Proposal for GSK3β inhibitor CHIR99021 (Tocris 4423)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
CHIR99021 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule aminopyrimidine that potently inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), with common use and profiling as a GSK3β-selective tool compound and canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway agonist in cell systems (notably embryonic stem cell self-renewal and iPSC generation) (Rethineswaran et al., 2021; Lyssiotis et al., 2011). In ocular biology, CHIR99021 has been implemented as a defined, stage-specific Wnt activator to accelerate and improve directed differentiation of human ESC/iPSC to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), increasing MITF/OTX2, pigmentation, and RPE functional readouts (apical PEDF, basal VEGF, integrin αVβ5–dependent phagocytosis) when applied at 3 μM during a defined mid-specification window (days 8–14) (Leach et al., 2015). Beyond development and differentiation protocols, CHIR99021 (as CHIR trihydrochloride) has been developed into an in vivo pharmacology tool with validated LC/MS assays and tissue PK in mice; after a 25 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, it achieves rapid systemic distribution and measurable retinal exposure with prolonged ocular retention relative to plasma and liver (plasma Tmax ~30 min, liver Tmax ~30 min, retina Tmax ~30 min; terminal half-lives ~118, 120, and 405 min, respectively) (DiCesare et al., 2023).

As a GSK3 inhibitor, CHIR99021 belongs to a class leveraged widely across neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and retinal biology. In retinal preclinical systems this class has been used in models of retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve injury/regeneration, and steroid-induced glaucoma; clinically, lithium chloride (LiCl) remains the only FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor but with a narrow therapeutic window and mixed efficacy for neurodegenerative disease (DiCesare et al., 2023). In RPE disease–relevant preclinical work, low-dose CHIR99021 exposure in RPE-derived models reduces production/secretion of the EFEMP1/F3 glycoprotein and broadly represses extracellular matrix (ECM), complement, protease, and TGFβ-associated components linked to sub-RPE deposit biology; in vivo, systemic CHIR99021 prevents formation of basal laminar deposits (BLamD) in a homozygous EFEMP1 R345W knock-in mouse (ML/DHRD, an AMD-like pathology) without detectable retinal toxicity on scotopic ERG and H&E histology over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
Class history in neural/retinal indications: GSK3 is a central kinase with broad substrate scope (>100 substrates) and regulates Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, mTOR, NF-κB, and apoptosis pathways central to retinal homeostasis and degeneration (Hottin et al., 2022). Across retinal neurodegeneration models, GSK3 inhibitors have shown neuroprotection (e.g., in rd10 retinitis pigmentosa, NMDA excitotoxicity, and diabetic retinopathy), and GSK3 inhibition is mechanistically linked to CNS axon regeneration pathways (e.g., via CRMP2, mTOR), though effects are context-dependent and can diverge across cell types and disease stages (Hottin et al., 2022). The translational record for systemic GSK3 inhibition is mixed; lithium’s broad CNS history underscores both feasibility and risk of narrow windows and systemic effects, motivating localized ocular delivery or targeted strategies for retinal disease (Hottin et al., 2022; DiCesare et al., 2023).

CHIR99021 in ocular biology and disease: In vitro, CHIR99021 is a core Wnt agonist in hESC/hiPSC-to-RPE protocols where it improves RPE specification, pigmentation, and function when properly staged; its effects can be recapitulated by WNT3A (canonical) but not by WNT5A (non-canonical), consistent with a canonical Wnt readout (Leach et al., 2015). In applied disease models:

- Anti-deposit/ECM remodeling in EFEMP1-driven pathology: Using ARPE-19 edited lines expressing HiBiT-tagged F3 (WT and R345W), CHIR99021 reduced F3 transcript and protein in both intracellular and secreted compartments without overt cytotoxicity; genetic knockdown of GSK3α/β phenocopied and synergized, supporting an on-target mechanism (DiCesare et al., 2023). Low-dose, longer-term exposure (1 μM for 1 week) suppressed ECM, complement, metalloproteinase, and TGFβ-associated proteins in proteomics (≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens, MMP2, SERPINE1, LTBP2, TGFβ1; decreases in HMGB1/2, C3; reductions in FBLN1/2) and produced parallel RNA-seq changes (downregulation of genes linked to sub-RPE deposits and ECM crosslinking; upregulation of TYR/TYRP1 and PEDF) without detectable activation of canonical TCF reporters, establishing a low-dose on-target biochemical window (DiCesare et al., 2023). Functionally, 1 μM CHIR99021 for 1 week normalized the R345W F3–linked elevation in MMP2 activity and reduced HiBiT F3 secretion apically and basally in transwell cultures (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In vivo efficacy and PK: In EFEMP1 R345W+/+ mice (~8 months old), systemic CHIR trihydrochloride (25 mg/kg IP, weekdays for 1 month) reduced the fraction of retinal FOVs containing BLamD from 14.205% to 4.167% and halved the mean deposit area (0.817 to 0.416 μm²), with no detectable ERG or histological toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). LC/MS/MS PK in plasma, liver, and retina confirmed rapid tissue distribution at 30 min and prolonged retinal retention (retina terminal T½ ~405 min) with estimated intraocular concentrations on the order of the effective in vitro range over the first hours (e.g., ~1.3 μM at 30 min and ~0.36 μM at 6 h) (DiCesare et al., 2023). Analytical assay development and rigorous methodology are reported (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Regeneration/reprogramming contexts: CHIR99021 is a frequent component of small-molecule cocktails that reprogram Müller glia toward photoreceptor-like fates, induce Rho+ cells in vitro and in degenerate mouse retinas, and is used in multi-pathway modulation (Wnt activation combined with inhibitors of TGF-β, BMP, and Notch) to enhance MC-derived photoreceptor-like outputs; effects vary with species/model, and cocktails require careful balance (Fujii et al., 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 also appears in chemical reprogramming schemes that convert adult human RPE to dopaminergic neurons and in multi-factor protocols generating photoreceptor progenitors from RPE or iPSCs, generally in combination with other pathway modulators and epigenetic agents (Rzhanova et al., 2024).

- Safety and adverse contexts: Despite benefits in differentiation, in a large-lesion, macula-sized RPE wound-repair model designed to mimic GA, CHIR99021 hindered lesion closure and yielded morphologically suboptimal infiltrating cells, even though pigmentation outside the lesion increased; EMT-suppressing agents (RepSox, Y-27632) performed better for wound closure under those conditions (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). Reviews caution that GSK3 inhibition can activate VEGF via canonical Wnt and could exacerbate angiogenesis, raising a risk signal for wet AMD contexts and arguing for careful selection of indication (dry vs wet AMD), timing, and combination strategies (e.g., with anti-VEGF) (Hottin et al., 2022).

To our knowledge, no human clinical studies have evaluated CHIR99021 for dry AMD; the most advanced ocular efficacy package is the EFEMP1 R345W mouse, an AMD-like BLamD model, where CHIR achieved both biochemical (ECM/complement/protease remodeling) and morphologic (deposit reduction) endpoints with ocular exposure in the in vitro effective range and no detectable electroretinal toxicity over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
Direct target and pathway entry points: GSK3 exists as α and β isoforms (85% identity), is constitutively active under basal conditions, and is negatively regulated by serine phosphorylation (S21 on α, S9 on β). It phosphorylates primed substrates on Ser/Thr motifs often culminating in β-TrCP recognition and proteasomal degradation of targets including β-catenin in the absence of Wnt; Wnt pathway activation sequesters/inhibits GSK3 within the destruction complex, stabilizing β-catenin and altering transcription via TCF/LEF (Hottin et al., 2022). CHIR99021 pharmacologically inhibits GSK3β and thereby is a canonical Wnt/β-catenin activator in many contexts, explaining its frequent use to bias fate decisions in pluripotent and somatic reprogramming paradigms (Lyssiotis et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2015).

Dose-dependent Wnt signaling in RPE systems: In RPE-derived ARPE-19 models, CHIR99021 shows a clear dose window: at 1 μM for one week it decreases EFEMP1/F3 transcripts/protein and globally represses ECM/complement/TGFβ signatures without detectable activation of TCF reporters; at ≥2.5 μM, TCF reporter activation becomes detectable, indicating canonical Wnt activation above a threshold (DiCesare et al., 2023). This low-dose window was sufficient to reduce MMP2 activity associated with the R345W F3 secretory stress pathophysiology, consistent with broad extracellular remodeling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

On-target genetic support: siRNA knockdown of GSK3α and GSK3β individually reduces F3 and combined knockdown synergizes, phenocopying CHIR’s effect on F3 production and secretion, supporting a GSK3-dependent mechanism for its anti-F3/anti-ECM actions (DiCesare et al., 2023). The effect generalizes across cell types (ARPE-19, human dermal fibroblasts, NIH-3T3), consistent with GSK3’s broad role in secretory/ECM regulation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

Secretory/ECM/complement/TGFβ axis remodeling: One-week, low-dose CHIR caused ≥2-fold reductions in multiple collagens (α1(V), α2(IV), α1(IV), α3(IV)), MMP2, complement C3, HMGB1/2, and TGFβ-related proteins such as SERPINE1/PAI-1 and LTBP2, with transcript-level suppression of ECM crosslinking and EMT-proximal genes (e.g., FN1, LOX, WNT ligands), while upregulating RPE differentiation/pigmentation (TYR, TYRP1) and increasing PEDF (SERPINF1) (DiCesare et al., 2023). These data point to a coordinated shift of the RPE secretome toward reduced pathogenic ECM/complement burden and increased pro-RPE homeostatic factors (e.g., PEDF), in line with the observed mitigation of BLamD in vivo (DiCesare et al., 2023).

mTOR–lysosome/autophagy coupling: Outside the retina, CHIR99021 has been shown to inhibit the Rheb/mTOR axis and increase lysosomal activation and autophagy in late endothelial progenitor cells, with evidence that CHIR reduces phosphorylated mTOR and Rheb independent of β-catenin, via effects attributed to TSC2 and lysosomal mTOR localization (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). These studies connect GSK3β inhibition to increased autophagic flux through mTORC1 suppression at the lysosome, a mechanistic route that in principle converges on transcriptional lysosome biogenesis programs (e.g., TFEB) though TFEB itself was not directly assayed in these reports (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). In retinal disease biology, GSK3 interdigitates with oxidative stress (NRF2 regulation), inflammatory NF-κB signaling, and mTOR pathways that are all implicated in AMD pathogenesis; pharmacologic GSK3β inhibition can increase NRF2 and reduce ROS in diabetic contexts, and reduced GSK3 activity in microglia dampens LPS-induced NF-κB signaling, underscoring additional protective axes that may be engaged in RPE or choroid (Hottin et al., 2022).

Angiogenic and repair liabilities: GSK3 inhibition/Wnt activation can increase VEGF and angiogenesis; reviews caution this may be beneficial in dry AMD (neuroprotection/anti-inflammatory) but harmful in wet AMD, suggesting indication-specific selection and potential need for combination with anti-VEGF or restricted/local delivery (Hottin et al., 2022). In a large RPE wound model mimicking GA-scale atrophy, continuous CHIR exposure hindered repair, in contrast to EMT-suppressing agents that improved closure, highlighting a context where Wnt activation can be counterproductive for lesion repopulation (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Mechanistic net assessment for dry AMD: In RPE disease–proximal models, CHIR99021’s dominant effects at low dose are anti-secretory for F3/EFEMP1 and anti-ECM/complement/TGFβ, with reduced MMP2 and enhanced RPE differentiation markers, culminating in prevention of BLamD in vivo without electrophysiologic deficits over one month (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent data show CHIR increases autophagy and lysosomal function via mTOR inhibition in other cell types, a mechanistic route that could contribute to proteostasis restoration in the RPE but remains to be demonstrated directly in RPE/AMD systems (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level predictions under the stated hypothesis: The team’s hypothesis posits that CHIR99021 will inhibit GSK3β in RPE, facilitate TFEB nuclear localization, enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D (CTSD) maturation, increase autophagic flux, and thereby prevent RPE atrophy in dry AMD. Direct evidence for TFEB nuclear localization or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 in RPE is not yet provided in the extant literature summarized here; however, two mechanistic pillars are established:

- In RPE disease models, low-dose CHIR99021 reduces a causal secretory burden (EFEMP1/F3) and pathogenic ECM/complement/protease output, normalizes MMP2 activity, increases homeostatic PEDF, and prevents BLamD formation in vivo, providing a deposit-centric, mechanistically credible route to slow early and mid-stage dry AMD pathology that is driven by sub-RPE matrix remodeling and complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- In non-ocular cells, CHIR99021 inhibits mTOR signaling at the lysosome (reduced Rheb/p-mTOR) and increases lysosomal activation and autophagy independent of β-catenin, consistent with a mechanism that would be predicted to favor TFEB nuclear translocation, transcription of lysosome/autophagy genes, and maturation of proteases such as CTSD; these precise endpoints have not been measured in RPE with CHIR99021 and thus remain to be validated (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Given GSK3 expression in ARPE-19 and its manipulation in the cited experiments (use of anti-GSK3α/β antibodies and on-target siRNA phenocopy), RPE is a relevant target cell for CHIR99021’s kinase inhibition (DiCesare et al., 2023). Under oxidative and secretory stress common to dry AMD, one would expect CHIR99021 at sub-TCF-activating exposure (≈1 μM) to:

- Reduce EFEMP1/F3 transcription/secretion and broadly depress ECM and complement cues that seed and stabilize BLamD/drusen, thereby lowering sub-RPE deposit biogenesis and associated pro-inflammatory signaling (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Normalize MMP2 activity and reduce matrix proteolysis-driven remodeling that contributes to basal laminar/basal linear deposit architecture (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Enhance RPE homeostatic phenotype, reflected by increased pigmentation gene expression and PEDF secretion, which supports photoreceptor survival and RPE trophic function (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Potentially increase autophagic flux and lysosomal competence via mTOR inhibition, improving clearance of aggregation-prone or secretory-stressed substrates; this inference is supported mechanistically outside the retina and should be formally confirmed in RPE by LC3 flux, p62/SQSTM1 turnover, LAMP1/2, lysotracker, and cathepsin maturation assays (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Boundary conditions and risks for the expected effect: The low-dose window is critical; at ≥2.5 μM, CHIR99021 activates canonical Wnt/TCF reporters in RPE-derived cells, and continuous Wnt activation can impair large-lesion RPE repair and increase angiogenic drive (VEGF), both of which are undesirable in late-stage GA or in patients at risk of conversion to exudative AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Hottin et al., 2022). In vivo PK after 25 mg/kg IP yields retinal concentrations in the 0.15–1.3 μM range over the first 24 h, overlapping the RPE efficacy window for EFEMP1/ECM suppression and below the Wnt activation threshold in vitro; however, local ocular delivery and controlled-release formulations may be preferable to avoid systemic exposure and to maintain sub-TCF-activating intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
- Disease-proximal efficacy with mechanistic depth. CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 production (transcript and protein), broadly suppresses ECM/complement/TGFβ secretome programs, decreases MMP2 activity, upregulates pigmentation genes and PEDF, and prevents BLamD in an EFEMP1 R345W knock-in model—an AMD-like pathology characterized by sub-RPE matrix deposits (DiCesare et al., 2023). The convergence of proteomics, transcriptomics, reporter assays, and genetic knockdown around GSK3 establishes on-target pathway control in RPE-derived systems (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Ocular exposure and safety. Tissue PK demonstrates retinal penetrance and prolonged retention (terminal T½ ≈ 6.75 h), with estimated intraocular levels overlapping the in vitro effective window; one month of systemic dosing at 25 mg/kg produced no detectable ERG or histological abnormalities in adult mice, supporting a tolerability window (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Plausible extension to proteostasis/autophagy. Independent mechanistic data show CHIR99021 inhibits mTORC1 signaling at the lysosome and increases autophagy/lysosomal activation via the TSC2–Rheb axis in non-ocular cells, a route that could bolster RPE lysosomal function under drusen/BLamD-associated stress even if TFEB was not yet directly measured in RPE (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Modality versatility with established use. Extensive prior use of CHIR99021 as a defined Wnt agonist in RPE/retinal differentiation and reprogramming provides a deep operations base for dosing/timing and cell-specific responses, which can be leveraged to avoid undesired pathway activation during therapy (Leach et al., 2015; Fujii et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Translational maturity and source quality. The core anti-deposit efficacy and ocular PK/safety package resides in a bioRxiv preprint; while comprehensive and internally consistent, it lacks peer-reviewed confirmation and replication across independent labs and models (DiCesare et al., 2023). Moreover, the EFEMP1 R345W model (ML/DHRD) is a rare, early-onset macular dystrophy with AMD-like deposits; it does not recapitulate the full aging/inflammation/metabolic milieu of typical dry AMD (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Wnt/angiogenesis liability and wound repair. GSK3β inhibition is a canonical Wnt activator and can increase VEGF/angiogenesis, potentially contraindicating use in patients with neovascular risk; in RPE monolayers with macula-sized lesions, CHIR99021 impaired lesion repair despite increasing peripheral pigmentation, highlighting a deleterious effect in GA-like settings requiring repopulation (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Dose/timing and cell-type dependency. Benefits of GSK3 modulation are highly context-dependent in retinal disease; the same pathway promotes different outcomes across disease stage and cell types (photoreceptors, Müller glia, RPE, endothelium). Reviews emphasize that treatment timing, duration, and targeted retinal layer will determine benefit vs harm (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022). The in vitro window where 1 μM avoids TCF activation is narrow; in vivo pharmacology must control ocular exposure carefully (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Mechanistic gap for the autophagy/TFEB claim in RPE. Although CHIR99021 increases autophagy through mTOR suppression in other cell types, direct evidence in human RPE or RPE-derived models for TFEB nuclear translocation, lysosomal acidification improvements, or CTSD maturation with CHIR99021 is currently absent from the surveyed literature; this is an experimental gap relative to the team’s stated hypothesis (Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Development recommendations  
- Indication scoping to dry AMD segments with deposit-dominated pathology. Based on anti-ECM/complement and anti-BLamD efficacy, prioritize early/mid dry AMD segments characterized by drusen/sub-RPE deposits and low neovascular risk; de-prioritize active geographic atrophy where repopulation/repair of large RPE lesions is the therapeutic aim, given the CHIR-associated repair impairment in vitro (DiCesare et al., 2023; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

- Local ocular delivery to widen the therapeutic index. Intravitreal or suprachoroidal controlled-release systems should be evaluated to maintain intraocular concentrations in the ~0.1–1 μM range that achieve biochemical efficacy but remain below the canonical Wnt activation threshold, while minimizing systemic exposure and wet-AMD conversion risk; the reviews support local delivery as a strategy for GSK3-based ocular interventions (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

- Mechanistic validation in RPE for proteostasis endpoints. In primary hfRPE and iPSC-RPE, directly measure CHIR99021’s impact on autophagy and lysosome: LC3-II flux (±bafilomycin A1), p62/SQSTM1 turnover, TFEB nuclear localization (immunofluorescence/fractionation), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), LAMP1/2 expression, and CTSD maturation/activity; determine whether these benefits occur at sub-TCF-activating exposures and under relevant stresses (oxidative, lipid, complement) (DiCesare et al., 2023; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

- Angiogenic surveillance and combination strategies. Quantify VEGF and angiogenic markers (VEGFA mRNA/protein, HIF-1α targets) in RPE/choroid after CHIR, and consider anti-VEGF co-therapy if Wnt-VEGF coupling poses a risk; preclinical reviews support the rationale for combination or timing-restricted inhibition to avoid pro-angiogenic consequences (Hottin et al., 2022).

- Broaden efficacy across dry AMD models. Test CHIR in aging-related and inflammation-metabolism models (e.g., high-fat diet + complement stress; smoke exposure; ApoE variants) in addition to EFEMP1 R345W to ensure generalizability beyond monogenic ECM disease; define the minimal exposure and duration to alter drusen/BLamD dynamics and microglial/complement activation (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Dose-finding anchored to ocular PK/PD. Use the established LC/MS retinal assay to map intravitreal/subconjunctival/suprachoroidal dose to retinal/choroidal concentration–time profiles; overlay with PD markers (F3 secretion, ECM transcripts, complement, PEDF) to define a sub-TCF window in vivo; confirm absence of ERG deficits and retinal histopathology across multi-month dosing (DiCesare et al., 2023).

- Translational vigilance. Lithium’s status as the sole FDA-approved GSK3 inhibitor and mixed outcomes of GSK3 modulation in retinal disease underscore the need to target specific retinal layers or cell types and to avoid broad systemic inhibition; this aligns with adopting local ocular delivery and possibly RPE-targeted formulations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022).

Conclusion  
On balance, CHIR99021 has a compelling, disease-proximal efficacy package for dry AMD centered on sub-RPE deposit biology. At low doses that do not detectably activate canonical Wnt, CHIR99021 reduces EFEMP1/F3 and globally attenuates ECM/complement/protease pathways in RPE-derived systems, increases PEDF and pigmentation gene expression, and prevents BLamD formation in an EFEMP1 R345W mouse model, with retinal exposures matching in vitro efficacy windows and month-long dosing without ERG/histology toxicity (DiCesare et al., 2023). Independent mechanistic data demonstrate CHIR-mediated inhibition of Rheb/mTOR and increased lysosomal/autophagic activity in non-ocular cells, consistent with the proteostasis-restoring arm of the team’s hypothesis, but direct evidence for TFEB nuclear translocation and CTSD maturation in RPE with CHIR is currently lacking and should be considered a key validation gap (Rethineswaran et al., 2021). The principal risks are Wnt-linked angiogenesis (potentially harmful in wet AMD) and impaired RPE wound repair in GA-like lesions when Wnt activation is sustained; these risks argue for a dry-AMD, early/mid-stage positioning, careful intraocular dose control to remain below the TCF activation threshold, and consideration of local delivery and/or anti-VEGF combinations in higher-risk patients (Hottin et al., 2022; Bailey-Steinitz, 2021).

Overall, CHIR99021 is a promising repurposed candidate for dry AMD if developed within a well-defined exposure window and indication niche. Its strengths are a clear kinase target with on-target cellular genetics, strong anti-deposit and secretome remodeling data in RPE and in vivo, ocular exposure that aligns with cellular pharmacology, and plausible lysosome/autophagy engagement. Its weaknesses are translational maturity (preprint stage; single primary in vivo model), Wnt-associated angiogenesis and repair liabilities at higher/continuous exposure, and incomplete validation of the autophagy/TFEB axis in RPE. A go decision for preclinical advancement is justified, contingent on rapid mechanistic confirmation in RPE for autophagy/lysosome endpoints, rigorous angiogenesis/wound-repair safety pharmacology, and PK/PD-guided local delivery strategies that maintain sub-TCF intraocular concentrations (DiCesare et al., 2023; Hottin et al., 2022; Rethineswaran et al., 2021).

Proposal for Pegcetacoplan (APL-2; Apellis)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pegcetacoplan (APL-2, now marketed as Syfovre) is a synthetically engineered, PEGylated cyclic peptide that belongs to the family of compstatin analogs designed to inhibit complement component C3. Its origins lie in early peptide discovery via phage‐display and random peptide library screening, and successive rounds of medicinal chemistry optimization were applied to improve its binding affinity, solubility, and pharmacokinetic profile through PEG conjugation (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Ong et al., 2024). The PEGylation process not only grants enhanced resistance to enzymatic degradation but also prolongs the intravitreal residence time, an essential property for ocular applications requiring sustained drug exposure with limited dosing frequency (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). As a second‐generation compstatin analog, pegcetacoplan employs a bivalent design that enables high specificity for human C3, blocking its proteolytic cleavage into the active fragments C3a and C3b. These fragments are potent mediators that further amplify the inflammatory cascade through the formation of C3 convertases (Lamers et al., 2022). This therapeutic candidate is embedded within a broader class of complement inhibitors that have been actively explored in inflammatory disorders, and notably in ophthalmology for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where aberrant complement activation plays a central pathogenic role (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Its synthetic nature, coupled with its targeted molecular design, positions pegcetacoplan as an attractive candidate for addressing the degenerative processes in geographic atrophy (GA) associated with dry AMD by directly modulating the complement cascade (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Patel et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the evolution of pegcetacoplan reflects a successful translation from bench to bedside across multiple therapeutic domains. Initially, the compstatin class was primarily developed and evaluated in systemic disorders characterized by complement dysregulation, most notably in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Early clinical trials in PNH provided critical safety and efficacy data that underscored the value of targeting C3, paving the way for the repurposing of these molecules in ocular disease (Lamers et al., 2022). With the conceptual framework and preclinical data in hand, pegcetacoplan was advanced into the ophthalmology space. The pivotal Phase II FILLY trial enrolled 246 patients with GA secondary to dry AMD, and the study demonstrated that monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan resulted in a statistically significant reduction of GA lesion growth by approximately 29%, while an every-other-month dosing regimen yielded a 20% reduction relative to sham-control treatment (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These encouraging anatomical outcomes, evidenced by the slowed progression of GA and the concurrent reduction in photoreceptor loss as evaluated by SD-OCT imaging, provided a strong rationale for subsequent Phase III clinical trials (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition to its use in dry AMD, pegcetacoplan’s earlier regulatory approval for PNH helped establish it as a viable molecule with a favorable safety profile. Its journey through successive clinical phases—from Phase I safety and tolerability studies to Phase II efficacy studies and ultimately Phase III confirmation—has offered compelling evidence that targeted complement inhibition can modify the disease course in conditions characterized by chronic complement activation (Tzoumas et al., 2023). However, clinical experience with pegcetacoplan has also identified potential safety signals, including an observed increase in the incidence of new-onset exudative (wet) AMD among certain subpopulations, a factor that necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). Overall, the therapeutic history of pegcetacoplan—spanning its origin from fundamental compstatin research to its current application in treating geographic atrophy—demonstrates its potential for repurposing as a disease-modifying therapy in ocular settings (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, the pathogenic cascade in dry AMD is tightly linked to dysregulated complement activation, and pegcetacoplan intervenes at one of the central nodes of this pathway by inhibiting complement component C3. Under physiological conditions, C3 is cleaved by C3 convertases into C3a—an anaphylatoxin that drives inflammation—and C3b, which functions as an opsonin and further propagates complement amplification (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). Pegcetacoplan binds to a key epitope on C3, thereby sterically hindering the enzyme-driven cleavage that would otherwise generate these active fragments. By effectively arresting this pivotal step in the complement cascade, the drug prevents downstream events such as the assembly of terminal complement complexes and the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
The inhibition of C3 cleavage has several critical biochemical consequences. First, by lowering the concentrations of C3a and C3b, pegcetacoplan reduces the generation of pro-inflammatory mediators and the subsequent chemotactic recruitment of immune cells, which, in turn, diminishes local inflammation in the retinal environment (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Tzoumas et al., 2023). Second, the reduction in C3b deposition directly limits the formation of MAC on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces—a process that has been implicated in triggering lysosomal dysfunction within these critical cells (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Park et al., 2021). The MAC, when deposited sublytically on RPE cells, can compromise the function of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), the proton pump responsible for maintaining the acidic environment of lysosomes. Acidification of the lysosomal compartment is essential for optimal activity of proteolytic enzymes, such as cathepsin D, which are required to degrade photoreceptor outer segment debris and other cytotoxic by-products (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
Thus, by preventing excessive complement activation and subsequent MAC formation, pegcetacoplan indirectly safeguards the intracellular degradative machinery of the RPE. This preservation of v-ATPase function ensures proper lysosomal acidification, which in turn maintains cathepsin D activity and reduces lysosomal overload—a key mechanism implicated in the progressive atrophy of the RPE observed in dry AMD (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that complement blockade via agents such as pegcetacoplan lowers sub-RPE deposit formation and inflammasome priming, processes intimately linked to lysosomal dysfunction and chronic inflammation (Liao et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Collectively, the mechanism of action of pegcetacoplan encompasses both direct inhibition of complement-driven inflammatory processes and indirect protection of intracellular catabolic functions in the RPE, thereby addressing two core pathological contributors to geographic atrophy (Kassa et al., 2019; Rubner et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
Based on its detailed mechanism of action, pegcetacoplan is expected to exert a dual beneficial effect in the management of dry AMD. First, by binding to and inhibiting complement C3, it should markedly reduce the formation of inflammatory mediators (C3a, C3b) as well as downstream terminal pathway components such as the MAC. Clinical trial data support this expectation: in the Phase II FILLY study, monthly intravitreal injections of pegcetacoplan were associated with a roughly 29% reduction in the rate of GA lesion growth relative to control, while an alternate-month regimen achieved a 20% reduction (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022). These anatomical outcomes are presumed to correlate with a slowing of disease progression and a delay in the onset of irreversible retinal degeneration.  
Second, through the inhibition of MAC deposition on RPE cells, pegcetacoplan is anticipated to preserve the functional integrity of lysosomes by ensuring that v-ATPase activity is maintained and that cathepsin D retains its proteolytic function. The preservation of lysosomal function is critical not only for the proper degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris but also for protecting RPE cells from metabolic stress and subsequent cell death (Liao et al., 2020; Desai & Dugel, 2022). Consequently, the expected biochemical outcome is that pegcetacoplan will reduce lysosomal overload and the accumulation of toxic metabolic by-products—a process thought to contribute to the formation of sub-RPE deposits that further exacerbate tissue atrophy in dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022).  
At the cellular level, maintaining cathepsin D activity is imperative because this protease is responsible for degrading intracellular waste products that accumulate in RPE cells, and its functionality is closely tied to the acidic environment provided by lysosomes. By preserving this aspect of lysosomal physiology, pegcetacoplan should contribute to RPE cell survival and thereby delay the progression of geographic atrophy (Patel et al., 2022). Although improvements in functional endpoints such as visual acuity have not been immediately evident in short-term clinical trials, the principal therapeutic endpoint remains the deceleration of structural degeneration. This structural preservation is expected to eventually translate into a longer period of maintained retinal function and a postponed deterioration in vision, ultimately extending the window during which patients can retain functional vision (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Furthermore, the established dosing regimens—with monthly or alternate-month intravitreal injections—are designed to sustain local complement inhibition at therapeutic levels without causing excessive immunosuppression that might predispose patients to infections. However, some studies have raised concerns about an increased risk of conversion to exudative AMD (wet AMD) during treatment, signaling that while the inhibition of C3 can preserve RPE integrity, careful monitoring is warranted to manage potential adverse events (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Rubner et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
A comprehensive review of pegcetacoplan as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a well-substantiated rationale and a promising clinical profile, albeit with some challenges that must be addressed. One of the most compelling strengths of pegcetacoplan is its precise molecular targeting of complement component C3—a central mediator in the complement cascade. By inhibiting C3, pegcetacoplan effectively blocks the generation of both C3a and C3b, thereby reducing pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC) (Yu & Wykoff, 2021). This upstream blockade provides a broad-spectrum mechanism capable of modulating all three complement activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative), which is particularly important in a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Lamers et al., 2022).  
Clinically, the results from the Phase II FILLY study are extremely encouraging, demonstrating a 29% reduction in GA lesion growth with monthly intravitreal administration and a 20% reduction with alternate-month dosing, outcomes that have been replicated in additional studies and served as the basis for progressing to Phase III evaluations (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022; Desai & Dugel, 2022). These anatomical endpoints, while not immediately translating into measurable improvements in visual acuity, are critical surrogates for the long-term preservation of retinal structure and function—a key goal in the management of dry AMD (Regillo & Heier, n.d.; Patel et al., 2022).  
Biochemically, pegcetacoplan’s mechanism of action extends beyond the mere suppression of complement-mediated inflammation. Its ability to indirectly preserve lysosomal function by preventing MAC-induced dysfunction of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase) and maintaining cathepsin D activity introduces a novel paradigm in addressing the intracellular stress that accelerates RPE degeneration (Liao et al., 2020; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). In dry AMD, the accumulation of metabolic by-products due to deficient lysosomal degradation leads to the formation of drusen and sub-RPE deposits, which further stimulate complement activation and create a vicious cycle of cellular damage. Pegcetacoplan, by protecting lysosomal integrity, offers the potential to break this cycle and slow the progression of geographic atrophy (Park et al., 2021; Kassa et al., 2019).  
There are, however, certain weaknesses and challenges that must be taken into account. One notable concern is the increased risk of new-onset exudative AMD that has been reported in some clinical studies. This adverse event appears to be dose-dependent and may reflect a complex interplay between complement inhibition and pro-angiogenic pathways in the retina (Wu & Sun, 2019; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023). The occurrence of neovascular complications necessitates rigorous patient selection criteria, close imaging surveillance, and potentially the development of combination strategies to counterbalance this risk without compromising the therapeutic efficacy against GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Another challenge is the logistical and patient adherence issues related to frequent intravitreal injections. Although the PEGylation of pegcetacoplan aids in prolonging its ocular residence, the need for repeated injections every month or every other month represents a significant treatment burden. This may affect patient compliance and overall treatment outcomes, particularly when compared to therapies that require less frequent dosing or alternative delivery modalities (Piri & Kaplan, 2023; Petrukhin, 2020). Future work aimed at developing sustained-release formulations or implantable devices could potentially alleviate this drawback (Lamers et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2022).  
From a mechanistic standpoint, while the inhibition of C3 is expected to preserve lysosomal function by protecting v-ATPase activity and sustaining cathepsin D levels, further research is needed to fully elucidate the downstream biochemical consequences of long-term complement inhibition. Detailed studies evaluating biomarkers of lysosomal function—including cathepsin D activity, lysosomal pH, and the turnover of sub-RPE deposits—will be instrumental in correlating these molecular effects with clinical outcomes (Desai & Dugel, 2022; Rubner et al., 2022). Such investigations are essential not only for optimizing dosing regimens but also for refining patient selection strategies, ensuring that those most likely to benefit from complement inhibition are appropriately targeted (Rubner et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2022).  
In addition, it is worth noting that while the current clinical evidence has predominantly focused on anatomical endpoints such as GA lesion size, translating these findings into meaningful improvements in vision remains an ongoing challenge. The disconnect between structural preservation and functional outcomes is a well-recognized issue in dry AMD research and may require additional therapeutic interventions or combination approaches to achieve robust clinical benefits (Patel et al., 2022; Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023).  
Overall, the benefit–risk profile of pegcetacoplan remains favorable when considered in the context of a disease with a profound unmet medical need. Its dual-action mechanism—combining potent complement inhibition with the preservation of intracellular lysosomal function—addresses both extracellular inflammatory processes and the intracellular degradative pathways that contribute to RPE cell loss and GA progression (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Mastellos & Lambris, 2024). Moreover, the clinical trial data, particularly the significant reduction in GA lesion progression observed in the FILLY study, provide a compelling rationale for further investment in pegcetacoplan’s development for dry AMD (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022).  
Nevertheless, it is imperative that future studies incorporate long-term follow-up and incorporate both anatomical and functional endpoints to fully capture the therapeutic potential of pegcetacoplan. Further optimization of the dosing regimen, exploration of sustained-release formulations, and rigorous monitoring for conversion to exudative AMD are critical next steps that will determine the long-term viability of this agent in clinical practice (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Lamers et al., 2022). In addition, combination therapies targeting complementary pathogenic pathways—such as oxidative stress and dysregulated angiogenesis—may augment the efficacy of pegcetacoplan and help mitigate its potential adverse effects (Halawa et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2021).  
In summary, the body of biomedical, clinical, and biochemical evidence indicates that pegcetacoplan holds significant promise as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its innovative design as a PEGylated compstatin analog ensures potent and sustained inhibition of complement C3, addressing a critical upstream mediator in the inflammatory cascade that drives RPE cell dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Tzoumas et al., 2023). Through its targeted action, pegcetacoplan not only reduces the formation of deleterious inflammatory fragments and the deposition of MAC but also indirectly preserves the lysosomal function essential for RPE homeostasis (Mastellos & Lambris, 2024).  
While challenges remain—particularly the risk of neovascular conversion and the inherent burden of frequent intravitreal administration—the overall therapeutic profile of pegcetacoplan suggests that it can significantly slow the progression of GA and potentially preserve visual function in patients with dry AMD (Lamers et al., 2022; Rubner et al., 2022). With further clinical validation and optimization of treatment protocols, pegcetacoplan is poised to redefine the standard of care for dry AMD and serve as a blueprint for the development of future complement-targeted therapies (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2024).  
From an expert drug development perspective, pegcetacoplan exemplifies how targeted modulation of the complement system can address the multifactorial pathology of dry AMD. Its capacity to intersect both extracellular inflammatory processes and intracellular lysosomal homeostasis provides a mechanistically unique approach that directly addresses the underlying pathophysiology of geographic atrophy. The robust clinical efficacy data, particularly the demonstrated 29% reduction in GA lesion growth in Phase II trials, strongly justify the continued prioritization of pegcetacoplan in the development pipeline (Cruz-Pimentel & Wu, 2023; Patel et al., 2022; Lamers et al., 2022).  
In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review across biomedical, clinical, and biochemical domains confirms that pegcetacoplan is a highly promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its synthetic origin, advanced molecular design, and demonstrated efficacy in clinical trials provide a solid foundation for its continued development. Despite potential challenges—including the risk of wet AMD conversion and the practical hurdles of repeated intravitreal administration—the advantages conferred by its targeted mechanism of action and the preservation of critical lysosomal functions in RPE cells substantiate its potential to slow geographic atrophy progression and ultimately improve patient outcomes (Park et al., 2019; Petrukhin, 2020; Regillo & Heier, n.d.). Future research should focus on long-term outcome studies, refinement of dosing strategies, and the possible integration of complementary therapies to maximize the therapeutic benefit while mitigating risks. Based on the current evidence, pegcetacoplan merits continued investment and clinical research as a lead candidate in the quest for an effective disease-modifying treatment for dry AMD (Qin et al., 2021; Rubner et al., 2022).

Proposal for Fenofibrate (Sigma F6020)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic small‐molecule drug belonging to the fibrate class of compounds, originally developed and approved for the treatment of dyslipidemia. It acts predominantly as a peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. Fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that undergoes hepatic esterase hydrolysis to form its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, which binds to PPARα and modulates the transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism. This drug class has historically been used for lowering serum triglycerides and increasing high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, reflecting its well‐established lipid‐modulating properties. Although fenofibrate was not initially developed for ocular indications, its mechanism as a PPARα agonist has spurred interest for repurposing in retinal diseases. In particular, the broad class of fibrates has garnered attention because PPARα is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and its activation can regulate lipid oxidation, autophagy, and inflammatory processes—all of which are critically disturbed in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Fu et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a robust clinical history in the management of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk reduction, with extensive use in millions of patients worldwide. Its ocular benefits became apparent with large clinical trials, such as the FIELD and ACCORD Eye studies, which demonstrated that fenofibrate can reduce the progression of diabetic retinopathy and decrease the need for retinal laser therapy in diabetic patients (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Although these trials primarily addressed diabetic retinal disease, subsequent preclinical and clinical reports have indicated that the retina may benefit from the lipid‐modulatory, anti‐inflammatory, and neuroprotective actions of PPARα agonists. For instance, several studies have explored fenofibrate in animal models of retinal ischemia and neovascularization, showing protective effects on the retinal vasculature and RPE (Fu et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2017). While the majority of these ocular studies have focused on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD, emerging literature has pointed to the potential of targeting PPARα signaling to mitigate RPE dysfunction and lipid accumulation, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). This history of fenofibrate in retinal disease, combined with its proven clinical safety for dyslipidemia and established ocular pharmacokinetics (including studies on topical delivery), provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action is rooted in its role as a PPARα agonist. Upon conversion to fenofibric acid, the compound binds to PPARα—a nuclear receptor highly expressed in several tissues, including the liver and the retinal pigment epithelium. When activated, PPARα forms heterodimers with retinoid X receptors (RXR) and binds to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) within the promoters of target genes. This binding results in the upregulation of genes critical for fatty acid uptake, β-oxidation, and lipid catabolism. Key genes regulated by PPARα include those encoding enzymes that facilitate mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, which in turn reduces intracellular lipid accumulation and promotes energy homeostasis (Fu et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2023).

In the context of the RPE and dry AMD, the hypothesis is that fenofibrate will stimulate PPARα-mediated transcriptional programs that not only enhance lipid catabolism but also intersect with cellular degradative pathways. One of the central tenets of the proposed mechanism is the coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy through the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. Under normal conditions, TFEB is kept inactive in the cytosol by phosphorylation mediated by mTORC1. Under stress conditions or when lysosomal function is impaired, TFEB translocates to the nucleus to upregulate genes involved in lysosomal acidification, autophagy, and lipid metabolism. The therapeutic hypothesis posits that fenofibrate, through PPARα activation in RPE cells, will indirectly coactivate TFEB. This may occur through changes in cellular metabolism that reduce mTORC1 activity or via direct transcriptional crosstalk between PPARα target genes and the CLEAR network (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Moreover, TFEB activation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification—a process necessary for optimal degradation of phagocytosed outer segment debris and drusen precursors—and upregulate lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D. In AMD, RPE cells often show lysosomal dysfunction characterized by deficient cathepsin D activity and lipofuscin accumulation. By improving lysosomal function, fenofibrate may facilitate the clearance of lipid-rich drusen precursors, thereby reducing RPE stress and preventing progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023). In addition to these lysosome-centric effects, fenofibrate has anti-inflammatory properties, as PPARα activation suppresses NF-κB signaling, reduces the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α and IL-1β), and alleviates oxidative stress—all of which are exacerbating factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Lee et al., 2023; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Furthermore, the modulation of the FGF21 pathway, occasionally observed with fenofibrate treatment, may contribute to neuroprotection and further support retinal homeostasis (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Taken together, the molecular interactions initiated by fenofibrate converge on restoring lipid homeostasis, enhancing autophagic flux, and mitigating inflammatory insults in RPE cells—a multifaceted approach that aligns with the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Lee et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
In the assays proposed to evaluate fenofibrate’s efficacy for dry AMD, one anticipates several measurable cellular and biochemical outcomes. First, treatment of RPE cells with fenofibrate should lead to a consistent activation of PPARα target genes, as demonstrated by upregulation of markers for fatty acid oxidation and lipid catabolism. Such molecular signatures can be quantified using gene expression analyses and reporter assays for PPRE activity (Fu et al., 2019; Tomita et al., 2021). Concurrently, it is expected that fenofibrate will enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. This could be evident from increased LC3-II accumulation in the presence of lysosomal inhibitors and enhanced degradation of autophagic substrates, which would indicate an upregulation of the autophagic machinery (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

A critical aspect of the proposed mechanism involves TFEB. Upon fenofibrate treatment, one should observe increased nuclear translocation of TFEB in RPE cells, which can be assessed by immunocytochemistry and subcellular fractionation. The activation of TFEB would then be expected to drive the transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding lysosomal proteins, such as lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) and various components of the V-ATPase complex, leading to enhanced lysosomal acidification. Lysotracker assays and measurements of intralysosomal pH could be deployed to confirm that fenofibrate-treated cells exhibit more acidic lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023).

Furthermore, increased cathepsin D activity is a pivotal expected outcome, serving as a surrogate marker for improved lysosomal enzyme function in degrading waste products, including drusen precursors. Biochemical assays to quantify cathepsin D activity, alongside immunostaining for its protein levels, would help to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Functionally, the cumulative effect of these molecular changes should be a reduction in the accumulation of lipofuscin and other drusen-associated lipid-protein aggregates within the RPE. This reduction could be observed using autofluorescence imaging techniques and electron microscopy to assess cytoplasmic inclusions (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

Additionally, given that fenofibrate has established anti-inflammatory properties, one might expect a decrease in the secretion or expression of inflammatory mediators in RPE cultures, as well as improved cellular resistance to oxidative stress challenges. Cytokine assays and measurements of reactive oxygen species (ROS) would serve as corroborative evidence for an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effect. Importantly, because reduced autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central to dry AMD, the combined effect of enhanced lipid catabolism, improved lysosomal acidification, and increased cathepsin D activity should contribute to an overall reduction in cellular stress and preservation of RPE integrity (Falcão et al., 2025; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Taken together, these expected effects would validate the therapeutic hypothesis and provide a strong rationale for advancing fenofibrate into further preclinical models of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Fenofibrate emerges as a promising repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD based on several compelling lines of evidence. The drug’s long-established clinical safety profile and extensive use in dyslipidemia serve as major strengths in terms of its translational potential (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012). Additionally, the documented success of fenofibrate in slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy in large-scale clinical trials underscores its ability to exert beneficial effects in retinal tissues (Lu et al., 2014; Treacy & Hurst, 2012).

From a mechanistic standpoint, fenofibrate’s mode of action as a PPARα agonist is well characterized, and its ability to stimulate lipid oxidation and enhance fatty acid metabolism could directly address the lipid dysregulation observed in RPE cells in dry AMD (Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023). Crucially, the hypothesis that fenofibrate may also coactivate TFEB, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and function, positions it uniquely among therapeutic candidates. Improved lysosomal acidification and increased cathepsin D activity would facilitate the clearance of drusen precursors and reduce the cytotoxic accumulation of lipofuscin, which is a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020). The convergence of lipid catabolism enhancement, autophagy upregulation, and anti-inflammatory effects creates a multifaceted therapeutic profile that is particularly attractive for a complex, multifactorial disease such as dry AMD.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and challenges. Most of the current evidence supporting fenofibrate’s retinal benefits is derived from studies focusing on diabetic retinopathy or neovascular AMD rather than directly on dry AMD. Although there is supportive mechanistic rationale linking PPARα activation to improved lysosomal function in the RPE, direct evidence for fenofibrate’s efficacy in reducing drusen accumulation and alleviating RPE stress in dry AMD models remains sparse (Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; da Ana et al., 2023). The specific involvement of TFEB activation by fenofibrate in RPE cells has not been fully elucidated in the existing literature, and further in vitro and in vivo studies are needed to validate this aspect of the mechanism. Additionally, while fenofibrate is generally safe when used systemically, there have been concerns regarding potential renal side effects, which may be particularly relevant in the elderly population that predominantly suffers from AMD (Treacy & Hurst, 2012; Tomita et al., 2021). Thus, optimizing the route of delivery—possibly via topical formulations or nanoparticle-based systems—may be necessary to ensure sufficient retinal bioavailability while minimizing systemic exposure (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

Another potential limitation is the dose required to achieve sufficient PPARα activation in the RPE to modulate TFEB and lysosomal pathways effectively. Preclinical studies have sometimes required relatively high doses of fenofibrate to observe significant ocular effects, and the pharmacokinetic barriers posed by the blood-retinal barrier may further complicate translatability (Tomita et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Moreover, the current body of literature underscores the need for more targeted studies to determine whether the benefits seen with fenofibrate in models of diabetic retinopathy and neovascular AMD can be replicated in models of dry AMD, where the pathogenic processes are distinct in their emphasis on lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and RPE dysfunction (da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation remains cautiously optimistic. Fenofibrate’s mechanism of action aligns well with the pathophysiological features of dry AMD, particularly regarding the restoration of lipid homeostasis and the enhancement of lysosomal function. The dual potential for direct metabolic benefits via PPARα activation and indirect benefits through TFEB-mediated lysosomal enhancement represents an innovative therapeutic strategy that could fill a critical gap in the current treatment landscape for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, the availability of various delivery platforms—including systemic administration, topical eye drops, and nanoparticle formulations—provides flexibility in addressing bioavailability challenges and minimizing adverse effects (Huang et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2014).

In conclusion, fenofibrate (Sigma F6020) possesses significant potential for repurposing as a drug candidate for dry AMD based on its well-established pharmacological profile, robust clinical safety record, and mechanistic actions that target key pathological processes in the RPE. While further preclinical studies specifically focused on dry AMD models are warranted to validate the hypothesized coactivation of TFEB and subsequent enhancement of lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, the current literature provides a strong scientific basis for such investigations. The strengths of fenofibrate lie in its multifaceted mechanism—encompassing lipid catabolism, autophagy, anti-inflammatory, and possibly neuroprotective effects—which collectively offer a promising strategy to reduce drusen precursors and mitigate RPE stress. The primary weaknesses involve the need for direct evidence in dry AMD models, optimization of ocular delivery to overcome pharmacokinetic barriers, and careful monitoring of potential systemic side effects in an elderly population. Overall, fenofibrate represents a compelling and scientifically sound candidate that merits further exploration in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to significantly advance our therapeutic arsenal against this currently untreatable form of macular degeneration (Falcão et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2019; da Ana et al., 2023; Dou & Duerfeldt, 2020; Lee et al., 2023).
