Proposal for ML-SA1 (Tocris 475342)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 is a synthetic, cell-permeable small-molecule agonist of the endolysosomal mucolipin/TRPML family, with primary pharmacological activity at TRPML1, the Ca2+-permeable cation channel encoded by MCOLN1 that resides on late endosome/lysosome membranes and mediates lysosomal Ca2+ efflux into the cytosol (Wang et al., 2023). ML-SA1 and chemically related “ML-SA” agonists emerged from small-molecule discovery programs aimed at pharmacologically restoring TRPML1 function; the compound is frequently referred to in the literature as “mucolipin synthetic agonist 1,” reflecting its origin as a tool compound class designed to activate TRPML channels rather than as a derivative of a natural product scaffold (Yan et al., 2021). Although the chemical structure and synthetic route for ML-SA1 are not detailed in the cited records, its provenance traces to a specialized small-molecule therapeutics effort at Calporta Therapeutics, a company subsequently acquired by Merck in 2019, signaling substantial translational interest in TRPML1 agonism for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disorders (Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Functionally, ML-SA1 belongs to the broader class of TRPML1 agonists/activators that includes endogenous lipid ligands such as phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate, PI(3,5)P2, and other synthetic small molecules (e.g., SF-22, MK6-83, and newer ML-SA chemotypes like ML-SA5), all of which gate TRPML channels to increase endolysosomal Ca2+ release (Wang et al., 2023; Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). Within this class, ML-SA1 is reported to activate TRPML1 with potency comparable to or greater than the endogenous PI(3,5)P2 under certain conditions and can act in conjunction with PI(3,5)P2 to potentiate channel opening, thereby rescuing endo-lysosomal morphology and function in cellular disease models that exhibit lysosomal stress (e.g., after PIKfyve inhibition) (Wang et al., 2023). Across preclinical research, TRPML1 agonists have been deployed as mechanistic probes and candidate therapeutics to restore lysosomal Ca2+ signaling, normalize lysosomal pH/acidification, promote autophagosome maturation and autolysosome formation, enhance lysosomal exocytosis, and induce TFEB-dependent lysosomal biogenesis in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

In ocular systems directly relevant to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, ML-SA1 has been used to interrogate TRPML1 function. In mouse primary RPE, human embryonic stem cell–derived RPE (hesRPE), and ARPE-19 cells, ML-SA1 produced rapid, robust, reversible increases in cytosolic Ca2+ that persisted in Ca2+-free external solutions and were blunted by lysosomal disruption, indicating a lysosomal Ca2+ source (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Critically, ML-SA1 failed to evoke Ca2+ signals in RPE from TRPML1 knockout mice, confirming channel specificity in this tissue (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The same study demonstrated that lysosomal lipid accumulation—induced pharmacologically or present in disease models—impairs ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, mechanistically linking lysosomal lipidization to diminished TRPML1 function in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018). These data situate ML-SA1 squarely within a mechanistic toolkit for modulating RPE lysosomal physiology implicated in retinal degenerations associated with lipid/lipofuscin accrual (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History  
There is no record in the provided corpus of ML-SA1 being used clinically in humans or specifically in trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA) (Más Gómez et al., 2018). However, extensive preclinical use across cell and animal models supports the biological rationale relevant to dry AMD. In RPE systems, ML-SA1 has been applied acutely to evoke TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release as described above (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In vivo, subretinal ML-SA1 administration in a rat retinal detachment model preserved outer nuclear layer thickness, reduced photoreceptor apoptosis, lessened cleaved caspase-3, increased autophagy markers (LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1), decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and prevented TRPML1 degradation, collectively demonstrating functional rescue via autophagy activation and oxidative stress mitigation in injured retina (Yan et al., 2021).

Beyond the eye, multiple studies in neuronal and disease-model systems have used ML-SA1 to correct lysosomal/autophagy defects and proteostasis. In cultured neurons and HEK293T cells, ML-SA1 enhanced maturation of autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and reduced α-synuclein accumulation/aggregates; ML-SA1 could override bafilomycin-induced fusion/acidification blocks in both HEK293T cells and neurons, and these effects required lysosomal PI(3,5)P2 and cytosolic Ca2+ consistent with TRPML1 channel gating (Pollmanns et al., 2022). In primary cortical neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidified endolysosomes and prevented LDL-induced amyloidogenesis by reducing Aβ and BACE1 mislocalization/activity; TRPML1 knockdown abrogated ML-SA1’s effects and exacerbated LDL-driven Aβ production (Hui et al., 2019). In lysosomal storage disease (LSD) contexts, ML-SA1 was used as a TRPML1 activator to elicit lysosomal Ca2+ release responses that were impaired in Niemann–Pick type C (NPC1) patient fibroblasts; BK channel activation partially rescued the reduced ML-SA1 response, and BK upregulation lowered lipofuscin accumulation via lysosomal exocytosis, establishing pharmacological synergies that might be exploited in lipid storage states (Zhong et al., 2016).

Importantly for RPE-relevant lysosomal storage phenotypes, the more potent TRPML1 agonist ML-SA5 was used in ARPE-19 CLN3-knockout cells (a juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis model) to reduce lysosomal accumulation of subunit C of mitochondrial ATPase (SubC), Gb3, and lysosomal glycerophosphodiesters, accompanied by TFEB nuclear translocation and increased surface LAMP1 consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis; however, BMP/LBPA lipid deficits and maturation of cathepsin D (CatD) and TPP1 remained impaired, indicating incomplete restoration of lysosomal hydrolase processing (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference). Patch-clamp experiments in these cells confirmed that ML-SA1 variants evoke TRPML1 currents fully blocked by the antagonist ML-SI3, supporting pharmacological specificity in RPE lysosomes (Unknown Reference). Collectively, the body of preclinical work shows that TRPML1 agonism has repeatedly restored facets of lysosomal function (Ca2+ release, acidification, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, exocytosis, TFEB activation) across cell types and in injured retina, though complete correction of all lysosomal abnormalities (e.g., hydrolase maturation) is not assured in all disease contexts (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021; Unknown Reference).

No studies in the present corpus demonstrate ML-SA1 use in dry AMD animal models, in RPE models of drusen/lipofuscin accumulation specific to AMD, or in clinical AMD studies; however, in RPE, lipid accumulation was shown to blunt ML-SA1–evoked TRPML1 Ca2+ release, and TRPML1 KO RPE exhibited increased autofluorescence, mechanistically connecting TRPML1 functionality to handling of autofluorescent/neutral lipid material relevant to AMD pathophysiology (Más Gómez et al., 2018). The class of TRPML1 agonists (including ML-SA1) is being investigated preclinically for lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative indications, reinforcing translational plausibility even in the absence of AMD-specific studies (Wang et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
TRPML1 is a lysosomal six-transmembrane TRP superfamily channel permeable to Ca2+ and other cations that localizes primarily to late endosomal/lysosomal membranes via cytosolic dileucine motifs, where it mediates lumen-to-cytosol ion efflux in response to endogenous and pharmacological gating (Wang et al., 2023; Unknown Reference). Physiological activation is conferred by the late endosomal/lysosomal phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2, whose 3′ phosphate directly stabilizes an open-channel conformation; PI(4,5)P2 acts as an antagonist enriched at the plasma membrane, ensuring compartmental specificity (Wang et al., 2023). TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release acts as a master regulator of lysosomal/autophagic homeostasis via several calcium-sensitive effectors: calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB to drive its nuclear translocation and induce the CLEAR network (lysosomal biogenesis and function genes), whereas CaMKKβ activation promotes autophagosome biogenesis; additional roles include regulation of vesicle trafficking, membrane fusion/fission, lysosomal reformation, exocytosis, and mitochondria–lysosome contacts (Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025; Unknown Reference).

ML-SA1 is a synthetic agonist that binds TRPML channels and increases channel open probability, functionally mimicking or synergizing with PI(3,5)P2 to produce lysosomal Ca2+ efflux (Wang et al., 2023). In multiple cell systems, ML-SA1 triggers rapid lysosomal Ca2+ release measured by cytosolic Ca2+ reporters and genetically encoded TRPML1-proximal indicators; responses are abolished or blunted by TRPML1 gene knockout, lysosomal rupture, or pharmacological inhibitors, confirming that cytosolic Ca2+ rises originate from lysosomes through TRPML1 (Más Gómez et al., 2018). In RPE cells, ML-SA1-evoked Ca2+ signals were insensitive to extracellular Ca2+ removal and ER Ca2+ depletion with thapsigargin, but were eliminated by lysosomal disruption with GPN and absent in TRPML1−/− RPE, demonstrating the specificity and lysosomal source in the cell type of interest (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Downstream of TRPML1 activation, ML-SA1 drives a coordinated set of lysosome-centric responses:  
- Autophagosome–lysosome fusion and maturation: ML-SA1 increases conversion of LC3-positive autophagosomes into acidic autolysosomes and shifts cargo (e.g., α-synuclein) into LAMP1-positive, acidified vesicles; notably, ML-SA1 can partially override bafilomycin A1 blocks on fusion/acidification, consistent with a Ca2+-dependent maturation/fusion mechanism (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Lysosomal acidification: In primary neurons, ML-SA1 rapidly acidifies endolysosomes in a TRPML1-dependent manner, coincident with reduced LDL-induced amyloidogenesis and BACE1 localization/activity in endolysosomes (Hui et al., 2019).  
- TFEB signaling and lysosomal biogenesis/exocytosis: TRPML1 activation promotes TFEB nuclear translocation and transcription of lysosomal/autophagy genes; in ARPE-19 CLN3-KO cells, ML-SA5 triggered TFEB translocation and increased surface LAMP1 within 90 minutes, consistent with enhanced lysosomal exocytosis, and reduced lysosomal glycerophosphodiester loads (Tedeschi et al., 2025; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Proteostasis correction: ML-SA1 reduces α-synuclein protein/aggregates in cell models by steering cargo into maturing autolysosomes and promoting degradative flux; these effects require autophagy, PI(3,5)P2, and cytosolic Ca2+, aligning with TRPML1’s canonical signaling dependencies (Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Neuroprotection via autophagy induction and oxidative stress reduction: In vivo in retinal detachment, subretinal ML-SA1 increased LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, reduced cleaved caspase-3, decreased ROS, preserved photoreceptors, and prevented injury-induced TRPML1 degradation (Yan et al., 2021).

Two mechanism-linked constraints merit emphasis for AMD translation. First, lysosomal lipid accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE: desipramine (ASM inhibition), PIKfyve inhibition (YM201636), and chloroquine/U18666A-induced neutral lipid/lipofuscin models decreased ML-SA1–evoked Ca2+ release without reducing TRPML1 mRNA or total lysosomal Ca2+, indicating functional channel inhibition by lipidized lysosomal membranes—an AMD-relevant condition (Más Gómez et al., 2018). Second, in CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation improved substrate clearance and TFEB signaling but did not restore the mature, active forms of CatD and TPP1 despite increased transcripts and precursor/intermediate protein levels, pointing to persistent hydrolase processing defects not corrected by TRPML1 agonism alone (Unknown Reference). These observations suggest that while ML-SA1 should restore key steps (Ca2+ efflux, fusion/acidification, TFEB), lysosomal lipid environments typical of aged RPE may constrain efficacy, and hydrolase maturation deficits—if present in AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Expected Effect  
Assay/System: RPE cells relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology, focusing on phagosome–lysosome fusion, lysosomal acidification, TFEB signaling, and clearance of drusen precursors.

Expected pharmacodynamic cascade:  
1) Channel activation and lysosomal Ca2+ efflux. ML-SA1 will directly activate TRPML1 on RPE lysosomes, eliciting cytosolic Ca2+ rises that persist in Ca2+-free external medium and are abolished by lysosomal disruption, as shown in mouse primary RPE, hesRPE, and ARPE-19 models; absence of response in TRPML1−/− RPE confirms target dependence (Más Gómez et al., 2018). TRPML1 expression in ARPE-19 is documented at the mRNA and functional current levels, supporting target presence in the proposed assay system (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference).

2) Calcineurin-TFEB pathway activation and lysosomal program induction. TRPML1-mediated Ca2+ release will activate calcineurin, drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and upregulate CLEAR network genes that boost lysosomal biogenesis and function, as established for TRPML1 signaling; in RPE (CLN3-KO), ML-SA5 triggered TFEB nuclear import in both WT and mutant cells, indicating pathway engagement in ARPE-19 (Wang et al., 2023; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).

3) Lysosomal acidification and maturation of degradative organelles. ML-SA1 is expected to increase autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, based on multiple cell models where ML-SA1 shifts LC3-positive vesicles toward acidic autolysosomes and augments LAMP1 colocalization; ML-SA1 also acidified neuronal endolysosomes within minutes in a TRPML1-dependent manner (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Hui et al., 2019). In retinal tissue in vivo (detachment model), TRPML1 activation promoted autolysosome formation by EM and upregulated LC3-II/LC3-I and Beclin-1, consistent with increased degradative flux (Yan et al., 2021).

4) Enhancement of degradative capacity and cargo clearance. By accelerating fusion and acidification, ML-SA1 should facilitate catabolic processing of outer segment phagosomes and lipoprotein-like cargoes that contribute to drusen precursors; in RPE knockout models of TRPML1, basal autofluorescence increases, supporting a role for TRPML1 in handling autofluorescent material, and ML-SA1-evoked TRPML1 activity is diminished by lysosomal lipid accumulation typical of aged RPE, highlighting both the therapeutic rationale and a potential barrier (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Unknown Reference).

Mechanistic uncertainties relevant to the hypothesis include the extent to which ML-SA1 will normalize hydrolase maturation (and consequently proteolysis) in aged or AMD RPE, given the CLN3-KO observation that mature CatD and TPP1 were not restored despite TFEB activation; while acidification generally supports protease activity, direct evidence of increased CatD activity post-TRPML1 activation in RPE is not provided here, and in CLN3-KO the maturation block persisted (Unknown Reference). Nevertheless, the acidic shift and fusion acceleration documented with ML-SA1 in neurons and the autophagy induction in retina argue for improved lysosomal degradative competence, which, together with increased exocytosis, should reduce accumulation of drusen precursors, albeit potentially incompletely if hydrolase processing bottlenecks remain (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).

Two context-specific modifiers should be anticipated:  
- Lysosomal lipid load: ML-SA1 responses are blunted by lysosomal lipid accumulation in RPE; thus, efficacy in dry AMD may require co-strategies that reduce lysosomal lipid burden or potentiate TRPML1 gating under lipidized conditions (e.g., via synergistic endogenous PI(3,5)P2, or adjuncts such as BK channel activators shown to enhance ML-SA1 responses in lipid storage contexts) (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- TRPML isoform engagement: ML-SA1 can activate TRPML3 under certain expression conditions; while TRPML3’s role in RPE is less defined, off-target TRPML3 activation may modulate lysosomal transport and ion fluxes, warranting selectivity profiling in RPE (Unknown Reference).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct target validation in RPE: ML-SA1 elicits TRPML1-dependent lysosomal Ca2+ release in primary mouse RPE, hesRPE, and ARPE-19 cells, with responses absent in TRPML1−/− RPE and abolished by lysosomal disruption; this is the critical first step in the proposed mechanism and is robustly documented (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Disease-mechanism alignment with AMD biology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation—central to AMD—functionally inhibits TRPML1 signaling in RPE, directly linking a hallmark AMD stressor to the TRPML1 pathway that ML-SA1 targets; RPE from ABCA4−/− mice (linked to retinal lipid/lipofuscin pathology) exhibit impaired TRPML1-mediated Ca2+ release (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This alignment makes TRPML1 activation a rational corrective lever.  
- Downstream pathway evidence: ML-SA1/ML-SA agonism reproducibly enhances autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, reduces proteotoxic burden (α-synuclein), and activates TFEB-dependent and TFEB-independent lysosomal functions across cell systems; in retina, subretinal ML-SA1 invokes autophagy, reduces ROS/apoptosis, and preserves structure/function after detachment, supporting ocular pharmacology and neuroprotection (Pollmanns et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2021).  
- Translational momentum: The TRPML1 agonist class is actively explored preclinically for LSD and neurodegenerative indications; Merck’s acquisition of Calporta underscores perceived therapeutic potential of TRPML1 agonism, supporting feasibility of a development path if RPE-specific efficacy is confirmed (Wang et al., 2023; Van Acker et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No AMD-specific in vivo data: There are no reports here of ML-SA1 tested in dry AMD or GA animal models, nor in clinical AMD studies; all AMD relevance is inferential from RPE biophysics, lipid-induced TRPML1 impairment, and generalized lysosomal/autophagy correction (Más Gómez et al., 2018). This gap means translational extrapolation to drusen clearance and GA slowing remains unproven.  
- Lipid-dependent resistance: Lysosomal lipid accumulation diminishes ML-SA1 responses in RPE without reducing TRPML1 expression or total lysosomal Ca2+, implying that aged/AMD RPE may exhibit attenuated pharmacodynamics; combination strategies or higher potency agonists (e.g., ML-SA5) may be needed to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Hydrolase maturation not universally rescued: In CLN3-deficient RPE, TRPML1 activation failed to restore mature CatD and TPP1 despite TFEB induction, indicating that some degradative deficits—potentially relevant to AMD—may not normalize solely via TRPML1 activation; this could limit improvements in cathepsin-dependent proteolysis of drusen precursors (Unknown Reference).  
- Selectivity considerations: ML-SA1 can activate other TRPML family members (e.g., TRPML3) in overexpression systems, and pan-TRPML agonism in RPE may have uncharacterized effects on lysosomal trafficking and axonal transport; selectivity profiling in RPE and concentration-response mapping are needed to de-risk off-target TRPML isoform engagement (Unknown Reference).  
- Context-dependent acidification: ML-SA1 acidifies neuronal endolysosomes and enhances degradative flux, but direct demonstrations of increased CatD activity in RPE after ML-SA1 are not provided here; given the CLN3-KO findings on hydrolase maturation, reliance on acidification alone may not guarantee improved protease activity in diseased RPE (Hui et al., 2019; Unknown Reference).

Development guidance  
Given the strong RPE target validation and consistent downstream biology, ML-SA1 (or a more potent TRPML1 agonist such as ML-SA5) is a credible mechanistic candidate for dry AMD; however, AMD-relevant pharmacology must be demonstrated directly. The most decision-informative steps are:  
- Establish efficacy in AMD-relevant RPE contexts: Test ML-SA1 in iPSC-derived human RPE from older donors and/or RPE cultured with A2E/lipofuscin and oxidized lipids to recapitulate lysosomal lipidization; quantify TRPML1 Ca2+ responses, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and cargo clearance (e.g., ApoE/cholesterol-rich particles, complement-containing deposits), benchmarking against the lipid-impairment reported in RPE (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Measure hydrolase activity and maturation: Directly assay CatD and other cathepsin activities and maturation states post-ML-SA1 in lipidized RPE; if maturation remains deficient, evaluate combinations with agents that restore hydrolase processing (e.g., modulators of endolysosomal trafficking or mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathways) (Unknown Reference).  
- Explore potentiation strategies: Consider co-targeting known TRPML1 modulators to overcome lipidized lysosomal membranes—examples include augmenting PI(3,5)P2 availability or adding BK channel activators, which rescued impaired ML-SA1 responses and reduced storage in NPC-related settings (Wang et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2016).  
- Prioritize potency and exposure: Given blunted responses in lipidized RPE, evaluate higher-potency ML-SA chemotypes (ML-SA5 EC50 ~80 nM in a TFE3/TFEB-related translocation assay vs. ML-SA1 in the µM range) for superior pharmacodynamics; subretinal tolerability is supported by RD studies but needs AMD-model confirmation (Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2021).  
- In vivo validation in AMD models: Move to aged/multiple-hit models that accumulate sub-RPE deposits (e.g., high-fat diet, light exposure, Abca4−/− backgrounds) to test whether TRPML1 agonism reduces drusen-like material, preserves RPE function, and slows GA-like endpoints; note that Abca4−/− RPE exhibited impaired TRPML1 Ca2+ release, making it a relevant sensitized background to assay pharmacological rescue (Más Gómez et al., 2018).

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a tractable, mechanistically well-supported TRPML1 agonist with direct RPE target validation and robust evidence that its downstream effects—lysosomal Ca2+ release, TFEB activation, autophagosome–lysosome fusion/acidification, and exocytosis—can correct core lysosomal deficits that plausibly drive drusen precursor accumulation in dry AMD (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Pollmanns et al., 2022; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). The principal risks are the lipid-dependence of TRPML1 dysfunction in RPE and the incomplete rescue of hydrolase maturation observed in CLN3-deficient RPE, both of which may attenuate the magnitude of effect on complex AMD cargoes and necessitate combination strategies or use of more potent agonists (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024). On balance, the mechanistic specificity, ocular proof-of-concept in retinal detachment, and extensive preclinical precedent for lysosomal restoration argue that ML-SA1 (or next-generation TRPML1 agonists) merits prioritized evaluation in AMD-relevant RPE assays and in vivo models, with an early focus on overcoming lipidized lysosomal resistance and verifying improvements in both acidification and hydrolase function (Yan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Tedeschi et al., 2025).

Strength of evidence for the dry AMD hypothesis: moderate, driven by strong RPE target biology and retinal neuroprotection data but constrained by the absence of AMD-specific in vivo studies and by lipid-imposed pharmacodynamic limits (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2021). If forthcoming AMD-relevant experiments confirm that TRPML1 activation restores lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and degradative capacity in lipidized RPE, and that drusen precursors are reduced, ML-SA1/ML-SA5 would represent a differentiated, mechanism-based approach compared with broad mTOR inhibition, with the potential to correct proximal lysosomal defects underlying GA progression (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).

Detailed, component-wise assessment  

- Target presence and engagement in RPE: TRPML1 expression and function are present in ARPE-19 and primary RPE; ML-SA1 evokes lysosomal Ca2+ release that is TRPML1-dependent (absent in TRPML1−/− RPE), establishing on-target engagement (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Relevance of TRPML1 signaling to AMD pathobiology: Lysosomal lipid/lipofuscin accumulation impairs TRPML1 function in RPE and is germane to AMD; RPE autofluorescence increases in TRPML1 KO, linking the channel to handling of drusen-like material (Más Gómez et al., 2018).  
- Downstream mechanisms aligned with therapeutic hypothesis: ML-SA1 triggers calcineurin-TFEB signaling, augments autophagosome–lysosome fusion and acidification, and enhances exocytosis—mechanisms expected to improve clearance of drusen precursors (Wang et al., 2023; Pollmanns et al., 2022).  
- Evidence for improved degradative flux: In neurons, ML-SA1 acidifies endolysosomes and reduces Aβ/BACE1 pathology; in retina in vivo, ML-SA1 increases autophagy markers and preserves photoreceptors; in RPE disease models, TRPML1 activation decreases stored substrates and reduces lysosomal surface area (Hui et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; Wünkhaus et al., 2024).  
- Constraints/unknowns: Lipid-imposed TRPML1 inhibition in RPE may limit efficacy; CatD/TPP1 maturation not rescued in CLN3-KO RPE; no direct AMD data; potential TRPML3 co-activation (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Unknown Reference).

Recommendation  
Advance ML-SA1 (and evaluate ML-SA5 as a higher-potency comparator) into AMD-relevant RPE assays with lipidized lysosomes, incorporating quantitative readouts of TRPML1 Ca2+ signaling, TFEB translocation, lysosomal pH, hydrolase maturation/activity, and cargo clearance, and then proceed to in vivo testing in drusen-accumulating models if in vitro data are supportive; in parallel, explore combination strategies (e.g., BK channel activation) to overcome lipid-dependent resistance to TRPML1 agonism (Más Gómez et al., 2018; Wünkhaus et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2016).

Proposal for Sulforaphane (Sigma S4441)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from glucoraphanin in cruciferous vegetables via myrosinase-mediated hydrolysis; as an electrophilic small molecule, SFN was identified through its unusually potent induction of phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant defenses in mammalian tissues via the KEAP1–NFE2L2/NRF2 stress-response axis (classically termed “phase 2 induction”) (Qin, 2007; Hyttinen et al., 2019). Isothiocyanates and related electrophiles covalently modify reactive cysteine residues on KEAP1, disrupting the KEAP1–NRF2 “hinge-and-latch” ubiquitin ligase complex and stabilizing NRF2 to drive ARE-dependent transcription of cytoprotective enzymes including NQO1, GCLM, HO-1, and glutathione pathway genes (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). Beyond canonical NRF2 activation, SFN is now recognized to engage lysosome-centered adaptive transcription by inducing nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB/TFE3 through a mild, ROS-triggered Ca²⁺–calcineurin pathway that is largely MTOR-independent, thereby upregulating CLEAR-network genes controlling lysosome and autophagy biogenesis (Li et al., 2021). In ocular contexts, SFN has been used experimentally as a cytoprotective agent in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models subjected to oxidative or phototoxic stress, and as a modulator of autophagy markers, situating SFN within a dual-modality class that can activate antioxidant defenses and augment lysosome-autophagy function (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
SFN and other NRF2 activators have been widely studied as cytoprotective chemopreventive agents and as protectants in oxidative-stress paradigms across tissues; in RPE models, SFN has repeatedly demonstrated NRF2-dependent protection and modulation of stress and quality-control pathways, although direct clinical testing in dry AMD is not reported in the provided literature (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016). In ARPE-19 cells exposed to blue light, SFN promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, induced HO-1 and glutathione production, reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and its cytoprotective effect was blocked by the NRF2 inhibitor ML385, indicating a mechanistic dependence on NRF2; SFN also increased LC3B-II and p62, and the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA blunted its protective action, linking SFN’s benefit to autophagy engagement in this RPE stress model (Yang et al., 2021). In a separate ARPE-19 inflammatory model (TGF-β), SFN (alone or combined with vitamin D) lowered ROS and VEGF and restored epithelial junction markers; in that system, the authors did not detect NRF2 pathway modulation and instead implicated ERK1/2 downregulation, underscoring context-dependence of the upstream signaling mediating protection (Bergandi et al., 2024). Reviews and experimental summaries further report that SFN protects retinal/epithelial tissues and can recover cone function in an NRF2-dependent manner in mice undergoing RPE oxidative stress, although primary data for those specific in vivo outcomes are not detailed in the provided text (Falcão et al., 2025). Mechanistically adjacent precedents in RPE include robust protection by the electrophilic NRF2 activator RTA 408 in primary human RPE subjected to H₂O₂, with genetic evidence for NRF2 dependence; while not SFN, this validates the KEAP1–NRF2 axis as druggable and protective in human RPE (Liu et al., 2016). With respect to lysosome-autophagy axes central to dry AMD, TFEB activation (via rapamycin or constitutively active TFEB) reduces photoreceptor outer segment–derived autofluorescent granules in RPE POS-feeding models, and TFEB-directed interventions (including trehalose or constitutively nuclear TFEB) restore cathepsin D/L abundance and activity and increase LAMP1 in AMD-relevant human RPE models, establishing the lysosome/transcriptional arm as therapeutically tractable in RPE; however, these TFEB-driven rescues have not been directly demonstrated with SFN in RPE in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
- NRF2 engagement via KEAP1 cysteine sensing: SFN, as an electrophile, reacts with specific redox-sensitive cysteines on KEAP1 (notably Cys151 among others), impairing KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination of NRF2 and permitting NRF2 stabilization, nuclear accumulation, and heterodimerization with small Maf proteins to bind AREs and induce a large gene battery of antioxidant, detoxification, and proteostasis regulators (e.g., NQO1, HO-1, GCLM, GSTs), increasing GSH and related defenses (Hyttinen et al., 2019; Qin, 2007). In RPE and ocular tissues, SFN and related NRF2 activators have induced phase II enzymes and HO-1 and conferred resistance to photooxidative injury, with biochemical readouts that include increased NQO1, thioredoxin, GSH, and reduced ROS (Qin, 2007; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021). Aging impairs inducible NRF2 signaling in RPE under oxidative challenges (e.g., sodium iodate), supporting the rationale for exogenous NRF2 activation in older RPE (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB/TFE3 activation and lysosome-autophagy biogenesis: SFN provokes a mild increase in ROS that sensitizes lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 channels to agonist-evoked Ca²⁺ release; resultant cytosolic Ca²⁺ engages calcineurin to dephosphorylate TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of CLEAR-network transcription independently of acute MTORC1 inhibition (TFEB activation is blocked by antioxidants, BAPTA-AM, and attenuated by FK506) (Li et al., 2021). The SFN-induced TFEB program upregulates autophagy and lysosome genes (SQSTM1, ULK1, LC3) and multiple lysosomal components including LAMP1, v-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V1H), hydrolases (CTSB, TPP1), and MCOLN1, and increases LysoTracker and LAMP1 signals, consistent with enhanced lysosomal mass and acidotropic probe accumulation (Li et al., 2021). Critically, TFEB is necessary for SFN-induced upregulation of NFE2L2/NRF2 and for SFN-mediated suppression of ROS in mitochondrial and lysosomal stress models, documenting a TFEB→NRF2 dependency in SFN’s antioxidant protection (Li et al., 2021). Reviews synthesizing TFEB–NRF2 crosstalk add that TFEB can directly or indirectly promote NRF2 by repressing its E3 ligase (DCAF11) and via p62-mediated KEAP1 sequestration; reciprocally, NRF2 activation can induce TFEB-related gene sets and promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion, indicating bidirectional reinforcement (Falcão et al., 2025).

- RPE-specific TFEB/lysosome biology relevant to AMD: In human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells, TFEB controls lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; nutrient deprivation and lysosomal stress increase TFEB and MITF and induce CLEAR genes including LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1, and autophagy factors (BECN1), with calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation regulating nuclear translocation (Pan et al., 2019). In AMD-relevant RPE models, TFEB activation (via mTORC1 inhibition or constitutively active TFEB) reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules through a hydrolase-dependent mechanism, and inhibition or genetic loss of CTSD increases autofluorescent burden and abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, tying TFEB-driven rescue to functional lysosomal proteolysis (Falcão et al., 2024). In human AMD donor RPE and CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, elevated p-TFEB/p-TFE3 associates with reduced CTSD/CTSL abundance and activity; interventions that restore TFEB nuclear activity (AAV2-TFEB-S467A) or TFEB activators (trehalose) rescue CTSD/CTSL levels and activities and increase LAMP1, while AKT2 inhibition counters secretory-autophagy bias and improves degradative flux (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

- Cathepsin D biochemistry and lysosomal pH: Cathepsin D (CTSD) is an abundant lysosomal aspartyl protease synthesized as an inactive proenzyme that undergoes maturation and activation in the acidic late endosome/lysosome; cathepsins generally require a reducing, mildly acidic lumen and lose activity at neutral pH, linking lysosomal acidification (v-ATPase function) tightly to CTSD proteolysis (Sharif, 2015). In AMD, lysosomal dysfunction (including LMP, impaired proton-pump function, and hydrolase inhibition by lipofuscin-derived oxidized products) is prominent, and CTSD leakage and reduced hydrolase activity are reported in AMD RPE, mechanistically supporting the therapeutic objective to normalize lysosomal pH and restore cathepsin activity (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Safety and pathway caveats: Constitutive or excessive activation of NRF2 or TFEB can carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks, and chronic KEAP1–NRF2 perturbation can yield accumulation of non-degradative organelles, emphasizing the need for cell-specific, dose-titrated modulation and rigorous safety assessment in the AMD context (Falcão et al., 2025).

Taken together, SFN stands out for concurrent engagement of NRF2 antioxidant programs and TFEB-driven lysosome/autophagy biogenesis—mechanisms that align with central oxidative and degradative defects in dry AMD RPE—yet it is important to note that direct biochemical evidence demonstrating SFN-mediated normalization of lysosomal pH and restoration of CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under AMD-relevant oxidative stress is not present in the supplied literature (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Under the stated hypothesis—SFN engages NRF2 and TFEB in oxidatively stressed RPE to normalize lysosomal pH and restore CTSD proteolysis—the expected proximate and downstream effects in rigorously designed assays are:  
- Antioxidant response and ROS control: SFN should increase NRF2 nuclear accumulation and ARE target expression (HO-1, NQO1, GCLM, Trx1, GSH biosynthesis enzymes) in RPE cells subjected to oxidative paradigms (e.g., blue light, sodium iodate, hydroquinone, or POS feeding with photooxidative stress), lowering ROS burden and oxidative damage; this is strongly supported in ARPE-19 under blue light (and in other epithelial systems), and the effect shows functional dependence on NRF2 (ML385-sensitive) (Yang et al., 2021; Qin, 2007). Aging-associated defects in inducible NRF2 signaling suggest exogenous NRF2 activation may be especially beneficial in aged RPE, further motivating this outcome measure (Sachdeva et al., 2014).

- TFEB activation and lysosome-autophagy program: SFN should induce TFEB nuclear translocation through ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin signaling, upregulate CLEAR-network transcripts (including LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1, LC3), increase lysosomal biogenesis and LysoTracker staining, and enhance autophagic flux; these outcomes are well documented for SFN in multiple human cell models and provide mechanistic plausibility for analogous effects in RPE (Li et al., 2021). In RPE specifically, TFEB is inducible and drives LAMP1 and CTSD expression under stress, while TFEB activation improves degradative capacity in AMD-relevant settings, supporting the assay logic to monitor TFEB localization and CLEAR targets in RPE (Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Lysosomal acidification and CTSD proteolysis: If SFN increases v-ATPase subunit expression and lysosomal mass (as in other cells), one would expect improved lysosomal acidification (lower pH) and more efficient CTSD maturation (pro- to intermediate- to mature forms) and activity, read out by calibrated pH probes (e.g., LysoSensor or ratiometric genetically encoded sensors), Western blots for CTSD processing, and fluorometric CTSD activity assays. This is biologically plausible given SFN-induced lysosomal gene expression and LysoTracker increases in vitro, and given that TFEB activation rescues hydrolase-dependent POS processing in RPE; however, direct evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal pH and increases CTSD maturation/activity in RPE under oxidative stress is not shown in the provided literature and must be generated (Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Functional RPE outcomes: Improved degradative clearance of POS-derived material and reduced accumulation of autofluorescent granules (lipofuscin-like AFG) are expected functional correlates. Rapamycin and constitutively active TFEB reduce AFG in RPE POS-feeding models in a hydrolase-dependent manner, and TFEB activation or AKT2 inhibition restores CTSD/CTSL activity and LAMP1 levels in human AMD RPE models; SFN could converge on these endpoints via TFEB activation, but this remains to be established experimentally (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).

Assay implementation considerations:  
- Cell systems and paradigms: iPSC-derived human RPE (including CFH Y402H risk background) and ARPE-19, subjected to blue light, hydroquinone/cigarette smoke mimetics, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and/or complement challenge, to model oxidative and degradative stress relevant to dry AMD (Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Readouts: NRF2 nuclear translocation and ARE target induction; TFEB nuclear translocation and phosphorylation state; CLEAR-network gene expression (LAMP1, CTSD, ATP6V1H, MCOLN1, ULK1, SQSTM1); lysosomal pH (calibrated probes); lysosomal mass (LAMP1 immunostaining, LysoTracker); CTSD processing (pro/mature Western blots) and enzymatic activity; autophagic flux (LC3 turnover with and without lysosomal inhibitors); POS processing kinetics and AFG quantification (Li et al., 2021; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024).

- Controls and mechanism validation: Antioxidant blockade (NAC, catalase) to test ROS-dependence of TFEB activation; Ca²⁺ chelation (BAPTA-AM) and calcineurin inhibition (FK506) to probe TFEB activation pathway; NRF2 inhibitor (ML385) to test NRF2 dependence; TFEB loss-of-function (siRNA/CRISPR) to test TFEB dependence; rapamycin/trehalose/AAV-TFEB as positive controls for lysosomal biogenesis; cathepsin inhibitors and CTSD KO/knockdown to test hydrolase dependence; use of AKT2 pathway modulators to deconvolve TFEB repression in AMD-relevant models (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Dosing: Based on mechanistic studies, SFN at 5–15 µM for 4–9 h is effective for TFEB activation in several cell lines; in ARPE-19 blue-light studies, SFN modulated NRF2 and autophagy markers, and in TGF-β models, SFN was tested at 1–10 µM with ERK pathway modulation observed (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Interpretation caveats: In TGF-β–treated RPE, investigators did not detect NRF2 modulation with SFN, implying model-specific pathway engagement; this further justifies running multiple oxidative-stress paradigms and confirming pathway activation per condition (Bergandi et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with AMD pathobiology: SFN targets two validated, convergent axes implicated in non-neovascular AMD—NRF2-mediated antioxidant defense and TFEB-driven lysosomal-autophagy competence—addressing both oxidative injury and impaired degradative capacity in RPE (Pinelli et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2019; Falcão et al., 2024). The KEAP1–NRF2 pathway is protective in RPE and becomes inducibly impaired with age, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolase function and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence in RPE models (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024).

- Robust cellular mechanism for dual-pathway engagement: High-quality mechanistic studies show SFN activates TFEB via ROS→Ca²⁺→calcineurin independent of acute MTORC1 inhibition, induces CLEAR genes, increases lysosomal mass and LysoTracker staining, and requires TFEB to drive NFE2L2 transcription and antioxidant protection; this dual activation positions SFN to coordinate detoxification and lysosomal biogenesis (Li et al., 2021).

- RPE-relevant efficacy signals: In ARPE-19 blue-light stress, SFN confers NRF2-dependent cytoprotection and requires autophagy; SFN also reduces ROS and preserves epithelial integrity in an inflammatory RPE model (albeit via ERK1/2 modulation), indicating protective breadth across RPE-relevant stressors (Yang et al., 2021; Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Translational plausibility: SFN (and class analogs) have measurable bioavailability in humans and have long been explored as chemopreventive agents, supporting feasibility of repurposing if ocular exposure and dosing can be optimized; as a comparator, RTA 408’s efficacy in primary RPE confirms the druggability of KEAP1–NRF2 in human RPE (Qin, 2007; Liu et al., 2016).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
- No direct evidence for lysosomal pH normalization or CTSD rescue by SFN in RPE: Although SFN upregulates lysosomal genes and LysoTracker signal in other cell types, the literature provided does not report calibrated lysosomal pH measurements, CTSD maturation patterns, or CTSD enzymatic activity in RPE after SFN under AMD-relevant oxidative stress; this is the critical gap relative to the stated hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Li et al., 2021).

- Model-dependent pathway engagement: In TGF-β ARPE-19, SFN protection tracked with ERK1/2 modulation rather than detectable NRF2 activation, underscoring that the upstream route by which SFN confers benefit can vary with the stressor and cellular context; robust pathway biomarker panels will be required in each model (Bergandi et al., 2024).

- Safety and liability considerations: Persistent activation of NRF2 or TFEB may carry oncogenic or maladaptive risks; KEAP1–NRF2 dysregulation can drive accumulation of non-degradative organelles, and TFEB activation must be titrated to avoid excessive catabolic or proliferative shifts; this risk profile necessitates careful dose finding, exposure control, and long-term safety assessment (Falcão et al., 2025).

- Ocular delivery/exposure unknowns: The provided literature notes systemic bioavailability with detection in non-ocular tissues; however, data establishing therapeutic concentrations in the RPE/choroid following systemic or local administration are absent here and will need to be generated to support translational feasibility (Qin, 2007).

- Disease-network complexity: In AMD-relevant RPE, AKT2 upregulation suppresses TFEB/TFE3 and reduces cathepsin expression/activity, while complement dysregulation, iron overload, and lipofuscin-associated proton-pump/hydrolase inhibition further stress lysosomes; whether SFN’s TFEB activation suffices under these multi-hit conditions, or whether combination with AKT2/MTOR modulators is required, remains to be determined (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Programmatic recommendation  
- Proceed to focused preclinical validation with a decision gate on lysosomal biochemical rescue. The mechanistic case for SFN’s dual NRF2/TFEB action is strong, and RPE protection data exist; however, the program’s value hinges on demonstrating that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and restores CTSD maturation/activity in stressed human RPE—outcomes not yet shown (Li et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

- Experimental plan (key go/no-go criteria):  
  1) Pathway engagement: SFN dose–time response for NRF2 and TFEB activation in iPSC-RPE (±CFH Y402H) under blue light, hydroquinone, sodium iodate, POS feeding, and complement challenge; use ML385, FK506, BAPTA-AM, and TFEB LOF to assign mechanism (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2024).  
  2) Lysosomal function: Calibrated lysosomal pH; CTSD pro/mature processing and activity; LAMP1 and LysoTracker; autophagic flux; POS degradation kinetics and AFG load; requirement for CTSD confirmed by CTSD knockdown and cathepsin inhibitors (Falcão et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
  3) Comparative controls: Rapamycin, trehalose, and AAV2-TFEB-S467A as positive controls for lysosomal rescue; AKT2 inhibition as a disease-relevant comparator; RTA 408 or DMF as NRF2-pathway comparators (Ghosh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2016).  
  4) In vivo signal-seeking: Acute oxidative RPE injury (e.g., sodium iodate) and chronic stress models to test functional endpoints (ERG, OCT) and histology with RPE lysosomal markers and CTSD activity ex vivo; assess whether SFN improves cone/RPE function in an NRF2-dependent manner as suggested by prior reports (Sachdeva et al., 2014; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  5) Safety/tolerability: Proliferation, TFEB/NRF2 target overactivation, lysosomal membrane integrity (LMP markers), and non-degradative organelle accumulation with extended SFN exposure; aim for intermittent dosing to minimize chronic pathway hyperactivation (Falcão et al., 2025).

If SFN demonstrates robust TFEB/NRF2 engagement in human RPE, normalizes lysosomal pH, and restores CTSD maturation/activity with concomitant functional improvements in POS clearance and AFG reduction, it would represent a differentiated candidate addressing both oxidative and degradative lesions central to geographic atrophy; absent those biochemical rescues, SFN should be deprioritized in favor of TFEB-directed agents (e.g., trehalose or gene-based TFEB activation) or combinations that address AKT2–TFEB repression and complement-driven lysosomal injury (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023).

In summary, sulforaphane is a scientifically credible, mechanistically dual-action candidate for dry AMD based on strong evidence of NRF2 activation in RPE and TFEB-driven lysosome-autophagy induction in multiple cell systems, with supportive RPE protection data; yet the decisive evidence that SFN normalizes lysosomal acidity and rescues cathepsin D proteolysis in oxidatively stressed human RPE is currently lacking in the provided literature and must be established to justify advancement (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025).

Proposal for Rapamycin (Sigma R0395)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin (sirolimus), commercially available as Sigma R0395, is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus, a discovery that dates back to studies on soil samples from Easter Island. As a naturally derived compound now synthesized and purified for clinical use, rapamycin belongs to the macrolide class and is best known for its potent immunosuppressive properties, having been used extensively to prevent organ rejection in transplantation. Over time, its application expanded beyond transplantation to include areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and age-related diseases due to its ability to inhibit the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The rationale for repurposing rapamycin in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically geographic atrophy (GA), stems from its established pharmacological profile, extensive safety record, and well-characterized biochemical functions. Its clinical approval and long-term safety data in other contexts provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential in ocular indications, particularly given its capacity to modulate autophagy in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Rapamycin’s development began with its use as an immunosuppressant in organ transplantation, and over the ensuing decades, its application has broadened considerably. Biochemical and preclinical studies have demonstrated that rapamycin is an effective inhibitor of mTORC1, a critical regulator not only of cell proliferation but also of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. Early investigations revealed that rapamycin could induce autophagy in various cell types, including RPE cells, by inhibiting mTORC1, thereby facilitating the clearance of toxic aggregates and damaged organelles. This mechanism has been explored extensively for neurodegenerative conditions, and more recently, there has been focused investigation into its utility for dry AMD. Clinical trials have tested rapamycin in forms ranging from intravitreal to subconjunctival injections in patients with GA; for example, a clinical trial by the National Eye Institute aimed to evaluate intravitreal injections of sirolimus for GA, although this study was terminated due to safety concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012). Similarly, other studies using subconjunctival injections demonstrated that while rapamycin appears safe and well-tolerated, significant benefits in terms of preventing GA progression have not been conclusively demonstrated (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011). In animal studies and in vitro RPE models, rapamycin enhanced autophagic flux, increased the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), and reduced the accumulation of toxic material such as A2E—an effect that is consistent with a potential for slowing GA progression (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Thus, rapamycin’s therapeutic history encompasses a combination of robust preclinical evidence supporting its mechanistic action and mixed clinical outcomes in ocular trials, setting the stage for further investigation into optimal dosing, delivery methods, and patient selection criteria (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
Rapamycin exerts its biological effects primarily through direct inhibition of mTORC1, a serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates signals from nutrients, growth factors, and cellular energy status to regulate cell growth, proliferation, and autophagy. In the absence of rapamycin, active mTORC1 phosphorylates downstream targets such as S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, thereby promoting anabolic processes and suppressing autophagy. When rapamycin binds to its intracellular receptor, FKBP12, the resulting complex interacts with the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTORC1, leading to its inhibition. This inhibition results in dephosphorylation and subsequent activation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy-related genes. Activated TFEB then translocates to the nucleus, where it enhances the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, acidification, and the production of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016). In the context of dry AMD, the proposed mechanism hinges on rapamycin’s ability to restore cellular homeostasis in RPE cells by increasing autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance of accumulated drusen components, which include toxic aggregates like A2E. Preclinical studies have shown that treatment of RPE cells with rapamycin results in a marked reduction in the accumulation of autofluorescent granules (AFGs) that are indicative of impaired lysosomal degradation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascade initiated by rapamycin—mTORC1 inhibition, TFEB activation, and enhanced expression of lysosome-associated proteins such as LAMP1 and pro-cathepsin D—forms the crux of its proposed therapeutic action in mitigating the progression of GA by promoting the dismantling and clearance of pathological deposits (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
In RPE cells, the inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin is expected to release the inhibitory phosphorylation on TFEB, enabling its nuclear translocation and activation of a transcriptional program that drives lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and the production of key lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D. This molecular shift is anticipated to markedly enhance the autophagic capacity of the RPE, leading to increased degradation of drusen components, including lipofuscin and A2E, which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. The activation of autophagy not only facilitates the clearance of accumulated toxic material but also mitigates oxidative stress by removing damaged mitochondria and other organelles that may contribute to reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, preclinical evidence indicates that, in ARPE-19 cell models, rapamycin improves cellular viability in the face of oxidative injury and reduces markers of cellular senescence by enhancing autophagic flux. These cellular effects are directly linked to the expression of critical proteins in RPE cells; for example, TFEB is known to be expressed in these cells and its activation correlates with increased lysosomal gene expression and function (Falcão et al., 2024) while cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease, is vital for the degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (Chang et al., 2022; Sinha et al., 2016). The intended therapeutic outcome is to slow or potentially halt the progression of GA by reducing the burden of drusen and preserving RPE function, which could translate into better preservation of visual acuity over time. However, it is important to note that while these mechanisms are promising in vitro, clinical translation has encountered challenges related to dosing, delivery, and the stage of disease at which intervention occurs (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin presents itself as a scientifically promising yet clinically challenging candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. One of the key strengths of rapamycin is its well-established mechanism of action: as a potent mTORC1 inhibitor, it leverages a well-characterized pathway involving TFEB activation that directly targets the core pathology observed in dry AMD—the accumulation of drusen components and impaired lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies have consistently demonstrated that rapamycin can enhance autophagic flux, lower levels of toxic aggregates such as A2E, and increase the activity of lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, thereby supporting its target validation in the context of RPE health (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, rapamycin has an extensive history of clinical use in other indications, and its safety profile, while not without concerns, is well documented from its use as an immunosuppressant in transplantation and in various oncology settings (Wang et al., 2022).

However, the clinical translation of rapamycin for dry AMD has not been straightforward. Multiple clinical trials have assessed its application using different routes of administration, such as intravitreal and subconjunctival injections, with mixed results. While safety and tolerability have generally been acceptable, the efficacy endpoints—specifically, the prevention or slowing of GA progression—have not been definitively met in these studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008, 2011, 2012; Wang et al., 2022). Furthermore, some trials encountered complications such as sterile endophthalmitis or observed decreases in visual acuity relative to untreated eyes, suggesting that even if the underlying molecular mechanisms are engaged, the overall benefits in late-stage disease might be limited (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Another potential weakness is the complexity inherent in mTOR signaling itself. The pathway plays a dual role in cellular homeostasis—while its inhibition can promote autophagy and lysosomal clearance, inappropriate or excessive inhibition could lead to adverse effects such as increased retinal neuron apoptosis, particularly in advanced stages of AMD where the cellular milieu is significantly altered (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Moreover, the optimal dosing regimen and delivery method for achieving the desired ocular concentration without incurring systemic side effects remain unresolved. Some studies have suggested that modifications to the formulation, such as encapsulation in synthetic nanoparticles, could enhance ocular penetration and prolong the effective duration of rapamycin within the eye, thereby minimizing side effects and improving efficacy (Jo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

Despite these challenges, the strength of rapamycin’s mechanism—the inhibition of mTORC1 and consequent activation of TFEB leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—remains compelling. The molecular rationale is robust, and the repeated demonstration of reduced levels of autofluorescent granules in RPE cells following rapamycin treatment is particularly encouraging (Falcão et al., 2024). The concept of using a repurposed, clinically approved drug to address a significant unmet need in dry AMD is attractive, especially given the limited treatment options currently available for this degenerative condition. In this light, further investigations—ideally, in earlier stages of AMD and with innovative delivery modalities—may reveal a niche where rapamycin can exert a clinically meaningful benefit (Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019).

In conclusion, while rapamycin has significant potential grounded in sound molecular pharmacology and extensive preclinical validation, its clinical application for dry AMD warrants careful optimization. The candidate’s strengths lie in its potent and well-understood mechanism of mTORC1 inhibition, the activation of TFEB, and subsequent improvements in lysosomal function and autophagic clearance in RPE cells. Conversely, clinical challenges including mixed efficacy outcomes in GA trials, potential adverse effects related to mTOR pathway modulation in vulnerable retinal neurons, and limitations in current dosing/delivery strategies represent hurdles that must be surmounted. Based on these comprehensive literature insights, rapamycin remains a promising candidate for further investigation, albeit with recommendations to explore its use in earlier disease stages and in combination with advanced ocular delivery systems to maximize its therapeutic benefit while minimizing risks (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2012; Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).

Proposal for 2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD; Sigma C0926)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
2-Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of natural β-cyclodextrin—a cyclic oligosaccharide consisting of glucose units linked via α-1,4 glycosidic bonds. This modification, achieved by the introduction of hydroxypropyl groups, improves its solubility and reduces its inherent cytotoxicity relative to unmodified cyclodextrins. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin class, molecules that have been widely used in pharmaceutical formulations as solubilizing agents and excipients due to their ability to encapsulate hydrophobic molecules within their lipophilic interior, thereby increasing bioavailability. Over the years, these agents have gained attention as cholesterol-binding molecules, and HPβCD is no exception, being repurposed for diseases characterized by pathological cholesterol accumulation such as Niemann–Pick type C1 (NPC1). Its structural properties permit the formation of inclusion complexes with cholesterol and other lipids, facilitating their mobilization and removal from cells. Given its established role in NPC1 disease and emerging evidence supporting its ability to cross the blood–retina barrier, HPβCD is now being evaluated as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), specifically targeting drusen-associated cholesterol accumulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Calias, 2018; Roney, 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, HPβCD has been extensively investigated as a therapeutic intervention for lysosomal storage diseases, with a particular focus on Niemann–Pick disease type C (NPC), a condition characterized by the pathological accumulation of cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in cells. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that systemic administration of HPβCD can lower intracellular cholesterol levels, thereby ameliorating disease-related cellular dysfunction. However, its pharmacokinetic limitations—most notably, its minimal penetration of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) when administered intravenously—have necessitated alternative routes of delivery, such as intrathecal administration, to achieve sufficient central nervous system (CNS) exposure (Calias, 2018). In the context of retinal diseases, several studies have investigated the effects of HPβCD in animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. In these models, HPβCD treatment has been associated with significant reductions in cholesterol crystals, diminished lipid deposition in structures such as Bruch’s membrane, and decreased activation of retinal macrophages and microglial cells (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Although HPβCD has been repurposed from its application in NPC to target retinal pathologies, a focused investigation into its use for dry AMD remains to be performed clinically, as systematic searches on ClinicalTrials.gov indicate that no registered trials have specifically addressed cyclodextrin use in AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HPβCD acts primarily as a cholesterol extractor by leveraging its toroidal structure, which is characterized by a hydrophilic exterior and a relatively hydrophobic interior cavity. This unique architecture enables HPβCD to form inclusion complexes with cholesterol, effectively sequestering the lipid from cellular membranes. In the setting of RPE cells, where lysosomal cholesterol accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, HPβCD is hypothesized to mobilize cholesterol from lysosomal membranes. Excess cholesterol in these membranes disrupts the lipid microdomains necessary for the optimal assembly and functioning of protein complexes such as the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), which is essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017). By extracting cholesterol, HPβCD is expected to restore these lipid microdomains, thereby facilitating the proper assembly and function of the v-ATPase complex. This normalization of v-ATPase assembly is critical for reestablishing an acidic environment within lysosomes, which in turn is necessary for the optimal activity of lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D (CTSD).

In neurons and other cell types, studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a reduction in both luminal and membrane-associated cholesterol levels, a process that not only improves lysosomal trafficking but also induces lysosomal exocytosis under certain conditions (Roney, 2020). Furthermore, the improvement in lysosomal acidification following HPβCD-mediated cholesterol extraction has been correlated with enhanced autophagic flux due to increased CTSD-mediated proteolysis. Although direct evidence for this mechanism in RPE cells is still emerging, it is reasonable to extrapolate that similar molecular events would occur in retinal cells. The restoration of lysosomal pH and the subsequent improvement in autophagy are critical because they directly contribute to the clearance of intracellular debris, including drusen lipids, thereby potentially reducing the lipid burden that characterizes the progression of dry AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is that it will mobilize cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby restoring the integrity of lipid microdomains that are essential for v-ATPase assembly. In practical terms, treatment with HPβCD is expected to yield several interrelated outcomes. First, the reduction in membrane cholesterol is anticipated to alleviate the inhibitory effect of cholesterol excess on v-ATPase assembly, leading to improved proton pump activity and a consequent normalization of lysosomal pH. Given that the activity of CTSD is pH-dependent—with optimal function occurring under acidic conditions—the normalization of lysosomal pH should enable enhanced CTSD activity and improved autophagic degradation of lipid aggregates (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Second, by promoting the removal of excess cholesterol, HPβCD should reduce the formation of cholesterol crystals, a pathological hallmark associated with retinal lipid dyshomeostasis and drusen formation. Animal studies have demonstrated that HPβCD treatment leads to a significant reduction in the number of cholesterol crystals per unit area in retinal tissues, which is strongly correlated with improvements in retinal lipid processing and decreased inflammatory responses mediated by macrophage and microglial activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Third, in laboratory assays using RPE cell cultures, one would expect to observe a decrease in the proportion of lipid-laden lysosomes, accompanied by measurable improvements in lysosomal acidification—parameters that serve as surrogate markers for enhanced autophagic capacity. Additionally, given the evidence that HPβCD can cross the blood–retina barrier when administered via systemic routes, there is a strong rationale for expecting that appropriate dosing regimens will yield sufficient retinal tissue concentrations to exert these beneficial effects (El-Darzi et al., 2023). Ultimately, these molecular and cellular changes are anticipated to culminate in the reduction of drusen lipid volumes, thereby slowing or potentially halting the progression of dry AMD (El-Darzi et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of HPβCD for the treatment of dry AMD is underpinned by a robust mechanistic rationale, a substantial preclinical history, and an acceptable clinical safety profile observed in other indications. One of the greatest strengths of HPβCD is its dual functionality: the ability to form effective inclusion complexes with cholesterol and the resultant improvement in lysosomal function. In several animal models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD has yielded promising results by lowering total, unesterified, and esterified cholesterol levels, reducing the number of cholesterol crystals, and mitigating inflammatory responses in the retina (El-Darzi et al., 2023). These data provide a compelling basis for its evaluation in conditions such as dry AMD where drusen formation is closely linked to aberrant cholesterol metabolism. Furthermore, its prior use in the treatment of NPC—a condition that shares certain pathogenic features with AMD in terms of lysosomal dysfunction—adds credence to the hypothesis that HPβCD may exert similar therapeutic effects in RPE cells (Calias, 2018).

A significant advantage of HPβCD is its established safety record in clinical studies for NPC. Although challenges remain regarding optimal dosing—especially given the compound’s limited ability to cross the BBB when administered systemically—the retinal application appears more favorable, as preclinical studies suggest that HPβCD is capable of traversing the blood–retina barrier and achieving therapeutic concentrations in retinal tissues (El-Darzi et al., 2023). However, it should be noted that the safety profile in the context of chronic ocular exposure remains to be fully characterized. Notably, clinical studies in NPC have observed adverse effects such as hearing loss with certain routes of administration, and while these effects may not directly translate to ocular toxicity, rigorous ocular safety studies will be essential to ensure that any repurposing for dry AMD is both efficacious and safe (Calias, 2018).

Another potential strength lies in the specificity of the lipid‐targeting strategy. Unlike therapies that broadly modulate inflammatory or oxidative stress pathways, HPβCD acts directly on the cholesterol burden—the underlying driver of drusen lipid accumulation in dry AMD. This mechanistic specificity has the potential to result in a more direct impact on the disease process, rather than merely modifying secondary symptoms. Mechanistically, the extraction of cholesterol by HPβCD is anticipated to restore the lipid environment within RPE lysosomal membranes, thereby re-enabling the proper assembly of v-ATPase complexes. This, in turn, can lead to improved lysosomal acidification, enhanced cathepsin D activity, and accelerated autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—a cascade of events that would address one of the root causes of retinal degeneration in AMD (Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and uncertainties must be acknowledged. First, while the preclinical data in animal models are promising, there remains a lack of clinical trial data specifically focusing on the use of HPβCD in dry AMD. A search using the relevant keywords indicates a paucity of clinical evidence in this particular indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.), which means that translational hurdles remain before HPβCD can be confidently recommended for dry AMD therapy. Second, although the mechanism by which HPβCD affects v-ATPase assembly and CTSD activity is supported by data in neuronal models, direct evidence of these molecular events in RPE cells is still emerging, leaving some uncertainty regarding the depth of its effects on lysosomal autophagy in the retinal environment (Nociari et al., 2017). Third, formulation and administration routes will be critical considerations. While systemic dosing has been used in other indications, the optimal approach for targeting the retina might require localized delivery techniques—such as intravitreal injection or the development of a sustained-release ocular formulation—to maximize retinal exposure while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target effects. Finally, the potential for adverse events, particularly those related to over-extraction of cholesterol or unintended disruption of lipid homeostasis, must be carefully evaluated in the context of chronic ocular treatment.

In summary, HPβCD is a well-characterized compound with a history of successful application in disorders of cholesterol accumulation, notably NPC. Its ability to extract cholesterol from cellular membranes, restore lipid microdomains, and thereby normalize lysosomal function forms a strong mechanistic basis for its evaluation as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models provide encouraging evidence that HPβCD can reduce retinal cholesterol accumulation, lower the number of cholesterol crystals, and improve markers of lysosomal function in retinal tissues. This directly aligns with the therapeutic hypothesis that the mobilization of cholesterol from RPE lysosomal membranes will restore v-ATPase activity, normalize lysosomal pH, enhance cathepsin D activity, and ultimately reduce the drusen lipid burden characteristic of dry AMD (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).

However, the translation of these preclinical findings into a clinically effective therapy for dry AMD will require addressing several critical challenges. These include the absence of direct clinical data in AMD, the need for detailed mechanistic studies in RPE cells to confirm that the cholesterol-lowering effects observed in other tissues are recapitulated in the retina, and the optimization of dosing and delivery methods to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are achieved safely in the target tissue. Additionally, any potential side effects—such as those noted in NPC patients, including auditory toxicity—must be rigorously monitored in ocular studies to ensure that treatment remains safe over the long term (Calias, 2018).

Overall, the repurposing of HPβCD for dry AMD is scientifically compelling due to its targeted mechanism of action and its established clinical history in related indications. Its ability to mobilize cholesterol and restore lysosomal function addresses fundamental pathogenic processes implicated in dry AMD, and the preclinical evidence supports its potential efficacy. Nevertheless, the absence of clinical trials in this particular indication, combined with uncertainties regarding the precise molecular interactions in RPE cells and the optimization of drug delivery to the retina, suggests that further preclinical and early-stage clinical studies are warranted before HPβCD can be advanced as a treatment for dry AMD. Continued research should focus on elucidating the detailed molecular mechanisms within RPE cells, assessing long-term safety in ocular models, and exploring various delivery modalities to maximize efficacy while minimizing potential risks. In conclusion, while HPβCD demonstrates substantial promise as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, a measured, stepwise approach in future research is essential to address outstanding questions and to establish its full therapeutic potential (Calias, 2018; El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017; Roney, 2020).
