Proposal for Torin2 (Selleckchem S2813)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Torin2 is a synthetic, second-generation ATP-competitive inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase designed to inhibit both mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and complex 2 (mTORC2) with high potency and favorable pharmacodynamic properties compared to first-generation allosteric mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin/rapalogs) and earlier catalytic mTOR kinase inhibitors (TORKi) such as PP242 and AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Chemically optimized by structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts, Torin2 exhibits rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates S6K1 (T389) and 4E-BP1 (T37/46) including rapamycin-insensitive sites, and of the mTORC2 substrate Akt (S473), reflecting dual-complex inhibition that is superior to rapamycin’s mTORC1-limited activity (with incomplete suppression of 4E-BP1) (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). In head-to-head comparisons with other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors, Torin2 maintains stronger and more sustained suppression of mTORC1/2 signaling after drug washout, attributable to its slow off-rate, with durable pathway inhibition persisting for approximately four hours in cellular assays, contrasting with rapid recovery observed with PP242 and shorter-duration suppression by AZD8055 (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). Torin2 is highly selective for mTOR over PI3K (>800-fold) and shows approximately 100-fold selectivity over the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR; these latter off-targets remain relevant at higher concentrations and inform safety margins and dose selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 9–10).

Mechanistically, Torin2 robustly induces autophagy across multiple cell lines (e.g., LC3-II accumulation, acridine-orange–positive acidic vesicle formation), consistent with its potent inhibition of mTORC1, a master negative regulator of autophagy initiation and flux (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9). As a drug class, ATP-competitive TORKi have been widely investigated in oncology and proliferative diseases given their ability to fully suppress both mTOR complexes, thereby impacting protein synthesis, cell-cycle progression, metabolism, and survival signaling (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10). Outside oncology, dual mTORC1/2 inhibition has demonstrated disease-modifying potential in organ systems where mTOR hyperactivation drives pathology; for example, Torin2 reduced S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation and curtailed cyst burden in a mouse model of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with efficacy comparable to sirolimus and a potentially more favorable side-effect profile (Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7).

In the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), dysregulated mTOR signaling (particularly chronic mTORC1 activation with age) is strongly implicated in degradative/clearance failure, lysosomal dysfunction, metabolic reprogramming, and structural degeneration that recapitulate key features of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including lipid-rich subretinal deposits and RPE dedifferentiation (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13; Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). RPE expresses and functionally engages both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, providing a mechanistic rationale for evaluating dual-complex catalytic inhibitors like Torin2 as therapeutic candidates to correct core pathogenic processes in dry AMD (Intartaglia et al., 2022, pp. 15–17).

Therapeutic History  
The mTOR pathway has been studied extensively in retinal and RPE biology, with strong preclinical evidence linking mTOR hyperactivation to RPE degeneration and dry AMD-like pathology, and corresponding benefits from mTOR inhibition; however, direct ocular data with Torin2 itself are currently lacking and must be extrapolated from pharmacology in other tissues and from surrogates (Torin1, PP242, INK-128/MLN0128) and rapamycin (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–10; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Genetic and pharmacologic mTOR activation in RPE induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suppresses autophagy, disrupts metabolism, and yields an AMD-like phenotype; in a knock-in model that overexpresses mLST8 (a core mTORC component) in RPE, both mTORC1 and mTORC2 are upregulated, and dual-complex inhibition with TORIN1 (a TORKi closely related to Torin2) normalized signaling and restored autophagy and RPE function in vitro, including rescue of autophagy regulators Atg9b and Atg7 and recovery of autophagy flux (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13). These data directly support the therapeutic relevance of dual mTORC1/2 inhibition in RPE conditions that model early AMD pathogenesis (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–13).

In a complementary RPE disease model focused on amyloid-β (Aβ)-induced lysosomal/autophagy impairment—a pathology linked to dry AMD—Torin (a first-generation mTOR inhibitor in this study; not explicitly Torin2) restored lysosomal activity via LAMP2 activation, corrected p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, facilitated Aβ aggregate clearance, and ameliorated Aβ-driven tight junction disruption in vitro and in Aβ-challenged mouse RPE in vivo, directly addressing the barrier degradation and clearance deficits central to AMD (Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2). In multiple RPE cell systems modeling autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation and lipofuscinogenesis after photoreceptor outer segment (POS) challenge, mTOR inhibition (rapamycin; INK-128) decreased AFG load by approximately 30% and activated a TFEB-dependent lysosome biogenesis program; these effects required intact lysosomal proteases/lipases and were associated with LAMP1 upregulation and GADD34 induction, supporting the concept that mTOR→TFEB pathway modulation can restore lysosomal clearance in RPE (albeit these studies were preprints and should be interpreted accordingly) (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 10–18). Constitutively active TFEB dramatically reduced POS-dependent AFGs in preventive and resolving paradigms, further validating TFEB activation as a mechanistic goal for pharmacologic mTOR inhibition in early AMD models (Falcão et al., 2024, pp. 1–6, 13–18).

In genetic models where RPE mTORC1 is hyperactivated through Tsc1 deletion, chronic mTORC1 activity causes progressive RPE degeneration, lipid accumulation, and subretinal drusenoid deposits, and rapamycin treatment restored RPE markers (e.g., RPE65), improved ERG responses, and partially normalized metabolomic derangements, providing in vivo proof-of-concept that mTOR pathway suppression improves RPE structure and function in AMD-like degeneration (Huang et al., 2019, pp. 1–2, 7–9; Zhao et al., 2011, pp. 10–11). At a mechanistic level, age-driven increases in lysosome mass and mTORC1 docking in RPE create a vicious cycle of mTORC1 hyperactivation that impairs phagolysosomal function, promotes lipogenesis, suppresses lipolysis, and degrades autophagy, converging on classic dry AMD phenotypes; mTOR inhibition breaks this cycle and restores degradative capacity (Go et al., 2020, pp. 1–3, 11–13).

Beyond ocular systems, Torin2 has been used preclinically in oncology and in non-ocular degenerative models; its dual mTORC1/2 suppression, sustained pharmacodynamics, and autophagy induction underlie anti-proliferative activity and apoptosis in cancer models, while in an ADPKD model Torin2 demonstrated pathway inhibition with efficacy comparable to sirolimus, suggesting that torin-class agents may be tolerable with appropriate dose and schedule selection (Liu et al., 2013, pp. 7–9; Holditch et al., 2019, pp. 6–7). Notably, second-generation mTOR inhibitors can be cytotoxic in RPE due to potent mTORC2 suppression with downstream Akt inhibition, a survival pathway for metabolically stressed RPE; this risk emphasizes the importance of dose titration and local ocular delivery strategies for Torin2 in AMD (Huang et al., 2018, pp. 7–8).

To our knowledge, Torin2 has not been reported in clinical trials for dry AMD or directly tested in RPE/retinal models in vivo; however, the strength of the translational prior—mTOR hyperactivation as a convergent mechanism in RPE degeneration; rescue with catalytic mTOR inhibitors such as TORIN1; and reversible ALP defects with Torin-class inhibition—warrants rigorous preclinical testing of Torin2 in dry AMD-relevant models (Chowdhury et al., 2025, pp. 1–2, 8–11; Jo et al., 2023, pp. 1–2).

Proposal for Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN; Sigma N3501)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is an endogenous intermediate in the mammalian NAD⁺ salvage pathway, generated by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM) and 5-phosphoribosyl‐1‐pyrophosphate (PRPP) and converted to NAD⁺ by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN belongs to the vitamin B3–derived NAD⁺ precursor class and is one of several precursors (others include nicotinamide [NAM], nicotinic acid [NA], and nicotinamide riboside [NR]) used to augment cellular NAD⁺ pools in aging and disease (Cimaglia et al., 2020). NMN was prioritized as a practical intervention because direct NAD⁺ delivery to tissues is not straightforward, whereas in vivo administration of NMN elevates tissue NAD⁺ and supports mitochondrial function and cellular stress defenses in multiple systems (Ebeling et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Transport and uptake mechanisms include the Slc12a8 transporter described in mouse small intestine, as well as extracellular dephosphorylation to NR followed by NR uptake via equilibrative nucleoside transporters; intracellular NR is re‐phosphorylated by NRK1 to NMN for resynthesis of NAD⁺ (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Rahman et al., 2024). Notably for RPE models, ARPE‐19 cells have been reported to express transporters supporting NMN uptake but not NR uptake, favoring NMN over NR in this system (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In RPE and retinal contexts, NMN and related precursors have been deployed preclinically to restore NAD⁺, improve mitochondrial function, modulate sirtuin‐dependent pathways, and mitigate features of neurodegeneration and cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ebeling et al., 2020; Lin, 2020).

Therapeutic History  
NAD⁺ decline with age is conserved across tissues, including the retina and RPE, and is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial function, heightened oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to degeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020). In the outer retina, rod‐ or cone‐specific Nampt deletion produces NAD⁺ deficiency and photoreceptor degeneration; systemic NMN at 150 mg/kg i.p. restored retinal function by ERG and preserved photoreceptor structure, establishing that exogenous NMN can replenish retinal NAD⁺ and mitigate degeneration linked to impaired salvage (Lin, 2020). NMN also protected in models of acute retinal injury: daily systemic NMN reduced photoreceptor death and oxidative stress after retinal detachment and increased retinal SIRT1 and HO‐1, consistent with NAD⁺‐dependent sirtuin activation in vivo (Chen et al., 2020). In ischemia models, NMN administration protected against retinal dysfunction (Lee et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024). In a cholesterol efflux–deficient murine model that recapitulates key dry AMD features driven by senescent subretinal macrophages (Abca1/g1‐deficient), systemic NMN reduced subretinal drusenoid deposits (SDDs), decreased lipofuscin‐positive macrophage burden, and improved electrophysiological and structural endpoints, supporting a role for NAD⁺ augmentation in reversing senescence‐driven outer retinal pathology in vivo (Terao et al., 2024). In RPE‐directed models, pharmacologic NAMPT inhibition with FK866 is widely used to mimic age‐related NAD⁺ decline; in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, NMN co‐treatment preserved NAD⁺, SIRT1 protein, viability, and reduced senescence markers, and in vivo systemic NMN preserved RPE NAD⁺ and SIRT1 after subretinal FK866 (Jadeja et al., 2018). Oxidant injury with sodium iodate (NaIO₃) induced RPE senescence, NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and subretinal inflammation; NMN restored RPE NAD⁺, reduced DNA damage and senescence markers, improved mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP in ARPE‐19, and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment in vivo, with intact Sirt1 signaling required for NMN benefit (Ren et al., 2022). Outside strictly RPE biology, NMN improved RPE phagocytosis and mitochondrial ultrastructure in the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration, with a mechanistic link to a NAD⁺/GAPDH axis that modulated actin/cytoskeletal phagocytosis machinery in RPE; GAPDH knockdown abrogated NMN’s benefits, supporting a causal chain from NAD⁺ repletion to enhanced RPE POS clearance via GAPDH‐dependent pathways (Zhang et al., 2024).

Clinical translation of NAD⁺ precursors has begun with nicotinamide and NR in ophthalmology-adjacent indications (e.g., glaucoma), demonstrating tolerability and retinal functional protection in mice, and documenting NAD⁺ elevation in adult humans, but direct clinical data for NMN in dry AMD are not available in the provided context (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Long-term NMN treatment in mice mitigated age-associated physiological decline systemically and reportedly ameliorated eye function, but detailed ocular pharmacology and human NMN ocular safety are not established here (Rahman et al., 2024). Collectively, the preclinical record supports NMN as an NAD⁺ augmenting therapy with demonstrated efficacy in retina and RPE-relevant models of NAD⁺ deficiency, oxidative injury, and senescence; however, there is no direct published clinical trial evidence in dry AMD patients in this context set (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Core biochemistry  
- NAD⁺ salvage. In mammalian cells, the salvage pathway supplies most NAD⁺ (~80%), with NAMPT catalyzing NAM → NMN and NMNAT1–3 completing NMN → NAD⁺; this pool fuels redox reactions and serves as substrate for NAD⁺‐consuming enzymes including sirtuins, PARPs, and the NAD glycohydrolase CD38 (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAMPT-mediated biosynthesis is essential for vision, and its decline in RPE with age causally links to reduced NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 expression/activity, and enhanced cellular senescence (Jadeja et al., 2018).  
- Uptake and intracellular handling. NMN can enter cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 shown in mouse gut) and/or after extracellular dephosphorylation to NR with re-phosphorylation by NRK1, routes that are cell type–dependent; ARPE-19 preferentially transport NMN in vitro, supporting the choice of NMN over NR in these RPE models (Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Rahman et al., 2024).

Downstream signaling nodes relevant to RPE and dry AMD  
- Sirtuins. NAD⁺ is an obligate co-substrate for sirtuins; increased NAD⁺ drives sirtuin deacetylase/deacylase activities across SIRT1–7 with consequences for mitochondrial function, antioxidant defenses, DNA repair, and autophagy/mitophagy (Cimaglia et al., 2020). In aging RPE, NAD⁺ and SIRT1 decline in parallel; restoring NAD⁺ with NMN rescues SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo, and reduces senescence markers p16^INK4a and p21^Waf/Cip1 (Jadeja et al., 2018). SIRT3, the mitochondrial sirtuin, maintains mitochondrial integrity by deacetylating and activating SOD2 and coordinating antioxidant responses, mitophagy, and UPR^mt; retinal NAD⁺ deficiency impairs SIRT3, linking NAD⁺ loss to mitochondrial vulnerability (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In a retinal detachment model, systemic NMN increased SIRT1 protein and HO‐1, with mechanistic in vitro data supporting a SIRT1 → HO‐1 protective axis (Chen et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and NAMPT/SIRT1 crosstalk. AMPK upregulates NAMPT expression and thus supports NAD⁺ salvage; reciprocally, SIRT1 deacetylates/stabilizes LKB1 to activate AMPK, forming a positive feedback loop that coordinates energy sensing and catabolic responses (Luján et al., 2022). In RPE senescence induced by NaIO₃, AMPK activation occurs downstream of ATP depletion and is modulated by NMN treatment, though overactivation of Sirt1 by a direct agonist (SRT1720) produced mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, arguing for physiological NAD⁺‐driven Sirt1 activation rather than pharmacologic overdrive (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy/mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. SIRT1 promotes autophagosome formation and Rab7‐dependent autophagosome–lysosome fusion; together with AMPK, it enhances expression of mitophagy effectors (PINK1, Parkin) and co-activates PGC‐1α to drive mitochondrial biogenesis programs via transcriptional partners (NRF‐1, ERRα, PPARα) (Luján et al., 2022). Reviews and preclinical observations indicate that NAD⁺ repletion can restore mitophagy, activate UPR^mt, and normalize mitochondrial metabolic profiles, including evidence that “NAD⁺ inhibits the metabolic reprogramming of RPE cells in early AMD by upregulating mitophagy,” supporting the hypothesis that NMN-driven NAD⁺ gain could favorably reprogram RPE mitochondrial quality control (Rahman et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function in vitro; the same study used mitophagy reporter assays (mKeima-mito), underscoring the feasibility of measuring NMN’s effects on mitophagy in human RPE although specific NMN → mitophagy data were not detailed in the excerpt (Fisher et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- PARP and CD38 as NAD⁺ sinks. DNA damage and SASP/inflammation drive PARP and CD38 activities that deplete NAD⁺; CD38 in particular contributes to age-related NAD⁺ decline and mitochondrial dysfunction and is induced by LXR signaling and SASP, creating a self-reinforcing senescence–NAD⁺ depletion loop (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Terao et al., 2024). In photoreceptor cells, PARP inhibition partially rescues viability under NAMPT inhibition, highlighting the vulnerability of NAD⁺ pools to consumption pathways and the value of reducing NAD⁺ sinks in parallel with NMN supplementation (Lin & Apte, 2018).  
- Inflammation and inflammasome. NAD⁺ augmentation via NMN or increased NAMPT/NAD⁺ can reduce NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 via a SIRT1‐dependent mechanism in RPE aging models, pointing to anti‐inflammatory benefits of the NAMPT/NAD⁺/SIRT1 axis (Wu et al., 2021). In the Abca1/g1 macrophage senescence model of dry AMD, NAD⁺ repletion (NMN or CD38 inhibition) eliminated senescent macrophages and reversed drusenoid pathology and RPE functional deficits, extending the anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory reach of NAD⁺ augmentation to subretinal immune cells central to AMD pathobiology (Terao et al., 2024).

Critically, although TFEB (a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis) and lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D (CTSD) are highly relevant to RPE oxidative‐debris clearance in dry AMD, the provided literature does not demonstrate direct NMN‐induced TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, or increased CTSD activity in RPE or retina; these remain plausible but unproven links in this context set (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectations in RPE models of dry AMD  
- NAD⁺ repletion in RPE. In ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with NMN restores cellular NAD⁺ reduced by NAMPT inhibition, with partial to robust recovery depending on media and dosing; in ARPE‐19, FK866 sharply lowers NAD⁺/NADH and ATP, while NMN rescues both metrics and normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis balance measured by Seahorse assays (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c). ARPE‐19 cells express NMN but not NR transporters, predicting superior uptake and intracellular conversion for NMN in this model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b). In NaIO₃‐stressed ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM NMN restored NAD⁺, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, reduced ROS and DNA damage, and reduced senescence markers, with Sirt1 activity required for these benefits (Ren et al., 2022).  
- Sirtuin engagement. In FK866‐inhibited RPE, NMN co‐treatment restored SIRT1 protein and activity in vitro and in vivo; in photoreceptor injury, NMN increased retinal SIRT1 and induced HO-1, suggesting a SIRT1‐dependent antioxidant arm (Jadeja et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020). In primary AMD donor RPE, NMN improved mitochondrial function, consistent with engagement of mitochondrial sirtuins and/or PGC-1α programs, though specific sirtuin readouts were not reported in that excerpt (Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- AMPK and mitophagy. AMPK will be sensitive to changes in ATP/AMP driven by mitochondrial recovery after NMN; in RPE senescence models, AMPK activation was observed under oxidant injury and modulated by NMN, and the NAD⁺/Sirt1/AMPK network is positioned to restore mitophagy via ULK1 activation, mTORC1 attenuation, and PINK1/Parkin induction (Ren et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022). The hypothesis that NAD⁺ supplementation restores RPE metabolic dysfunction by inducing mitophagy is supported conceptually and by limited preclinical data cited for NAD⁺ effects on RPE mitophagy, making mitophagy flux (e.g., mKeima‐mito) a reasonable expected readout under NMN treatment (Jadeja et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022).  
- Autophagy-lysosome system and debris clearance. TFEB governs lysosomal biogenesis and function and is a rational target in dry AMD; Sirt1 and AMPK facilitate autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7) and thus could secondarily enhance lysosomal throughput after NMN (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022). However, direct evidence that NMN increases lysosomal number, lysosomal acidification, TFEB nuclear translocation, or CTSD activity in RPE is not provided here; these are testable but as yet unvalidated expectations (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a). By contrast, NMN increased RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and restored actin‐mediated phagocytic machinery in vivo in the RCS rat, revealing a complementary route by which NMN could improve outer segment turnover independent of direct TFEB activation (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Anti‐senescence and anti‐inflammatory effects. In RPE and subretinal myeloid cells, NMN suppresses senescence phenotypes and reduces inflammatory mediators, which should reduce SASP‐driven bystander stress on RPE and photoreceptors and may indirectly lower CD38‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion in the subretinal compartment (Jadeja et al., 2018; Terao et al., 2024).

Collectively, in an RPE assay aligned to dry AMD pathophysiology, NMN is expected to: (1) restore NAD⁺ and ATP; (2) engage Sirt1/Sirt3 and normalize mitochondrial function; (3) reduce senescence and inflammatory signaling; and (4) enhance POS phagocytosis via cytoskeletal machinery, with plausible but unproven enhancement of lysosomal biogenesis/function via Sirt1/AMPK-mediated autophagy pathways and TFEB cross-talk (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022).

Assay design notes  
- Use ARPE‐19 and primary human RPE including AMD donor–derived cultures for translational relevance; confirm NMN uptake advantages versus NR in each model (Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Quantify NAD⁺ by enzymatic assay, SIRT1 activity fluorometrically, mitochondrial ATP production via Seahorse ATP rate assay, and senescence markers (SA‐β‐gal, p16, p21) per established protocols (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b).  
- Test TFEB nuclear translocation (immunocytochemistry), lysosomal mass (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor/LysoTracker), and cathepsin D maturation/activity explicitly, recognizing these endpoints are not yet shown for NMN in RPE (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Assay mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), PINK1/Parkin expression, and autophagosome–lysosome fusion (LC3‐II, p62, Rab7 localization) (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Measure RPE phagocytosis of POS and handling of phototoxic bisretinoids/lipofuscin surrogates to capture clearance outcomes (Zhang et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease‐mechanism alignment. Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance, and chronic para‐inflammation; age‐associated NAD⁺ decline in RPE and retina connects this pathobiology to a targetable metabolic axis (NAMPT/NAD⁺), and restoring NAD⁺ is causally protective in multiple retinal models (Jadeja et al., 2018; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Lin, 2020). In vitro and in vivo, NMN replenishes NAD⁺ in RPE and retina, rescues SIRT1 and mitochondrial function, and reduces senescence and inflammation—key drivers of RPE failure in dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020).  
- Direct RPE benefits with functional readouts. Under NAMPT inhibition and oxidant stress, NMN restores NAD⁺/ATP, normalizes OXPHOS/glycolysis, rescues RPE gene expression, lowers ROS and DNA damage, and blunts senescence markers; in RCS rats, NMN enhances RPE POS phagocytosis through a NAD⁺/GAPDH-actin axis (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Reversal of senescence-driven dry AMD phenotypes in vivo. In the Abca1/g1 model where subretinal macrophage senescence drives SDDs and RPE dysfunction, NAD⁺ augmentation by NMN reduces SDDs, lipofuscin‐positive macrophages, and functional/structural pathology, demonstrating disease‐relevant efficacy in a model that captures hallmark dry AMD features (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Mechanistic tractability and biomarkerability. The NAMPT/NMN → NAD⁺ → sirtuin/AMPK network is well studied and offers clear pharmacodynamic biomarkers (NAD⁺ levels, SIRT1 activity, mitochondrial respiration) and pathophysiological readouts (senescence markers, mitophagy flux), supporting a high‐confidence translational path (Jadeja et al., 2018; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- RPE uptake feasibility. ARPE‐19 transport NMN but not NR, favoring NMN for in vitro RPE work; broader literature identifies NMN transport and NR conversion pathways that together ensure NMN bioavailability in ocular cell types (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020a).

Limitations and risks  
- TFEB/lysosome claims remain unproven for NMN in RPE. While TFEB‐driven lysosomal biogenesis/function is a compelling therapeutic target in dry AMD, direct evidence that NMN activates TFEB, increases lysosomal number/acidification, or enhances cathepsin D activity in RPE is not present in the provided literature; these are critical, testable hypotheses that should not be presupposed in development plans (Falcão et al., 2025; Will‐Orrego, 2020a; Ebeling et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).  
- Context‐dependent AMPK/Sirt1 dynamics. In NaIO₃‐induced RPE senescence, AMPK activation accompanied ATP loss and was suppressed upon NMN treatment; further, pharmacologic Sirt1 overactivation caused mitochondrial hyperfusion and stress signaling, underscoring that pathway set points matter and that NMN’s benefits likely hinge on physiologic tuning rather than maximal activation (Ren et al., 2022). This complexity argues for careful titration of NMN exposure and for avoiding assumptions about AMPK activation being uniformly beneficial in all RPE contexts.  
- Model caveats. ARPE‐19 harbor genomic abnormalities and do not recapitulate all RPE functions (e.g., missing RPE65), and media composition strongly modulates metabolic readouts; corroboration in primary human RPE (including AMD donors) and in vivo models is essential (Will‐Orrego, 2020c; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Target competition with NAD⁺ sinks. PARPs and CD38 can drain NAD⁺; in photoreceptors and macrophages these sinks materially influence disease, suggesting that combining NMN with PARP/CD38 modulation may be superior to NMN alone in some settings, and that patient subgroups with high NAD⁺ consumption (e.g., inflammatory phenotypes) may require tailored strategies (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024).  
- Translation and clinical data gaps. Although nicotinamide and NR have human safety/PK data, direct human ocular PK/PD and safety data for NMN are limited here, and no clinical testing in dry AMD is documented in the provided sources (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2024). Dosing translation must reconcile effective rodent exposures (150–1,000 mg/kg/day in various models) with human tolerability and ocular exposure (Lin, 2020; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024).

Program implications and next steps  
- Mechanistic validation in RPE. Prioritize experiments that directly test the unproven parts of the hypothesis: TFEB activation (nuclear translocation), lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1/2), acidification (LysoSensor), and cathepsin D maturation/activity after NMN in primary human RPE from AMD and non‐AMD donors, and in iPSC‐RPE, with parallel readouts of NAD⁺, SIRT1, SIRT3, and AMPK (Falcão et al., 2025; Ebeling et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk. Quantify mitophagy flux (mKeima‐mito), autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Rab7 co‐localization), and PINK1/Parkin dynamics under NMN, leveraging assays already applied in AMD donor RPE studies (Fisher et al., 2022; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Functional clearance endpoints. Test NMN effects on RPE POS phagocytosis, lipofuscin/bisretinoid handling, and oxidative debris clearance in vitro and in vivo, building on the strong RCS rat evidence for NMN‐mediated enhancement of RPE phagocytosis via a GAPDH‐actin mechanism (Zhang et al., 2024).  
- Inflammation and senescence. Extend evaluation to subretinal macrophage phenotypes and SASP factors in RPE–macrophage co‐culture and in vivo, given NMN’s ability to eliminate senescent macrophages and reverse SDDs in the Abca1/g1 model (Terao et al., 2024).  
- Dosing/PD strategy. Calibrate NMN dose–response carefully: in ARPE‐19 and primary RPE, co‐treatment with 0.05–1.0 mM NMN rescued FK866‐induced NAD⁺ loss within 72 h, while NMN alone did not elevate ATP above baseline; in NaIO₃ ARPE‐19, 800–1,000 µM was required to adequately restore NAD⁺ (Jadeja et al., 2018; Will‐Orrego, 2020b; Ren et al., 2022). In vivo, effective rodent doses ranged from 150 mg/kg i.p. to 1,000 mg/kg oral depending on model and endpoint (Lin, 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Engage PK/PD modeling to bridge to human‐equivalent dosing and to support ocular exposure.  
- Combination hypotheses. Consider rational combinations with PARP inhibition (to reduce NAD⁺ consumption) or CD38 inhibition in inflammatory phenotypes, consistent with partial rescue by PARP inhibitors in NAMPT‐deficient contexts and CD38’s role in macrophage senescence (Lin & Apte, 2018; Terao et al., 2024). Also consider pairing with agents that more directly activate TFEB where justified, while monitoring for unintended mTORC1 perturbations (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
NMN is a biologically credible and mechanistically tractable candidate for dry AMD focused on RPE rescue through NAD⁺ repletion and sirtuin‐centric mitochondrial restoration, with strong preclinical support in RPE senescence, oxidant injury, and phagocytosis assays, and compelling in vivo evidence in retinal injury and senescence‐driven dry‐AMD–like pathology (Jadeja et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Terao et al., 2024). The hypothesized downstream impacts on TFEB, lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and cathepsin D activity are plausible given the Sirt1/AMPK/autophagy network architecture but remain unvalidated in RPE after NMN and should be explicitly de‐risked experimentally before clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2025; Luján et al., 2022; Ebeling et al., 2020). Strengths include a coherent disease‐mechanism target, measurable PD, multi‐compartment benefits (RPE, photoreceptors, subretinal macrophages), and favorable uptake in RPE models; weaknesses include reliance on models with limitations, the need to control for NAD⁺ sinks and pathway set points, and gaps in lysosome‐specific mechanistic evidence and human ocular PK/PD (Will‐Orrego, 2020b, 2020c; Lin & Apte, 2018; Rahman et al., 2024). Overall, NMN merits advancement to a rigorous preclinical validation package focused on lysosome‐mitophagy endpoints in primary human RPE and AMD‐relevant in vivo models, with a translational plan that integrates mitochondrial function, senescence/inflammation control, and debris clearance readouts as co‐primary pharmacology objectives (Ebeling et al., 2020; Fisher et al., 2022; Terao et al., 2024).

Proposal for Temsirolimus (Torisel; Pfizer)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Temsirolimus (CCI-779; Torisel) is a semi-synthetic ester prodrug of sirolimus (rapamycin) discovered during rapamycin medicinal chemistry optimization to improve formulation properties and pharmacokinetics; it is a first-generation “rapalog” that inhibits mTOR by forming an intracellular complex with FKBP12 and binding the FRB domain of mTOR, thereby allosterically inhibiting mTORC1 catalytic signaling (and only indirectly affecting mTORC2) (Wang et al., 2022). As a class, rapalogs are derived from the natural macrolide rapamycin originally isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus; they have been used systemically as immunosuppressants and anti-proliferative/anti-angiogenic agents in oncology and transplant medicine by suppressing mTORC1-dependent growth and inflammatory programs (Wang et al., 2022; Johnson, 2013). mTORC1 is a lysosome-proximal signaling hub that integrates amino acid sufficiency via the Ragulator–Rag GTPase machinery and growth/energy signals via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating anabolism (protein synthesis via S6K and 4E-BP1), and repressing catabolism (autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis) (Johnson, 2013). In ocular biology, temsirolimus has been evaluated preclinically in human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), consistently demonstrating dose-dependent inhibition of proliferation and migration and decreased VEGF/PDGF expression through mTOR pathway inhibition, supporting target engagement in retinal cell types relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Liegl et al., 2014). Compared with rapamycin, temsirolimus has higher aqueous solubility and stability but is administered intravenously in approved oncology indications; adverse events include metabolic and mucosal toxicities typical of systemic mTOR inhibition (Wang et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Rapamycin/sirolimus and rapalogs have a long clinical history across transplantation and oncology; in ophthalmology, mechanistic and translational work has targeted mTOR for AMD and other retinal diseases because mTORC1 suppresses autophagy/lysosomal programs and promotes inflammatory and angiogenic signaling (Wang et al., 2022; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). In RPE models that recapitulate daily phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), mTORC1 activity is dynamically regulated: POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1, followed by inhibition during phagosome maturation; however, in aged RPE and AMD, mTORC1 activity is relatively elevated and TFEB is retained in the phosphorylated cytosolic state, impairing lysosomal responses and favoring lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granule (AFG) accumulation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025). In these systems, rapamycin reduces POS-dependent AFGs by about 30% while increasing TFEB activity and lysosomal biogenesis markers (e.g., LAMP1) in ARPE-19 and human fetal RPE cells; efficacy generalizes to other mTOR pathway inhibitors (e.g., INK-128), and constitutively active TFEB provides larger effects, supporting a TFEB-centric mechanism (Falcão et al., 2024). These effects require intact lysosomal proteolysis; pharmacologic blockade of lysosomal acid lipase, cathepsin inhibition, or cathepsin D (CTSD) knockout abrogates rapamycin’s benefit, highlighting a dependence on functional lysosomes (Falcão et al., 2024). Although these data do not directly test temsirolimus in lysosome-TFEB endpoints, temsirolimus is mechanistically a rapalog mTORC1 inhibitor, and in RPE it engages mTOR biology by suppressing growth factor signaling outputs (VEGF/PDGF) and cell motility/proliferation, thereby validating target engagement in the relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).

Clinically, multiple sirolimus trials have evaluated mTOR inhibition in geographic atrophy (GA), a late stage of dry AMD, with disappointing outcomes. Subconjunctival sirolimus (440 µg every 3 months for 24 months) in a bilateral-eye, fellow-eye-control study did not slow GA enlargement and was associated with a treatment-associated decrease in visual acuity relative to untreated fellow eyes, despite an acceptable safety profile in that study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; Wang et al., 2022). An intravitreal sirolimus Phase I/II study in bilateral GA was discontinued early, and separate trials reported ocular adverse events including accelerated retinal thinning, abnormal perilesional autofluorescence, and sterile endophthalmitis; overall, no structural or functional benefit was demonstrated across these programs (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2011; Wang et al., 2022). These clinical observations raise concern that chronic mTOR inhibition in established GA may be ineffective or even detrimental, potentially due to disease stage–specific network effects of autophagy and survival signaling in degenerating retina (Wang et al., 2022). In contrast, preclinical data in other retinal contexts (e.g., glaucoma) show neuroprotective correlates of mTOR inhibition, underscoring the context- and stage-dependence of therapeutic effects (Wang et al., 2022). For wet AMD and retinal vascular pathology, temsirolimus (and rapamycin) exert anti-angiogenic actions in vitro and in animal models by downregulating VEGF/PDGF and endothelial proliferation, which are less directly relevant to GA biology but establish ocular pharmacology for the class (Liegl et al., 2014; Johnson, 2013). Drug delivery innovations such as synthetic HDL nanoparticles carrying rapamycin have been explored preclinically to optimize ocular delivery, suggesting format-dependent translatability may be important for this class (Falcão et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Temsirolimus acts as a prototypical rapalog: it binds FKBP12 to form a gain-of-function complex that docks to the FKBP12-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain of mTOR and selectively inhibits mTORC1 signaling; mTORC2 is generally spared acutely, with potential indirect effects chronically depending on cellular context (Wang et al., 2022). mTORC1 normally phosphorylates TFEB on multiple serine residues, retaining it in the cytosol and preventing nuclear entry; when mTORC1 is inhibited, TFEB becomes dephosphorylated, translocates to the nucleus, and drives the CLEAR network that upregulates autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., LAMP1), enhancing degradative capacity and organelle biogenesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024). In RPE cells, POS phagocytosis engages mTORC1 transiently, but aged/AMD RPE exhibit enhanced mTORC1 activity that suppresses appropriate TFEB activation; rapamycin reverses this, promoting TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear entry, GADD34 upregulation, and increased lysosomal mass, collectively reducing AFGs by approximately 30% in POS-challenged RPE (Falcão et al., 2024). The TFEB dependency has been functionally validated via TFEB gain-of-function, which markedly decreases AFGs in both preventive and “therapeutic” paradigms after lipofuscin-like material has already formed (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic relevance to mTOR pathway modulation beyond rapamycin was supported using INK-128 and other mTOR inhibitors, which replicated the AFG reduction and TFEB-lysosome signature (Falcão et al., 2024).

At the biochemical level, mTORC1 integrates amino acid signaling at the lysosomal surface via Ragulator-Rag GTPases and growth/energy cues via Rheb/AMPK, coordinating downstream phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4E-BP1 to activate translation while repressing catabolic programs including initiation of autophagy (partly by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and by blocking TFEB) (Johnson, 2013; Chang et al., 2022). In retinal tissues, mTOR inhibition is expected to relieve brakes on autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis; in diabetic retinopathy models, mTOR inhibition with rapamycin restored impaired lysosomal proteolysis by normalizing cathepsin L activity and autophagic flux, mechanistically consistent with TFEB-driven CLEAR network activation and improved lysosomal protease capacity (Wang et al., 2022). Although direct evidence for temsirolimus effects on RPE TFEB phosphorylation state, lysosomal acidification, or CTSD maturation is not available, the shared mechanism of FKBP12-dependent mTORC1 inhibition and the RPE-cell mTOR engagement demonstrated by temsirolimus (antiproliferative/anti-migratory, VEGF/PDGF suppression) support pathway perturbation in the correct cellular context (Liegl et al., 2014).

In the context of AMD pathophysiology, RPE lysosomal dysfunction and impaired clearance of POS-derived material drive lipofuscin accumulation and downstream toxicity; TFEB has emerged as a master regulator to restore lysosomal capacity, while AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D and L levels/activities, highlighting protease insufficiency as a plausible node of therapeutic rescue (Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, in POS-fed RPE, the rapamycin benefit is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibition or CTSD knockout, indicating that mTORC1 inhibition enhances clearance only when lysosomal protease function is preserved, and suggesting that concomitant strategies to support lysosomal acidification/protease maturation could be synergistic (Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, some reports have suggested low immunoreactivity of mTORC1/2 components in RPE, but this observation contrasts with multiple functional studies demonstrating mTORC1 signaling in RPE during POS handling and aging; taken together, functional responsiveness to mTOR inhibitors in RPE likely depends on model system and detection sensitivity (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
In a POS-pulse/chase AFG assay using ARPE-19 or human fetal RPE, temsirolimus is expected to inhibit mTORC1 (decreased pS6 phosphorylation), dephosphorylate TFEB, increase TFEB nuclear localization, upregulate CLEAR network/lysosomal biogenesis genes (e.g., GADD34, LAMP1), and reduce AFG burden by enhancing degradation of phagocytosed material; this mirrors rapamycin’s effects (~30% AFG reduction) and those of other mTOR inhibitors in these models (Falcão et al., 2024). To confirm on-target activity and pathway alignment, assays should include pS6/S6 and pTFEB/TFEB immunoblotting at 2–24 h, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LAMP1 immunostaining for lysosomal mass, and flow cytometry quantification of AFGs after 24–72 h chase, consistent with established methodologies (Falcão et al., 2024). Because rapamycin’s benefits are abolished by lysosomal protease blockade and in CTSD-deficient backgrounds, temsirolimus-dependent AFG reduction is predicted to require functional cathepsin D and lipases; co-assaying CTSD maturation (pro-/mature CTSD ratio), lysosomal pH, and acid lipase activity is therefore crucial to mechanistic validation (Falcão et al., 2024). In parallel, transcriptomic or targeted RT-qPCR panels for CLEAR genes will validate TFEB program engagement (Falcão et al., 2024).

Regarding lysosomal acidification and protease activity, there is mechanistic plausibility but no direct demonstration that temsirolimus enhances lysosomal pH or CTSD maturation in RPE; nevertheless, the TFEB-centric model predicts improved lysosomal proteostasis, and related retinal models show that mTOR inhibition can restore impaired lysosomal proteolysis (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux, supporting the hypothesis that temsirolimus could favorably influence protease maturation/activity in RPE (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Notably, independent approaches in RPE can acidify lysosomes and reduce AFGs, underscoring the tractability of the acidification axis, though this was not via mTOR inhibition; combining mTORC1-TFEB activation with direct acidification strategies could be additive (Falcão et al., 2024). The expectation for disease modification in GA derives from the idea that sustained enhancement of lysosomal clearance will reduce lipofuscin burden, preserve RPE function, and slow atrophic expansion; however, prior GA trials with sirolimus showed no benefit and potential harm, implying that either the disease stage, delivery/exposure, or network consequences of chronic mTORC1 inhibition negate the anticipated benefit in late disease (Wang et al., 2022).

Temsirolimus target expression and pharmacology in RPE are supported by in vitro data showing dose-dependent inhibition of RPE proliferation and migration and suppression of hypoxia-induced VEGF/PDGF increases without overt cytotoxicity at low micromolar to millimolar nominal concentrations; these endpoints corroborate mTOR pathway engagement in RPE and provide pharmacodynamic markers (e.g., VEGF suppression) that can be measured alongside TFEB-lysosomal readouts in AFG assays (Liegl et al., 2014). The drug class’s ocular delivery options range from systemic dosing (with significant class-typical adverse events) to local delivery; sirolimus trials used subconjunctival or intravitreal administration but encountered safety/tolerability signals including sterile endophthalmitis and accelerated retinal thinning with no efficacy in GA, emphasizing the need for alternative delivery technologies (e.g., nanoparticles) and stage-appropriate patient selection if pursuing this mechanism (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2024). Finally, given AMD donor RPE deficiencies in cathepsins D/L, co-therapies or genetic activation strategies that more directly drive TFEB or augment lysosomal protease capacity could be required to realize the full benefit of mTORC1 inhibition in human disease (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanism-based rationale with cell-type congruence: RPE lysosomal dysfunction is central to AMD, and mTORC1 directly represses TFEB and lysosomal programs; in POS-fed RPE, mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin reduces AFG burden by ~30%, increases lysosomal biogenesis (LAMP1), and requires intact lysosomal proteases, aligning precisely with the hypothesized MoA (Falcão et al., 2024). The effect generalizes across mTOR inhibitors and is amplified by TFEB gain-of-function, strengthening the pathway argument (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Direct evidence that temsirolimus engages mTOR signaling in RPE: temsirolimus suppresses proliferation/migration and reduces VEGF/PDGF in primary human RPE, indicating pharmacodynamic activity and target engagement in the disease-relevant cell type (Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Broad mechanistic plausibility for enhancing lysosomal proteolysis: mTORC1 inhibition activates TFEB; retinal disease models show restoration of lysosomal protease activity (cathepsin L) and autophagic flux with rapamycin, consistent with improved lysosomal proteostasis, which could translate to better CTSD maturation in RPE even though that specific nexus is unproven for temsirolimus (Wang et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Drug class knowledge base and formulation opportunities: extensive class experience informs safety risk assessment; emerging ocular delivery strategies (e.g., sHDL rapamycin nanoparticles) might overcome exposure constraints seen in prior sirolimus GA trials (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative/unsafe clinical precedents in GA with class analog: multiple sirolimus trials in GA failed to slow lesion growth and revealed adverse ocular events, including accelerated retinal thinning and procedure-related sterile endophthalmitis, suggesting either mechanistic inadequacy at late stages, harmful network effects of chronic mTORC1 inhibition, or delivery-related issues; this materially lowers clinical plausibility for GA-stage disease (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Absence of temsirolimus-specific TFEB/lysosome data in RPE: while rapamycin demonstrates TFEB activation, lysosomal biogenesis, and AFG reduction, comparable mechanistic data for temsirolimus in RPE are lacking; the program would therefore carry translatability risk until head-to-head, mechanistic RPE assays confirm TFEB engagement and AFG reduction with temsirolimus (Falcão et al., 2024; Liegl et al., 2014).  
- Dependence on intact lysosomes and proteases: rapamycin’s benefit disappears with lipase inhibition or CTSD deficiency; AMD donor RPE show reduced cathepsin D/L, implying that many patient retinas may not have sufficient residual lysosomal capacity for mTORC1 inhibition alone to succeed without adjuncts that restore acidification/protease maturation (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context and stage dependence of mTOR biology: autophagy upregulation that is protective in early disease can exacerbate neuronal apoptosis in late AMD; cell-type–specific and duration-dependent consequences of mTOR inhibition complicate chronic treatment in GA and may negate benefits or cause harm (Wang et al., 2022).  
- Systemic formulation constraints and ocular delivery safety: temsirolimus is an IV drug with known systemic toxicities; local ocular administration for a chronic indication must overcome prior safety/tolerability issues observed with sirolimus injections while achieving sustained, intraretinal/RPE-targeted exposure (Wang et al., 2022).

Go/No-Go Perspective and Development Recommendations  
- Indication selection: Given the negative GA clinical history with sirolimus, prioritize early/intermediate dry AMD with measurable lipofuscin/AFG burden and residual RPE lysosomal capacity, rather than established GA, where class effects have been neutral or detrimental (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Mechanistic bridging for temsirolimus: Run definitive RPE mechanistic studies comparing temsirolimus to rapamycin and an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor (e.g., INK-128) using POS-pulse/chase AFG assays, pS6/pTFEB readouts, TFEB nuclear localization, LAMP1, lysosomal pH, acid lipase, and CTSD maturation/activity, with rescue and block experiments to confirm TFEB dependence and lysosome-requirement (Falcão et al., 2024).  
- Combination strategies: Evaluate temsirolimus with lysosome-acidifying agents or TFEB-direct activators/gene transfer to overcome the protease dependency bottleneck evident in AMD RPE; mechanistic review suggests dual TFEB/mTOR and NRF2/KEAP1 modulation could be synergistic but requires careful control to avoid oncogenic risk (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Delivery innovation: Avoid frequent intravitreal bolusing; explore sustained-release local delivery or targeted nanoparticles (e.g., sHDL-like) to deliver rapalogs selectively to RPE/retina at sub-toxic exposures, learning from prior sirolimus delivery failures (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).  
- Translational biomarkers: In early clinical exploration, incorporate pharmacodynamic biomarkers of TFEB activation (e.g., aqueous humor proteomics for CLEAR targets, retinal LAMP1 imaging if feasible), structural endpoints sensitive to RPE health (fundus autofluorescence for lipofuscin load), and stringent safety monitoring for retinal thinning and inflammation to detect class-typical adverse signals early (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Bottom line: The TFEB-lysosome rationale is robust at the cellular level in RPE, but the rapalog class has failed to translate benefit in GA; temsirolimus lacks direct RPE TFEB/lysosomal evidence and carries delivery/safety liabilities observed with sirolimus in GA. As a repurposing candidate, temsirolimus merits mechanistic validation in RPE with TFEB/lysosome endpoints and, if positive, a carefully designed, stage-appropriate pilot in early/intermediate dry AMD using optimized delivery; it is not a priority candidate for GA without compelling new mechanistic and translational data that overcome the class’s negative clinical precedent (Falcão et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022).

Proposal for Nicotinamide riboside (NR; ChromaDex Niagen)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR), marketed as ChromaDex Niagen, belongs to the vitamin B3 family and is a naturally occurring precursor of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+). Originally discovered in trace amounts in milk and other food sources, NR has been isolated and subsequently synthesized to yield a high‐purity form for nutritional and pharmaceutical applications. As a member of a class of compounds designed to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, NR has attracted significant attention in the fields of metabolism, aging, and neuroprotection. Its chemical structure—a combination of a nicotinamide moiety bound to ribose—enables it to enter salvage pathways in cells with minimal metabolic conversion losses. In this regard, NR is comparable to other NAD+ boosters such as nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), though differences in bioavailability and cellular transporter expression have been noted in some studies. Preclinical research has documented retinal distribution of NR in rodent models, suggesting that it reaches ocular tissues in pharmacologically relevant concentrations, an essential prerequisite for any agent intended to treat dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Braidy et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has been extensively investigated for its potential to modulate cellular energy metabolism and mitigate the effects of aging in diverse tissues. Early studies revealed that supplementation with NR effectively elevates NAD+ levels in multiple cell types, including neurons, skeletal muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and cellular stress resistance (Dovijarski, 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, while much of the direct experimental work has been performed using NMN, the close biochemical relationship between NMN and NR—as NAD+ precursors—has led investigators to propose that NR could produce similar outcomes in RPE cells. Models of retinal degeneration, including glaucoma and optic nerve injury, have demonstrated that NAD+ boosting via NR administration can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting its potential repurposing for dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies investigating NR’s safety in humans have shown that it is well tolerated at doses that elevate systemic NAD+ levels; doses in the gram-range have been employed without significant adverse effects (Jadeja et al., 2020). Although direct clinical trials targeting dry AMD are still forthcoming, the overall therapeutic history of NR—encompassing robust preclinical ocular benefit across neurodegenerative models and a favorable safety profile in human subjects—strongly supports further investigation for eye diseases where NAD+ depletion is a central pathophysiological feature (Dovijarski, 2019; Braidy et al., 2019; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The proposed mechanism of NR in dry AMD centers on its capacity to elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, thereby fueling a cascade of beneficial biochemical events. After cell entry, NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRKs) to generate NMN, which is subsequently converted to NAD+ through the activity of NMN adenylyltransferase. The resultant increase in NAD+ acts as a vital cofactor for sirtuins—primarily SIRT1 and SIRT3—which are NAD+-dependent deacetylases involved in regulating numerous cellular processes. SIRT1, in particular, has been implicated in deacetylating key transcription factors such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; its deacetylation leads to its nuclear translocation and binding to CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in the promoter regions of autophagy and lysosomal genes. Such activation promotes lysosomal acidification and increases the activity of hydrolases like cathepsin D, which are critical for the degradation of damaged proteins and organelles. Concurrently, SIRT3, which localizes predominantly to mitochondria, enhances mitochondrial function by deacetylating enzymes crucial for mitochondrial bioenergetics and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. The overall effect of NR supplementation is therefore hypothesized to be a restoration of cellular homeostasis in RPE cells—improving both autophagic clearance and mitochondrial function, two processes known to be compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Lin & Apte, 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). Such a mechanism is consistent with a substantial body of literature demonstrating that the NAD+-sirtuin axis plays a critical role in regulating neuroprotective and anti-aging functions across various tissues (Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2018; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

At the molecular level, the cascade initiated by NR begins with its metabolic conversion to NAD+, which then serves as an essential substrate for SIRT1 activation. Activated SIRT1 deacetylates TFEB, facilitating its nuclear accumulation and binding to the CLEAR network promoters, thereby upregulating genes responsible for autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lysosomal acidification. This process is expected to boost cathepsin D activity and overall lysosomal proteolytic function. Parallel activation of SIRT3 in mitochondria further strengthens cellular defenses by enhancing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and reducing ROS generation through deacetylation of key metabolic enzymes. These reconstructed pathways directly address the deleterious effects of oxidative stress and metabolic dysfunction that drive RPE cell death in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018). While several studies using NMN have validated these pathways in RPE and retinal cells (Ren et al., 2022), the mechanistic rationale for NR’s effectiveness remains compelling given its similar mode of action and previously documented retinal distribution (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the experimental setting, the administration of NR is expected to lead to a marked elevation of intracellular NAD+ levels within RPE cells, setting off a chain reaction of intracellular adjustments. The immediate consequence of increased NAD+ availability will be the enhanced activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3. Once activated, SIRT1 is anticipated to deacetylate TFEB, resulting in its translocation to the nucleus. In the nucleus, TFEB binds to target gene promoters, thereby upregulating a suite of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis and the autophagic process. Critically, improvements in lysosomal acidification are expected to boost cathepsin D activity—a protease essential for the degradation of intracellular waste and damaged organelles. Simultaneously, SIRT3-mediated deacetylation events within the mitochondria are projected to improve mitochondrial respiratory capacity and enhance ATP production, while also reducing the production of ROS that ordinarily contribute to oxidative damage. The net effect of these cellular modifications should be an increase in RPE cell viability, particularly under conditions of induced oxidative stress (for example, H₂O₂ exposure), which mimics the pathological environment observed in dry AMD (Zhu et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2022).

Additionally, the NR-induced NAD+ boosting is hypothesized to initiate a beneficial feedback loop wherein improved mitochondrial function further supports cellular energy demands and sustains autophagic flux. This dual action—simultaneously targeting lysosomal and mitochondrial dysfunction—addresses two major hallmarks of dry AMD pathophysiology. RPE cells, which are crucial for the maintenance of photoreceptors, suffer from cumulative oxidative damage and impaired clearance of cellular debris as a result of aging and environmental stress. By restoring efficient autophagic processes and ensuring proper mitochondrial function, NR treatment is expected to reduce the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysfunctional organelles, thereby staving off cellular senescence and death. This is especially salient given that recent studies have linked improved NAD+ metabolism to increased cellular resilience in models of age-related neurodegeneration (Jadeja et al., 2018; Jadeja et al., 2020). The expected outcomes in these assays include measurable increases in NAD+/NADH ratios, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of TFEB, elevated cathepsin D activity, and ultimately, improved cell survival following oxidative challenge. Such effects have been reported in various in vitro and in vivo studies employing NAD+ precursors, strengthening the biological plausibility of the NR hypothesis for treating dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
An overall evaluation of NR as a candidate for treating dry AMD reveals both promising strengths and areas requiring further elucidation. Among the principal strengths is NR’s robust ability to elevate systemic and intracellular NAD+ levels, a key factor in numerous regulatory processes implicated in aging and cellular stress response. Its well-characterized pharmacokinetics, combined with documented safety in human supplementation studies, position NR as an attractive candidate for rapid clinical translation (Jadeja et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). The underlying mechanism—that is, the activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3 leading to deacetylation and activation of TFEB—is supported by a breadth of biochemical and preclinical studies, albeit many of these have been performed with related compounds such as NMN. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis is critical for autophagic and mitochondrial homeostasis in RPE cells—a process compromised in dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Further strengths include NR’s potential to confer dual-organellar benefit. Restoration of lysosomal function, as evidenced by improved acidification and protease activity (e.g., cathepsin D), is a novel therapeutic target that addresses the accumulation of cellular debris—a key factor in the progression of dry AMD. Concurrently, the enhancement of mitochondrial quality and bioenergetics through SIRT3 activation can mitigate oxidative stress and improve cell survival in metabolic stress conditions. Together, these actions provide a mechanistically coherent rationale for repurposing NR in a disease context that currently lacks effective treatments (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020).

However, several challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, while preclinical data offer promising insights, direct evidence of NR’s efficacy in RPE cells specifically challenged by dry AMD-like oxidative stress is still limited. Much of the supportive evidence comes from studies employing NMN or from models of other neurodegenerative conditions such as glaucoma and optic nerve degeneration (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2024). Given differences in uptake and metabolic processing between NR and NMN (Will-Orrego, 2020), it will be important to confirm that NR is adequately taken up by RPE and that its metabolic conversion is efficient in these cells.  

Furthermore, the full cascade—from NAD+ elevation through SIRT1/SIRT3 activation, subsequent TFEB deacetylation, and eventual lysosomal and mitochondrial improvements—remains to be validated within the specific context of dry AMD. Although the general biology of the NAD+–sirtuin axis is well established, its quantitative impact on TFEB activity and cathepsin D function in RPE under conditions of oxidative stress has not been directly demonstrated. This gap in the literature raises questions regarding the optimal dosing regimen, the timing of supplementation, and the potential for compensatory metabolic changes that might blunt the predicted benefits (Ren et al., 2022).

Another consideration is the heterogeneity inherent in dry AMD pathology. RPE cell dysfunction in AMD is multifactorial, involving not only oxidative stress and defective autophagy, but also inflammation, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Whether NR’s NAD+ boosting effect alone can sufficiently address the multifaceted nature of dry AMD remains uncertain. There is also the possibility that chronic administration might lead to unforeseen metabolic imbalances or off-target effects, particularly if prolonged high-dose supplementation alters systemic NAD+ homeostasis or affects non-target tissues in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2023; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Despite these challenges, the candidate’s favorable safety profile and the mechanistic soundness of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB hypothesis underpin a strong case for further investigation. In vitro experiments using ARPE-19 cells and primary RPE cultures under oxidative stress conditions should be prioritized to determine whether NR supplementation can reproducibly induce TFEB nuclear translocation, enhance lysosomal acidification, and improve mitochondrial function. In addition, in vivo studies in animal models that recapitulate dry AMD pathology will be essential to assess the translational potential of NR. These studies might include detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses to ascertain the retinal bioavailability of NR, as well as dose-response studies to define the therapeutic window. Finally, controlled clinical trials in patients with early dry AMD would be necessary to confirm efficacy and to optimize treatment protocols (Martucci et al., 2025; Oshitari, 2024; Lin & Apte, 2018).

In summary, the current body of evidence suggests that NR is a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to efficiently elevate intracellular NAD+ levels, combined with the downstream activation of SIRT1 and SIRT3, provides a strong mechanistic rationale for improving both autophagic flux and mitochondrial function in RPE cells. These cellular processes are crucial for maintaining retinal health and combating the oxidative and metabolic stress that drives dry AMD progression. Moreover, the extensive preclinical investigation of NAD+ precursors and the favorable safety record of NR in human studies further support its potential for fast-tracking into clinical evaluation for retinal disorders (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Nonetheless, key uncertainties remain regarding the direct applicability of NR’s effects to the complex microenvironment of the retina in dry AMD. Issues such as differential cellular uptake, the efficiency of NR’s metabolic conversion to NAD+ in RPE cells, and the precise threshold of NAD+ elevation required to trigger beneficial deacetylation of TFEB must be addressed. Furthermore, given the multifactorial nature of AMD pathology, combinatorial therapeutic approaches may ultimately be necessary to achieve clinically significant improvements. Therefore, while NR emerges as a highly promising candidate with a compelling mechanistic framework, rigorous experimental validation tailored specifically to the ocular setting is imperative. Future studies should elucidate whether the activation of the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB axis translates into meaningful improvements in lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and RPE cell survival in both in vitro models of oxidative stress and in vivo models of dry AMD (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2018; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Looking forward, systematic exploration through well-designed preclinical trials is recommended to confirm the predicted molecular events. These experiments should include detailed time-course and dose-response analyses of NAD+ levels, sirtuin activities, TFEB deacetylation status, and lysosomal function in retinal cells exposed to oxidative insults. Such data will not only clarify the effectiveness of NR in restoring cellular homeostasis but also help refine dosing strategies and identify potential biomarkers of response. Ultimately, if subsequent research affirms the predicted benefits of NR in improving RPE function and survival, this therapeutic candidate could represent a major advancement in the pharmacological management of dry AMD—a condition for which current treatment options remain notably limited (Kitaoka et al., 2020; Mehmel et al., 2020; Dovijarski, 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021).

Overall, the promising preclinical evidence supporting the NAD+–sirtuin–TFEB pathway, combined with the safety profile demonstrated in human trials, renders NR a highly attractive candidate for drug development in dry AMD. While further direct experimental evidence is required to confirm its efficacy in retinal cells, the mechanistic insights gleaned from various studies provide a sound scientific basis for proceeding with additional preclinical and clinical investigations. Thus, repurposing nicotinamide riboside for dry AMD holds significant potential and merits further exploration as part of an integrated strategy to address the unmet therapeutic need in this degenerative retinal disease (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Ebeling et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Pîrvu et al., 2021; Lin & Apte, 2018).
