Proposal for VX-765 (Belnacasan; Selleckchem S2731)

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of VX-765 (Belnacasan; Selleckchem S2731) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
VX-765 is an orally bioavailable small‐molecule agent belonging to the caspase-1 inhibitor class. It is a synthetically derived peptidomimetic prodrug that, once metabolized, yields an active derivative capable of selectively binding to and inhibiting caspase-1. Originally developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, VX-765 was designed to address the shortcomings of earlier peptide-based caspase inhibitors by improving bioavailability, stability, and selectivity. As a caspase-1 inhibitor, it falls within a broader category of agents that have been used to blunt excessive inflammasome responses in various inflammatory and immune-mediated conditions. In the context of drug discovery, caspase-1 inhibitors have been of keen interest because caspase-1 is the key enzyme responsible for converting pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their active cytokine forms, thereby playing a central role in mediating inflammation and the programmed cell death process known as pyroptosis. VX-765 has been evaluated primarily in systemic inflammatory and cardiovascular settings, where its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and excellent oral bioavailability have been demonstrated (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of VX-765 underscores its extensive preclinical development and early clinical evaluation in several inflammatory settings. In preclinical cardiovascular models, for instance, VX-765 demonstrated significant cardioprotection when administered during reperfusion, reducing infarct size and preserving mitochondrial enzyme activities (Audia et al., 2018). It has undergone Phase I and Phase II clinical studies—its Phase II safety data indicate that it is well tolerated at doses that achieve a suppression of proinflammatory cytokines in plasma (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). Although the major clinical investigations with VX-765 have focused on disorders such as epilepsy and other inflammatory diseases rather than ophthalmic disorders, the rationale for its use in dry AMD stems from overlapping inflammatory mechanisms. Specifically, dry AMD shares underlying pathological processes such as chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Prior experimental studies in RPE models using caspase-1 inhibitors like Z-YVAD-FMK have demonstrated that inhibiting caspase-1 activity reduces IL-1β release and can influence cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). However, despite this promising mechanistic background, VX-765 itself has not yet been directly evaluated in preclinical models of dry AMD or in similar ocular diseases. This gap in ophthalmic precedent is notable, but given its established safety profile in nonocular clinical settings and robust anti-inflammatory activity, VX-765 remains an attractive candidate for repurposing into the dry AMD arena (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, VX-765 exerts its effect primarily through selective inhibition of caspase-1, a cysteine protease critically involved in the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Under conditions of cellular stress—such as those occurring in RPE cells in response to lipofuscin accumulation and photooxidative damage—lysosomal destabilization can occur. This lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) leads to the release of cathepsins and other proteases into the cytosol, which, in turn, can serve as an activator of the NLRP3 inflammasome. Once assembled, the inflammasome facilitates the autocatalytic cleavage of caspase-1 into its active p10/p20 subunits, thereby enabling it to convert pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms. VX-765 binds to the active site of caspase-1, thereby preventing this proteolytic cleavage and subsequent cytokine release. This action not only blunts the inflammatory cascade but, by inhibiting caspase-1–dependent processing, may also prevent the activation of gasdermin-D (GSDMD) which is responsible for forming membrane pores during pyroptosis (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

The hypothesis for using VX-765 in dry AMD is that inhibition of caspase-1 will disrupt a pathological amplification loop. In RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress and lipofuscin-related photooxidative damage, inflammasome activation has been shown to promote rapid pyroptotic cell death rather than a slower apoptotic process. This results in an autocrine/paracrine loop where secreted IL-1β further primes neighboring cells for inflammasome activation, exacerbating cell death and causing tissue dysfunction. By blocking caspase-1 activity, VX-765 is expected to prevent this destructive cascade, thereby preserving lysosomal function. More specifically, there is a hypothesized link between caspase-1 activity and alterations in lysosomal integrity—a process involving LMP that is associated with a loss of vacuolar (V-) ATPase activity and disturbances in cathepsin D maturation. The V-ATPase is critical for maintaining an acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal enzyme activity, including that of cathepsin D, which is involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments. Some studies have shown that under conditions of inflammasome activation, RPE cells demonstrate not only an increase in cytokine secretion but also a decline in the functionality of lysosomal hydrolases, which may further compromise cell viability (Brandstetter, 2016). Although direct evidence linking VX-765 to the preservation of V-ATPase activity or cathepsin D function in RPE is currently lacking, the mechanistic framework provided by previous studies using other caspase-1 inhibitors supports the notion that caspase-1 blockade may confer lysosomal protection and attenuate pyroptotic RPE death (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed in vitro and in vivo assays, VX-765 is expected to reduce the levels of active caspase-1 and consequently diminish the secretion of IL-1β and IL-18 from RPE cells stressed by inflammatory stimuli such as lipofuscin photooxidative damage. In validated ARPE-19 cell models that mimic the conditions of dry AMD—where priming with IL-1α and subsequent exposure to lysosomal stressors (for example, the photooxidative effects of lipofuscin components) lead to inflammasome activation and rapid pyroptotic cell death—treatment with caspase-1 inhibitors has been shown to reduce cell lysis and cytokine release (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). By extrapolation, VX-765 should produce similar results. Endpoints for such studies might include decreased levels of IL-1β and IL-18 measured by ELISA, preservation of cell viability as determined by metabolic assays (such as MTT or LDH assays), and a reduction in markers of pyroptosis including the cleavage of GSDMD.

Furthermore, because the hypothesis posits that caspase-1 activity contributes to inflammasome‐mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization, VX-765 is anticipated to stabilize lysosomal integrity. This stabilization should help maintain the acid–base balance within lysosomes—reflected by sustained V-ATPase activity—which is critical for the proper maturation and function of cathepsin D. In healthy RPE cells, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease responsible for degrading photoreceptor outer segment debris. In the context of dry AMD, a decline in cathepsin D activity may contribute to the accumulation of undegraded material, exacerbating cellular stress and death. Although direct measurements of V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation following VX-765 treatment have not yet been published, the overall expectation is that by interrupting the caspase-1–driven inflammatory signaling cascade, VX-765 can prevent the deleterious loss of lysosomal function and thereby reduce RPE cell death (Brandstetter, 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Tseng et al., 2013).

Additionally, in in vivo models of AMD (for example, those induced by Aβ₁₋₄₀ or other drusen mimetics), the inhibition of caspase-1 should theoretically reduce the incidence or severity of geographic atrophy by preserving RPE structure and function. This is of particular interest given that RPE degeneration is a critical event in the progression of dry AMD. Markers of efficacy would include improved retinal morphology on OCT imaging, better electrophysiological responses (as measured by ERG), and a decrease in inflammatory cellular infiltrates. Collectively, these anticipated outcomes support the hypothesis that VX-765’s inhibition of caspase-1 may interrupt the cascade of inflammasome activation, LMP, and lysosomal enzyme failure that leads to RPE death in dry AMD (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation:  
Our overall evaluation of VX-765 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic but recognizes several critical hurdles. One of the major strengths of VX-765 is its well-characterized mechanism of action as a selective caspase-1 inhibitor, along with its demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects in non-ocular preclinical models. The clinical safety profile established in Phase I and II studies—particularly its ability to reduce circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines—lends support to its potential use in a chronic disease setting such as dry AMD (Audia et al., 2018; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). From a mechanistic standpoint, the centrality of caspase-1 in mediating inflammasome-driven cytokine maturation and pyroptosis is well established, and there is compelling evidence from RPE cell models that caspase-1 inhibition can reduce IL-1β secretion and potentially modify cell death pathways (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). These observations provide a strong rationale for the hypothesis that VX-765 could prevent the lysosomal destabilization and subsequent inflammatory cascade responsible for RPE degeneration.

However, there are also several weaknesses and gaps that must be addressed before VX-765 can be fully endorsed for dry AMD. Although the mechanistic data support the role of caspase-1 inhibition in reducing inflammatory cytokine release and possibly preserving lysosomal function, there is currently no direct evidence that VX-765 can stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity, preserve V-ATPase activity, or maintain proper cathepsin D function specifically in RPE cells. Most of the available literature has utilized generic caspase-1 inhibitors such as Z-YVAD-FMK as proof-of-principle tools rather than VX-765 itself in ocular models (Brandstetter, 2016; Tseng et al., 2013). Furthermore, although numerous studies have demonstrated that inflammasome activation and caspase-1–dependent pyroptosis are features of RPE injury in vitro and in some in vivo models of dry AMD, the translation of these findings into effective therapies has proven challenging. The eye’s unique anatomy and the need for adequate drug delivery to the retina raise additional concerns. For an orally administered agent like VX-765, it is not yet clear whether systemic dosing can achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the RPE, or whether intravitreal or alternative delivery methods would be necessary.

Another potential weakness lies in the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. In addition to inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction, dry AMD pathogenesis involves complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and other pro-inflammatory pathways. It remains possible that targeting caspase-1 alone may not be sufficient to arrest disease progression, and a combination approach might be necessary. Moreover, previous caspase inhibitor candidates (for example, pralnacasan) have encountered issues with liver toxicity or other off-target effects in long-term studies, raising concerns about the safety of chronic caspase-1 inhibition (MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010). These potential challenges underscore the need for rigorous preclinical studies in relevant dry AMD models that not only assess the anti-inflammatory and anti-pyroptotic effects of VX-765 but also directly measure lysosomal functional parameters such as V-ATPase activity and cathepsin D maturation.

In summary, while VX-765 offers a promising and mechanistically coherent approach to perturbing the detrimental caspase-1–mediated signaling cascade implicated in RPE degeneration, significant gaps remain in linking its action to improved lysosomal function and reduced RPE death in the specific context of dry AMD. The strengths of VX-765 include its established safety data, oral bioavailability, and selective inhibition of a central inflammatory enzyme; however, its application to AMD is currently supported only by indirect evidence extrapolated from non-ocular models and generic caspase-1 inhibitor studies (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013). To move this candidate forward, we recommend that targeted preclinical studies be undertaken in sight-relevant in vitro systems (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE models) and in vivo models of dry AMD to assess whether VX-765 can indeed prevent or reverse lysosomal membrane permeabilization, sustain V-ATPase activity, and preserve cathepsin D function, in addition to reducing downstream cytokine release and pyroptotic cell death. Only with such data can we determine whether VX-765 holds true promise as a therapeutic for dry AMD.

Overall, while VX-765 has scientifically robust credentials as a caspase-1 inhibitor with proven anti-inflammatory potential in other systems, its repurposing for dry AMD will depend on demonstrating that its molecular actions translate into preservation of RPE function and structure in ocular models. The candidate is promising, but further focused studies are needed to address drug delivery, ocular pharmacokinetics, and the precise impact on lysosomal pathways within the RPE before clinical translation can be considered (Audia et al., 2018; Brandstetter, 2016; MacKenzie & Schipper, 2010; Tseng et al., 2013).

Proposal for Urolithin A (Sigma SML1791)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Urolithin A is a naturally derived small molecule that originates from the gut microbial metabolism of dietary polyphenols, particularly ellagitannins and ellagic acid, which are abundant in fruits such as pomegranates, berries, and nuts (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Heilman et al., 2017). Unlike synthetic drug candidates, Urolithin A is generated endogenously following dietary intake, a process that relies on a healthy gut microbiome to convert these precursors into bioactive urolithins. This compound belongs to the broader class of nutraceuticals and microbiota‐derived metabolites that have been widely investigated for their capacity to modulate mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). These compounds, which have historically been explored mostly within the context of nutritional interventions and age-related muscle decline, are now being repurposed as potential drugs for other degenerative conditions. Urolithin A, in particular, has attracted significant attention due to its ability to enhance mitochondrial quality control through the activation of pathways such as PINK1/Parkin and modulation of autophagy-related mechanisms. Its synthesis in the human body, as well as its isolation from natural sources for research-grade applications such as Sigma SML1791, underscores its dual status as both a naturally occurring metabolite and a drug candidate with therapeutic potential across a variety of disease models (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, as a member of this emerging class, Urolithin A has been shown to be well tolerated, which gives it an advantage over many synthetic compounds that may pose safety concerns due to their off-target toxicities (Wang & Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). The natural origin and well-characterized safety profile of Urolithin A lend support to its development as a repurposed therapeutic agent, particularly for diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired lysosomal clearance play central roles.

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of Urolithin A spans several preclinical and clinical studies that have established its safety, bioavailability, and efficacy in improving mitochondrial function. In numerous animal studies, Urolithin A has demonstrated a high no‐observed‐adverse‐effect level (NOAEL), with doses in the range of several thousand mg/kg demonstrating a remarkable safety margin (Djedjibegović et al., 2020). Early-phase clinical trials, including randomized placebo-controlled studies in healthy elderly subjects, have corroborated its safety; these trials reported no serious adverse events even at doses as high as 2000 mg, and significant improvements were observed in mitochondrial gene expression and muscle function (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). This safety profile has been further supported by work that shows Urolithin A’s favorable pharmacokinetic properties. For instance, following oral administration, Urolithin A is rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations reached around 6 hours post-dose and a half-life of approximately 17–22 hours for the compound and its glucuronide conjugates (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Raimundo et al., 2021). Its systemic bioavailability is advantageous when considering repurposing for systemic degenerative conditions such as AMD.

Historically, the focus of Urolithin A research has been on its role in mitigating age-associated muscle decline by improving mitochondrial quality, a property that has been linked to its induction of mitophagy, which is the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2019). However, growing evidence from both in vitro studies and animal models indicates that Urolithin A’s benefits extend to other tissues, particularly those that are highly dependent on mitochondrial health such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the eye (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Although direct clinical studies using Urolithin A for dry AMD are still pending, the preclinical data suggest that its ability to improve mitochondrial function by promoting mitophagy and lysosomal clearance mechanisms could be beneficial in counteracting RPE degeneration, a hallmark of dry AMD. The therapeutic candidate thus finds support from both its legacy in muscle studies and emerging evidence in neurodegenerative disease models, including studies related to Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central themes (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Skeie et al., 2021). This therapeutic history, spanning several decades of research on mitochondrial modulators, positions Urolithin A as a promising candidate for repurposing toward diseases that involve similar cellular and molecular derangements.

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Urolithin A is multifaceted and central to its potential as a therapeutic agent for dry AMD. At a molecular level, Urolithin A functions primarily as a mitophagy enhancer. In cells experiencing mitochondrial damage or oxidative stress, the kinase PINK1 accumulates on the outer mitochondrial membrane, thereby recruiting the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin; together, they tag dysfunctional mitochondria for autophagic degradation (Borsky et al., 2025; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). This PINK1/Parkin-mediated pathway is essential for maintaining mitochondrial quality and cellular energy metabolism, particularly in high-energy demanding tissues such as the RPE where mitochondria are crucial for photoreceptor support (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Borsky et al., 2025). In addition to inducing mitophagy through PINK1/Parkin signaling, Urolithin A has been shown to activate AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key energy sensor in cells. AMPK activation leads to the phosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of transcription factor EB (TFEB), which acts as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025). Once translocated into the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the expression of genes encoding lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D (CTSD), thereby enhancing the capacity of cells to clear autophagic cargo through improved lysosomal degradation (D’Amico et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025).

The biochemical interactions involved in these processes are well supported by in vitro data showing that Urolithin A not only reduces mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) but also ameliorates the disruption of autophagic flux that is often observed under oxidative stress conditions (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). This reduction of oxidative stress is particularly relevant for the RPE because elevated oxidative damage is a significant contributor to cellular senescence and apoptosis in patients with dry AMD. Furthermore, Urolithin A has been noted to induce p62-dependent lysophagy, a specialized form of autophagy that targets lysosomal components for recycling and repair, ensuring that even when conventional lysosomal biogenesis is impaired, cellular proteostasis can be maintained (Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The dual activation of mitophagy and lysosomal biogenesis creates a synergistic effect, where damaged mitochondria are efficiently recognized, isolated, and degraded, and the lysosomal compartment is concurrently replenished with new, fully functional enzymes, ensuring an optimal degradative environment (Auguste, 2022; Borsky et al., 2025). Moreover, studies have shown that Urolithin A can favorably influence other signaling pathways that contribute to mitochondrial biogenesis, such as the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis, further supporting its role in restoring mitochondrial homeostasis (Borsky et al., 2025; D’Amico et al., 2021). In summary, Urolithin A’s multifaceted mechanism—which encompasses the induction of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, activation of AMPK–TFEB signaling to enhance lysosomal biogenesis, and reduction of oxidative stress—forms a robust foundation for its proposed therapeutic application in the treatment of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis for Urolithin A in dry AMD rests on its ability to restore mitochondrial quality and enhance lysosomal clearance in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the proposed assay, Urolithin A is expected to activate the PINK1/Parkin pathway in RPE cells, thus facilitating the selective removal of damaged mitochondria that contribute to oxidative stress and cellular dysfunction (Borsky et al., 2025). Concurrently, through the activation of AMPK, Urolithin A is anticipated to drive the nuclear translocation of TFEB, thereby upregulating lysosomal genes such as LAMP1 and cathepsin D. This upregulation is expected to enhance lysosomal acidification, an essential component for the proper degradation of autophagic cargo, including damaged mitochondria and photoreceptor outer segments (POS) that accumulate with age (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025).

In oxidative stress RPE models, where mitochondrial ROS levels are elevated due to chronic insult, Urolithin A is projected to reduce ROS production by promoting the clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria, thereby mitigating the cascade of oxidative damage (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). This is expected to result in the stabilization of mitochondrial membrane potential and the maintenance of energy homeostasis, both of which are crucial for the survival of RPE cells under stress. Additionally, the enhanced lysosomal function driven by TFEB activation is likely to lead to increased activity of cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease that plays a pivotal role in degrading autophagosomal substrates and in processing debris from phagocytosis of POS (D’Amico et al., 2021; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). The net effect of these actions would be a reduction in cellular stress markers, improved cellular clearance, and preservation of RPE cell integrity, which are fundamental in slowing down the progression of dry AMD.

The expected pharmacological outcomes are supported by prior studies demonstrating that Urolithin A can modulate key proteins known to be expressed in RPE cells. For instance, PINK1 is well documented to be present in RPE cells and plays an essential role in initiating mitophagy in response to mitochondrial damage (Hyttinen et al., 2018; García‐Villalba et al., 2020). Similarly, proteins such as LAMP1 and CTSD are integral to the function of the lysosomal system in RPE cells, and their upregulation has been associated with improved cellular clearance and resistance to stress-induced apoptosis (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025). Thus, by simultaneously targeting both the mitophagic and lysosomal arms of the cellular clearance machinery, Urolithin A is expected to exert a comprehensive protective effect in the diseased state. This integrative approach is particularly relevant in dry AMD, wherein the accumulation of damaged cellular components and impaired lysosomal degradation are key pathological features (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). Ultimately, the anticipated effects of Urolithin A administration include enhanced mitochondrial turnover, reduced oxidative stress, reinvigorated lysosomal function, and overall RPE cell survival, all of which are envisioned to culminate in a slowing or possible arrest of the degenerative processes underlying dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Urolithin A as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge that underscore its potential while also highlighting critical areas that warrant further investigation. One of the most significant strengths of Urolithin A is its well-established safety profile. Preclinical toxicology studies have demonstrated that Urolithin A has a high NOAEL, and early-phase human clinical trials have shown that it is effectively tolerated at doses ranging from 250 to 2000 mg without significant adverse events (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025). This establishes a favorable risk–benefit ratio that is particularly advantageous when considering the chronic administration likely required for a degenerative condition such as dry AMD. Additionally, its oral bioavailability and favorable pharmacokinetic parameters, including a consistent half-life and effective systemic distribution, further support its potential for use as a repurposed drug (Zhang et al., 2025; Raimundo et al., 2021).

Mechanistically, Urolithin A addresses two core pathological processes implicated in dry AMD: mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal insufficiency. Its ability to trigger the PINK1/Parkin pathway ensures that damaged mitochondria are selectively removed, thereby reducing mitochondrial ROS production and mitigating oxidative injury—a process that is particularly beneficial in the energy-intensive environment of the RPE (Borsky et al., 2025). Simultaneously, the activation of AMPK and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB primes the lysosomal system for enhanced biogenesis and improved degradative capacity, thus tackling the accumulation of cellular debris and phagocytosed POS that are hallmarks of AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025).

From a translational perspective, the therapeutic history of Urolithin A provides a strong foundation for its repurposing. Although much of the direct evidence pertains to skeletal muscle and neurodegenerative models, the underlying mechanisms—mitochondrial clearance and autophagic enhancement—are universally relevant to cellular systems burdened by degenerative stress, including the RPE (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024). However, a notable limitation remains in the current literature: there is a paucity of direct experimental data specifically utilizing RPE models or clinical cohorts with dry AMD. Although the extrapolation from other systems is promising, targeted studies are needed to validate the efficacy and optimize the dosing regimen for ocular applications (Zhang et al., 2025; Makarov & Korkotian, 2023).

Another potential challenge is the inherent variability in the bioactivation of ellagitannins to Urolithins among individuals, owing to differences in gut microbiota composition. While direct administration of Urolithin A circumvents this challenge, variability in metabolic processing and individual pharmacodynamic responses may still influence therapeutic outcomes (Wang & Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Moreover, the translation of systemic improvements in mitochondrial function to localized effects within the retina is not entirely straightforward; the blood–retinal barrier and unique ocular microenvironment may affect drug distribution and efficacy (Makarov & Korkotian, 2023; Harper, 2023). These challenges underscore the need for comprehensive ocular pharmacokinetic studies and the development of delivery strategies that ensure adequate drug concentration in the RPE.

Despite these limitations, the overall evidence supports the advancement of Urolithin A as a candidate for treating dry AMD. Its dual mechanism of enhancing both mitophagy and lysosomal function is particularly well-suited to counteracting the complex pathophysiology of AMD, where mitochondrial decay and lysosomal failure converge to induce cellular apoptosis and dysfunction (Auguste, 2022; Borsky et al., 2025). In addition, the compound’s ability to reduce oxidative stress, a critical driver of AMD progression, further bolsters the rationale for its use (Djedjibegović et al., 2020; Jayatunga et al., 2021). Importantly, the wealth of preclinical data demonstrating Urolithin A’s beneficial effects in animal models and cell culture systems provides a compelling argument for its continued evaluation in ocular models of AMD (Hyttinen et al., 2018; Jiménez-Loygorri et al., 2024).

In summary, Urolithin A presents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing against dry AMD. Its natural origin, excellent safety profile, favorable pharmacokinetics, and robust mechanism of action—characterized by the activation of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and AMPK–TFEB-mediated lysosomal biogenesis—render it an attractive candidate for further investigation. The expected beneficial effects in reducing oxidative stress, clearing damaged mitochondria, and re-establishing lysosomal function in RPE cells align well with the therapeutic needs in dry AMD. Nevertheless, critical gaps remain in direct evidence from ocular models and in addressing potential interindividual variability in drug response. If these challenges are successfully navigated through targeted preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, Urolithin A could fill a significant unmet need in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a novel, mechanism-based intervention that targets the underlying cellular dysfunctions driving the disease (Jayatunga et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025; Borsky et al., 2025; Hyttinen et al., 2018). Ultimately, while further research is necessary to refine dosing strategies and confirm ocular efficacy, the overall evaluation indicates that Urolithin A is a strong candidate worthy of pursuit in the quest for effective therapies for dry age-related macular degeneration.

Proposal for MCC950 (AdipoGen AG-CRID3)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
MCC950 (AdipoGen AG‐CRID3) is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the diarylsulfonylurea chemical class and was originally discovered during investigations aimed at identifying potent inhibitors of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its chemical scaffold was designed to specifically interfere with the ATPase function of the NLRP3 NACHT domain, thereby preventing the oligomerization of NLRP3 and subsequent formation of the ASC speck complex that is essential for inflammasome activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This compound has been synthetically optimized for high potency, with reported effective concentrations in the nanomolar range in various disease models, and its structure–activity relationship has been refined in numerous preclinical studies over the past several years (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). As a representative of its drug class, diarylsulfonylureas have been broadly explored in inflammatory contexts due to their capacity to modulate innate immune pathways; however, MCC950 has emerged as a prototype NLRP3-targeting agent with potential applications across inflammatory and degenerative diseases, including those affecting ocular tissues (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
MCC950 was initially characterized in systemic inflammatory disease models, where it demonstrated remarkable efficacy in reducing the production of proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18, by directly inhibiting the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical evaluations in nonocular contexts—such as experimental colitis, myocardial infarction, and atherosclerosis—have consistently shown that MCC950 can markedly mitigate pathology by blocking the inflammasome cascade (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the ocular arena, several studies have examined MCC950’s impact in diverse rodent models of retinal disease. For example, in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models, MCC950 administration led to reductions in IL-1β mRNA and secreted protein levels, albeit with a paradoxical increase in overall CNV lesion volume, suggesting a complex interplay between inflammasome inhibition and immune cell recruitment (Dieckmann et al., 2024). Furthermore, intravitreal delivery of MCC950 in an OPTN(E50K) mouse model of normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) showed functional and structural retinal improvements through decreased expression of inflammasome components and glial activation markers (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023). In vitro investigations using ARPE-19 and R28 retinal cell lines have also highlighted MCC950's ability to decrease NLRP3, caspase-1, IL-1β, and IL-18 levels, thus attenuating inflammasome-mediated inflammatory responses (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). Despite these promising preclinical data in models of retinal inflammation and vascular dysfunction, MCC950 has not yet progressed into clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or geographic atrophy (GA), and its use in ocular conditions remains primarily in the preclinical and exploratory phase (Wooff et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
MCC950 exerts its pharmacological effects by specifically targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic multiprotein complex that mediates the innate immune response to both pathogen-associated and damage-associated molecular patterns (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). At the molecular level, MCC950 is believed to bind to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, thereby inhibiting its ATPase activity—a critical step required for the conformational changes and oligomerization that lead to the formation of the active inflammasome complex (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025). This blockade prevents the recruitment of the adaptor protein ASC, thus halting the maturation and activation of caspase-1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Consequently, the cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their bioactive forms is suppressed, which results in diminished secretion of these potent proinflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2025; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Importantly, MCC950’s mechanism is selective for NLRP3, as it does not interfere with the activation of other inflammasome platforms, such as those mediated by AIM2, NLRC4, or NLRP1 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). In the context of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells—a cell type critical for the maintenance of the outer blood–retina barrier and implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—NLRP3 activation has been linked to chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and lysosomal destabilization. Inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 is postulated to preserve lysosomal integrity by preventing excessive caspase-1 activation, which is known to contribute to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and the subsequent loss of v-ATPase–dependent acidification along with aberrant cathepsin D (CTSD) activity (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). Although direct experimental evidence demonstrating the preservation of CTSD activity or v-ATPase function by MCC950 in RPE cells is not yet firmly established in the literature provided, the underlying rationale is supported by the well-documented role of caspase-1 in mediating pyroptosis and lysosomal dysfunction in models of RPE degeneration (Korhonen, 2024; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

Expected Effect:  
In a therapeutic scenario for dry AMD, the expected effect of MCC950 is to inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation within RPE cells, thereby reducing the downstream activation of caspase-1 and the cleavage of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18. This dampening of the inflammatory cascade is anticipated to prevent or attenuate the lysosomal membrane destabilization that is often observed in RPE cells under stress conditions such as those induced by Alu RNA accumulation secondary to DICER1 deficiency—an event that has been strongly implicated in geographic atrophy (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). With reduced caspase-1 activity, it is hypothesized that MCC950 will preserve the integrity of the lysosomal compartment by maintaining proper v-ATPase function and ensuring that cathepsin D is correctly matured and compartmentalized, thereby mitigating autophagic and lysosomal stress (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Ildefonso et al., 2016). In preclinical RPE models, inhibitors of NLRP3 have been shown to decrease IL-1β/IL-18 release and reduce inflammatory cell death (pyroptosis), which in turn supports cellular homeostasis and may prevent the progressive loss of RPE cells that drives the clinical progression of dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020). Overall Evaluation:  
MCC950 offers several notable strengths as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its high potency and selectivity as an inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a central mediator of innate immune inflammatory responses that has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various retinal degenerative disorders, including AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Its mechanism of action—binding to the NACHT domain to inhibit ATPase activity and subsequently block caspase-1 activation—provides a targeted approach that directly addresses a proximal event in the inflammatory cascade (Wang et al., 2025; Wooff et al., 2020). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that MCC950 can successfully reduce the release of IL-1β and IL-18 in various cell types, including retinal endothelial cells and RPE-like cells, which underscores its potential to ameliorate the chronic inflammatory environment observed in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Li, 2020). While the compound effectively reduces inflammasome activity in multiple settings, its performance in models that closely recapitulate dry AMD pathology, particularly those focusing on geographic atrophy and RPE degeneration, remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Wooff et al., 2020). A further limitation is the relative paucity of data regarding the pharmacokinetic properties and ocular bioavailability of MCC950 when administered via routes that would be clinically relevant for AMD, such as intravitreal or topical delivery. Although some studies have begun to characterize its ocular distribution and short-term safety in rodent models (Chen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025), comprehensive long-term toxicity profiles, dose–response evaluations, and assessments of potential off-target effects in the highly specialized environment of the eye have yet to be established. These studies are essential not only for confirming the anti-inflammatory efficacy of MCC950 in RPE cells but also for ensuring that long-term inhibition of NLRP3 does not inadvertently impair other cellular processes critical for retinal health.

In summary, the evaluation of MCC950 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is promising yet remains preliminary. Its well-characterized ability to selectively inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome, reducing caspase-1 activation and downstream IL-1β/IL-18 release, aligns with the mechanistic rationale for targeting chronic inflammation in RPE cells—a key driver of geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Korhonen, 2024). The compound’s preclinical efficacy in reducing inflammatory biomarkers in various ocular and non-ocular models supports the hypothesis that MCC950 may alleviate the inflammatory milieu that underlies RPE degeneration and lysosomal dysfunction. However, mixed outcomes observed in certain retinal models, along with the absence of direct evidence linking MCC950 to improved lysosomal v-ATPase function and cathepsin D maturation in RPE cells, underscore the need for further detailed studies (Wooff et al., 2020). Moreover, optimizing the ocular delivery method, establishing a robust pharmacokinetic profile in the eye, and conducting dedicated preclinical trials in models that accurately mimic dry AMD pathophysiology are critical next steps before this candidate can be considered for clinical translation. 

Overall, while MCC950 exhibits significant mechanistic and pharmacological strengths that support its evaluation as a potential treatment for dry AMD, its clinical viability will depend on resolving several key uncertainties. These include (1) the demonstration of its capacity to restore and maintain lysosomal integrity and CTSD activity in stressed RPE cells, (2) the establishment of an optimal dosing regimen with minimal ocular toxicity, and (3) clarification of the complex immunological consequences of long-term NLRP3 inhibition within the retinal environment. Addressing these questions through a comprehensive series of biochemical, cellular, and animal studies will be essential for determining whether MCC950 can be effectively repurposed to combat the progressive RPE loss and chronic inflammatory state that drive geographic atrophy in dry AMD (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016).

In conclusion, MCC950 is a highly attractive candidate from a drug development perspective due to its potent, selective inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a pathway increasingly implicated in the inflammatory cascade that underlies dry AMD. Its synthetic origins as a diarylsulfonylurea and its extensive preclinical evaluation in inflammatory disease models lend strong support to its potential utility. Nevertheless, the complex biology of the retinal environment and the conflicting preclinical results observed in some models necessitate cautious optimism. Further targeted studies that rigorously assess MCC950’s effects on RPE-specific endpoints—including lysosomal acidification, v-ATPase function, and cathepsin D maturation—will be pivotal in establishing its efficacy for dry AMD. Additionally, comprehensive ocular safety and pharmacokinetic studies are required to ensure that the benefits of MCC950 can be realized without incurring off-target toxicities in this delicate tissue. Based on the current literature, MCC950 holds promise as a means to directly address inflammasome-driven inflammation in dry AMD; however, its advancement into clinical trials will depend on the outcomes of these critical preclinical investigations (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Wooff et al., 2020; Li, 2020; Ildefonso et al., 2016; Dieckmann et al., 2024).

Proposal for MK-2206 (Selleckchem S1078)

Below is a detailed evaluation of MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), structured into five sections.

─────────────────────────────  
Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
─────────────────────────────  
MK-2206 is a synthetically derived, orally bioavailable small‐molecule inhibitor that functions as an allosteric modulator of the serine/threonine kinase AKT. Unlike classical ATP‐competitive agents, MK-2206 binds to an allosteric site outside the catalytic pocket, thereby altering the conformation of AKT and preventing its full activation. Originally discovered and optimized for oncological indications, its development was driven by the need to inhibit aberrant AKT signaling observed in multiple cancers. The compound belongs to a class of drugs known as allosteric AKT inhibitors, which historically have been explored for their ability to modulate critical intracellular signaling pathways that govern cellular proliferation, survival, and metabolism. More specifically, MK-2206 has been demonstrated in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of AKT at key regulatory residues (for example, S473) in multiple cell types, including primary retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures where its application at 1 μM for 24 hours was shown to inhibit AKT phosphorylation and promote nuclear translocation of TFEB (Transcription Factor EB) – the master regulator of lysosomal gene expression (Karim et al., 2020). Although the detailed synthetic route is not fully delineated within our context, the compound has been thoroughly characterized for its bioavailability, metabolic stability, and cell‐penetrant properties during its extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation in oncology (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). These attributes underpin its suitability for repurposing; its well‐defined medicinal chemistry profile and advanced clinical development stage (availability of Phase I data) position MK-2206 as an attractive candidate for investigating autophagy regulation in non‐oncologic contexts such as AMD (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Therapeutic History  
─────────────────────────────  
Historically, MK-2206 has been developed and evaluated predominantly as an anticancer agent. During its clinical evolution, it was subjected to multiple Phase I and combination Phase I/II clinical trials in patients with advanced solid tumors, HER2-positive cancers, and other malignancies. The compound has been administered on both an every-other-day (QOD) schedule and on a once-weekly (QW) regimen in dose‐escalation studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). These early clinical studies provided valuable safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) data that have now established an acceptable safety profile in humans. Outside the field of oncology, no published clinical study has yet directly evaluated MK-2206 in ocular indications. However, a separate body of preclinical research has increasingly linked dysregulated AKT activation in RPE cells with impaired lysosomal function and defective autophagy – two pathological hallmarks of dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020). In immunoproteasome‐deficient RPE models (for example, LMP2 knockout [KO] cells), hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT is associated with reduced nuclear TFEB and compromised autophagic flux, features that correlate with RPE stress and lipofuscin accumulation (Karim et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro data have demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of AKT using MK-2206 leads to decreased AKT phosphorylation, increased nuclear TFEB localization, and enhanced autophagy flux in RPE, rescuing some of the defects observed in these models (Karim et al., 2020). Although MK-2206 per se has not been directly tested in animal models of AMD, related preclinical evidence based on the modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE supports its potential utility in the AMD context (Karim et al., 2020). In addition, several patent reviews have discussed MK-2206 within the broader portfolio of AKT inhibitors that are being repurposed for indications beyond oncology, further reinforcing the plausibility of using MK-2206 to target cellular pathways implicated in AMD (Guo et al., 2021).

─────────────────────────────  
Mechanism of Action  
─────────────────────────────  
The established mechanism of MK-2206 is anchored in its ability to inhibit AKT signaling through an allosteric mechanism. Under normal conditions, the AKT kinase is activated by phosphorylation events – typically at threonine 308 and serine 473 – in response to upstream signals from receptor tyrosine kinases and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathways. AKT then phosphorylates a wide range of substrates that control cell survival, growth, and metabolism. One of the downstream effects of activated AKT is the phosphorylation of TFEB (and possibly other MiT/TFE family members such as TFE3) at specific serine residues (for example, S467). This phosphorylation event hampers TFEB’s capacity to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, thereby repressing its transcriptional activity on the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a gene set that drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Karim et al., 2020).

MK-2206 exerts its effect by binding to an allosteric site on AKT, a mode of inhibition that distinguishes it from ATP‐competitive inhibitors. In doing so, it reduces the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473, thereby lowering its kinase activity (Karim et al., 2020). In RPE cells – particularly under pathogenic conditions such as immunoproteasome deficiency that leads to AKT hyper‐phosphorylation – MK-2206 administration has been shown to result in a marked decrease in AKT activity. This decrease, in turn, permits the dephosphorylation of TFEB, facilitating its nuclear import (Karim et al., 2020). Once in the nucleus, TFEB upregulates the transcription of genes involved in lysosomal function, autophagosome formation, and the expression of critical enzymes such as cathepsin D and components of the V-ATPase, which are necessary for maintaining lysosomal acidification (Karim et al., 2020).

Although the research cited does not explicitly verify isoform‐specific inhibition of AKT2 by MK-2206, the underlying hypothesis – that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE suppresses TFEB nuclear localization – provides a strong rationale for repurposing MK-2206 in AMD. Some studies have proposed that AKT2, among the three isoforms, may predominantly drive the inflammatory and autophagy‐related deficits encountered in RPE in AMD models (Ghosh et al., 2019). This hypothesis is further supported by evidence showing that AKT2 inhibition can attenuate inflammatory cascades (such as IFNλ–LCN-2–driven neutrophil infiltration) that contribute to early RPE pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the mechanism of action of MK-2206 – namely, its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT activity leading to increased nuclear translocation of TFEB and subsequent upregulation of lysosomal/autophagy pathways – directly addresses key pathobiological mechanisms implicated in dry AMD.

─────────────────────────────  
Expected Effect  
─────────────────────────────  
Based on the hypothesis under review, the administration of MK-2206 to RPE cells is expected to yield several critical downstream effects that are therapeutically desirable in the context of dry AMD. First, MK-2206 should decrease the hyper‐phosphorylation of AKT observed in stressed or disease‐impacted RPE, which is thought to be a major contributing factor to the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization in these cells (Karim et al., 2020). By relieving this inhibitory phosphorylation, MK-2206 should facilitate the dephosphorylation and subsequent nuclear translocation of TFEB. Once TFEB is allowed to enter the nucleus, it can promote the transcription of a broad array of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, including those involved in the expression of vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase) components and cathepsin D (CTSD) (Karim et al., 2020).

The restoration of nuclear TFEB activity is expected to lead to several beneficial cellular effects. In the RPE – which relies on robust autophagy for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of cellular homeostasis – enhanced TFEB‐driven gene expression should improve lysosomal acidification and enzymatic activity, including that of cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Karim et al., 2020). Improved lysosomal acidification is critical for the maturation and function of cathepsin D, which in turn is essential for the degradation of protein aggregates and lipofuscin. Since drusen and lipofuscin accumulation represent major pathological hallmarks of dry AMD, the normalization of cathepsin D function could help to clear these toxic deposits, potentially slowing or reversing disease progression (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019).

Furthermore, other reports suggest that AKT activation in RPE not only hinders autophagy but also promotes pro‐inflammatory pathways that contribute to tissue degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2019). Thus, the inhibition of AKT signaling by MK-2206 is anticipated to diminish such inflammatory cascades (Ghosh et al., 2019). In aggregate, the expected net effect is a re‐establishment of cellular proteostasis within the RPE via two interrelated mechanisms: (1) an enhancement of autophagic flux and lysosomal clearance via the TFEB pathway, and (2) a reduction in deleterious inflammatory and stress responses mediated by aberrant AKT2 signaling. Given that RPE dysfunction, lipofuscin accumulation, and drusen formation underlie the pathogenesis of dry AMD, MK-2206 could thereby serve to counteract disease progression at a mechanistic level (Karim et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
Overall Evaluation  
─────────────────────────────  
In evaluating MK-2206 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key points emerge. On the strength side, MK-2206 is a well-characterized small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the AKT pathway – a pathway increasingly implicated in the regulation of autophagy and lysosomal function in RPE cells. Preclinical studies in immunoproteasome-deficient RPE have demonstrated that MK-2206 can inhibit AKT phosphorylation, restore nuclear TFEB localization, and promote autophagic flux (Karim et al., 2020). This mechanistic link is especially relevant, as dry AMD is characterized by reduced autophagy, impaired lysosomal clearance, and resultant accumulation of drusen and lipofuscin. Moreover, the rationale that AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE cells suppresses TFEB function – thereby weakening the cell’s proteolytic capacity – is well supported by the available preclinical data (Ghosh et al., 2019). In addition, MK-2206 has already been through several Phase I oncology trials, meaning that its safety and pharmacokinetic profiles are largely established in humans, which dramatically de-risks its repurposing for a different indication such as AMD (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010). This could accelerate the clinical development timeline, as much of the initial toxicity and dosing work has been completed.

Nonetheless, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses to be addressed. First, while the available studies support that MK-2206 can modulate the AKT–TFEB axis in RPE cells under preclinical conditions, many of these studies do not provide isoform‐specific data; our hypothesis hinges on the idea that AKT2 is the critical isoform to be inhibited. MK-2206 is generally described as a pan-AKT inhibitor, which means that it may also affect AKT1 and AKT3. The lack of isoform specificity could lead to unanticipated off-target effects or impact cellular processes in non-RPE tissues if systemic exposure is not tightly controlled (Karim et al., 2020). Second, although the mechanism of promoting nuclear TFEB activity through AKT inhibition is conceptually sound and supported by cellular data, direct measurements of downstream endpoints critical to AMD – such as lysosomal acidification (e.g., via V-ATPase activity assays) and cathepsin D maturation or activity – are limited or indirect in the current literature (Karim et al., 2020). Without robust evidence that MK-2206 improves these specific lysosomal functions in RPE cells, the link between restored autophagy and actual therapeutic benefit in terms of drusen clearance remains inferential. Third, previous clinical development of MK-2206 in oncology has encountered variable efficacy when used as a monotherapy, prompting its evaluation predominantly in combination regimens (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). The implications of these findings for a non‐oncologic, degenerative condition such as AMD are not straightforward, and careful attention must be paid to optimizing both delivery routes (for example, local versus systemic administration) and dosing strategies that are tailored to the ocular microenvironment.

Furthermore, while the literature provides a strong rationale linking AKT hyperactivation to impaired autophagy in RPE, dry AMD is a multifactorial disease with complex pathophysiology that includes oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic risk factors such as CFH variants. It is not yet fully clear whether correcting the autophagy defect alone will suffice to produce clinically meaningful outcomes in all patients with dry AMD. In addition, toxicity concerns must be carefully revisited: although MK-2206’s safety profile is defined in the context of oncology, potential ocular toxicity – such as RPE cell toxicity, off-target retinal effects, or interference with normal retinal cellular turnover – must be rigorously evaluated via dedicated preclinical ocular studies before clinical translation. Finally, the intellectual property and regulatory landscape for repurposing a cancer drug to treat an ocular disease will require further scrutiny, although the existing clinical data on MK-2206 do provide an important head-start compared to wholly novel compounds (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).

In summary, the strengths of MK-2206 as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD include:  
• A well-characterized mechanism of action that aligns with pathobiological insights from RPE autophagy studies, namely the inhibition of aberrant AKT signaling leading to enhanced nuclear TFEB activity and autophagy restoration (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Established clinical safety and PK data from multiple Phase I oncology trials, which reduce translational risk and may accelerate repurposing efforts (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2008; 2010).  
• A plausible hypothesis that links AKT2 hyperactivity in RPE (observed in CFH-risk models and immunoproteasome-deficient systems) to lysosomal dysfunction, drusen accumulation, and ultimately, AMD pathology (Ghosh et al., 2019).

Conversely, potential weaknesses include:  
• Limited evidence regarding isoform specificity toward AKT2, as MK-2206 is generally considered a pan-AKT inhibitor, which may inadvertently modulate other AKT isoforms and lead to systemic side effects (Karim et al., 2020).  
• Incomplete preclinical data linking MK-2206 directly to improvements in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity in RPE, which remain key therapeutic endpoints predicted to counteract drusen formation (Karim et al., 2020).  
• The challenge of adapting systemic dosing regimens used in oncology to the ocular setting, where achieving therapeutic retinal concentrations without causing off-target toxicity is paramount (Guo et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009).  
• The multifactorial nature of dry AMD that may require combination approaches, meaning that modulation of the AKT–TFEB axis alone might not be sufficient to achieve robust clinical benefit in all patients.

Overall, MK-2206 represents a promising candidate to repurpose for dry AMD based on its ability to allosterically inhibit AKT, a central node in a pathway that has been implicated in RPE autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction. The preclinical rationale – that inhibition of AKT releases the block on TFEB nuclear translocation, thereby improving lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity – is well founded in the literature (Karim et al., 2020). Moreover, the favorable clinical safety profile gleaned from its extensive evaluation in oncology serves as an important asset when considering repurposing strategies. However, critical questions remain regarding isoform specificity, the optimal route and dosing for ocular application, and whether restoring autophagy via this pathway is sufficient to reverse or halt the progression of dry AMD in patients. Future studies should focus on establishing robust preclinical data in AMD-relevant animal models —including direct measures of lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D function, and drusen clearance —as well as refining ocular delivery strategies that minimize systemic exposure. Addressing these gaps will be essential for de-risking MK-2206’s application in the AMD setting and for paving the way toward clinical trials specifically targeting the AKT–TFEB pathway in the context of retinal degeneration.

─────────────────────────────  
Conclusion  
─────────────────────────────  
In conclusion, our comprehensive literature review supports the repurposing of MK-2206 for dry AMD on the following grounds: it is a well‐studied allosteric AKT inhibitor with a known safety profile from Phase I oncology trials; preclinical investigations in RPE models implicate AKT hyperactivation in the suppression of TFEB nuclear localization and consequent lysosomal dysfunction; and mechanistic hypotheses derived from these models suggest that inhibiting AKT (and, by extension, AKT2) can restore autophagy, improve lysosomal acidification, boost cathepsin D activity, and potentially counteract drusen accumulation – a key driver of dry AMD pathology. While challenges remain, particularly with respect to isoform selectivity and the translation of dosing paradigms from oncology to ocular applications, the existing data provide a strong rationale for advancing MK-2206 into more focused preclinical studies for dry AMD. Such work should include detailed analyses of lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and the overall impact on RPE proteostasis in in vivo models that recapitulate the human disease. With these additional studies, MK-2206 could emerge as a viable candidate in our therapeutic pipeline for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021).

Proposal for Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (R&D Systems 1869-CD)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Recombinant human pro-cathepsin D (rhCTSD), as exemplified by R&D Systems product 1869-CD, is a bioengineered form of a naturally occurring lysosomal aspartyl protease that is synthesized as an inactive precursor (pro-cathepsin D) (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). This therapeutic candidate belongs to the enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) class, a category of biotherapeutics developed to supplement or correct deficient lysosomal enzymes in various disorders. The natural cathepsin D enzyme is normally produced and processed intracellularly through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and Golgi apparatus, undergoing critical post-translational modifications—including the removal of the N-terminal signal peptide, glycosylation, and addition of a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag—that are essential for its subsequent targeting to the lysosome (Sharif, 2015, pp. 60–64). The recombinant version is produced under conditions aimed at ensuring high purity and biological activity conforming to GMP standards, thus making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in conditions where lysosomal proteolytic capacity is compromised. The candidate has been designed in the context of neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorders, where enzyme supplementation has been shown to restore proteolytic flux by directly replacing a rate-limiting hydrolase (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Enzyme replacement therapies have been a cornerstone in the management of several lysosomal storage disorders since the early 1990s, with the first approved treatment for Gaucher’s disease setting a precedent for this therapeutic strategy (Saftig, 2005; Lerussi et al., 2025). In the specific case of cathepsin D, recombinant forms have been employed in preclinical models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) and other neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders, where the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D was able to rescue functional deficits associated with genetic CTSD deficiency (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Animal studies using CTSD-deficient mouse models have demonstrated that both intracranial and localized injections of recombinant CTSD can correct defects in proteolysis and autophagy, leading to improvements in neuropathological markers and even extending lifespan in treated animals (Bassal et al., 2021; Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Although most of these studies have focused on neurodegenerative conditions of the central nervous system, similar principles of lysosomal dysfunction apply to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis in the context of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Klettner et al., 2013). Notably, the literature suggests that cathepsin D is highly expressed in RPE cells and plays a vital role in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), with its deficiency or reduced function being implicated in the accumulation of toxic deposits and drusen formation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Despite the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD using rhCTSD, the extensive preclinical evidence from both neurodegenerative and retinal disease models provides a compelling rationale for exploring the repurposing of this enzyme replacement strategy in dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of recombinant human pro-cathepsin D is rooted in its ability to restore lysosomal proteolytic function, which is often impaired in disease states such as dry AMD. Under physiological conditions, pro-cathepsin D is synthesized in the rough ER as an inactive precursor that undergoes several post-translational modifications, including the cleavage of an N-terminal signal peptide, N-linked glycosylation, and critical mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging in the Golgi apparatus (Sharif, 2015). The M6P tag facilitates the binding of pro-cathepsin D to M6P receptors within the trans-Golgi network (TGN), directing the enzyme to late endosomes and, eventually, to lysosomes where the acidic environment promotes its maturation into its active form (Sharif, 2015). Once active, cathepsin D contributes to the degradation of a wide range of substrates, including the photoreceptor outer segments in RPE cells, thereby playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and preventing the accumulation of deleterious debris that can lead to drusen formation (Klettner et al., 2013). The proposed therapeutic strategy involves subretinal delivery of the recombinant enzyme to bypass systemic limitations such as the blood-brain barrier and to achieve localized uptake into RPE cells via the M6P receptor-mediated endocytosis pathway (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Once internalized, the enzyme can replenish endogenous levels of cathepsin D, thereby enhancing autophagic flux and proteolytic degradation processes that are essential for the health and function of the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). This targeted mechanism is a direct, molecularly specific approach that aims not only to compensate for maturation defects in the enzyme but also to overcome upstream acidification abnormalities that often hinder proper activation of endogenously produced cathepsin D in aging RPE cells (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015).

Expected Effect:  
The anticipated outcome of employing recombinant human pro-cathepsin D for the treatment of dry AMD is multifaceted. First, the subretinal administration of the enzyme is expected to lead to efficient uptake by RPE cells via the M6P receptor, thereby supplementing or restoring the lysosomal pool of active cathepsin D where it is most critically needed (Sharif, 2015). This direct enzyme replacement should result in improved degradation of cellular waste such as spent photoreceptor outer segments, mitigating the build-up of lipofuscin and drusen that are characteristic of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). In animal models of CTSD deficiency—specifically those that mimic aspects of neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders—the administration of exogenous pro-cathepsin D has yielded significant improvements in proteolytic function, reduction of pathological markers, and even extensions in lifespan (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020), which suggest that similar therapeutic benefits might be achievable in the context of dry AMD. Enhancing the proteolytic flux within the lysosomes of RPE cells is expected to restore autophagy and maintain cellular homeostasis, thereby reducing the incidence of apoptotic cell death and preserving retinal structure (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015). Additionally, by compensating for potential maturation deficits and bypassing defective acidification processes through localized delivery, the therapeutic candidate offers a targeted approach that is likely to be both efficacious and specific compared to more indirect modulators of lysosomal function (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020; Sharif, 2015). Ultimately, the expected effect is an overall improvement in RPE health, which should translate into slowed progression of dry AMD, decreased drusen accumulation, and preserved visual function.

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating recombinant human pro-cathepsin D as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths emerge from the literature, though some challenges remain. One of the primary strengths of this candidate lies in its specificity; unlike indirect modulators of lysosomal function, the exogenous delivery of a rate-limiting hydrolase such as CTSD offers a mechanistically driven, targeted replacement therapy that directly addresses a known biochemical deficit in the retinal pigment epithelium (Klettner et al., 2013; Liu, 2021). The robust body of preclinical evidence supporting the efficacy of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in models of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, where similar lysosomal impairments are present, lends further credence to its potential applicability in AMD (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020). Moreover, the formulation's GMP-compatibility and prior demonstration of safety in the context of genetic CTSD deficiency are significant advantages that can accelerate its translational potential (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021).

The enzyme’s molecular mechanism, which involves uptake via mannose-6-phosphate receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent activation in the lysosomal compartment, is well-characterized and aligns with the pathological requirements for restoring RPE function in dry AMD (Sharif, 2015). This targeted approach provides a direct means to enhance proteolytic activity and autophagic flux, crucial processes that are disrupted in the aging retina and contribute to drusen accumulation (Klettner et al., 2013). The ability of the exogenously delivered pro-cathepsin D to overcome defects in lysosomal maturation and acidification further reinforces its potential role in reversing or mitigating the deleterious effects of the disease (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

On the other hand, several weaknesses or challenges must be acknowledged. Although the mechanistic rationale is robust, the translation of preclinical successes in neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models to the complex, multifactorial pathology of dry AMD remains uncertain (Benes et al., 2008; Liu, 2021). Dry AMD is influenced by a host of factors—including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, and genetic predispositions—that may not be fully addressed by simply supplementing CTSD activity. Therefore, while the normalization of proteolytic flux in RPE cells is a critical component, it may not suffice on its own in the context of the broader pathophysiological milieu present in AMD (Klettner et al., 2013; Sharif, 2015).

Furthermore, delivery challenges inherent to subretinal injections must be considered. Although localized delivery methods help bypass systemic barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, subretinal injections are technically demanding, carry inherent risks of infection, and may provoke local immune responses due to repeated interventions (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The emergence of neutralizing antibodies, as observed in some ERT studies when alternative routes of administration were explored, could compromise the long-term efficacy of the therapy if systemic leakage occurs or if repeated dosing is required (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). Additionally, the stability and persistence of the enzyme in the subretinal space represent important pharmacokinetic questions that must be addressed through rigorous preclinical pharmacodynamic studies.

Another potential shortcoming is the specificity of the enzyme’s action. While cathepsin D is indeed a critical protease in RPE cells, there is an intricate interplay between cathepsin D and other lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsins B, L, and S, as well as regulatory proteins like cystatin C, which modulate proteolytic activity (Sharif, 2015). This interdependence implies that augmenting CTSD activity alone might lead to compensatory changes in other proteases that could either enhance the therapeutic effect or, conversely, result in unforeseen off-target consequences. Moreover, given the complexity of the RPE cell’s lysosomal network and the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis, combination approaches targeting several aspects of lysosomal dysfunction might be necessary to achieve optimal clinical outcomes.

In summary, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D presents a therapeutically attractive and mechanistically rational candidate for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its origins as a naturally occurring lysosomal precursor that, when supplemented exogenously, has been shown to restore enzyme activity in preclinical models of lysosomal dysfunction (Bassal et al., 2021; Marques et al., 2020) underscores its potential for addressing the proteolytic deficits seen in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Klettner et al., 2013). The candidate’s well-defined molecular processing pathway—from synthesis as an inactive proenzyme to activation within the acidic environment of the lysosome—ensures that it is both functionally and biologically suited to compensate for endogenous maturation deficits (Sharif, 2015). This detailed understanding of its biochemistry and cellular uptake mechanisms via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor supports the hypothesis that subretinal delivery of rhCTSD could enhance proteolytic flux, reduce drusen accumulation, and ultimately contribute to the preservation of retinal function in patients with dry AMD (Liu, 2021; Marques et al., 2020).

Despite these promising attributes, the candidate’s clinical translation will require addressing several key challenges. Future studies must rigorously evaluate the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of subretinally delivered rhCTSD, with particular emphasis on its stability, local retention time in the subretinal space, and potential immunogenicity. It will also be critical to determine whether augmenting CTSD activity alone is sufficient to counteract the multi-factorial processes underlying dry AMD or if the therapeutic strategy should be integrated into a broader, combination-based treatment regimen. Additionally, long-term safety studies are necessary to monitor for potential adverse effects, such as immune-mediated clearance or detrimental off-target proteolytic activity that might impair retinal structure and function (Marques et al., 2020; Thiessen, 2023).

Ultimately, the overall evaluation is cautiously optimistic. The mechanistic rationale is strong—supported by extensive preclinical data from related neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disorder models—and the therapeutic candidate is produced under rigorous, GMP-compliant conditions, offering a level of quality assurance that is imperative for clinical advancement (Marques et al., 2020; Liu, 2021). The specificity of recombinant pro-cathepsin D in directly addressing a rate-limiting step in lysosomal degradation makes it an especially compelling candidate in a disease setting where impaired autophagy and proteolysis are central to pathology (Klettner et al., 2013). However, challenges related to effective subretinal delivery, the potential for immune responses, and the need to integrate its action within the broader context of AMD pathogenesis must be rigorously addressed in subsequent preclinical and clinical studies before a definitive therapeutic benefit can be confirmed (Marques et al., 2020; Benes et al., 2008). In light of these considerations, recombinant human pro-cathepsin D stands out as a promising avenue for therapeutic intervention in dry AMD, meriting further investigation to delineate its efficacy, safety, and long-term benefits in the appropriate animal models and ultimately in clinical trials.
