Proposal for ZLN005 (Sigma SML1649)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic, small-molecule benzimidazole identified by high-throughput screening of ~48,000 compounds using a HEK293 cell line harboring a human PGC-1α promoter–driven luciferase reporter; it was selected for its ability to transcriptionally induce the Ppargc1a (PGC-1α) gene and validated in follow-up orthogonal assays and cell types (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021). Chemically, ZLN005 is 2-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1H-benzimidazole with a reported molecular weight of 250.3; it is repeatedly described as a “small-molecule PGC-1α transcriptional activator/agonist” and a “specific and selective transcriptional inducer of PGC-1α expression” (Bleckwehl et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2013; Maurice et al., 2022). The initial discovery campaign also yielded a related backbone compound (ZLN027) that showed cytotoxicity, whereas ZLN005 did not under the reported in vitro conditions, and ZLN005 was later found to inhibit luciferases—an assay interference red flag that necessitates careful interpretation of luciferase-based readouts (Zhang et al., 2013).

Pharmacologic class and precedent: ZLN005 belongs to the class of tool/investigational small molecules that transcriptionally upregulate PGC-1α and thereby stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty-acid oxidation in a tissue-selective fashion (Zhang et al., 2013). This class has been deployed broadly in preclinical systems—skeletal muscle, cardiomyocytes, neurons, kidney, lung epithelium, vascular smooth muscle, and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)—to probe whether enhancing PGC-1α can restore mitochondrial capacity, reduce oxidative stress, and improve cell/tissue resilience (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021). A subset of studies emphasizes that ZLN005 acts upstream of AMPK→PGC-1α/MEF2 transcriptional circuits and engages canonical mitochondrial biogenesis regulators (NRF1/2, TFAM, ERRs), while in some tissues it promotes downstream fatty-acid oxidation via CPT-1α, aligning with the recognized role of PGC-1α as a master coactivator of oxidative metabolism (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
ZLN005 has no reported clinical use. Its portfolio of preclinical applications includes:

- Metabolic disease: In diabetic db/db mice, chronic oral ZLN005 (15 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks) improved glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, and dyslipidemia, with induction of PGC-1α and mitochondrial/FAO gene programs in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic gluconeogenic transcripts; AMPK/ACC phosphorylation rose in muscle but not liver, consistent with tissue selectivity (Zhang et al., 2013). Basic single-dose oral pharmacokinetics in db/db mice showed rapid plasma absorption and high initial liver exposure, with relatively stable muscle exposure over 4 hours (Zhang et al., 2013). A short-term rat safety study (75 mg/kg/day, 14 days) reported survival with no obvious changes in body weight gain or gross metabolic parameters (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Skeletal muscle cells: In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 dose-dependently increased PGC-1α mRNA, glucose uptake, and palmitate oxidation; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increased, PGC-1α induction was AMPK-dependent (Compound C–sensitive), and MEF2 promoter integrity was required, consistent with a transcriptional mechanism (Zhang et al., 2013).

- Kidney ischemia–reperfusion injury (AKI): In mouse I/R models and H/R-injured renal tubular cells, ZLN005 restored PGC-1α and CPT-1α expression, improved mitochondrial ultrastructure/membrane potential, reduced ROS and lipid peroxidation (H₂O₂, MDA), lessened apoptosis, and required CPT-1α activity for benefit; high concentrations were toxic to HK2 cells (Wang et al., 2021).

- Neuronal injury: ZLN005 improved viability in OGD/R-injured PC12 cells, induced PGC-1α and antioxidant genes (SOD1/HO-1), and post-ischemia administration reduced infarct volume and neurological deficit in rat tMCAO, indicating neuroprotection likely via PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial and antioxidant programs; in a separate study, ZLN005 crossed the blood–brain barrier and protected against PBDE-47 neurotoxicity via PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis (Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).

- Cardiomyocytes: In hESC-derived cardiomyocytes, brief ZLN005 exposure (10 μM, 48 h) increased PGC-1α and ERRγ, upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS/FAO genes (NRF1, TFAM, respiratory subunits, CPT1b), increased mtDNA copy number, basal OCR and ATP, and drove structural/electrophysiological maturation (longer sarcomeres, more negative RMP, enhanced Ca²⁺ handling, increased CX43) (Liu et al., 2020).

- Lung epithelium/infection: In AECs (A549 and primary AEC2), ZLN005 increased PGC-1α and NRF1, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane potential, ATP, decreased ROS and senescence markers (p21, SA-β-gal), and these effects required PGC-1α (shPGC-1α attenuated benefit); in a P. aeruginosa pneumonia model, ZLN005 pretreatment (15 mg/kg × 3) reduced bacterial load and IL-1β and rescued SIRT3 in lung, consistent with PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis activation (Ma et al., 2023; Maurice et al., 2022).

- Vascular smooth muscle cells: ZLN005 increased PGC-1α, ESRRA, NRF1, mtDNA, and ATP, shifted mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion (↑MFN2, ↓DRP1), and dispersed perinuclear aggregates, indicating enhanced mitochondrial function (Zou et al., 2025).

- Retinal and RPE models: In ARPE-19, ZLN005 robustly increased PGC-1α, upregulated transcription factors, antioxidant enzymes and mitochondrial genes, improved basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and protected against oxidative insults (H₂O₂, oxLDL, NaIO₃); protection was PGC-1α-dependent; in primary human RPE (H-RPE), 10 μM ZLN005 selectively induced PGC-1α and blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, with smaller fold-change than in ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In ex vivo rd1 retinal explants (inherited photoreceptor degeneration), ZLN005 reduced overall calpain activity, shifted calpain isoform balance toward neuroprotective calpain-1 and away from calpain-2, and enhanced photoreceptor viability, supporting retinal neuroprotection via PGC-1α activation (Wang et al., 2025).

There are no reports that ZLN005 has been tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) animal models, nor direct demonstrations that it improves RPE phagosome clearance, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, lipofuscin burden, or drusen in AMD contexts; TFEB-targeted rescue of lysosomal function and cathepsin activity in RPE has been achieved with other agents (e.g., trehalose) or genetic TFEB activation, but ZLN005 has not been evaluated in those axes in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Transcriptional induction of PGC-1α. ZLN005 increases PGC-1α transcription via the PGC-1α promoter, requiring an intact MEF2 binding site; it increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein across multiple cell types where responsive, including myotubes, cardiomyocytes, lung epithelium, VSMCs, and RPE; reliance on MEF2 sites suggests ZLN005 engages upstream signaling and chromatin/transcriptional complexes that drive Ppargc1a expression (Zhang et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025; Shu et al., 2021).

AMPK activation via mild mitochondrial uncoupling. In L6 myotubes, ZLN005 increases the cellular ADP:ATP ratio and mildly increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption in isolated mitochondria, consistent with weak uncoupling that activates AMPK; AMPK and ACC phosphorylation increase, and pharmacologic AMPK inhibition (Compound C) blocks PGC-1α induction and glucose uptake; the pathway is further modeled as AMPK-phosphorylated PGC-1α engaging MEF2C to amplify its own gene expression via positive feedback (Zhang et al., 2013). AMPK-dependence extends functionally: glucose uptake and PGC-1α induction in muscle cells require AMPK activation (Wang et al., 2021).

Downstream PGC-1α programs. Across tissues, ZLN005 induces the canonical PGC-1α program: coactivation of ERRs/PPARs/NRF1/2, upregulation of TFAM, increases in mtDNA copy number, OXPHOS complex gene products, fatty-acid oxidation enzymes (e.g., CPT-1, MCAD), and functional increases in basal/maximal OCR, ATP production, and mitochondrial content/number—data are robust in cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle, and consistent in lung epithelial cells and RPE (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2022). In kidney I/R, PGC-1α induction by ZLN005 increased CPT-1α, restored mitochondrial FAO, reduced ROS and MDA, and decreased apoptosis; genetic or pharmacologic CPT-1α inhibition abrogated ZLN005 benefit, placing FAO downstream of PGC-1α as a necessary mediator of cytoprotection in that model (Wang et al., 2021).

PGC-1α–SIRT axis and anti-inflammatory effects. In lung infection models, ZLN005 activated the PGC-1α–SIRT3 axis, rescued SIRT3 expression, and lowered IL-1β expression in infected lungs, aligning with the role of SIRT3 in mitochondrial antioxidant function (activation of SOD2, glutathione system) and with PGC-1α’s coactivation of oxidative metabolism and antioxidant defense (Maurice et al., 2022).

Cell-type specificity and paradoxical tissue effects. ZLN005 shows a cell-type- and tissue-selective response: skeletal muscle and diverse non-hepatic cells robustly induce PGC-1α, whereas primary hepatocytes do not; in db/db mice, liver PGC-1α was paradoxically downregulated, with concurrent suppression of gluconeogenic genes, possibly via indirect systemic mechanisms (Zhang et al., 2013). In RPE, primary cells (H-RPE) exhibited modest PGC-1α fold-induction relative to ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α expression, yet ZLN005 still blocked TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration in H-RPE (Shu et al., 2021).

Assay caveats. ZLN005 potently inhibits luciferases, necessitating caution and orthogonal validation for any conclusions drawn from luciferase reporters, including those targeting TFEB/TFE3 or PGC-1α target promoters (Zhang et al., 2013).

Linking to TFEB/lysosomal axis: rationale vs evidence. AMPK primes lysosomal biogenesis and function partly by inducing TFEB/TFE3, while simultaneously regulating mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; a combined AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition strategy has been proposed as superior for mitochondrial disease contexts (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/retina, genetic and pharmacologic activation of TFEB restores lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSL), improves autophagosome–lysosome fusion and catabolism, and reduces disease-relevant lipid accumulation; these TFEB-centered effects are well documented in RPE but have not been demonstrated for ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023). Some evidence in non-retinal systems places PGC-1α upstream of TFEB-regulated lysosomal activity (e.g., in Huntington disease models), supporting a conceptual link between mitochondrial biogenesis and lysosomal/autophagy competence; however, ZLN005-specific co-activation of TFEB or enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD in RPE has not been shown (Blasiak et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathobiology—RPE mitochondrial–lysosomal dysfunction. Dry AMD features RPE oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, reduced OXPHOS, fewer/disorganized mitochondria), defective mitophagy, impaired proteostasis, and lysosomal/autophagy defects that promote lipofuscin and drusen biogenesis (Hyttinen et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019). PGC-1α is highly expressed in retina/RPE and is a potent regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defenses in these cells; genetic deficiency of PGC-1α (especially combined with NRF2 loss) fosters RPE degeneration with proteostatic/lysosomal stress reminiscent of dry AMD (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK→PGC-1α signaling induces mitochondrial biogenesis and interacts with NRF2/ARE antioxidant programs; reciprocally, AMPK can promote TFEB/TFE3-driven lysosomal biogenesis, providing a bidirectional mito–lyso coupling framework relevant to RPE homeostasis (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

What ZLN005 is expected to do in RPE assays. In ARPE-19 and H-RPE, ZLN005 selectively induces PGC-1α, improves mitochondrial respiration, upregulates mitochondrial/antioxidant gene expression, and protects against oxidative insults; PGC-1α dependence of cytoprotection has been demonstrated in ARPE-19 (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In H-RPE, ZLN005 prevents TGFβ₂-induced EMT and migration, linking PGC-1α induction to preservation of epithelial phenotype and metabolic competence under stress (Shu et al., 2021). Based on these data, in RPE assays ZLN005 is expected to:

- Increase PGC-1α transcript/protein and downstream mitochondrial biogenesis (e.g., NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS genes), raising basal/maximal respiration and spare capacity, and boosting ATP (Tong et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020).  
- Lower ROS and improve mitochondrial membrane potential and structure, thereby reducing oxidative injury susceptibility (Tong et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023).  
- Preserve epithelial features and reduce EMT/migration under profibrotic stress (TGFβ₂), maintaining RPE barrier function (Shu et al., 2021).

Hypothesized effects on lysosomes/TFEB/CTSD and phagosome clearance. The proposal posits that ZLN005 will “cooperate with TFEB to enhance lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D activity, thereby improving phagosome clearance” and that improved mito–lyso coupling will reduce lipofuscin. Available evidence supports the general biological framework—AMPK can activate TFEB/TFE3 and PGC-1α in parallel, PGC-1α/NRF2 promote mitochondrial homeostasis and antioxidant capacity in RPE, and TFEB activation restores lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic flux in diseased RPE—but there are no direct data that ZLN005 activates TFEB, increases lysosomal acidification, elevates cathepsin D activity, or enhances phagosome clearance in RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). In fact, the TFEB-centric rescue of CTSD/LAMP1 and lysosome function in AMD-model RPE has been demonstrated with trehalose or genetic TFEB activation, not with ZLN005; therefore, any expectation that ZLN005 alone will enhance lysosomal acidification/CTSD or phagosome clearance is a plausible but unproven hypothesis that requires explicit testing with lysosomal pH probes, CTSD activity assays, and POS phagocytosis/phagosome clearance metrics in primary human RPE (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Important caveats for experimental design:  
- Reporter interference: ZLN005 inhibits luciferases and may confound TFEB/E-box luciferase or PGC-1α reporter assays; use non-luciferase readouts (e.g., immunoblots, qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, RNA-seq, proteomics, TFEB nuclear translocation imaging, LysoTracker/DQ-BSA/CTSD activity assays) (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Primary vs cell line responsiveness: Primary H-RPE shows smaller PGC-1α fold-induction than ARPE-19 due to higher baseline PGC-1α; dosing windows and exposure times must be optimized in H-RPE to achieve functional gains without undue mitochondrial uncoupling (Shu et al., 2021).  
- Cross-talk assessment: If synergy with TFEB is a key aim, include a TFEB activator arm (e.g., trehalose) as comparator/combination and measure canonical TFEB outputs (CTSD/L, LAMP1/2, CLEAR network gene expression), while maintaining AMPK/mTORC1 pathway controls to dissect mechanism (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Direct RPE activity. ZLN005 selectively upregulates PGC-1α in ARPE-19 and primary H-RPE, enhances mitochondrial respiration, and protects ARPE-19 from oxidative stress in a PGC-1α-dependent manner; it also suppresses TGFβ₂-induced EMT/migration in H-RPE, linking mitochondrial competence to epithelial stability—both highly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Robust mitochondrial biogenesis/transcriptional program. Across cardiomyocytes, muscle, and lung epithelium, ZLN005 reproducibly induces PGC-1α and downstream transcriptional programs (NRF1/TFAM/OXPHOS/FAO), increasing mtDNA, OCR, and ATP, establishing a mechanistic basis for improving RPE mitochondrial deficits observed in dry AMD (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023; Hyttinen et al., 2023).  
- Systems-level cytoprotection. In AKI and neuronal ischemia/toxicity models, ZLN005 reduces ROS and apoptosis, improves mitochondrial integrity, and requires key downstream effectors (CPT-1α in kidney), demonstrating that PGC-1α activation can translate to organ protection, which conceptually extends to RPE under oxidative/energetic stress (Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2023).  
- Disease relevance of the target. Extensive genetic/pathophysiologic evidence places PGC-1α at the center of RPE mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant defense, and senescence control; PGC-1α or PGC-1α/NRF2 loss causes AMD-like degeneration, and AMPK→PGC-1α and NRF2/ARE axes are validated protective mechanisms in RPE (Felszeghy et al., 2019; Hyttinen et al., 2018; Hyttinen et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).  
- Translational feasibility. ZLN005 has oral bioactivity with favorable metabolic endpoints in mice, rudimentary short-term rat safety, and a breadth of preclinical efficacy across tissues; it penetrates the CNS, implying some potential for ocular exposure via circulation, though eye PK is unknown (Zhang et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2023).

Limitations and risks  
- No direct evidence for TFEB/lysosomal activation by ZLN005. There are no data showing that ZLN005 increases TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, or phagosome clearance in RPE; TFEB-dependent improvements in lysosome function and CTSD have been demonstrated with other interventions (trehalose or genetic TFEB activation), not with ZLN005 (Ghosh et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021). The hypothesized mito–lyso crosstalk is biologically plausible via AMPK signaling but remains to be demonstrated for this compound (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Potential pro-angiogenic signaling. PGC-1α/ERRα activation in RPE has been linked to VEGF upregulation under certain conditions; in a chronic retinal setting, inadvertent promotion of angiogenic signaling could be undesirable, especially near neovascular AMD thresholds; careful assessment of VEGF/angiogenic gene expression in RPE and choroid is warranted (Blasiak et al., 2021).  
- Dose window and uncoupling toxicity. ZLN005 acts at least partly via mild mitochondrial uncoupling to activate AMPK; while beneficial in moderation, uncoupling can exacerbate ROS and bioenergetic stress if overdosed; high ZLN005 concentrations were toxic in HK2 cells, underscoring the need for careful titration in primary H-RPE (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2021).  
- Cell-type and species specificity. ZLN005 does not induce PGC-1α in primary hepatocytes and downregulated hepatic PGC-1α in db/db mice; responsiveness varies by cell context (e.g., smaller fold-change in H-RPE than ARPE-19), complicating dose translation and efficacy prediction in human RPE in vivo (Zhang et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2021).  
- Reporter assay interference. The compound inhibits luciferases; any reliance on luciferase readouts for PGC-1α or TFEB activity risks artifact and demands orthogonal assay confirmation (Zhang et al., 2013).  
- Ocular pharmacokinetics unknown. Oral PK demonstrates high liver exposure and moderate muscle exposure; there are no data on ocular distribution, RPE exposure, or retinal bioavailability, making formulation and dosing strategies for eye delivery an open question (Zhang et al., 2013).

Decision-critical gaps and suggested de-risking experiments  
- TFEB/lysosomal axis: Directly test whether ZLN005 increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR network gene expression, lysosomal pH acidification (ratiometric probes), CTSD/CTSL protein/activity, and autophagosome flux (LC3B-II/p62 turnover) in primary H-RPE; benchmark versus trehalose and/or genetic TFEB activation and evaluate additivity or synergy in ZLN005+trehalose combination, with AMPK/mTORC1 pathway readouts to mechanistically link signaling (Ghosh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Phagosome processing: Quantify photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and phagosome clearance kinetics, including cathepsin-dependent proteolysis and lipofuscinogenic adduct accumulation, under oxidative/complement stress ± ZLN005; include PGC-1α knockdown to confirm dependence (Tong et al., 2022; Felszeghy et al., 2019).  
- In vivo efficacy in AMD-relevant models: Test in complement/CFH risk allele iPSC-RPE xenograft or sodium iodate/aging mouse models focusing on RPE structure/function, lipofuscin proxies, sub-RPE deposit formation, and ERG endpoints; incorporate TFEB activation arms where possible to validate the dual-axis hypothesis (Ghosh et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022).  
- Safety pharmacology: Titrate ZLN005 dosing in ocular delivery paradigms (intravitreal, periocular, or systemic) with eye PK, retinal/RPE exposure, retinal function (ERG), and VEGF expression profiling to exclude pro-angiogenic shifts; assess off-target mitochondrial stress at higher exposures in H-RPE (Blasiak et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

Conclusion: fit for further evaluation with focused lysosome endpoints. ZLN005 has strong mechanistic and preclinical support as a PGC-1α activator that improves mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative resilience in RPE and retina-adjacent systems, and it produces protective effects across diverse tissues via PGC-1α-dependent programs (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). However, the core elements of the present hypothesis—enhancement of TFEB activity, lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and phagosome clearance, plus reduction of lipofuscin and drusen—are not yet evidenced for ZLN005 and remain inferential based on pathway crosstalk (AMPK→TFEB/TFE3, PGC-1α–NRF2) and TFEB-targeted rescue in RPE by other agents (Boya et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Consequently, ZLN005 is a promising mitochondrial-centric candidate for dry AMD that merits accelerated, targeted validation on lysosomal/phagosome endpoints and ocular delivery feasibility. The compound’s strengths—a validated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism in RPE, demonstrated oxidative stress protection in ARPE-19, primary H-RPE EMT suppression, and broad cross-tissue efficacy—justify this investment, provided that the risks of off-target uncoupling, reporter assay interference, cell-type specificity, and potential pro-angiogenic signaling are actively managed in the experimental plan (Tong et al., 2022; Shu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2013; Blasiak et al., 2021).

Proposal for T0901317 (Sigma T2320)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
T0901317 is a fully synthetic small‐molecule agonist originally identified through screening for compounds that activate liver X receptors (LXRs). It belongs to the class of nuclear receptor ligands and is structurally designed to mimic endogenous oxysterols, the natural activators of LXRs. LXRs, comprising two isoforms, LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), are master transcriptional regulators of cholesterol, lipid, and glucose metabolism. T0901317 was first characterized for its capacity to bind and stimulate these receptors, thereby upregulating target genes involved in cholesterol efflux such as ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) and apolipoprotein E (APOE) (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). The compound has been widely used in preclinical studies to investigate cholesterol homeostasis, inflammation modulation, and emerging neuroprotective pathways. Its chemical synthesis follows standard procedures for developing derivatives that confer high receptor affinity and bioactivity while allowing researchers to dissect LXR-dependent pathways in multiple cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The rationale behind using such LXR agonists, including T0901317, in ocular disorders like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) stems from their demonstrated ability to restore cholesterol efflux, ameliorate lipid deposition, and reduce inflammatory stress in target tissues (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, T0901317 has been utilized extensively within the biomedical research arena as a tool compound to elucidate the role of LXRs in metabolic and inflammatory diseases. Preclinical work has demonstrated that LXR activation in key tissues, including the retina, can reestablish lipid homeostasis and reduce pathological lipid accumulation. Several studies indicate that in LXR-deficient models, there is an accumulation of neutral lipids and extracellular deposits—features that are remarkably similar to drusen formation observed in early dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10). In animal models, particularly in mice lacking the Nr1h3 isoform, the phenotype includes RPE dysfunction, inflammatory microenvironment formation, and structural changes that closely mimic human dry AMD pathology (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). Although T0901317 has not advanced to clinical trials for AMD, its efficacy has been primarily established in vitro using human RPE cell models and in vivo in murine models. The compound has shown potential for correcting the dysregulated cholesterol metabolism that contributes to the chronic buildup of lipid-rich drusen—a central pathological hallmark of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 15–16). Outside of ocular applications, compounds from this class have been investigated for atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration, further emphasizing the critical link between cholesterol metabolism and chronic inflammatory conditions (Malek & Lad, 2014, pp. 13–15).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of T0901317 is fundamentally tied to its role as a potent activator of LXRs. Upon binding to LXRα and LXRβ within retinal cells, T0901317 facilitates heterodimerization with retinoid X receptors (RXRs), forming a transcriptionally active complex that binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. This activation cascade results in upregulation of numerous genes critical for cholesterol efflux and lipid metabolism, most notably ABCA1 and APOE (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16). Upregulation of ABCA1 increases the efflux of excess cholesterol and oxidized lipids from RPE cells into the extracellular environment, thereby reducing the intracellular lipid load that predisposes cells to toxicity and drusen accumulation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Wu et al., 2023, pp. 10–12).

Beyond cholesterol efflux, T0901317 activates additional gene networks that modulate lysosomal function and autophagy. Experimental data suggest that T0901317 enhances the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and promotes the assembly of vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPases (v-ATPase), essential for maintaining lysosomal acidity (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). This increase in active lysosomal enzymes and reinforced acidification contributes to the improved clearance of debris, particularly drusen components composed of lipid and protein aggregates. Furthermore, LXR activation by T0901317 has been shown to increase autophagy gene expression, thereby inducing a mitophagy response that removes damaged organelles and supports cellular metabolic renewal (Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10; Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). In addition, T0901317 exerts significant anti-inflammatory effects by downregulating NF-κB signaling. It has been observed to inhibit the phosphorylation of IκBα, which prevents the nuclear translocation of NF-κB and subsequent transcription of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17; Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). This dual role in lipid regulation and inflammation attenuation is central to its therapeutic promise in AMD, where chronic inflammation and disrupted lipid processing are major determinants of disease progression.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, with its hallmark drusen deposits and RPE dysfunction, the expected therapeutic effect of T0901317 is multifold. By activating LXRs in RPE cells, T0901317 is expected to upregulate the expression of ABCA1 and other cholesterol efflux mediators, thereby reducing the intracellular build‐up of cholesterol and oxidized lipids that contribute to drusen formation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4). This increase in cholesterol efflux would allow the RPE to better clear lipid debris, lowering the overall lipid burden on Bruch’s membrane. Concomitantly, the drug’s capacity to augment lysosomal function is anticipated to result in improved clearance of extracellular drusen components via a cathepsin D–dependent mechanism. Enhanced v-ATPase assembly and lysosomal acidification, as demonstrated by increased CTSD activity in vitro, should restore the degradative capacity of the lysosomal system, thereby facilitating the removal of protein-lipid aggregates (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33).

Furthermore, the activation of autophagy pathways and promotion of mitophagy are expected to counteract the mitochondrial dysfunction that characterizes aged RPE cells—an integral pathological feature of dry AMD (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 7–9, 2–4). The anticipated result is a restoration of cellular homeostasis, improved energy metabolism, and reduction in oxidative stress, all of which are essential for maintaining RPE cell integrity. RPE cells have been shown to express both LXRα and LXRβ, and their expression is frequently diminished in AMD-affected eyes (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Lyssenko et al., 2018, pp. 1–3). Therefore, by boosting LXR activity, T0901317 not only counteracts lipid dysregulation but also provides a neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory benefit by modulating cytokine production and dampening microglial activation in the outer retina (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6).

Overall Evaluation:  
The overall assessment of T0901317 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration is cautiously optimistic, with several key strengths as well as notable limitations that warrant further investigation.  

Strengths:  
One of the primary advantages of T0901317 is its well-documented ability to activate LXRs and thereby induce a broad spectrum of beneficial responses relevant to dry AMD pathology. The compound’s capacity to upregulate ABCA1 expression is critical, as impaired cholesterol efflux is a central mechanism underlying the accumulation of lipid-rich drusen (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 15–16, 12–13). Moreover, its ability to enhance lysosomal enzyme expression and promote v-ATPase assembly is particularly promising for the restoration of lysosomal acidity—a key defect in aged RPE cells that contributes to decreased clearance of toxic lipid deposits (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 13–17, 20–22). In addition, the induction of autophagy and mitophagy following LXR activation offers a dual therapeutic benefit by promoting the removal of damaged mitochondria and reducing oxidative stress, thereby preserving RPE cell viability (Xie et al., 2022, pp. 1–2). The anti-inflammatory properties of T0901317, demonstrated by its inhibition of NF-κB signaling and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, further support its potential utility in addressing the chronic low-grade inflammation often observed in AMD (Choudhary & Malek, 2016, pp. 4–6). Collectively, these mechanisms directly target the multifactorial aspects of dry AMD pathology—namely, lipid dysregulation, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammatory stress—making T0901317 an attractive candidate for repurposing in this indication (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Another significant strength is the potential for ocular delivery strategies to mitigate the systemic side effects associated with T0901317. Given that systemic administration of LXR agonists has been linked to adverse metabolic effects such as hypertriglyceridemia and off-target activation of nuclear receptors like FXR and PXR (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16), localized ocular delivery could concentrate the drug’s therapeutic effects in the retina while minimizing systemic exposure. This approach may overcome one of the principal limitations of T0901317 and reposition it as a viable option specifically for retinal applications.

Weaknesses and Challenges:  
Despite these promising attributes, there are several challenges that temper the enthusiasm for T0901317 as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. A well-recognized limitation of T0901317 is its lack of absolute specificity for LXRs. Its ability to activate other nuclear receptors such as FXR and PXR raises concerns about off-target effects that could lead to dysregulated lipid metabolism in non-ocular tissues, systemic toxicity, and unwanted metabolic side effects such as hepatic steatosis and hyperlipidemia (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22). Moreover, while preclinical evidence in cell culture and murine models has shown that LXR activation can reverse lipid accumulation and partially restore RPE cell function, the translation of such effects to the human condition—especially over the chronic time course of dry AMD—remains to be conclusively demonstrated (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13, 7–9).

Another challenge lies in the fact that many preclinical studies have used alternative LXR agonists such as GW3965, which may exhibit a more favorable safety profile compared to T0901317 (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 9–11; Peters et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). The potential differences in selectivity and off-target activity between T0901317 and these other compounds necessitate a careful comparison. It is possible that while T0901317 has provided invaluable mechanistic insights into LXR biology in the retina, compounds with improved specificity may eventually be more amenable to clinical development. Furthermore, the specific hypothesis regarding T0901317’s ability to enhance lysosomal acidity and cathepsin D-dependent clearance of drusen components is based on in vitro observations, and there is still a need for more comprehensive studies that document these effects in animal models that recapitulate the chronic aspects of dry AMD pathology (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 25–33; Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4).

Additionally, because the retinal environment is highly specialized and the RPE plays a central role in maintaining photoreceptor health, any therapeutic approach must carefully balance metabolic reprogramming with preservation of essential RPE functions. Overactivation of autophagy or lysosomal pathways might conceivably lead to other cellular stresses if not properly calibrated. Thus, while the theoretical framework for T0901317’s benefit in dry AMD is strong, detailed pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies in appropriate models are essential before moving this candidate further along the drug development pathway.

Conclusion:  
In conclusion, T0901317 demonstrates considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration based on its ability to activate LXR in RPE cells, thereby inducing cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 upregulation, enhancing lysosomal function through increased expression of hydrolases like cathepsin D, promoting autophagy and mitophagy, and reducing inflammation by dampening NF-κB signaling (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 12–13; Terao et al., 2024, pp. 8–10).

The strengths of T0901317 lie in its robust mechanistic rationale, the preclinical evidence supporting LXR-mediated restoration of cholesterol homeostasis, and the potential for localized ocular delivery to minimize systemic toxicities. However, its known off-target effects, particularly activation of other nuclear receptor pathways that can lead to metabolic side effects, present a significant hurdle that must be addressed through formulation optimization and dosing strategies (Lei et al., 2017, pp. 20–22; Storti et al., 2019, pp. 15–16). Furthermore, while the mechanistic underpinnings are appealing, further in vivo validation in chronic, clinically relevant AMD models is essential to confirm that the improvements in cholesterol efflux and lysosomal function translate into meaningful therapeutic outcomes—in terms of slowing or reversing the progression of dry AMD. Overall, T0901317 represents a promising, though challenging, candidate for addressing the unmet need in dry AMD therapy. Investment in additional preclinical studies focusing on ocular bioavailability, long-term safety in the retinal microenvironment, and optimization of dosing regimens will be critical in determining whether T0901317 or a similarly acting, perhaps more selective, LXR agonist can progress into clinical evaluation for dry AMD. The strategic focus on lipid-driven dysfunction, particularly in lysosomal clearance pathways, offers a novel mechanism of action that could complement or serve as an alternative to current therapeutic approaches, making T0901317 (or its optimized derivatives) a compelling candidate for further investigation (Choudhary et al., 2020, pp. 2–4, 7–9, 13–17).

Proposal for AZD9056 (Axellus)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AZD9056 is a small‐molecule, orally active P2X7 receptor antagonist developed by AstraZeneca that belongs to the class of synthetic adamantane‐based compounds. Although its precise chemical structure has not been fully disclosed in the public domain, multiple reports indicate that it emerges from a medicinal chemistry program focused on adamantyl benzamide scaffolds discovered through high‐throughput screening and subsequent structure–activity relationship (SAR) optimization (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). The compound is understood to maintain the essential adamantane moiety linked through a methylene spacer to an aromatic benzamide, which is thought to force a twist in the benzamide conformation critical for high P2X7 antagonism (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007). In general, the adamantane class of compounds has been explored for its lipophilic and sterically constrained properties that can impart favorable bioavailability and receptor selectivity; indeed, the adamantane scaffold has also been exploited in a number of antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents. In the case of AZD9056, this design strategy was implemented to yield a molecule that potently blocks the ATP‐driven activity of the P2X7 receptor—a ligand‐gated ion channel implicated in inflammation and cell death—while offering the oral bioavailability and acceptable pharmacokinetic properties required for systemic application (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). The overall discovery process appears to have combined hit identification with parallel synthetic approaches in order to establish an SAR profile that ultimately led to a candidate with nanomolar potency in cell‐based assays of P2X7 function, such as inhibition of Bz-ATP–induced Ca2+ influx and dye uptake, although the specific synthetic steps remain proprietary (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
AZD9056 has been evaluated extensively in non‐ocular inflammatory disease contexts. Early-phase clinical trials established its safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers through single- and multiple-dose studies that characterized its pharmacokinetic profile, with parameters such as a moderate oral bioavailability (~62%), a terminal half-life in the range of 16–18 hours, and the capacity for once-daily dosing (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Its development program initially focused on rheumatoid arthritis (RA). In a 4-week phase IIa trial in RA patients, AZD9056 was found to be safe and well tolerated at the doses assessed, and target engagement was evidenced by significant inhibition of ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release (Chrovian et al., 2014). However, a subsequent larger phase IIb study in RA, enrolling up to 385 or more patients and including an open etanercept comparator arm, failed to demonstrate superior clinical efficacy over placebo across several objective endpoints, even though tolerability remained acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Lepre et al., 2023). In parallel with its RA development, AZD9056 also underwent evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), specifically in patients with Crohn's disease, where a phase IIa trial using a 200 mg once-daily regimen showed nominal improvements in the Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (CDAI) but no accompanying improvement in inflammatory biomarkers (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Rech et al., 2016). Aside from these clinical endeavors in systemic inflammatory disorders, a dedicated ocular safety study was conducted in healthy volunteers; in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, retinal function was directly assessed by measures including electroretinography and visual acuity—an indication that the eye was considered as a potential compartment of interest, even though no efficacy studies in ocular disease states such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) have been reported (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). Overall, while the compound has been repurposed extensively for anti-inflammatory indications and has an established human safety profile, its clinical history thus far has not included a trial specifically targeting dry AMD or any direct veterinary employments for ocular diseases (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Mechanism of Action:  
The P2X7 receptor (P2X7R) is an ATP-gated, nonselective cation channel predominantly expressed on immune cells and, importantly for the intended application, on the retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) (Calzaferri et al., 2020). Under physiological conditions, P2X7R is quiescent; however, in the presence of elevated extracellular ATP—a phenomenon noted in inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including AMD—the receptor becomes activated, mediating several deleterious downstream events. Upon activation, P2X7R undergoes a conformational change that not only allows the influx of Ca2+ and Na+ but also promotes the formation of large membrane pores owing to its ability to transition into a state that permits the passage of molecules as large as 900 Da (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015). This pore formation results in cytotoxic calcium overload and is directly linked to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex responsible for the processing of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). In the retinal pigment epithelium, this ATP-driven activation has been shown to contribute to lysosomal alkalization—a process that impairs the optimal acidic environment required by lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsins—and ultimately leads to defective clearance of cellular debris (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Specifically, experimental studies in ARPE-19 cells (a human RPE cell line) have demonstrated that stimulation of P2X7 induces lysosomal dysfunction; conversely, pharmacological inhibition of P2X7 using antagonists such as Brilliant Blue G (BBG) can reverse this lysosomal impairment (Tempest-Roe, 2017). Mechanistically, AZD9056 is designed to bind to the P2X7 receptor with high potency and selectivity, thereby preventing the receptor’s activation by ATP. By doing so, it is anticipated to block the cascade of events that lead from receptor activation to pore formation, inflammasome assembly, and subsequent IL-1β release (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Lee et al., 2023). Although the exact molecular binding mode of AZD9056 has not been detailed in available literature, it is presumed to interact with key residues involved in channel gating and pore formation, thereby stabilizing the receptor in a closed, inactive conformation (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023). Additionally, its ability to reduce ex vivo ATP-induced monocyte IL-1β release in healthy volunteers has served as a functional biomarker for target engagement, reinforcing the hypothesis that P2X7 antagonism can modulate inflammasome-driven inflammatory signaling (Chrovian et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2023).  

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry age-related macular degeneration, the central hypothesis for repurposing AZD9056 is that it will antagonize P2X7 receptors on retinal pigmented epithelium cells, thereby preventing a cascade of ATP-driven pathological events. Elevated extracellular ATP levels have been documented in the vitreous of AMD patients, which suggests a pathological activation of purinergic signaling in the retina (Calzaferri et al., 2020). When ATP activates P2X7 receptors on RPE cells, it leads to two major deleterious outcomes. First, the receptor’s activation results in sustained Ca2+ influx and large pore formation, triggering cytotoxicity and subsequent cell death mechanisms, including apoptotic and inflammasome-dependent cell death pathways (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Second, P2X7 activation has been mechanistically linked to lysosomal alkalization in RPE cells, which impairs the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D; this enzyme is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other cellular debris (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The hypothesis posits that by blocking P2X7 receptor activation with AZD9056, one would preserve the normal acidic environment of the lysosomes, thereby maintaining or even restoring optimal cathepsin D activity. In turn, these effects are anticipated to protect the RPE from inflammasome-mediated apoptosis and lysosomal dysfunction, which are key drivers of geographic atrophy, the advanced clinical manifestation of dry AMD (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Calzaferri et al., 2020). Preclinical studies support the role of P2X7 in mediating RPE degeneration; for example, genetic knockout of P2X7 in mouse models has been shown to protect against Alu RNA-induced RPE toxicity, an established model of dry AMD pathology (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Furthermore, in vitro studies using human RPE cell cultures have indicated that P2X7 receptor blockade can reverse lysosomal impairment, suggesting that AZD9056 could produce measurable improvements in functional assays that evaluate lysosomal protease activity, such as cathepsin D activity assays, and overall RPE viability assays (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Ultimately, if the protective effects seen in preclinical studies translate into the clinical setting, AZD9056 may reduce the accumulation of undigested cellular debris (drusen) and slow or halt the progression of geographic atrophy in patients with dry AMD by dampening the inflamed state and preserving RPE function (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018).  

Overall Evaluation:  
From a drug development perspective, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD presents a compelling but challenging opportunity. One of the primary strengths of this therapeutic candidate lies in its robust mechanistic rationale. The P2X7 receptor plays a central role in mediating ATP-induced inflammasome activation, lysosomal dysfunction, and subsequent RPE cell death—pathophysiological processes that have been repeatedly implicated in dry AMD and geographic atrophy models (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). The ability of P2X7 antagonists to block these processes has been demonstrated in various in vitro and in vivo models, where blockade of the receptor reduces IL-1β release, reverses lysosomal alkalization, and confers protection against RPE degeneration (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). Furthermore, AZD9056 has gone through extensive clinical safety evaluations in multiple inflammatory disease indications; its pharmacokinetic profile—characterized by acceptable oral bioavailability and a half-life conducive to once-daily dosing—has been well established in early phase studies (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This pre-existing clinical safety data is an asset in reducing the risk profile typically associated with novel drug candidates and may streamline early-stage clinical trial designs for an ocular indication. Additionally, preliminary ocular safety assessments in healthy volunteers, which included measures such as retinal electroretinography and visual acuity testing, suggest that systemic administration of AZD9056 does not produce overt ocular toxicity—an encouraging sign for its potential repurposing in dry AMD (Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Nevertheless, there are several notable limitations and challenges associated with using AZD9056 in the treatment of dry AMD. First, the prior clinical development history of AZD9056 in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease revealed limited or inconsistent efficacy despite demonstrable target engagement. In the phase IIb studies for RA, the compound failed to outperform placebo across objective outcome measures even though safety endpoints were met (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014). This raises concerns about whether P2X7 receptor blockade alone is sufficient to generate a meaningful clinical outcome, particularly in a complex and multifactorial disease process such as dry AMD. Moreover, the inflammatory milieu in rheumatoid arthritis or IBD differs significantly from that in the retina, and systemic inflammation may not accurately recapitulate the localized, chronic degenerative processes occurring in the RPE (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Guile et al., 2009).  

Another concern relates to the dual and sometimes paradoxical roles of the P2X7 receptor. While its pathological activation is linked to pro-inflammatory signaling, P2X7 also appears to have a scavenger or phagocytic function under conditions of low ATP levels (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Newman, 2024). In the context of the RPE, which is specialized for high-volume phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, complete blockade of P2X7 might inadvertently impair beneficial clearance processes that serve to prevent debris accumulation. In animal models, alternative data has shown that the loss of P2X7 function can result in changes reminiscent of early AMD, such as reduced phagocytosis, suggesting that finely balanced modulation rather than total inhibition may be necessary (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Such duality underscores the potential risk that while AZD9056 may ameliorate inflammasome activation and lysosomal destabilization, it might simultaneously disrupt physiologic functions of RPE cells that are critical for maintaining retinal homeostasis.  

The lack of direct evidence for AZD9056’s efficacy in ocular models of dry AMD is another major gap. While the preclinical literature supports a role for P2X7 signaling in RPE dysfunction and geographic atrophy (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017), the specific application of AZD9056 in these models remains largely inferential. There are no published studies documenting that AZD9056, when administered at doses achieving retinal penetration, effectively preserves cathepsin D activity or prevents RPE cell death in animal models of dry AMD. Furthermore, the translation of systemic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data to ocular compartments is nontrivial; disparities in drug distribution, blood–retinal barrier permeability, and local metabolism could limit effective target engagement in the retina even if systemic safety is acceptable (Arulkumaran et al., 2011). The undisclosed chemical structure of AZD9056 also complicates any efforts to optimize the compound specifically for ocular bioavailability or to better understand its off-target profile relative to other P2X7 antagonists that have been more thoroughly characterized in the literature (Chrovian et al., 2014; Gunosewoyo et al., 2007).  

In summary, the overall evaluation of AZD9056 for treatment of dry AMD is one of cautious enthusiasm tempered by several unresolved questions. On the strength side, the compound leverages a clear mechanistic rationale by antagonizing the P2X7 receptor—a key mediator of ATP-induced inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction known to be active in the RPE of AMD patients—and it comes with an established clinical safety record in inflammatory disorders (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018). Its ability to suppress IL-1β release in ex vivo assays supports its functional engagement with the P2X7/IL-1β pathway, and preclinical data suggest that P2X7 inhibition can protect against RPE degeneration (Gu & Wiley, 2018; Tempest-Roe, 2017). However, significant challenges persist: prior clinical trials in RA and IBD have yielded mixed efficacy results, casting doubt on whether P2X7 blockade alone can significantly modify disease progression in complex conditions; the potential for interference with beneficial receptor functions in the RPE may compromise its utility; and the lack of direct preclinical data in dry AMD models means that much of the benefit remains theoretical at this stage (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Territo & Zarrinmayeh, 2021). Additionally, uncertainties related to ocular pharmacokinetics and the inability to adjust the synthetic structure for improved retinal targeting (given the proprietary nature of the molecule’s chemistry) further complicate its repositioning for an ocular indication (Chrovian et al., 2014; Eser et al., 2015).  

Given the current state of the literature, it would be advisable to conduct targeted preclinical studies that specifically address the effects of AZD9056 on RPE cells and retinal tissue. These studies should include assays for lysosomal pH stability, cathepsin D activity, inflammasome assembly (e.g., NLRP3 activation and caspase-1 processing), and overall RPE cell viability under conditions of ATP stress. Furthermore, careful evaluation of retinal drug levels following systemic dosing—or the development of a topical formulation—might be necessary to ensure that sufficient drug concentrations can be achieved in the retina without systemic toxicity. A parallel investigation into the potential compensatory roles of P2X7 in RPE phagocytosis would also be warranted to minimize any risk of disrupting beneficial cellular functions (Calzaferri et al., 2020; Gu & Wiley, 2018; Arulkumaran et al., 2011).  

Overall, while AZD9056’s strong mechanistic basis and favorable early-phase clinical safety profile make it an attractive candidate for repurposing, the translational challenges and previous clinical setbacks in other indications necessitate rigorous preclinical validation in dry AMD models before further clinical development is considered. The compound’s capacity to specifically maintain lysosomal function and cathepsin D activity in the RPE represents a promising therapeutic opportunity if these effects can be reliably recapitulated in the ocular setting. However, caution is advised due to the dual roles of P2X7 signaling in both pathological and physiologic processes and the potential non-optimal receptor occupancy in the retina. In conclusion, the repurposing of AZD9056 for dry AMD holds potential but would require a focused, mechanistically guided preclinical program to address the unique challenges posed by the ocular environment and the complex biology of the P2X7 receptor (Arulkumaran et al., 2011; Chrovian et al., 2014; Calzaferri et al., 2020; Tempest-Roe, 2017).

Proposal for Bexarotene (Sigma B1269)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bexarotene, commercially known as Targretin and referenced here as Sigma B1269, is a fully synthetic rexinoid that was originally designed as a selective agonist for the retinoid X receptor (RXR). It is structurally distinct from naturally occurring retinoids such as 9‐cis‐retinoic acid; its chemical structure consists of a lipophilic tetramethyltetralin moiety connected through an ethynyl linker to a benzoic acid group, a design that confers high binding affinity (nanomolar EC50 values) and specificity for RXR subtypes (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). As a member of the rexinoid class, bexarotene belongs to a group of therapeutic compounds that were developed to overcome the limitations of pan‐retinoid receptor activation by offering a more targeted means of modulating nuclear receptor signaling. RXRs have the unique ability to form either homodimers or heterodimers with a wide range of nuclear receptors—including peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptors (PPARs), liver X receptors (LXRs), thyroid hormone receptors (TRs), and vitamin D receptors (VDRs)—thereby influencing diverse gene expression programs that control cell growth, differentiation, and lipid metabolism (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). The synthetic origin of bexarotene, achieved through sophisticated organic synthesis that optimizes its lipophilic and acidic domains, enables it to engage conserved ligand‐binding residues (for example, key arginine and hydrophobic amino acids) in the RXR ligand‐binding domain, ensuring potent activation of the receptor (Chitranshi et al., 2019, p. 9; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 11–13). This profile not only underlies its efficacy in its original oncologic indications but also supports its potential for repurposing in other diseases where RXR signaling is of therapeutic interest.

Therapeutic History:  
Bexarotene is well established in clinical practice as the first FDA-approved RXR-selective agonist, primarily indicated for the treatment of refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients who have failed at least one systemic therapy (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3). Over the years, extensive clinical experience with bexarotene has been accrued in oncology, with studies demonstrating its capacity to induce cancer cell arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis by modulating the transcriptional landscape via RXR-mediated gene regulation (Heck et al., 2016, pp. 1–2, 9–10). Beyond its original role in oncology, bexarotene has been investigated in various other contexts; preclinical studies have explored its effects in non-small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and even in some hormone-sensitive malignancies—owing to its ability to interfere with proliferative signaling pathways (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Notably, recent investigations have also assessed bexarotene in neurodegenerative disease models, particularly Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease, where its RXR-mediated upregulation of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) and cholesterol transporters such as ABCA1 have been postulated to facilitate amyloid-beta clearance and neuronal protection (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). Although the compound has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its mechanism of action—centered on modulating lipid metabolism and cellular clearance pathways—suggests that its repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically plausible, especially given the involvement of dysregulated lipid homeostasis and lysosomal dysfunction in this condition (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Furthermore, RXR signaling is known to be critical in maintaining retinal homeostasis, and studies in animal models have shown that disruption of RXR function can lead to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) abnormalities, providing an indirect rationale for evaluating RXR agonists like bexarotene in ocular applications (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, bexarotene exerts its effects by binding selectively to the ligand-binding domain of RXRs with high affinity, thereby promoting conformational changes that favor the release of co-repressor proteins and the recruitment of co-activators containing LxxLL motifs. This binding event induces RXR to function either as a homodimer or, more importantly, as a heterodimer with other nuclear receptors such as LXR and PPAR, which are central to the regulation of lipid homeostasis and inflammatory responses (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3). In its role as an RXR agonist, bexarotene has been shown to markedly upregulate the transcription of genes involved in cholesterol efflux, including those coding for ATP-binding cassette transporters like ABCA1 and for apolipoproteins such as ApoE; these factors are critical for mobilizing and clearing excess cholesterol in various tissues (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, RXR agonism by bexarotene can stimulate the activity of permissive heterodimers—such as RXR/PPARα—which are known to play pivotal roles in fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism. This activation is hypothesized to extend to downstream transcriptional regulators like TFEB, the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, though direct evidence in retinal cells is still emerging (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). In several preclinical models, bexarotene has been associated with the modulation of lysosomal pathways; for instance, it can alleviate endoplasmic reticulum stress and prevent the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins, which are important contributors to intracellular lipid accumulation and cellular dysfunction (Farol & Hymes, 2004, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Moreover, its selective RXR activity circumvents the adverse effects associated with pan-retinoid receptor activation, particularly the hypercalcemic and other toxicities seen with non-selective retinoids, by limiting cross-reactivity with RARs (Jurutka et al., 2022, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). In summary, bexarotene’s multifaceted mechanism includes (1) robust activation of RXR-mediated transcription of lipid transporter genes, (2) modulation of heterodimer partners such as PPARα and LXR that indirectly regulate lipid metabolism and energy balance, and (3) potential upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis and function via TFEB-associated pathways—collectively contributing to improved cellular lipid clearance and metabolic homeostasis (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-related Macular Degeneration:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of bexarotene for dry AMD posits that activation of RXR in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells will lead to beneficial metabolic remodeling, specifically through enhancing cholesterol efflux and promoting lysosomal function. In the context of dry AMD, pathologic drusen formation is largely a consequence of chronic accumulation of lipids and misprocessed extracellular debris under the RPE. Through the activation of RXR, bexarotene is expected to upregulate key mediators of cholesterol transport such as ABCA1 and ApoE, thereby facilitating the removal of excess cholesterol and lipid deposits from the RPE (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2). In addition, RXR activation, particularly when partnered with PPARα, has been associated with the induction of a lysosomal program that involves enhanced expression of genes regulating lysosomal acidification—potentially via the upregulation of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits—and the activation of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Although direct demonstrations of TFEB activation in RPE models with bexarotene treatment are limited in the provided literature, the established role of RXR agonists in modulating lipid-rich, lysosomal compartments in other cell types supports the likelihood that a similar upregulation would occur in RPE cells (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Dheer et al., 2018, pp. 1–2). Given that TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and function, its coactivation alongside PPARα could enhance the degradative capacity of the cell, resulting in improved clearance of drusen-associated lipid aggregates. This dual action—promoting cholesterol efflux while simultaneously enhancing lysosomal catabolism—addresses two of the key pathogenic mechanisms underlying dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In vitro, one might anticipate that bexarotene treatment of cultured RPE cells will lead to increased transcript and protein levels of ABC transporters, elevated markers of lysosomal acidification such as V-ATPase subunits, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D, collectively contributing to the reduction of lipid overload at a cellular level (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9). Moreover, given its extensive clinical use in oncology with a tolerable ocular safety profile, bexarotene is well situated for repurposing, provided that its systemic adverse effects (e.g., hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism) can be managed or mitigated through controlled dosing strategies or targeted delivery approaches (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bexarotene emerges as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its well-characterized pharmacological profile and multifaceted mechanism of action. One of its primary strengths lies in its selective activation of RXR, which has been shown to trigger transcriptional programs that enhance cholesterol efflux via the upregulation of key transporters such as ABCA1 and ApoE—pathways that are directly relevant to the clearance of drusen-associated lipids in dry AMD (Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2). In addition, the potential for RXR agonism to engage PPARα and, by extension, coactivate TFEB offers a novel approach to correcting lysosomal dysfunction—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. This dual action addresses both the extracellular accumulation of lipids and the intracellular deficits in degradative capacity that contribute to RPE dysfunction. The extensive clinical experience with bexarotene in cancer therapy provides an added advantage, as its pharmacokinetics, dosing regimens, and safety profiles are well documented, thereby facilitating a more rapid transition into repurposing studies. However, several challenges and weaknesses need to be acknowledged. Bexarotene is known to cause significant metabolic side effects, including hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism, which may necessitate adjunctive treatments (such as lipid-lowering agents) or the development of targeted ocular delivery systems to minimize systemic exposure (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 2–3). Furthermore, although preclinical data in neurodegenerative models have demonstrated beneficial effects on lipid metabolism and lysosomal pathways, direct evidence in retinal pigment epithelial models is still limited. This gap underscores the need for rigorous in vitro and in vivo studies specifically designed to evaluate bexarotene’s efficacy in RPE cells and animal models of dry AMD (Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Lalloyer et al., 2009, pp. 1–2). Another potential risk involves the compound’s polypharmacological nature; while its ability to interact with multiple nuclear receptors can be advantageous for targeting complex diseases, it also raises the possibility of off-target effects, such as its documented antagonism at PPARγ in certain contexts, which could have unforeseen impacts on retinal cell physiology (Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Heck et al., 2016, pp. 7–9). The balance between therapeutic benefits and adverse effects will need to be carefully managed, perhaps by optimizing dosing regimens or by designing analogues with improved selectivity and reduced side effect profiles. In summary, the repurposing of bexarotene for dry AMD is supported by its robust activation of RXR-driven pathways related to lipid efflux and lysosomal function, as well as by its safe clinical history in ocular settings when used topically or in controlled systemic regimens. Nonetheless, additional preclinical work is essential to directly demonstrate its efficacy in RPE models and to delineate any ocular-specific pharmacodynamic parameters. Overall, the candidate shows promise as a multi‐pathway therapeutic approach for dry AMD, with strengths including its defined mechanism of action and extensive clinical history, and weaknesses largely centered on potential systemic side effects and the need for targeted delivery strategies (de Almeida & Conda‐Sheridan, 2019, pp. 8–9; Marshall et al., 2015, pp. 2–3; Chitranshi et al., 2019, pp. 1–2; Mallick et al., 2021, pp. 1–2; Marciano et al., 2015, pp. 1–2).
