Proposal for SRT1720 (Sigma SML0271)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT1720 is a first-generation synthetic small-molecule sirtuin 1 (SIRT1)–activating compound (STAC) originally discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals and optimized around an imidazo[1,2-b]thiazole chemotype to yield higher apparent potency and selectivity than the natural product resveratrol in early assay systems (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018). Subsequent mechanistic work across the STAC class resolved that many apparent activation signals were substrate/context dependent and, in some assay configurations, artifactual; nevertheless, later kinetic/biophysical and structural studies established that STACs can directly engage SIRT1 via an assisted allosteric mechanism that stabilizes the enzyme–substrate complex, with mutational data showing that E230K/A SIRT1 variants abolish both binding and activation by STACs (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). While most STACs are SIRT1-selective, SRT1720 exhibits notable polypharmacology, including reported inhibitory activity against Sirt3, highlighting potential off-target risks intrinsic to this first-generation class (Mazzone, 2018). As a class, STACs have been widely evaluated for metabolic, inflammatory, neurodegenerative, and aging phenotypes predicated on SIRT1’s broad substrate repertoire (for example, PGC-1α, NF-κB p65/RelA, FOXO family, p53), which link to mitochondrial biogenesis, anti-inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, and cell survival programs (Chang et al., 2024; Mazzone, 2018).

Therapeutic History  
SRT1720 has extensive preclinical use, but there is no evidence in the provided corpus that it has been tested in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), in the eye, or in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models (cellular or in vivo) (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Bononi et al., 2022). In non-ocular systems, SRT1720 increased mitochondrial biogenesis and rescued mitochondrial function after oxidant injury in renal proximal tubule cells, providing proof-of-concept that STAC activation can drive PGC-1α–linked mitochondrial programs in mammalian cells under oxidative stress (Ji et al., 2021). In metabolic disease models, SRT1720 is reported to improve hepatic lipid metabolism via SIRT1-dependent pathways regulating PGC-1α, AMPK, PPARα, FOXO1, SREBP-1c and FGF21, with consistent decreases in lipogenesis and inflammation and increases in fatty-acid β-oxidation in NAFLD models (Ding et al., 2017). Multiple lifespan/healthspan studies reported benefits in mice—improved survival and healthspan in diet-induced obese animals and lifespan extension on standard diet—again consistent with systemic SIRT1-axis engagement (Mazzone, 2018). At the same time, substantial controversy surrounds both mechanism and safety. Pacholec et al. argued SRT1720 (and related first-generation STACs) are not direct SIRT1 activators under specific biochemical conditions, although later work provided structural and kinetic support for allosteric activation with specific substrates (Lee et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022). Importantly for repurposing risk, SRT1720 promoted tumor cell migration and lung metastasis in a breast cancer model, and SRT1720 can trigger SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in some hematologic malignancy cells, underscoring unresolved off-target liabilities (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). No pharmacokinetic (PK), ADME, or clinical tolerability data for SRT1720 are supplied in the present corpus; by contrast, the second-generation STAC SRT2104 has human PK/tolerability and multiple preclinical and clinical signals across diseases, including ocular/neurologic models (but those data cannot be extrapolated to SRT1720 without qualification) (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024). Collectively, the historical record supports that SRT1720 is a pharmacologically active first-generation STAC with broad preclinical use, mixed mechanistic interpretations, and safety concerns; critically, there is no published use in AMD or RPE models in the material provided here (Ji et al., 2021; Bononi et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action  
- Biochemical pharmacology and target engagement: SRT1720 belongs to the STAC class that can directly activate SIRT1 through an assisted allosteric mechanism requiring specific substrate motifs; mutating SIRT1 E230 disrupts both activator binding and activation, and co-crystal structures of SIRT1 with SRT-like activators support an allosteric binding pocket that enhances deacetylation efficiency in a substrate-dependent manner (Lee et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018). Early reports of direct activation were contested due to labeled peptide assay artifacts, but subsequent kinetic and structural data reconciled these findings with an allosteric model; nonetheless, the field recognizes pharmacological caveats including context-dependent activation and off-targets, such as reported Sirt3 inhibition by SRT1720 (Mazzone, 2018; Lee et al., 2021).  
- Canonical SIRT1 substrates and pathway biology: SIRT1 deacetylates transcriptional regulators and autophagy/mitophagy machinery that converge on mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress defense, and inflammatory tone—each relevant to AMD pathogenesis. These include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis/oxidative metabolism), FOXO1/FOXO3a (antioxidant/autophagy transcription), NF-κB p65/RelA (inflammatory gene programs), p53 (apoptosis/senescence), and Nrf2 (antioxidant transcription), as well as autophagy proteins (e.g., ATG family members and LC3) and trafficking nodes such as Rab7 that promote autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Chang et al., 2024; Luján et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025). In multiple cell types, SIRT1 activation or NAD⁺ elevation increases PGC-1α activity and mitochondrial biogenesis and can suppress NF-κB signaling via p65 deacetylation, consistent with anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory effects that are therapeutically desirable in RPE (Ding et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2025).  
- RPE-specific SIRT1/autophagy linkage: In ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress, PARP1 activation depletes NAD⁺, inhibits SIRT1 (elevated p53 acetylation), and selectively impairs late-stage autophagy by blocking autolysosome formation without preventing autophagosome formation; restoring NAD⁺ or inhibiting PARP1 preserves SIRT1 activity and rescues late autophagic flux, whereas PARP1 inhibition fails to rescue autophagy when SIRT1 is depleted—placing SIRT1 as the essential downstream effector for recovering autophagy in oxidatively stressed RPE (Jang et al., 2020). In vivo, PARP1 inhibition protected the retina in sodium iodate (SI) injury and the benefit was autophagy-dependent, reinforcing the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1→autophagy axis as a mechanistic driver of RPE/retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020). AMD donor RPE exhibits decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1 levels, increased acetylated (inactive) PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and hyperactive mTOR—all changes expected to depress SIRT1-dependent autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis and to contribute to lysosomal/autophagic abnormalities (Zhang et al., 2020).  
- TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal acidification context: TFEB is the master transcription factor for lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy gene networks (CLEAR), whose nuclear translocation is negatively regulated by mTORC1; CLEAR target upregulation increases lysosomal capacity and flux, while lysosomal ion/pH homeostasis (v-ATPase–dependent proton pumping) determines enzyme activation, including cathepsins such as CTSD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In AMD/RPE-relevant literature, TFEB/CLEAR is positioned as a principal lever for lysosomal rejuvenation, and lysosomal acidity and calcium handling are identified as key determinants of autophagic flux and RPE health (Boya et al., 2023). Although sirtuin family members can intersect TFEB signaling (e.g., AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis in non-neovascular AMD), direct evidence for SIRT1-driven TFEB deacetylation/activation is not provided in the present corpus; however, PGC-1α has been placed upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, linking SIRT1→PGC-1α activity to potential TFEB–CLEAR induction by inference (not by direct RPE data) (Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Critical gaps relevant to the working hypothesis: Within the provided literature, there is no direct evidence that SRT1720 activates SIRT1 in RPE, no demonstration that SRT1720 promotes TFEB deacetylation or nuclear activation, and no reports that SRT1720 enhances lysosomal acidification or cathepsin D (CTSD) activity in RPE or AMD models; any such assertions remain unsubstantiated by the references supplied here (Ji et al., 2021; Mazzone, 2018; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Therefore, while the SIRT1→autophagy/mitophagy rationale in RPE is strong, the specific mechanistic chain “SRT1720→SIRT1 activation in RPE→TFEB deacetylation→CLEAR upregulation→lysosomal acidification/CTSD enhancement” lacks direct experimental support in RPE/AMD contexts in these sources and should be treated as a testable, not established, hypothesis (Falcão et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020).

Therapeutic biology of the disease target supports SIRT1 activation in RPE. Multiple AMD-relevant datasets show NAD⁺ depletion and SIRT1 downregulation in AMD RPE (primary donor-derived cultures and iPSC-RPE), accompanied by impaired PGC-1α activity, AMPK suppression, and mTOR hyperactivation, together with autophagy/lysosome structural and functional abnormalities; the PARP1-dependent late-autophagy block under oxidative stress in RPE is SIRT1-dependent for rescue, further bolstering SIRT1 as a target for restoring autophagic flux and organelle quality control (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). However, these observations do not establish which pharmacologic SIRT1 activator is optimal for RPE/AMD, and they do not establish TFEB deacetylation as a SIRT1-dependent event in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History in Related Ocular Systems (Class Precedent)  
Although direct SRT1720 ocular data are absent here, SRT2104—a second-generation STAC with improved specificity and exposure—shows SIRT1-linked protection in retinal ischemia/reperfusion and TNF-induced optic nerve injury, including deacetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (p53, NF-κB p65, STAT3), reduced apoptosis/inflammation, and induction of autophagy in optic nerve, which provides class-level ocular precedent that SIRT1 activation can be neuroprotective and autophagy-enhancing in the visual system (Chang et al., 2024). These results should not be extrapolated to SRT1720 without direct data, but they reinforce the biological plausibility that a STAC could benefit retinal tissues if target engagement and safety can be achieved (Chang et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
The proposed assay hypothesis is that SRT1720 will activate SIRT1 in RPE, leading to TFEB deacetylation/activation, increased lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity, and improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material. Based on the literature provided here, the following expectations are reasonable and aligned with evidence, and several components are speculative:

- Supported expectations tied to SIRT1 biology in RPE:
  - If SRT1720 achieves bona fide SIRT1 activation and target engagement in RPE, it should decrease acetylation of canonical SIRT1 substrates (for example, p53 K382ac, p65 K310ac, PGC-1α), restore late-stage autophagic flux under oxidative stress, and enhance autophagosome–lysosome fusion, given the demonstrated requirement for SIRT1 to rescue late-stage autophagy in H₂O₂-stressed ARPE-19 cells (Jang et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025).  
  - Biomarkers: recovery of p62 turnover, normalization of LC3-II/LC3-I dynamics in flux assays, increased autolysosome signal in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3 imaging, and potentially increased Rab7 activity/localization to autophagosomes are anticipated if SRT1720 strengthens late-stage autophagy via SIRT1 (Jang et al., 2020; Luján et al., 2022).  
  - Mitochondrial endpoints: increased PGC-1α deacetylation/activity and improved mitophagy markers (PINK1, Parkin induction) would be consistent with SIRT1 activation; SRT1720 has driven PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis after oxidant injury in renal cells, supporting feasibility of this axis in oxidatively stressed epithelia (Ji et al., 2021; Luján et al., 2022).  

- Plausible, but not demonstrated within the provided literature:
  - TFEB deacetylation/activation: the present corpus does not document SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation or STAC-induced TFEB activation in RPE. TFEB/CLEAR is a validated master lysosomal program, and PGC-1α can lie upstream of TFEB in other disease contexts, so an indirect route “SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB→CLEAR” is biologically plausible but remains unproven in RPE here and should be tested directly (Falcão et al., 2025).  
  - Lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity: lysosomal pH and hydrolase activation are central to RPE proteostasis and AMD; however, no experiment in the supplied sources demonstrates that SRT1720 or any STAC increases lysosomal acidification or CTSD activity in RPE. These readouts (e.g., LysoTracker/LysoSensor ratio, DQ-BSA, cathepsin activity assays) should be considered exploratory endpoints for SRT1720, not expected outcomes (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
  - LAMP2 expression: likewise, no provided reference shows SRT1720 increasing LAMP2 in RPE. While CLEAR activation generally elevates lysosomal genes (e.g., LAMP family, cathepsins), this requires evidence of TFEB activation in the same system and has not been shown for SRT1720 in RPE in the available literature (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  

- Target presence/assay feasibility:
  - SIRT1 is expressed in human RPE and is reduced in AMD donor RPE and AMD iPSC-RPE models, with associated increases in acetylated PGC-1α and deficits in mitochondrial/autophagic programs, confirming the presence of the pharmacological target and a disease-relevant deficit that SIRT1 activation could address (Golestaneh et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020).  
  - The disease cell biology is well-aligned with a SIRT1-centric intervention: in RPE, autophagy and phagocytic digestion converge on lysosomes to clear POS; impaired lysosomal enzyme activity and acidification reduce flux and increase oxidative stress and protein/organelle damage—phenotypes linked to AMD and to which SIRT1’s autophagy/mitophagy-promoting actions are mechanistically relevant (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
On balance, the therapeutic rationale “activate SIRT1 to restore autophagy/mitophagy and lysosomal competence in RPE for dry AMD” is well-supported by AMD-relevant cell biology and human donor data; however, the specific choice of SRT1720 has substantial evidentiary and safety gaps relative to alternatives in the STAC space, and the asserted TFEB/lysosome mechanistic specifics are not demonstrated in the provided literature.

Strengths  
- Strong target biology and disease alignment in RPE and AMD: Multiple independent datasets demonstrate that AMD RPE exhibit decreased NAD⁺, reduced SIRT1, increased acetylated PGC-1α, impaired AMPK signaling, and mTOR hyperactivity concurrent with autophagy/lysosomal abnormalities, which together point to an actionable SIRT1 deficit in AMD pathology (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020). In oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 cells and an SI mouse model, preserving NAD⁺ and thereby SIRT1 activity was necessary and sufficient to rescue late-stage autophagy and protect retina, placing SIRT1 centrally in autophagy restoration and retinal resilience (Jang et al., 2020).  
- Class-level ocular precedent for SIRT1 activation: SRT2104, a later-generation STAC with better drug-like properties, increases SIRT1 activity in retina/optic nerve, promotes SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of p53, NF-κB p65, and STAT3, reduces apoptosis/inflammation, and upregulates autophagy in optic nerve, establishing that STAC-mediated SIRT1 activation can be protective and autophagy-enhancing in ocular tissues (Chang et al., 2024).  
- Mitochondrial stress/biogenesis axis engagement by SRT1720: In non-ocular epithelia, SRT1720 induces PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial biogenesis and rescues function after oxidant injury, a desirable capability for stressed RPE; SRT1720 also modulates metabolic signaling via SIRT1–PGC-1α/AMPK/PPARα/FOXO1 pathways, consistent with correcting mitochondrial oxidative metabolism defects that characterize AMD RPE (Ji et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Therapeutic tractability of lysosome/autophagy endpoints: TFEB/CLEAR biology, lysosomal acidification, and cathepsin function are well-defined levers in RPE; measuring autophagic flux (LC3, p62, RFP-GFP-LC3), lysosomal pH (LysoSensor), and hydrolase activity (e.g., CTSD) is straightforward and interpretable in RPE assays, enabling rapid validation of the hypothesis in vitro (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Absence of direct RPE/AMD data for SRT1720: No provided reference shows SRT1720 engaging SIRT1 in RPE, improving autophagic flux in RPE, activating TFEB/CLEAR in RPE, or enhancing lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity in RPE or AMD-like models. The core elements of the hypothesis (TFEB deacetylation and CLEAR induction by SRT1720 in RPE) are not documented here and require de novo demonstration (Ji et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).  
- Mechanistic controversy and off-targets: The STAC field’s historical assay artifacts, substrate dependence, and the assisted allosteric mechanism place a premium on rigorous target engagement readouts in the specific cellular context; SRT1720 additionally shows Sirt3 inhibitory activity and has been associated with SIRT1-independent cytotoxicity in certain cells, complicating mechanistic attribution (Mazzone, 2018; Chang et al., 2024).  
- Safety signal: SRT1720 increased tumor cell migration and metastasis in a breast cancer mouse model; while AMD is not a malignancy, a pro-migratory/pro-metastatic signal raises a red flag for systemic exposure and suggests careful ocular delivery strategies and off-target profiling if pursued (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  
- Lack of PK/ADME and clinical data for SRT1720 in this corpus: Unlike SRT2104, which has human PK/tolerability data and CNS/retinal preclinical activity, SRT1720 lacks disclosed PK/ADME and clinical reports here, hindering translational assessment and dose/exposure design for ocular studies (Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  
- TFEB/lysosome-specific uncertainty: While CLEAR network activation and lysosomal acidification are compelling RPE targets, the present sources do not show SIRT1-dependent TFEB deacetylation in RPE, nor do they link STACs to lysosomal pH regulation or CTSD activation in RPE; asserting this mechanism is premature without experimental support (Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Recommendation and Development Path  
- Scientific merit: Pursuing SIRT1 activation to normalize late-stage autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in RPE is well-justified by the PARP1→NAD⁺→SIRT1 axis in RPE and AMD donor biology; however, SRT1720 is not, on current evidence, the optimal first-in-class molecule to test this hypothesis in RPE (Jang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).  
- Prioritization: If the team’s objective is target validation, consider tool-compound triage: compare SRT1720 with a second-generation clinical-stage STAC (SRT2104) and with an orthogonal approach that is known to restore SIRT1 activity in RPE (e.g., NAD⁺ boosting) in parallel RPE assays, using target-engagement and autophagy/lysosome endpoints defined a priori (Chang et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2020).  
- Minimal dataset to proceed (go/no-go):  
  1) Demonstrate SIRT1 activation in human RPE by SRT1720 at non-toxic concentrations via decreased acetyl-p53 (K382), decreased acetyl-PGC-1α, and decreased acetyl-p65 (K310), with rescue by SIRT1 knockdown or a SIRT1-dead mutant to confirm on-target action (Luo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2020).  
  2) Show restoration of late-stage autophagy under H₂O₂ or A2E stress: increased autolysosome formation in tandem RFP-GFP-LC3, decreased p62, and restored LC3-II flux in the presence/absence of lysosomal inhibitors; confirm loss of effect with SIRT1 knockdown (Jang et al., 2020).  
  3) Test TFEB/CLEAR explicitly: TFEB nuclear translocation, TFEB transcriptional reporter, and CLEAR target induction (e.g., LAMP2 and CTSD mRNA/protein) with and without mTORC1 modulation; test necessity of SIRT1 by knockdown and sufficiency by PGC-1α gain-of-function to probe the SIRT1→PGC-1α→TFEB chain (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
  4) Quantify lysosomal acidification and hydrolase activity: LysoSensor/LysoTracker measurements and CTSD activity assays; relate outcomes to TFEB activation and to autophagic flux to determine whether SRT1720 enhances lysosomal function or acts predominantly on pre-lysosomal steps (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
  5) Evaluate mitophagy and mitochondrial function: PINK1/Parkin recruitment, mt-Keima flux, mitochondrial respiration/ATP, and ROS after SRT1720 in stressed RPE to connect SIRT1–PGC-1α engagement to mitochondrial quality control (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Luján et al., 2022).  
  6) Safety pharmacology in RPE: assess proliferation/migration, EMT markers, and off-target sirtuin activity (Sirt3) to de-risk pro-migratory liabilities observed in cancer models (Bononi et al., 2022; Mazzone, 2018).  

- If SRT1720 fails to deliver on TFEB/CLEAR and lysosomal pH/hydrolase endpoints but still rescues late-stage autophagic flux, the program can pivot to an autophagy-centric mechanism of action (MoA) without TFEB claims; conversely, if TFEB/CLEAR induction is robust, the candidate may differentiate from mTOR inhibitors via epigenetic/cofactor-driven CLEAR activation, contingent on confirming SIRT1 dependency (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- For in vivo progression, the SI model used to establish PARP1→SIRT1/autophagy dependency provides a tractable retinal degeneration context, but ocular delivery and safety (especially with first-generation STACs) will require localized dosing strategies (intravitreal/subretinal) and careful dosing to minimize systemic exposure (Jang et al., 2020).

Bottom Line  
- The hypothesis that SRT1720 can correct RPE proteostasis in dry AMD via SIRT1 activation is mechanistically credible with respect to autophagy/mitophagy restoration, but the specific claims of TFEB deacetylation, CLEAR network activation, and enhancement of lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity by SRT1720 in RPE are not supported by the present literature and must be treated as untested (Jang et al., 2020; Falcão et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Given the safety concerns and off-target profile of SRT1720, and the existence of a later-generation STAC (SRT2104) with human PK and ocular neuroprotection, SRT1720 should not be advanced beyond in vitro RPE validation until it demonstrates clear, on-target superiority in RPE assays and acceptable safety margins; otherwise, the team should prioritize either SRT2104 or NAD⁺ augmentation/PARP1 modulation for translational efforts (Chang et al., 2024; Bononi et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2020).  

Summary assessment  
- Pros: Strong disease–target alignment in RPE; robust class biology for SIRT1-driven autophagy/mitophagy; SRT1720 can activate SIRT1 pathways in other oxidative-stress contexts; feasible, discriminating assays exist to test the MoA (Zhang et al., 2020; Jang et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Cons: No direct evidence of efficacy/mechanism in RPE; TFEB/lysosome mechanistic claims unsupported; safety/off-target risks; no PK/clinical data in this corpus; better-characterized STAC alternatives exist (Falcão et al., 2025; Bononi et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2024).  

Decision guidance: Proceed with a narrowly scoped, mechanism-first in vitro validation of SRT1720 in human RPE focused on SIRT1 target engagement and late-stage autophagy rescue under oxidative/phagolysosomal stress, with explicit tests for TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal acidification/CTSD activity; in parallel, benchmark against SRT2104 and NAD⁺ repletion, and use pre-specified go/no-go criteria tied to on-target mechanistic readouts and safety signals to decide whether SRT1720 merits in vivo exploration in retinal degeneration models (Jang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

Proposal for Fingolimod (FTY720; Selleckchem S5002)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fingolimod (FTY720) is a synthetic, sphingoid-base mimetic that is phosphorylated in vivo by sphingosine kinase 2 (SphK2) to yield the active metabolite FTY720-phosphate (FTY720-P), which binds sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1PRs) with sub-micromolar affinity comparable to endogenous S1P (primarily S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5) (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). As a small-molecule modulator of S1PRs, fingolimod belongs to the class of GPCR-targeting immunomodulators that regulate lymphocyte trafficking and vascular/endothelial signaling; this class has been deployed extensively in neuroinflammatory disease (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and investigated across ocular inflammatory and vascular pathologies (Gesualdo et al., 2021; Sorenson et al., 2022). In ocular biology, endogenous S1P signaling is pleiotropic: it is detected in, and acts upon, multiple retinal cell types including RPE, endothelium, neurons, and glia, where it can protect photoreceptors from oxidative stress–induced apoptosis and modulate wound repair and barrier function, underscoring the translational appeal of S1PR modulators for retinal degenerations (Gupta et al., 2012). At the same time, the S1P axis exhibits context-dependent outcomes—anti-S1P antibodies reduce subretinal fibrosis in AMD models—so receptor-subtype selectivity, ligand presentation (e.g., apoM/HDL-bound vs free), and cell-type–specific responses will be critical to therapeutic design (Gupta et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
Fingolimod is an approved oral therapy that reduces lesion formation in multiple sclerosis through S1PR-mediated immunomodulation, providing an extensive clinical safety and pharmacology dataset for potential repurposing (Mondal & Mandal, 2019). In ocular indications, preclinical studies demonstrate that S1PR pathway manipulation alters retinal/choroidal vascular pathology: intravitreally delivered S1P chaperoned by apolipoprotein M (apoM) activates endothelial S1PR1 and suppresses choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and vascular leak, and separate approaches show that anti-S1P antibodies or S1PR1-selective agonists can suppress CNV and stabilize endothelial barriers (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). Fingolimod itself (as FTY720) reduces choroidal endothelial migration and capillary morphogenesis in vitro and mitigates CNV in vivo, indicating that systemic or intraocular S1PR modulation impacts ocular neovascular disease biology (Sorenson et al., 2022). In diabetic retinopathy models, fingolimod reduces retinal angiogenesis and VEGFA levels, aligning with its anti-angiogenic/vascular-stabilizing profile (Gesualdo et al., 2021). Importantly for the dry AMD context, none of these studies directly evaluate atrophic AMD outcomes, RPE autophagy/lysosome endpoints, or complement-driven injury after fingolimod, and there is no prior clinical use of fingolimod for dry AMD (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). A material safety consideration for retinal indications is fingolimod-associated macular edema (FAME), reported in clinical settings and relevant to dosing, route, and patient selection if repurposed for macular disease (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Mechanism of Action  
Receptor pharmacology of fingolimod and ocular S1P biology. Fingolimod is phosphorylated by SphK2 to FTY720-P, which behaves as a functional agonist at S1PR1, S1PR4, and S1PR5 and a partial agonist at S1PR3, triggering receptor internalization and signaling adaptation that sequesters lymphocytes and modulates vascular responses (Gupta et al., 2012; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In ocular tissues, S1PR1 is prominently expressed in multiple cell types, with experimental evidence demonstrating S1PR1 expression in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) where S1PR1 appears as the predominant S1PR subtype alongside dynamic regulation of S1PR1/S1PR3 by oxygen tension (Sorenson et al., 2022). RPE also expresses the S1P-generating enzymes SphK1 and SphK2 and can synthesize and release S1P, providing the local pathway components to respond to pharmacologic S1PR modulation (Wang et al., 2023). S1P ligands elicit cell-type–specific responses in the retinal neurovascular unit: endothelial S1PR1 activation stabilizes adherens junctions and quells sprouting angiogenesis, apoM/HDL-bound S1P reduces choroidal leakage and CNV, and S1P/S1PR signaling influences RPE barrier function and angiogenic or inflammatory outputs (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022). These features render S1PR1 a biologically plausible target in RPE and choroid for modulating disease-relevant pathways in AMD, while also highlighting that the net effect of S1P pathway modulation depends on receptor subtype and ligand context (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022).

RPE autophagy–lysosome biology, lysosomal acidification, and AMD. The RPE is a post-mitotic, highly phagocytic epithelium that performs daily heterophagy of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and constitutive macroautophagy, processes that converge on lysosomal degradation; failure at the lysosomal step produces lipofuscin accumulation, proteotoxic stress, and drusen formation that characterize AMD (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal acidity, maintained by the vacuolar H^+-ATPase (V-ATPase), is essential for cathepsin activity and cargo hydrolysis; AMD-relevant lipofuscin bisretinoids such as A2E elevate lysosomal pH by inhibiting V-ATPase, impairing phagolysosomal digestion of POS and promoting a feed-forward cycle of oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction (Sinha et al., 2016). Lysosomal signaling couples to mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPase complexes, integrating luminal amino acids and energy status to regulate autophagy; in RPE, βA3/A1-crystallin (Cryba1) binds the V0 domain of V-ATPase and its loss produces mTORC1 hyperactivation, inefficient lysosomal clearance, and AMD-like pathology, functionally tying V-ATPase activity and mTORC1–TFEB signaling to disease (Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy protects RPE from oxidative stress, and genetic or age-related declines in macroautophagy correlate with mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, inflammasome activation, and lipofuscin accumulation in human AMD eyes and animal models (Sinha et al., 2016). These data establish that increasing autophagic flux and restoring lysosomal acidification are mechanistically central interventions for RPE protection in AMD.

The AMPK–mTOR–ULK1/TFEB axis: a mechanistic route to autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis. AMPK and mTOR are canonical, opposing regulators of autophagy: AMPK stimulates autophagy by activating ULK1 and inhibiting mTORC1 (including via TSC1/2–Rheb), whereas mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1/Atg13 to block initiation and phosphorylates Atg14 to dampen nucleation (Wang et al., 2023). TFEB/TFE3 are master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy; mTORC1 phosphorylation retains TFEB in the cytosol, and mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation to activate the CLEAR network of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Wang et al., 2023). AMPK-dependent phosphorylation is required for TFEB/TFE3 transcriptional activation, and AMPK activation increases V-ATPase assembly and activity under glucose starvation, providing a direct link from energy stress to lysosomal acidification machinery (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE/AMD-relevant systems, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), lysosomal proteins (LAMP2), and cathepsins (CTSB), and reduces accumulation of POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granules; trehalose- or rapamycin-mediated TFEB activation enhances autophagic flux and decreases A2E/lipofuscin load and inflammatory markers in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2025). Human AMD RPE displays increased TFEB phosphorylation and reduced nuclear TFEB, together with decreased cathepsin levels, consistent with mTORC1-mediated suppression of lysosomal function; TFEB reactivation in Cryba1-deficient RPE rescues CLEAR gene expression and degradative capacity, supporting TFEB as a viable target for lysosomal rejuvenation (Falcão et al., 2025).

Mitochondria–lysosome crosstalk, S1P, and oxidative damage. Mitochondrial quality control via PINK1/PRKN-driven mitophagy and mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) is coordinated with lysosomal function; AMPK acts bidirectionally to couple mitochondrial stress to lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy competence (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE and AMD models, mitochondrial dysfunction (mtDNA damage, impaired mitophagy) increases ROS and sensitizes cells to inflammasome activation and downstream damage; restoring lysosomal/mitochondrial clearance reduces oxidative injury (Boya et al., 2023). S1P signaling can induce mitochondrial biogenesis and thereby influence immunometabolic homeostasis; combined with AMPK–TFEB activation, S1P-related pathways could theoretically enhance both mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023).

Inflammation, complement, and autophagy–lysosome cross-talk in AMD. Autophagy negatively regulates inflammasome activation, and complement/inflammasome axes contribute to RPE pathology in AMD; for example, complement C5a primes inflammasomes, and high-risk CFH Y402H RPE exhibit swollen lysosomes with cathepsin D leakage and increased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Complement-related lysosomal stress provides a plausible injury modality that could be mitigated by lysosomal stabilization and increased autophagic flux; indeed, complement modulation can restore lysosomal function in a CFH Y402H RPE model (Boya et al., 2023). Because impaired lysosome/autophagy promotes secretory autophagy of inflammatory cargo, including HMGB1 and possibly amyloid species, enhancing lysosomal degradation should also reduce extracellular pro-inflammatory signals that propagate AMD pathology (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

What is known—and unknown—about fingolimod and the AMPK/TFEB–lysosome axis. In human cell models outside the eye, fingolimod can increase LC3B-II and alter Akt signaling (dephosphorylating Akt1 at Ser473), consistent with autophagy induction; yet the same studies report TFEB downregulation and induction of an inhibitory phosphorylation mark on TFEB (Ser211), with overall interpretations suggesting potential for stalling/saturation of autophagy under some conditions, and cell-type–dependent lysosomal enlargement and membrane permeabilization have also been described (Relic et al., 2021). Across the RPE/AMD literature summarized here, there is no direct demonstration that fingolimod or S1PR agonists activate AMPK, mobilize TFEB to the nucleus, increase V-ATPase–dependent lysosomal acidification, or enhance autophagic flux in RPE; nor are there data showing that fingolimod reduces complement-driven RPE injury in dry AMD models (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). These are critical gaps that must be addressed experimentally before the proposed mechanism can be accepted (Jung et al., 2025; Relic et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Target engagement and proximal signaling in RPE. Because S1PR1 is expressed in RPE and appears to be the predominant S1P receptor subtype in this cell type, fingolimod (as FTY720-P) should engage RPE S1PRs at pharmacologically relevant concentrations if present in the subretinal/choroidal milieu, although receptor subtype balance and receptor down-modulation dynamics will influence outcomes (Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021). In the hypothesized AMPK→TFEB pathway, proximal readouts would include increased AMPK phosphorylation/activation, decreased mTORC1 activity (e.g., phospho-S6K/4EBP1), and enhanced nuclear localization of TFEB/TFE3, followed by transcriptional upregulation of CLEAR genes (e.g., LAMP1/2, ATP6V0A1, CTSB/D) (Boya et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Because S1PR signaling is pleiotropic, it is critical to test whether fingolimod in RPE shifts Akt and mTORC1 activities toward a TFEB-permissive state, as opposed to inducing the inhibitory TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and autophagy stalling seen in some non-ocular cells (Relic et al., 2021).

Lysosomal acidification, degradative capacity, and autophagic flux. If fingolimod drives AMPK activation and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, predicted functional outcomes include increased V-ATPase assembly and activity (acidified lysosomes), higher cathepsin activity, and increased autophagic flux measurable by LC3-II turnover in the presence of bafilomycin or chloroquine, together with decreased steady-state p62/SQSTM1 under basal degradative conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). TFEB activation in RPE models reduces POS-dependent lipofuscin-like granule accumulation and increases lysosome number; pharmacologic TFEB induction (e.g., with trehalose) increases lysosomal biogenesis and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, so fingolimod engagement of this axis should phenocopy these protective changes if the postulated signaling is correct (Falcão et al., 2025). Restoration of lysosomal acidity would be expected to counteract A2E- and lipofuscin-induced V-ATPase inhibition, improving phagolysosomal degradation of POS and reducing waste buildup (Sinha et al., 2016).

Oxidative stress, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammasome/complement outputs. By increasing autophagic and mitophagic flux, and engaging TFEB-dependent antioxidant/clearance programs, the candidate mechanism should reduce mitochondrial ROS, stabilize mitochondrial biogenesis via AMPK–PGC-1 pathways, and decrease ROS-dependent priming of inflammasomes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016). Autophagy mitigates inflammasome activation, and restoring lysosome function reduces the release of DAMPs and secretory autophagy cargo (e.g., HMGB1), which together would be expected to blunt complement pathway amplification in stressed RPE; complement deposition (C5b-9) within lysosomes, especially in CFH risk-allele RPE, may be reduced if lysosomal integrity is preserved and capacity is restored (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). In aggregate, if fingolimod engages the AMPK–TFEB–lysosome axis in RPE as hypothesized, one would expect improvements in lysosomal pH, cathepsin activity (including CTSD), autophagic flux, reduced lipofuscin/A2E accumulation, lower mitochondrial ROS, and decreased inflammasome/complement readouts in RPE challenged with AMD-relevant stresses (oxidants, A2E, complement components) (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Caveats and contrary expectations. Fingolimod’s effects on TFEB and autophagy are cell- and context-dependent; in human synovial fibroblasts and HEK293 cells fingolimod induced TFEB Ser211 phosphorylation and TFEB downregulation despite LC3B-II accumulation, suggesting potential autophagy stalling and negative feedback on TFEB that could counter the desired lysosomal biogenesis in RPE (Relic et al., 2021). Moreover, S1P pathway manipulation can yield opposing outcomes in different compartments (e.g., anti-S1P strategies reduce ocular fibrosis/CNV), so nonselective S1PR modulation by fingolimod may not cleanly recapitulate the endothelial-protective, S1PR1-selective phenotypes observed with apoM/HDL–S1P delivery (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012). Finally, retinal safety signals—particularly macular edema—have been associated with fingolimod in clinical practice and would warrant stringent dose–exposure control and route optimization (e.g., local ocular delivery) in any AMD program (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Assay design implications. Given the mechanistic uncertainties, rigorous RPE-focused assays must be prioritized: (1) S1PR1/3/5 expression profiling in the chosen RPE system (primary human, iPSC-RPE) and receptor occupancy by fingolimod; (2) AMPK phosphorylation and mTORC1 readouts (p-AMPK, p-S6K, p-4EBP1) after fingolimod with and without S1PR antagonists; (3) TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR target induction; (4) lysosomal pH (ratiometric LysoSensor) and V-ATPase assembly/activity; (5) autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover ± lysosomal inhibitors; p62 dynamics); (6) cathepsin D/L activity assays; (7) oxidative stress resilience (mitoROS, mtDNA damage) and mitophagy markers; and (8) complement handling (C3 turnover, C5b-9 deposition) under CFH Y402H and amyloid/oxidant stress conditions (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Benchmarking to validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) and lysosomal acidification restorers will contextualize fingolimod’s performance on the most disease-relevant axes (Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong disease–mechanism alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by impaired lysosomal acidification, defective autophagic clearance, and oxidative/complement stress in RPE; AMPK–mTOR–TFEB signaling and V-ATPase activity are validated nodal controllers of lysosomal competence in RPE and AMD models, providing clear mechanistic targets that, if engaged, should be disease-modifying (Sinha et al., 2016; Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- On-target cellular expression: S1PR1 is present in RPE and is the predominant S1PR subtype, while RPE express SphK1/2, indicating the S1P/S1PR machinery required for pharmacologic modulation exists in the target cell (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).  
- Prior ocular efficacy signals via S1PR modulation: ApoM/HDL–S1P→S1PR1 suppresses CNV and leakage; FTY720 reduces choroidal endothelial angiogenic behaviors and mitigates CNV; in diabetic retinopathy, fingolimod decreases VEGF signaling—together confirming relevant ocular pharmacology and providing translational scaffolding for retinal use (Jung et al., 2025; Sorenson et al., 2022; Gesualdo et al., 2021).  
- Immunometabolic rationale: S1P signaling can promote mitochondrial biogenesis, and AMPK–TFEB signaling coordinates mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk; a single agent engaging the S1P–AMPK–TFEB axis might simultaneously improve mitochondrial and lysosomal resilience in oxidatively stressed RPE (Boya et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Repurposing tractability: Extensive human exposure, known PK/PD, and manageable formulation chemistry enable accelerated translational planning compared to de novo entities (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mechanistic gap in the target cell: There is currently no direct evidence that fingolimod activates AMPK or TFEB in RPE, increases autophagic flux, or acidifies lysosomes; likewise, no data show fingolimod reduces complement-driven injury in RPE/dry AMD models, and this is the central premise of the hypothesis (Jung et al., 2025; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Context dependence and potential for adverse lysosomal effects: In human non-ocular cells, fingolimod induced inhibitory TFEB phosphorylation and autophagy stalling, and lysosomal enlargement/permeabilization has been reported in some contexts—opposite to the desired lysosomal restoration—raising the possibility of deleterious effects in RPE unless carefully titrated (Relic et al., 2021).  
- Receptor- and ligand-context complexity: Beneficial vascular phenotypes are associated with endothelial S1PR1 stimulation—often via chaperone-bound S1P—while nonselective S1PR modulation or anti-S1P strategies can also be beneficial (e.g., anti-fibrotic effects in AMD), implying that fingolimod’s mixed S1PR agonism and functional antagonism could yield off-target or counterproductive outcomes in the RPE/choroid (Jung et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2012; Sorenson et al., 2022).  
- Retinal safety concerns: Fingolimod-associated macular edema is a documented adverse effect in humans, which is particularly concerning in a macular disease; any development plan must incorporate delivery strategies and exposure limits that mitigate this risk (Mondal & Mandal, 2019).  
- Evidence base skew: Much of the directly AMD-relevant S1P/S1PR ocular literature concerns neovascular endpoints (wet AMD/CNV) or endothelium, not atrophic RPE biology; the best lysosome/autophagy data are robust but are not linked to S1PR pharmacology, necessitating bridging studies to validate the specific drug–mechanism–disease chain (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Go/no-go perspective and experimental priorities  
On balance, fingolimod is a mechanistically plausible, but currently unvalidated, repurposing candidate for dry AMD via the proposed S1PR→AMPK→TFEB→lysosome axis. A limited, mechanism-first preclinical package in human RPE models is warranted before considering in vivo efficacy work. The minimum data package to de-risk the hypothesis should include:  
- Demonstration that fingolimod engages S1PRs on human RPE and increases AMPK activity while suppressing mTORC1, with consequent TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene induction; side-by-side with a S1PR1-selective agonist and apoM/HDL-S1P as positive controls for S1PR1 biology (Sorenson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025).  
- Functional lysosomal rescue: increased V-ATPase assembly/activity, lower lysosomal pH, increased CTSD/CTSL activity, improved POS digestion, reduced A2E and lipofuscin-like autofluorescence under static and diurnal POS feeding paradigms (Sinha et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Flux and mitochondrial outcomes: increased autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover, p62 dynamics), enhanced mitophagy under oxidant stress (PINK1/PRKN markers), and decreased mitoROS (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).  
- Inflammation/complement endpoints: reduced IL1B release after MG-132/BafA challenges, lowered NLRP3 activation, decreased lysosomal C5b-9 deposition and improved lysosomal integrity in CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE exposed to complement (Piippo, 2019; Falcão et al., 2025).  
- Safety liabilities: absence of lysosomal membrane permeabilization, cathepsin leakage, or TFEB Ser211 inhibitory phosphorylation with autophagy stalling at therapeutic exposure in RPE, in contrast to adverse signatures reported in other cell types (Relic et al., 2021).

Depending on these in vitro outcomes, a focused in vivo test in a dry AMD-relevant model (e.g., NaIO3 injury or Cryba1 cKO) with intraocular delivery and a retinal safety assessment (OCT for edema, ERG, histology) would be the logical next step (Falcão et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2016). If the AMPK–TFEB and lysosomal endpoints are not met, pivot to alternative S1PR strategies (S1PR1-selective agonists or apoM/HDL–S1P formulations) that have more consistent endothelial/retinal protective phenotypes may be warranted (Jung et al., 2025). If proximal signaling is partially engaged but lysosomal capacity remains limiting, combination approaches with validated TFEB activators (e.g., trehalose) or NRF2 activators that cross-reinforce lysosomal and antioxidant programs could be explored with attention to oncogenicity and cell specificity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Conclusion  
Fingolimod sits at the intersection of a compelling disease mechanism (lysosomal/autophagic failure in RPE), a plausible upstream target (S1PR1 in RPE), and a therapeutic class with ocular activity (S1PR modulators), but it lacks direct evidence for engaging the AMPK–TFEB–lysosomal biogenesis/acidification axis in RPE or for mitigating complement/oxidative injury in dry AMD models (Sorenson et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025). The strength of the lysosome/autophagy rationale and the existence of RPE S1PR1 expression support a mechanism-first exploration; however, cell-type–dependent fingolimod effects on TFEB and autophagy and the clinical risk of macular edema demand caution (Relic et al., 2021; Mondal & Mandal, 2019). Proceed only with a staged validation plan centered on RPE-intrinsic endpoints of AMPK/TFEB activation, lysosomal acidification, and complement/oxidative resilience; without those data, the hypothesis remains unsubstantiated for dry AMD, and alternative S1PR strategies or direct TFEB/lysosome-targeting interventions may be more tractable (Jung et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Proposal for Vorinostat (SAHA; Selleckchem S1047)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA; Selleckchem S1047) is a synthetic small molecule originally discovered through a screening process aimed at identifying inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) and belongs to the hydroxamic acid class of compounds. It was developed as an anticancer agent and later received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for the treatment of cutaneous T cell lymphoma; its chemical synthesis involves derivatization of an anilide moiety with a hydroxamic acid function, enabling a high degree of specificity for the zinc-dependent catalytic pockets of HDAC enzymes. As a pan-HDAC inhibitor, Vorinostat is designed to modulate epigenetic regulation by binding to the active site of multiple HDAC isoforms, thereby increasing histone acetylation and altering the transcriptional profile of target genes. This class of compounds has been broadly used in oncology, where the modulation of chromatin structure reactivates suppressed tumor suppressor genes and triggers cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In the context of drug repurposing, the rationale for exploring Vorinostat in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is centered on its potential to epigenetically reprogram retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells by enhancing the acetylation status and activation of key transcription factors such as TFEB and FOXO, which are critical regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—a mechanism distinctly different from kinase inhibition strategies (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Vorinostat’s clinical journey has predominantly revolved around its anticancer applications. Early-phase clinical trials in various solid tumors, including breast, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancer, as well as studies in metastatic thyroid cancer, relapsed or refractory leukemia, and multiple myeloma, have provided a robust safety profile and dosing regimen for this therapeutic candidate (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2004, 2005, 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). Although its use in oncology has been extensive—with studies demonstrating its ability to block cell growth by inhibiting key enzymes required for proliferation—the direct evidence for its application in ocular diseases, especially in dry AMD, remains limited. Nonetheless, the broader class of HDAC inhibitors has shown promising results in preclinical ocular models. For instance, several studies have demonstrated that HDAC inhibitors can attenuate choroidal neovascularization, protect retinal tissues from ischemic injury, and promote cellular differentiation in the retinal pigment epithelium (Luo et al., 2025). These findings provide an indirect validation of the concept that epigenetic modulators of HDAC activity may be repurposed to combat the autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD. Although Vorinostat itself has not been extensively studied in the context of dry AMD or similar RPE-driven degenerative diseases, its established pharmacological profile and ocular tolerability in other clinical contexts suggest that it could offer mechanistic benefits by modulating retinal epigenetic landscapes (Luo et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action:  
Vorinostat exerts its biological effects by inhibiting the activity of zinc-dependent histone deacetylases. Under normal physiological conditions, HDACs remove acetyl groups from the lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin condensation and transcriptional repression; by inhibiting these enzymes, Vorinostat results in the accumulation of acetylated histones and a more relaxed chromatin structure that promotes gene transcription. The current hypothesis contends that in RPE cells, Vorinostat-mediated HDAC inhibition will enhance the acetylation of the transcription factors TFEB (transcription factor EB) and members of the FOXO (forkhead box O) family. TFEB is a master regulator of the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which governs the transcription of genes encoding lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D (CTSD), and other proteins necessary for autophagy and lysosomal acidification (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). Similarly, FOXO transcription factors are implicated in cellular stress responses and can promote the expression of antioxidant enzymes as well as proteins involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity. In neuronal models, HDAC inhibition has been linked to increased expression, acetylation, and nuclear localization of TFEB, leading to upregulation of lysosomal gene expression and enhanced autophagic flux (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). It is anticipated that Vorinostat will operate through a similar mechanism in RPE cells by facilitating the dissociation of HDACs from the promoters of TFEB/FOXO target genes, thereby promoting their transcriptional activation. This would initiate a cascade of events that enhance lysosomal biogenesis, improve lysosomal acidification, and increase the activity of cathepsin D—the lysosomal protease that plays a critical role in degrading accumulated protein aggregates and damaged cellular organelles, which are pathognomonic of dry AMD pathology (Luo et al., 2025). Moreover, it is relevant that other HDAC inhibitors, such as trichostatin A (TSA) and valproic acid (VPA), have demonstrated the capacity to modulate similar pathways in retinal cells, thereby indirectly supporting the proposed mechanism of action for Vorinostat in restoring lysosomal function and autophagic balance in RPE cells (Luo et al., 2025).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed mechanism of action, the expected effect of Vorinostat in the context of dry AMD is multifaceted. The compound is anticipated to inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to an increase in overall protein acetylation, including that of histones and transcription factors. This epigenetic modulation should facilitate the nuclear translocation and activation of TFEB, thereby upregulating the CLEAR network of genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and autophagy. In turn, the increased expression and activity of cathepsin D will improve the degradative capacity of the lysosomes, fostering the clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious protein aggregates that accumulate with age in RPE cells. Additionally, enhanced FOXO activity could promote an improved antioxidant response and mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction, which together would reduce oxidative stress—a key driver of RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

The anticipated outcome in preclinical assays would be a measurable restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by reductions in markers of cellular stress and accumulation of autophagy substrates. Cellular assays may demonstrate increased lysosomal enzyme activities, such as that of cathepsin D, and improved acidification of lysosomes in treated RPE cells. In animal models engineered or induced to exhibit dry AMD-like pathology, treatment with Vorinostat is expected to lead to an improvement in retinal structure and function, potentially assessed through morphological analyses and electroretinography. Furthermore, the restoration of TFEB/FOXO activity should enhance the overall cellular resilience of RPE, thereby delaying or preventing the progression of degenerative changes associated with dry AMD. Given Vorinostat’s established oral bioavailability and systemic tolerability in oncology patients, there is potential for its repurposing with adjusted dosing regimens aimed at achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina with minimal systemic toxicity (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Vorinostat as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses emerge. One of the principal strengths of Vorinostat is its well-characterized pharmacological profile, which is supported by extensive clinical data in oncology. Its FDA-approved status and known systemic tolerability provide a translational advantage over novel compounds that are still in early developmental stages. The robust mechanism of action of HDAC inhibitors, with demonstrated capacity to modulate gene expression through epigenetic reprogramming, aligns well with the pathobiology of dry AMD, where impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are central features. The specific hypothesis that Vorinostat will promote the acetylation and activation of TFEB and FOXO transcription factors to drive lysosomal biogenesis, improve acidification, and enhance cathepsin D activity addresses well-validated therapeutic targets in the disease process (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

However, there are also significant weaknesses and potential challenges that must be carefully considered. First, while the mechanistic rationale is compelling, direct experimental evidence supporting Vorinostat’s efficacy in RPE cells or animal models of dry AMD is currently sparse. Much of the supporting data is extrapolated from studies using other HDAC inhibitors such as TSA, VPA, or AN7, and from cancer studies where the cellular context differs substantially from that of the RPE (Luo et al., 2025). Second, the pharmacokinetic profile and ocular tissue penetration of Vorinostat when administered systemically remain uncertain. The blood–retinal barrier presents a formidable challenge to achieving therapeutic drug concentrations in the retina, and while clinical trials in oncology have established systemic dosing guidelines, it is unclear whether these doses will translate into efficacious levels within the RPE while maintaining safety. Third, the potential for off-target effects and retinal toxicity cannot be overlooked; certain HDAC inhibitors have been associated with deleterious retinal effects when administered at inappropriate doses or over prolonged periods, emphasizing the need for careful dose optimization and possibly localized (e.g., intravitreal) delivery strategies (Luo et al., 2025). Fourth, the complex interplay between various HDAC isoforms in the retina may necessitate a more selective approach than that offered by the broad-spectrum inhibition provided by Vorinostat, as indiscriminate inhibition could disrupt other acetylation-dependent regulatory mechanisms critical for normal retinal function (Luo et al., 2025).

In addition, while the hypothesis posits that Vorinostat will upregulate TFEB and FOXO to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function, the regulation of these transcription factors is multifactorial. For example, TFEB activity is tightly controlled by phosphorylation events mediated by mTORC1 and AKT2 signaling pathways, and the interplay between these kinases, deacetylases such as SIRT5, and HDACs remains an active area of investigation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Buniello et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024). Thus, while there is mechanistic plausibility in promoting lysosomal biogenesis via HDAC inhibition, the precise molecular outcomes in the unique environment of aging RPE cells require further delineation. Furthermore, studies in other models have revealed that the beneficial effects of HDAC inhibition on autophagy and lysosomal function may vary depending on the timing, duration, and specific isoform selectivity of the inhibitor used (Luo et al., 2025).

Taking these factors into account, a cautious but optimistic view emerges regarding the repurposing of Vorinostat for dry AMD. The compound’s established clinical track record in oncology is a substantial advantage, providing a foundation for subsequent translational studies. The convergent evidence supporting the role of HDAC inhibition in enhancing autophagy and mitigating oxidative stress in retinal diseases further bolsters the rationale for this approach (Falcão et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). However, to fully validate the therapeutic potential of Vorinostat in dry AMD, rigorous preclinical studies are needed to (1) confirm its efficacy in restoring TFEB/FOXO activity and lysosomal function in RPE cells, (2) determine its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties in ocular tissues, (3) assess its safety profile within the retina over chronic dosing schedules, and (4) establish optimized dosing strategies that achieve target engagement without compromising retinal integrity.

Moreover, future investigations might explore alternative delivery mechanisms, such as nanoparticle-based systems or sustained-release intravitreal formulations, to circumvent the challenges posed by the blood–retinal barrier and achieve localized drug concentrations that are both effective and safe. In parallel, combinatorial therapeutic strategies that pair Vorinostat with other agents that modulate complementary pathways—such as antioxidants, SIRT1 activators, or agents that specifically target mTORC1 signaling—could be considered to provide a multifaceted approach to treating dry AMD. These strategies would leverage the ability of Vorinostat to reprogram epigenetic signatures in RPE cells while simultaneously addressing other pathogenic mechanisms contributing to AMD progression (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).

In summary, Vorinostat represents a promising candidate for drug repurposing in dry AMD due to its potent HDAC inhibitory activity, favorable clinical history in oncology, and a plausible mechanism by which it could restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux in RPE cells—a central defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. The strengths of this approach include the compound’s established approval and known pharmacology, coupled with emerging evidence that epigenetic modulation can address key cellular dysfunctions in retinal degeneration. Conversely, the critical weaknesses pertain to the lack of direct preclinical evidence in the context of AMD, uncertainties regarding effective ocular delivery, and potential risks of off-target effects in a delicate tissue such as the retina. A comprehensive series of translational studies, beginning with in vitro models of RPE dysfunction and progressing to in vivo dry AMD models, is essential to fully establish the therapeutic window, efficacy, and safety profile of Vorinostat for this new indication. If these studies yield positive results, Vorinostat could offer a novel, mechanistically precise approach to the treatment of dry AMD, addressing a significant unmet clinical need by restoring the autophagy–lysosome pathway and ultimately preserving vision in affected patients (Buniello et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025).
