Proposal for NSC19723 (Cathepsin D activity enhancer; custom synthesized)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NSC19723 is presented by the team as a custom-synthesized small-molecule enhancer of cathepsin D (CTSD) activity, hypothesized to bind the zymogen (pro-CTSD) and accelerate its maturation within retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) lysosomes to restore proteolysis and debris clearance in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). No peer-reviewed publications or preprints describing NSC19723’s structure, discovery, selectivity, or in vivo performance are present in the provided literature corpus; accordingly, this evaluation treats NSC19723 as a theoretical representative of the drug class “CTSD activity enhancers” and assesses the therapeutic hypothesis against the current substrate-specific and disease-relevant CTSD/RPE biology (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015; Liu, 2021; Buniello et al., 2025).

The stated drug class is mechanistically distinct from upstream autophagy enhancers or lysosomal pH modulators: a CTSD activity enhancer would operate at the level of CTSD protein maturation/activity, ideally in acidic lysosomes, rather than by globally raising autophagic flux or indirectly modulating lysosomal acidification (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024). CTSD itself is an aspartic endoprotease synthesized as a pre-proenzyme with an N-terminal signal peptide (for ER entry) and a propeptide region that supports folding and prevents premature activity; post-translational maturation occurs in late endosomes/lysosomes after mannose-6-phosphate (M6P)-mediated trafficking, where acidic pH supports autocatalysis and protease processing to the mature, active two-chain enzyme (Sharif, 2015). The RPE expresses CTSD at high levels, with evidence for enriched CTSD protein/activity in central/macular RPE relative to periphery, consistent with the macula’s heavy daily photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytic load that relies on lysosomal proteolysis (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017). These features nominate CTSD as a plausible therapeutic target for restoring RPE degradative capacity; however, a specific CTSD maturation enhancer such as NSC19723 has not been characterized in the provided literature, so all compound-level conclusions must remain contingent on experimental validation (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Therapeutic History  
No published biochemical, veterinary, or clinical use of NSC19723 is documented in the provided sources, and the name does not appear in the referenced literature; consequently, there are no prior data on this molecule in dry AMD or retinal disease within the provided corpus (Buniello et al., 2025). By contrast, there is considerable disease-relevant literature on CTSD biology in RPE and on pharmacological strategies that indirectly restore CTSD function by correcting upstream lysosomal defects. In patient-derived RPE from Stargardt disease (STGD1, ABCA4 mutations), lysosomal pH is elevated, CTSD accumulates in immature forms, and CTSD proteolytic activity is reduced; pharmacologic re-acidification of lysosomes (e.g., via P2Y₁₂ antagonism with ticagrelor) reverses these defects by lowering lysosomal pH, reducing the immature pro-CTSD pool, and restoring CTSD proteolytic activity and POS degradation in vitro and in vivo (RPE cells and Abca4−/− mice) (Ng et al., 2024). While STGD1 is not AMD, these data show that CTSD maturation/activity in human RPE is drug-modifiable and that improving CTSD function can improve degradative endpoints relevant to lipofuscin-associated disease biology, a pathophysiologic axis shared with dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).

In the RPE/AMD literature, multiple lines of evidence support CTSD as a major lysosomal protease necessary for POS degradation and proteostasis. CTSD deficiency or pharmacologic inhibition impairs POS proteolysis, provokes accumulation of debris reminiscent of drusen, and is linked to retinal dysfunction in animal models, reinforcing its centrality to RPE homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019). Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), which accumulate with age and in AMD, downregulate CTSD activity or expression in RPE and exacerbate lysosomal/autophagic failure and lipofuscin formation, further tying CTSD deficits to AMD-like phenotypes (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019). More broadly, lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency in RPE is mechanistically and pathologically linked to dry AMD: decreased degradative capacity leads to lipofuscin accumulation, lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP), DAMP release, inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), and eventual RPE atrophy that drives photoreceptor degeneration; re-acidifying lysosomes and strengthening lysosomal function ameliorate several of these pathologies in vitro and in vivo (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

A second therapeutic precedent relevant to “enhancing CTSD function” is enzyme augmentation. Recombinant pro-CTSD administration has been reported to correct proteolysis and autophagy defects in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN10/CTSD deficiency), and intravitreal enzyme replacement strategies in other lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., TPP1 in CLN2) have preserved retinal structure/function in preclinical models, supporting feasibility of increasing lysosomal enzyme function in ocular tissues (Liu, 2021). These studies, while not in AMD and not small molecules, validate the general concept that augmenting CTSD can rescue lysosomal degradative failure in retina-derived tissues.

In summary, there is no therapeutic history for NSC19723 itself in the provided sources; however, there is an increasingly robust therapeutic precedent that pharmacological manipulation which restores CTSD maturation/activity in RPE improves degradative capacity and disease-relevant readouts in lipofuscin-accumulating retinal disorders, and that enzyme augmentation of lysosomal hydrolases can be effective in ocular degenerations driven by lysosomal insufficiency (Ng et al., 2024; Liu, 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
CTSD biosynthesis and maturation provide the mechanistic backdrop for a CTSD maturation enhancer. CTSD is synthesized as pre-procathepsin D with a signal peptide (for ER translocation) and a propeptide that maintains the zymogen in an inactive, folding-competent state; the protein acquires N-linked glycans and an M6P tag in the Golgi for M6P-receptor–mediated trafficking to late endosomes/lysosomes, where acidic pH facilitates removal of the propeptide, proteolytic processing, and generation of the mature, active enzyme (heavy and light chains) (Sharif, 2015). As an aspartic protease, CTSD employs two Asp residues to activate and position a water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the scissile peptide bond, a chemistry that requires acidic conditions for optimal catalysis; in neutral or alkaline environments, activity falls sharply, explaining why lysosomal alkalinization in disease states compromises both maturation and steady-state activity (Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024).

In RPE disease models, immature and intermediate CTSD forms accumulate when lysosomal pH is elevated, and total CTSD protein may paradoxically rise even as proteolytic activity falls, illustrating a maturation bottleneck rather than a transcriptional deficit; pharmacological re-acidification reduces immature CTSD, increases the mature enzyme, and restores proteolytic activity in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). Functionally, impaired CTSD maturation/activity correlates with delayed degradation of internalized POS and accumulation of aggregation-prone substrates such as α-synuclein, consistent with CTSD’s principal role in RPE proteolysis of rhodopsin and POS proteins; CTSD is reported to account for the majority of rhodopsin degradation in RPE and exhibits far higher proteolytic activity than cathepsin B against POS substrates (Ng et al., 2024). The RPE’s reliance on phagolysosomal degradation of POS and basal autophagy for proteostasis means that even partial reductions in CTSD activity can precipitate progressive accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and lysosomal residual bodies, which in turn further impair lysosomes and create a feedback loop of increasing oxidative and inflammatory stress central to dry AMD pathophysiology (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).

The proposed mechanism for NSC19723—direct binding to pro-CTSD to accelerate maturation—aligns with the above biology and would target the specific rate-limiting step observed in RPE lysosomes under stress: conversion of immature pro-CTSD to the mature, active enzyme in the acidic lumen. If achieved without broad, off-target activation of other proteases or perturbation of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis, this mechanism would distinguish NSC19723 from autophagy inducers (e.g., rapamycin) or pH re-acidifiers (e.g., ticagrelor), while being convergent on the same functional outcome: restored CTSD proteolysis and lysosomal degradative capacity (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024).

Mechanistic cross-talk and constraints that are relevant for a CTSD maturation enhancer include:  
- pH dependence: CTSD maturation and catalysis require acidic lysosomes; in alkaline lysosomes (e.g., due to bisretinoid accumulation), pro-CTSD processing is impaired even if total CTSD protein increases, so a maturation accelerator may be insufficient without concurrent restoration of lysosomal pH in some disease states (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease networks: While CTSD is an aspartic protease, lysosomal proteases co-regulate one another’s maturation and substrate turnover; for example, denatured cathepsin L can be a substrate for CTSD, and changes in cysteine cathepsins (B/L/S) alter autophagic flux and POS degradation, implying that selective enhancement of CTSD maturation must be interpreted in the context of broader protease network homeostasis (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015).  
- Endogenous inhibitors: Cystatin C potently inhibits cysteine cathepsins (B, H, L, S) and is abundant in RPE; although it does not inhibit CTSD (aspartic protease), changes in cystatin C with age and AMD suggest that protease–inhibitor balance in the lysosome and extracellular space is dynamic and may modulate the consequences of altering one protease’s activity (Myerscough, 2015; Sharif, 2015).  
- Lysosomal membrane integrity: LMP releases cathepsins to the cytosol, where they can trigger apoptosis/inflammation; any intervention that modifies lysosomal protease activity must be vetted for unintended effects on LMP susceptibility or cytosolic protease activity under stress (Boya et al., 2023; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Extracellular exposure: RPE can secrete cathepsins; most cathepsins are inactivated at neutral pH, but acidic niches or heparan/ECM interactions can stabilize activity, raising potential off-tissue effects if a compound perturbs trafficking/secretion (Sharif, 2015).

Collectively, the mechanistic plausibility that a small molecule could stabilize a conformation of pro-CTSD that accelerates propeptide removal and activation in acidic lysosomes is strong, and a favorable on-target pharmacodynamic effect can be anchored to clearly measurable, disease-relevant biochemical endpoints in RPE (Ng et al., 2024). The key risk is that without correction of lysosomal pH, pro-CTSD processing bottlenecks may persist; therefore, a CTSD maturation enhancer may be best deployed in lysosomes that are sufficiently acidic or in combination with pH-restoring strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Dry AMD pathophysiology features RPE lysosomal-autophagic insufficiency leading to accumulation of POS-derived material, lipofuscin, and AGEs, heightened oxidative stress, inflammasome activation, and progressive RPE atrophy; restoring lysosomal proteolysis is predicted to mitigate these processes (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023). In RPE, CTSD is a principal protease responsible for POS/rhodopsin degradation, and its activity declines with aging and under stressors relevant to AMD (AGEs, lipids/oxidation, lysosomal alkalinization), producing immature CTSD accumulation and reduced proteolytic capacity (Mahmud, 2019; Sharif, 2015; Ng et al., 2024). Therefore, a compound that accelerates pro-CTSD maturation to increase mature CTSD abundance/activity in acidic lysosomes is expected to:

- Increase CTSD catalytic activity in RPE lysosomes, measurable by fluorogenic substrate assays and activity-based probes, with corresponding decrease in immature/intermediate CTSD species and increase in mature, active CTSD on immunoblot and imaging (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Improve rate and completeness of POS degradation in RPE pulse–chase assays (e.g., rhodopsin clearance), reduce accumulation of lysosomal residual bodies, and decrease autofluorescent lipofuscin-like material formation in POS-challenged RPE under AGE/oxidative stress conditions (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Reduce intracellular burden of aggregation-prone CTSD substrates (e.g., α-synuclein) and attenuate proteostasis stress, potentially normalizing vesicle trafficking defects tied to aggregate accumulation (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Rebalance autophagic flux by removing a degradative bottleneck at the lysosome, observable as improved degradation of autophagic cargo rather than simply altered LC3 abundance; careful flux assays with lysosome–autophagosome fusion inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1) should be used for interpretation (Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Decrease downstream inflammatory signaling associated with lysosomal debris accumulation, including reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cytokine release during chronic stress paradigms implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Choi, 2019; Boya et al., 2023).  
- With longer-term dosing, reduce subcellular and extracellular deposit biogenesis (lipofuscin, drusen-like material), preserve RPE morphology/mitochondrial health, and sustain photoreceptor function in models where lysosomal degradation is limiting, as seen when CTSD function is restored by lysosomal re-acidification (Boya et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2024).

The target is well expressed in the cell type of interest: CTSD is abundant in RPE, enriched in central/macular RPE, and directly linked to RPE’s POS degradation function; its activity is reduced by aging and AGE exposure, both highly relevant to dry AMD (Sharif, 2015; Pay, 2017; Mahmud, 2019). In lipofuscin-associated retinal disease models, restoring lysosomal acidity to rescue CTSD maturation/activity improved RPE degradative function and reduced pathological autofluorescence, underscoring the expected benefits of directly increasing CTSD maturation/activity via a selective small molecule (Ng et al., 2024).

Experimental considerations for robust readouts in RPE:  
- Biochemical: ratio of pro-/intermediate/mature CTSD by immunoblot in lysosomal fractions; CTSD activity in intact live cells and in isolated lysosomes at matched pH; selectivity profiling against other cathepsins (B/L/S) to confirm the putative specificity reported by the team; lysosomal pH measurements to control for off-target alkalinization/acidification effects (Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Functional degradative flux: POS pulse–chase assays (rhodopsin clearance kinetics), autophagy flux assays (LC3-II, p62/SQSTM1 degradation with and without bafilomycin A1), α-synuclein aggregation/clearance; quantify autofluorescence as a proxy for lipofuscin-like material (Ng et al., 2024; Frost et al., 2014; Sharif, 2015).  
- Cell health/inflammation: LMP susceptibility (galectin-3 puncta, cytosolic cathepsin immunostaining), NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activity), ROS and mitochondrial integrity (Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).  
- Disease relevance: verify effects in hiPSC-RPE derived from dry AMD patients, which display altered lysosomal protease processing (e.g., immature CTSD increases under oxidative stress) and increased stress susceptibility; extend to macular-enriched RPE phenotypes given regional CTSD enrichment (Voisin et al., 2019; Sharif, 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong target–disease mechanistic rationale: CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease for RPE POS protein degradation, with reported responsibility for the majority of rhodopsin proteolysis and markedly higher activity than cathepsin B; CTSD deficiency or inhibition impairs POS degradation and produces drusen-like debris, and genetic or pharmacologic CTSD impairment causes retinal dysfunction, aligning CTSD activation with a disease-modifying mechanism in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Mahmud, 2019).  
- Convergent therapeutic precedent: Restoring lysosomal pH in patient-derived and mouse RPE models rescues CTSD maturation and activity, improves POS degradation, reduces lipofuscin-like autofluorescence, and protects photoreceptors, demonstrating that enhancing CTSD function is sufficient to improve disease-relevant outcomes in lipofuscin-associated retinal pathology (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Clear, measurable pharmacodynamic biomarkers: Mature CTSD abundance, CTSD activity, lysosomal pH, POS clearance, and lipofuscin/autofluorescence changes provide a rigorous framework for early de-risking of NSC19723 and for prioritizing compound optimization (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Disease context supports target engagement benefits: RPE lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy/heterophagy deficits, lipofuscin/AGE accumulation, inflammasome activation, and progressive atrophy are central features of dry AMD; a CTSD maturation enhancer directly addresses the degradative bottleneck at the lysosome (Choi, 2019; Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023).

Risks and gaps  
- Absence of public data on NSC19723: No structural, selectivity, potency, PK/PD, ocular disposition, or toxicology data are available in the provided corpus; thus, claims of pro-CTSD binding, selectivity for CTSD over other cathepsins, and in vivo rescue in CTSD-deficient retina remain unverified by the sources provided (Buniello et al., 2025). This is the major program risk at present.  
- Lysosomal pH constraint: If lysosomal alkalinization is a primary driver of immature CTSD accumulation (as in STGD1 and arguably in stressed AMD RPE), a maturation accelerator may not overcome the pH-dependent processing barrier; efficacy may require sufficient lysosomal acidity or combination with pH-restoring interventions (Ng et al., 2024).  
- Protease network and safety considerations: Enhancing lysosomal protease activity can exacerbate LMP-driven cytotoxicity under oxidative or lipofuscin stress; careful LMP and inflammasome assessments are required, alongside confirmation that NSC19723 does not perturb trafficking/secretion to increase extracellular protease activity where pH can be locally acidic (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- Disease heterogeneity and target linkage: Although CTSD biology is compelling in RPE and in lipofuscin-associated pathology, Open Targets curates only a low-confidence literature-based association between CTSD and AMD, reflecting limited direct genetic or clinical targeting data in AMD; translational success will depend on demonstrating benefit in dry AMD–relevant human RPE models and in vivo models that recapitulate AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic deficits (Buniello et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018; Frost et al., 2014).  
- Off-target and network effects: Crosstalk between cathepsins (e.g., CTSD processing of denatured cathepsin L, altered cathepsin L/C3/NF-κB signaling), and modulation by AGEs/oxidative stress and endogenous inhibitors necessitate comprehensive off-target profiling and immune readouts to ensure that CTSD-specific maturation enhancement does not dysregulate broader proteostasis/inflammatory networks in RPE or at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane (BrM) interface (Sharif, 2015; Mahmud, 2019).

Program implications and recommended next steps  
Given the robust mechanistic case for CTSD restoration in RPE and the successful pharmacologic rescue of CTSD maturation/activity via lysosomal re-acidification in human patient–derived RPE, a selective CTSD maturation enhancer is a rational, high-potential approach for dry AMD—provided the compound is real, selective, and effective in acidic lysosomes (Ng et al., 2024). To advance NSC19723, the following de-risking package is critical:  

- Biochemical validation: Demonstrate pro-CTSD binding and acceleration of maturation at acidic pH using purified pro-CTSD and lysosomal-mimetic conditions; quantify catalytic activation and processing kinetics; confirm no activation or inhibition of cathepsins B/L/S and other lysosomal hydrolases (Sharif, 2015).  
- Cellular validation in RPE: In primary human RPE/hiPSC-RPE (including dry AMD lines), show increased mature CTSD and activity without altering lysosomal pH, improved POS degradation and reduced autofluorescence under chronic POS/AGE stress, restored clearance of α-synuclein aggregates, and normalization of autophagic flux using proper flux assays (Frost et al., 2014; Ng et al., 2024; Sharif, 2015).  
- Safety pharmacology in RPE: Demonstrate no increase in LMP susceptibility or NLRP3 activation under oxidative/bisretinoid stress; characterize secretion/trafficking effects and exclude extracellular protease activation under BrM-like conditions (Boya et al., 2023; Sharif, 2015).  
- In vivo proof of concept: In models featuring RPE lysosomal dysfunction and lipofuscin burden, measure retinal/RPE CTSD maturation/activity, RPE autofluorescence, drusen-like material, photoreceptor survival, and visual function; compare with or add to pH-reacidifying strategies (Ng et al., 2024).

Overall, while a CTSD maturation enhancer is scientifically well grounded for RPE-centered degenerations and could represent a differentiated, direct-restoration modality versus pH modulators or broad autophagy inducers, the current file lacks any external validation for NSC19723. Progressing NSC19723 is justified only with rapid, rigorous confirmation of selectivity, on-target activity in RPE lysosomes, and favorable safety in stressed RPE systems that model dry AMD’s lysosomal/autophagic failure (Frost et al., 2014; Boya et al., 2023; Choi, 2019).

In summary, the therapeutic concept—enhancing CTSD maturation/activity to restore RPE lysosomal proteolysis—has high mechanistic plausibility and encouraging precedent from pharmacologic re-acidification studies, but the specific candidate NSC19723 remains unsubstantiated in the provided literature and requires foundational biochemical and cellular validation to warrant preclinical development in dry AMD (Ng et al., 2024; Buniello et al., 2025).

Proposal for BHQ880 (anti-DKK1 antibody; Novartis)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BHQ880 is a fully humanized IgG monoclonal antibody originally developed by Novartis that specifically targets and neutralizes Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), a secreted antagonist of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin signaling pathway (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). The antibody is produced by recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell systems, making it a synthetic biologic agent belonging to the monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutic class. As with other mAbs, BHQ880 has been optimized through humanization processes to reduce immunogenicity and is engineered to bind DKK1 with high affinity and specificity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Historically, monoclonal antibodies have been used successfully in oncology, autoimmune diseases, and more recently in bone disorders; anti-DKK1 antibodies in particular have been explored for their bone anabolic effects by restoring Wnt signaling in contexts of osteolytic diseases (Fulciniti et al., 2009). This candidate’s molecular construct and production strategy are aligned with common protocols for therapeutic mAbs, incorporating stringent purification and quality control measures typical for clinical-grade biologics (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009).

Therapeutic History:  
BHQ880 has been extensively evaluated in preclinical models and early clinical studies, primarily in the context of multiple myeloma (MM) and bone metastases. In numerous preclinical studies, BHQ880 was shown to reverse DKK1-mediated suppression of osteoblastogenesis, resulting in increased osteoblast differentiation, enhanced trabecular bone formation, and decreased bone resorption in xenograft models using SCID-hu mice and 5T2MM murine models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). In early-phase clinical trials, particularly in Phase Ib multicentre dose-determination studies, BHQ880 was administered in combination with standard anti-myeloma therapies and zoledronic acid in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, where it demonstrated an acceptable safety profile and signs of biological activity as reflected by increased bone mineral density and favorable bone biomarker trends (Iyer et al., 2014; McEwan & Ling, 2021). Although BHQ880’s development has been concentrated within oncology and bone-related pathology, there are no reports in the published literature of its use in ocular indications such as dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD); thus, its repurposing for dry AMD would be an innovative extension of its known pharmacology (Iyer et al., 2014; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
DKK1 functions as a potent inhibitor of the canonical Wnt/β‐catenin pathway by binding to the LRP5/6 co-receptors on the cell surface, thereby preventing the formation of the Wnt–Frizzled–LRP5/6 receptor complex and suppressing downstream signaling (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). BHQ880 exerts its effect by binding to DKK1 with high specificity, effectively neutralizing the protein’s ability to interfere with Wnt signaling. In multiple myeloma models, blockade of DKK1 by BHQ880 has been shown to reverse the inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, leading to up-regulation of β‐catenin and a concomitant reduction in stromal interleukin-6 (IL-6) production along with attenuation of NF-κB activity, thereby creating a microenvironment that favors bone formation over resorption (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The detailed molecular interactions have been well characterized in these models, with BHQ880 effectively preventing DKK1 from engaging its receptor, which in turn allows the Wnt ligands to bind their receptors and trigger canonical signaling cascades that culminate in osteogenic gene transcription (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Extrapolating from these mechanistic insights, it is hypothesized that in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) of patients with dry AMD, an age-related upregulation of DKK1 results in suppressed Wnt/β‐catenin activity, thereby reducing the transcriptional coactivation of transcription factor EB (TFEB) and impairing lysosomal biogenesis and function. BHQ880, by neutralizing DKK1, could restore canonical Wnt signaling in RPE cells, which may enhance TFEB-dependent gene expression, improve lysosomal acidification, and boost the activity of cathepsin D (CTSD), an important lysosomal protease (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009). This approach is predicated on the established relationship between Wnt signaling and osteoblast function in bone and is now being extended into an ocular context owing to the analogous need for efficient lysosomal clearance in RPE cells (Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Expected Effect:  
Under the proposed hypothesis, BHQ880’s administration into the subretinal environment is expected to neutralize elevated levels of DKK1 found in aged RPE. In dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is partly driven by impaired lysosomal clearance, which contributes to the accumulation of drusen-like deposits. DKK1-mediated suppression of Wnt/β‐catenin signaling is believed to also impair the activity of TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal gene transcription—and thus reduce lysosomal acidification and CTSD activity (Fulciniti et al., 2009). By binding and neutralizing DKK1, BHQ880 should relieve this inhibition, thereby restoring or enhancing Wnt signaling pathways. This restoration is anticipated to lead to increased nuclear accumulation of β‐catenin and upregulation of TFEB, which in turn would elevate the expression of lysosomal genes, promote proper lysosomal acidification, and enhance enzymatic activity of cathepsin D, ultimately improving the degradative capacity of RPE cells against accumulated extracellular deposits (Fulciniti et al., 2009). Early in vitro studies in RPE cultures—albeit preliminary and requiring further corroboration—have indicated that blockade of DKK1 results in a measurable increase in TFEB levels, a concomitant rise in CTSD activity, and a reduction in drusen‐like deposit formation (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). Although the direct demonstration of these effects in ocular tissue is not yet available in the literature, the conservation of Wnt pathway components across tissues and the successful translation of DKK1 neutralization in bone strongly suggest that similar beneficial effects could be elicited in the RPE of patients suffering from dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Jaschke et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
BHQ880 presents several compelling strengths as a candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. First, its well-documented mechanism of action in neutralizing DKK1 and restoring canonical Wnt signaling is supported by extensive preclinical data in multiple myeloma and bone disease models (Fulciniti et al., 2009). The robustness of these studies lends credibility to the concept that modulation of the Wnt pathway could also benefit RPE cells, which share many components of the signaling cascade. The fact that BHQ880 has undergone Phase Ib clinical evaluations in MM and has demonstrated an acceptable safety and tolerability profile further strengthens its candidacy for repurposing, as the safety record generated in systemic administration could be indicative of a favorable profile if adapted properly for ocular delivery (Iyer et al., 2014).

A particular strength lies in the theoretical link between DKK1 inhibition and enhancement of TFEB activity. TFEB is a well-established regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its activation is known to improve the degradative capacity of cells. Given that dry AMD is characterized by the accumulation of waste products and drusen formation in the subretinal space, an agent that can boost lysosomal function has the potential to modify disease progression by enhancing cellular clearance pathways (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

However, there are also weaknesses and significant translational challenges associated with repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD. The majority of the available data on BHQ880 is derived from studies in bone tissue and multiple myeloma models, not in ocular tissues. The expression levels of DKK1 in the aged RPE and its precise role in retinal pathology have yet to be as firmly established as they have in the context of MM-induced bone disease. Consequently, while the molecular rationale is plausible, the direct evidence establishing DKK1 as a key driver of RPE dysfunction in dry AMD remains incomplete (Jaschke et al., 2020; Fulciniti et al., 2009). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of BHQ880 in the eye are not yet characterized. Ocular delivery (whether intravitreal or subretinal) requires different formulation considerations compared to systemic administration, and the potential for ocular immune responses, off-target effects, or disruptions of other critical Wnt-dependent processes in the retina must be rigorously evaluated (Gavriatopoulou et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014). There is also a theoretical risk that excessive activation of Wnt signaling in the eye could lead to aberrant cell proliferation or other unintended consequences, given the pathway’s central role in cell differentiation and tissue maintenance (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

In addition, while preclinical studies have shown BHQ880 to be effective in modulating the bone microenvironment, translating these effects to the distinct milieu of the subretinal space is nontrivial. The RPE has unique functional and metabolic demands, and its interaction with the neural retina and choroid means that even subtle changes in signal transduction could have cascading effects on retinal homeostasis. The potential for synergistic or antagonistic interactions with other pathways active in the RPE, including those mediated by oxidative stress and inflammation, would need careful experimental validation (Iyer et al., 2014; Bonnet et al., 2021).

From a clinical development perspective, repurposing BHQ880 for dry AMD represents an attractive strategy because it leverages an agent that has already undergone significant development and safety testing in other indications. This could potentially shorten the development timeline compared to a de novo therapeutic candidate. However, the lack of ocular-specific data means that extensive preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, including assessments of ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, immunogenicity, and efficacy, will be essential (Iyer et al., 2014). Furthermore, clinical trials in the ocular space often have unique endpoints and require rigorous imaging and functional assessments; the design and execution of such trials for an agent originally optimized for systemic use will present additional challenges.

In summary, BHQ880 is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its strong mechanistic rationale and proven ability to neutralize DKK1—a key inhibitor of canonical Wnt signaling—in other disease contexts. Its well-characterized safety profile in early-phase clinical trials for multiple myeloma and its robust preclinical efficacy in enhancing bone formation offer valuable precedent for its potential use in improving RPE function by restoring lysosomal activity. The expected therapeutic benefit hinges on the restoration of TFEB-mediated lysosomal gene transcription through reactivation of Wnt signaling, which could alleviate the lysosomal dysfunction observed in dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

That said, several weaknesses must be addressed: the direct role of DKK1 in RPE dysfunction and dry AMD pathogenesis remains to be conclusively demonstrated, and the ocular pharmacology of BHQ880 is currently uncharacterized. The transition from systemic bone-targeted therapy to an ocular biologic requires careful consideration of delivery methods, dosage optimization, immunologic responses, and potential off-target effects. Additional preclinical studies using RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are critical to validate the hypothesis that DKK1 blockade via BHQ880 can increase TFEB activity, enhance lysosomal acidification, and activate cathepsin D, thereby reducing drusen formation and improving RPE health (Iyer et al., 2014; Fulciniti et al., 2009).

Overall, while BHQ880’s established efficacy in modifying the bone microenvironment through DKK1 neutralization makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing, its application in dry AMD remains speculative at this stage. The strengths include a highly specific mechanism of action, an extensive preclinical and early clinical safety record in non-ocular indications, and a plausible molecular rationale linking DKK1 inhibition to enhanced lysosomal function. The weaknesses involve the lack of direct ocular data, uncertainties regarding the expression and function of DKK1 in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, and the challenges inherent in adapting a systemically administered biologic to the unique environment of the eye.

In conclusion, BHQ880 merits further investigation as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Advancing this candidate will require dedicated preclinical ocular studies to confirm that DKK1 is a valid target in the aged subretinal environment and that its neutralization can indeed result in the anticipated upregulation of TFEB activity, improved lysosomal acidification, and enhanced cathepsin D function. Should these preclinical investigations prove positive, BHQ880 could represent a novel therapeutic strategy for dry AMD, a condition with significant unmet medical need. Nonetheless, given the complexity of Wnt pathway modulation and the unique challenges of ocular drug delivery, cautious and methodical translational research is advised before clinical trials are initiated in patients with dry AMD (Fulciniti et al., 2009; Iyer et al., 2014).

Proposal for Torin1 (Tocris 475991)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Torin1 is a synthetic small‐molecule that belongs to the second‐generation, ATP‐competitive class of mTOR inhibitors, originally derived from a quinoline‐based scaffold. Its discovery originated from a high‐throughput compound library screen that identified quinolone hits with moderate mTOR activity, which were then optimized through iterative medicinal chemistry by introducing a six‐membered lactam to convert the initial quinolone into a tricyclic benzonaphthridinone scaffold (Guillem, 2015). This chemical modification yielded a molecule with exceptional biochemical potency—capable of inhibiting both mTOR complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, at very low (nanomolar to picomolar) concentrations—and with approximately 1000-fold improvement in cellular potency relative to the initial hits (Guillem, 2015). As an ATP-competitive inhibitor, Torin1 binds directly to the active (ATP-binding) site of mTOR, thereby circumventing the partial inhibition that is observed with first-generation mTOR inhibitors like rapamycin that act allosterically by binding FKBP12 (Liu et al., 2012). Torin1 has been widely used as a research tool to interrogate mTOR signaling in various cellular contexts, and its chemical lineage as a quinoline-derived molecule positions it within a well-characterized class of inhibitors that have been instrumental in expanding our understanding of mTOR-dependent regulation of autophagy and cellular metabolism (Liu et al., 2012).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Torin1 has been employed predominantly as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated its robust ability to inhibit mTOR signaling in cancer models, autophagy-deficient systems, and metabolic studies. For instance, Torin1 was shown to potently inhibit mTOR signaling pathways in glioblastoma and prostate cancer cells, significantly reducing cell-cycle progression and inducing apoptosis in certain contexts (Gu, 2017; Liu et al., 2012). Its use as an autophagy inducer is well documented, as experiments utilizing Torin1 have demonstrated increased autophagic flux and elevated lysosomal activity in multiple cell lines (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2012). Importantly, Torin1 is also used in studies with retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as evidenced by its ability to increase TFEB-driven luciferase reporter activity in ARPE-19 cells by effectively suppressing mTORC1 signaling (Huang et al., 2018). Despite these promising experimental findings, Torin1 has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication, including neurodegenerative disorders or dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Moreover, its intrinsic pharmacokinetic limitations—such as poor aqueous solubility, a short half-life, and low oral bioavailability—have been recognized in several studies, thereby limiting its potential as a direct therapeutic candidate without further structural optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Torin1 functions by competing with ATP for binding to the catalytic domain of mTOR, effectively blocking the phosphorylation of downstream substrates. Its ATP-competitive nature allows Torin1 to inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, thereby offering a broader inhibition profile than allosteric agents like rapamycin that primarily target mTORC1 (Guillem, 2015; Liu et al., 2012). Detailed molecular modeling and structure–activity relationship studies indicate that the tricyclic benzonaphthridinone core of Torin1 forms critical hinge-binding interactions with residues in the mTOR kinase domain (Liu et al., 2012). This interaction accounts for its high potency, as reflected in low nanomolar IC₅₀ values in cellular assays (Liu et al., 2012; Gros & Muller, 2014). Torin1 induces rapid dephosphorylation of canonical mTORC1 substrates, such as S6 kinase at Thr389 and 4E-BP1 at Thr37/46, which results in downregulation of protein synthesis and cellular growth signals (Misra & Pizzo, 2013). Moreover, by simultaneously inhibiting mTORC2, it reduces phosphorylation of Akt at Ser473—a site critical for full Akt activation—thus attenuating the feedback loops that typically reinvigorate upstream PI3K signaling in response to mTORC1 inhibition (Gu, 2017; Martina et al., 2014). A particularly notable feature of Torin1 is its slow off-rate, which leads to sustained inhibition of mTOR activity even after drug washout, a pharmacodynamic property that may confer prolonged downstream effects such as enhanced autophagic flux (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). The inhibition of mTOR by Torin1 correlates with dephosphorylation of transcription factors, particularly TFEB and TFE3; under normal nutrient-replete conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB (e.g., on S211 in TFEB) and TFE3, sequestering them in the cytosol through binding with 14-3-3 proteins (Huang et al., 2018; Martina et al., 2014). Upon mTOR inhibition by Torin1, TFEB is dephosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network genes that drive lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy (Li, 2018; Liu et al., 2013). This precise modulation of mTOR signaling and subsequent transcriptional reprogramming forms the biochemical basis for leveraging Torin1 as a candidate to ameliorate lysosomal clearance defects.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing Torin1 in the context of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is that potent inhibition of mTORC1/2 in RPE cells can lift the repressive phosphorylation that normally limits the activity of TFEB and TFE3. In RPE cells, as demonstrated by studies in ARPE-19 cell models, mTOR inhibition via Torin1 not only leads to decreased phosphorylation of S6 kinase but also results in marked activation of TFEB-driven transcription (Huang et al., 2018). When TFEB translocates to the nucleus, it binds to CLEAR elements present in the promoters of genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis, acidification (through the upregulation of V-ATPase subunits), and the maturation and activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD) (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018). In dry AMD, RPE cells exhibit a decline in lysosomal function along with accumulation of cellular debris and lipofuscin, which contribute to disease pathology. By inducing a robust CLEAR response, Torin1 is expected to restore lysosomal function through increased biogenesis, enhanced acidification, and elevated cathepsin D activity, thereby improving the clearance of toxic aggregates in RPE cells and ultimately mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Gu, 2017; Huang et al., 2018). Additionally, the sustained target engagement afforded by Torin1’s slow off-rate may provide prolonged therapeutic benefit even with intermittent dosing, an attractive feature given the chronic nature of AMD (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013). Recent evidence from preclinical iPSC models and autophagy-deficiency studies underscores the potential translation of mTOR-targeted strategies in restoring cellular homeostasis in degenerative diseases, lending further credence to this expected mechanism (Guillem, 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, Torin1 possesses a compelling mechanistic profile that aligns well with the therapeutic needs of dry AMD by targeting a fundamental pathway governing cellular homeostasis in RPE cells. Its origin from a quinoline-based scaffold and subsequent chemical optimization into a highly potent ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor underline its status as a valuable chemical probe in preclinical settings (Guillem, 2015). The dual inhibition of both mTORC1 and mTORC2 by Torin1, combined with its slow off-rate and sustained downstream effects—including dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3—make it an ideal tool for inducing lysosomal biogenesis and enhancing autophagic clearance (Martina et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2012). In cellular models, including ARPE-19 RPE cells, Torin1 has already demonstrated the ability to activate TFEB and upregulate CLEAR gene expression, which is directly relevant to counteracting the lysosomal clearance defects observed in dry AMD (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018).

However, significant challenges remain regarding the translational applicability of Torin1 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its reported poor aqueous solubility, short half-life, and low oral bioavailability present formidable barriers to clinical development unless addressed through formulation improvements or further medicinal chemistry optimization (Guillem, 2015; Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, while extensive preclinical literature supports its role as a robust mTOR inhibitor in cancer and autophagy research, there is a lack of direct in vivo evidence for its efficacy in ocular models, particularly in dry AMD or geographic atrophy (GA) mouse lines (Liu et al., 2013; Gu, 2017). Careful dosing will also be critical, as the broad and potent inhibition of mTOR can have unintended effects on cellular metabolism and protein synthesis beyond the intended enhancement of lysosomal function. Additionally, off-target effects have been observed in some biochemical screens at supraphysiologic concentrations, including binding to other PIKK family members such as ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK, although these are generally not manifested at the low nanomolar concentrations used in cellular assays (Settembre et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).

From the perspective of repurposing for dry AMD, Torin1’s deep mechanistic specificity is a double-edged sword: it offers a highly defined and robust approach to upregulating lysosomal biogenesis via the TFEB/TFE3 axis, yet its pharmacokinetic liabilities and the absence of any clinical history in ocular disease necessitate additional work. The promising in vitro data in RPE models (ARPE-19 cells) and iPSC-derived RPE systems provide valuable target validation, but before advancing to clinical trials a refined analog or an optimized delivery method (for example, local ocular administration to bypass systemic bioavailability issues) should be considered (Huang et al., 2018; Li, 2018; Wang et al., 2022).

In summary, Torin1 is an excellent candidate for preclinical proof-of-concept studies to validate mTOR inhibition as a strategy to combat lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD; however, further optimization to improve its stability and bioavailability, alongside rigorous in vivo testing in relevant AMD models, will be essential prior to clinical development (Guillem, 2015; Gu, 2017). The strengths of Torin1 lie in its potent, dual mTOR inhibition and its ability to robustly induce TFEB activation, whereas its weaknesses center on its pharmacokinetic shortcomings and the current lack of efficacy data in ocular disease models. Overall, with focused optimization and targeted delivery strategies, Torin1 or its derivatives may offer a promising therapeutic avenue for ameliorating the lysosomal clearance defects that underlie dry AMD pathology (Liu et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2018).

Proposal for Panobinostat (LBH589; Selleckchem S1030)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Panobinostat (LBH589) is a fully synthetic small‐molecule compound originally developed by Novartis and characterized chemically as a cinnamic hydroxamic acid analogue formulated as its anhydrous lactate salt. This molecule belongs to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), a group of compounds designed to inhibit the enzymatic activity of HDACs that regulate chromatin remodeling and transcription by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from histone proteins. Panobinostat’s chemical structure, defined by its hydroxamic acid moiety, is tailored to chelate the zinc ion in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby preventing deacetylation reactions that normally lead to a condensed chromatin state. In its initial development, panobinostat was formulated in multiple dosage forms, including oral hard capsules containing 10, 15, or 20 mg doses and earlier intravenous preparations, illustrating its versatility in administration routes for different clinical indications (Van Veggel, Westerman, & Hamberg, 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007). Compounds of this class have historically been employed in oncology, where their capacity to induce hyperacetylation of histone and non-histone substrates leads to altered gene transcription, cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and eventual apoptosis in malignant cells (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cea et al., 2013). Moreover, the broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC isoforms—spanning Classes I, II, and IV—distinguishes panobinostat as a “pan-HDAC inhibitor” with high potency at nanomolar concentrations, a characteristic that underlies its robust pharmacological profile and its subsequent regulatory approvals for certain cancer indications (Morabito et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Since its discovery, panobinostat has undergone extensive preclinical and clinical evaluation primarily targeting multiple myeloma and various hematologic malignancies. Early phase clinical trials established that, as a single agent, panobinostat had modest activity; however, its combination with proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib and corticosteroids like dexamethasone produced synergistic effects that translated into significant improvements in progression‐free survival in relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma patients. This positive clinical efficacy culminated in its approval by both the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2015 for the treatment of patients with multiple myeloma who had received at least two prior regimens (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Libby et al., 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021). Beyond multiple myeloma, panobinostat has been scrutinized in a variety of clinical settings—including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and several solid tumor malignancies—to explore its antitumor potential in combination therapies, given its capacity to potentiate the cytotoxic effects of other agents by modulating epigenetic regulation (Cea et al., 2013; Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). Despite its demonstrated efficacy in cancer, there is no recorded use of panobinostat in ophthalmological diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in any similar degenerative condition. The extensive body of clinical research on HDAC inhibitors has predominantly focused on antineoplastic applications, and while some mechanistic parallels exist between the cellular processes targeted in cancer and those disrupted in degenerative retinal diseases, panobinostat’s utility in dry AMD remains an uncharted territory that has thus far not been explored in preclinical or clinical trials (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016; Libby et al., 2015).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, panobinostat exerts its biological effects primarily through the inhibition of histone deacetylase enzymes. The compound’s hydroxamic acid group binds with high affinity to the zinc ion located in the catalytic domain of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking the deacetylation of lysine residues on histone tails as well as on several non-histone proteins. This blockade causes an accumulation of acetylated histones, which in turn results in a more open chromatin conformation that facilitates enhanced transcription of a multitude of genes, including those pivotal for cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and cellular differentiation (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). Beyond its classical role in modifying histone tail acetylation, panobinostat’s broad inhibition across HDAC classes implies that it can modulate the acetylation status of key transcription factors, chaperone proteins (such as heat shock protein 90), and structural proteins like α-tubulin. This wide-ranging impact on protein acetylation alters the functional activity of numerous signaling pathways and cellular processes, contributing to anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic outcomes in cancer cells (Morabito et al., 2016). The pleiotropic nature of its action is further evidenced by the induction of autophagy in various tumor models, an effect thought to be mediated by the increased acetylation and transcriptional activation of master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis such as transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although the provided literature does not explicitly detail TFEB upregulation in response to panobinostat, the general tendency of HDAC inhibitors to enhance acetylation-dependent transcription supports the hypothesis that TFEB and its downstream lysosomal genes could be upregulated—thereby promoting autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Libby et al., 2015). This complex interplay of molecular events not only underpins panobinostat’s established antitumor activity but also provides a rationale for its possible repurposing in degenerative diseases where enhanced cellular clearance mechanisms may be therapeutic (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD):  
Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by the progressive dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which is responsible for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and the clearance of cellular debris. A central pathological hallmark of dry AMD is the accumulation of drusen deposits beneath the RPE, partly attributable to impaired lysosomal degradation and autophagy. In the context of this disease, the hypothesis proposes that localized ocular administration of panobinostat could inhibit HDAC activity in RPE cells, leading to a global increase in histone acetylation. This epigenetic modulation is expected to activate acetylation-dependent transcription factors such as TFEB—a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy—that, once activated, upregulates a network of genes involved in lysosomal acidification and cathepsin D expression (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Cinek & Karalı, 2021). Enhanced expression of these lysosomal components is anticipated to restore or improve the degradative capacity of the RPE, facilitating the clearance of drusen deposits and ameliorating the pathological buildup of cellular waste characteristic of dry AMD.

In preclinical oncology studies, panobinostat has consistently induced autophagy and promoted lysosomal function in cancer cells, leading to growth inhibition and apoptosis. If similar cellular responses occur in RPE cells, then panobinostat may stimulate a beneficial autophagic flux that targets accumulated proteins and lipids for degradation (Libby et al., 2015). The expression of cathepsin D—a lysosomal protease critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments and other metabolic substrates—is well documented in RPE cells, and its activity is tightly regulated by lysosomal pH; thus, any intervention that improves lysosomal acidification is likely to have a favorable impact on RPE homeostasis (Mottamal et al., 2015; Morabito et al., 2016). These findings support the proposed mechanism whereby panobinostat’s inhibition of HDACs may indirectly enhance the transcriptional activation of TFEB, culminating in improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Moreover, the broad HDAC inhibitory profile of panobinostat ensures that multiple redundant deacetylation pathways are targeted simultaneously, offering the potential for robust and sustained activation of the cellular clearance machinery compared to more selective agents (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).

From a translational perspective, it is crucial to recognize that systemic toxicity has been an important limitation of panobinostat in oncologic settings, where adverse effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, thrombocytopenia, and cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation) have been observed. However, the concept of localized ocular dosing—via intravitreal injection or topical delivery—could potentially mitigate these risks by achieving high local drug concentrations with minimal systemic exposure (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). In the specific context of dry AMD, where chronic, localized pathology is present in the retina, targeted delivery of panobinostat could allow for the modulation of RPE cellular processes without triggering widespread adverse reactions. This targeted approach aligns with current trends in ocular pharmacotherapy, which increasingly favor local drug delivery systems designed to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity (Bondarev et al., 2021; Van Veggel et al., 2018). Ultimately, the expected outcome in the proposed assay is that panobinostat treatment will lead to measurable upregulation of lysosomal gene expression, restoration of lysosomal acidification, and enhanced activity of cathepsin D within RPE cells, thereby reducing the burden of drusen deposits and potentially slowing the progression of dry AMD (Cea et al., 2013; Libby et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of panobinostat for dry age-related macular degeneration presents an intriguing and biologically plausible strategy that leverages the compound’s well-documented HDAC inhibitory properties to modulate critical intracellular degradation pathways. One of the foremost strengths of this therapeutic candidate is its potent, broad-spectrum inhibition of HDAC enzymes at low nanomolar concentrations, which has been repeatedly demonstrated in various preclinical and clinical studies in oncology (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016). The resultant hyperacetylation of histones and non-histone proteins not only promotes cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in malignant cells but also facilitates the transcriptional activation of autophagy- and lysosome-related genes—a pathway that could be harnessed to restore faithful lysosomal degradation in retinal pigment epithelial cells affected in dry AMD (Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Cinek & Karalı, 2021).

In terms of mechanistic specificity, the broad inhibitory profile of panobinostat could be seen as an advantage in the context of dry AMD, where multiple deacetylation pathways may contribute to the impaired clearance of cellular debris. By simultaneously inhibiting several HDAC isoforms, panobinostat is likely to achieve a more robust activation of TFEB and other transcription factors central to lysosomal biogenesis, thereby amplifying the cellular clearance mechanisms required to remove drusen deposits (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). Additionally, the existing clinical experience with panobinostat in oncology provides a rich repository of pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and safety data that can inform dose optimization and risk management strategies—albeit with the caveat that ocular tissues may respond differently to HDAC inhibition than cancer cells (Bondarev et al., 2021; Libby et al., 2015).

Nevertheless, several significant weaknesses must be acknowledged in evaluating panobinostat as a candidate for dry AMD treatment. Chief among these is the potential for systemic toxicity. Panobinostat’s clinical utilization in cancer has been limited by adverse side effects including gastrointestinal toxicity, thrombocytopenia, and cardiac complications, and although localized ocular delivery may attenuate these concerns, the safety profile of panobinostat in retinal tissues remains largely unexplored (Libby et al., 2015; Karol et al., 2020). Moreover, the pharmacokinetic behavior of panobinostat when administered locally to the eye is unknown; challenges such as drug solubility, stability, and diffusion across retinal layers must be addressed rigorously in preclinical models. There is also the possibility of off-target effects in retinal cells that could exacerbate retinal stress or contribute to unwanted inflammation, particularly given the complex interplay of epigenetic regulation in non-dividing, highly specialized cells like the RPE (Cea et al., 2013; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015).

Another point of concern is the translational leap from oncology to ophthalmology. While the mechanistic rationale for using panobinostat to enhance autophagy and lysosomal function is supported by its effects in cancer cells, RPE cells possess distinctive metabolic and regulatory pathways that may not respond identically to HDAC inhibition. The degree to which TFEB and other autophagy or lysosomal genes are modulated by panobinostat in RPE cells has not yet been directly demonstrated, and significant differences in chromatin structure and gene expression profiles between cancer cells and differentiated RPE cells could impact both efficacy and safety outcomes (Morabito et al., 2016; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011). In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD necessitates long-term treatment, and the potential cumulative effects of continuous HDAC inhibition in ocular tissues raise concerns regarding retinal integrity, visual function, and overall ocular health over extended periods—a consideration that remains entirely speculative without targeted preclinical studies (Dokmanovic, Clarke, & Marks, 2007; Morabito et al., 2016).

From a drug development perspective, the strategy of repurposing panobinostat for dry AMD is compelling because it integrates a well-characterized molecular mode of action with an unmet clinical need. However, critical translational challenges must be overcome. These include reformulating panobinostat for localized ocular delivery, establishing appropriate dosing regimens that maximize local efficacy while minimizing toxicity, and conducting comprehensive preclinical evaluations in relevant in vitro and in vivo models of dry AMD. The potential benefit of enhancing lysosomal clearance through increased TFEB activation is a particularly attractive aspect of this proposal, as impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are recognized contributors to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Cinek & Karalı, 2021; Morabito et al., 2016). Nonetheless, a careful balance must be maintained, as excessive activation of autophagy pathways in non-proliferative tissues may inadvertently trigger cell death or exacerbated stress responses.

In summary, while panobinostat’s established efficacy in oncology and its well-documented ability to induce broad epigenetic changes provide a strong scientific foundation for its potential repurposing, a number of critical challenges remain. On the positive side, panobinostat is among the most potent HDAC inhibitors available, capable of eliciting profound changes in gene expression that might restore lysosomal function in RPE cells and thereby clear accumulated drusen deposits. In addition, modern advances in ocular drug delivery—such as intravitreal injections, biodegradable implants, or topical formulations enhanced by nanocarrier systems—offer promising routes to achieve the necessary drug concentrations in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and toxicity (Van Veggel et al., 2018; Morabito et al., 2016).

Conversely, the risk of adverse effects related to HDAC inhibition, the unknown ocular pharmacokinetics, and the potential differences in cellular responses between cancerous and retinal cells represent significant hurdles that must be rigorously addressed through targeted preclinical research. Furthermore, given that panobinostat’s clinical track record is largely confined to oncology, its application in a degenerative ocular disease such as dry AMD would require new, dedicated studies to validate its safety, efficacy, and optimal delivery modality in this context (Libby et al., 2015; Afifi et al., 2015).

Overall, panobinostat emerges as a promising yet challenging candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to robustly inhibit multiple HDAC isoforms and thereby potentially activate TFEB and lysosomal gene networks aligns well with the therapeutic strategy of improving autophagic clearance in RPE cells. However, substantial gaps in knowledge remain regarding its direct effects on retinal cells and the feasibility of its long-term use in an ocular setting. Consequently, while the mechanistic rationale is strong and the preclinical evidence from oncology provides useful insights, extensive additional research is needed to assess the translational potential, determine safe and efficacious ocular dosing parameters, and ultimately validate this approach in models that reliably mimic the pathophysiology of dry AMD (Prince et al., 2009; Morabito et al., 2016; Benedetti, Conte, & Altucci, 2015; Bondarev et al., 2021).

In conclusion, panobinostat’s repurposing for dry AMD is grounded in a robust understanding of epigenetic regulation and lysosomal biology. Its established clinical use in oncology offers a wealth of pharmacological data and a precedent for potent HDAC inhibition, while the hypothesis that HDAC inhibitors can reactivate latent clearance pathways in RPE cells is both innovative and scientifically plausible. The strengths of panobinostat lie in its potency, broad-spectrum activity, and documented ability to elicit autophagic responses, which collectively suggest that, under the right conditions and with a carefully optimized ocular delivery system, it could address one of the major pathophysiological mechanisms underlying dry AMD. Nonetheless, the weaknesses, including potential off-target toxicity, uncertain ocular pharmacokinetics, and the need for a comprehensive reevaluation of its effects in non-malignant, differentiated cell types, must be thoroughly investigated before advancing into clinical studies. Therefore, data from directed preclinical experiments employing RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD will be essential in determining whether the benefits of panobinostat can be safely and effectively harnessed to treat this common cause of vision loss in the elderly (Srinivas, 2017; Van Veggel et al., 2018; Bondarev et al., 2021; Carafa, Nebbioso, & Altucci, 2011).
