Proposal for Harmine (Sigma H1392)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Harmine is a naturally occurring β-carboline alkaloid that is abundant in Peganum harmala L., and has been investigated for neuropharmacological activities including acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition, antioxidant activity, and anti-inflammatory effects, with related β-carbolines such as harmaline frequently studied alongside it (Singh et al., 2024). As an alkaloid, harmine belongs to a class of nitrogen-containing, basic, often polycyclic natural products that have historically provided a rich source of neuroactive scaffolds and approved therapeutics across neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), with the literature situating harmine within a broader set of “neuroprotective alkaloids” considered for NDD drug discovery (Singh et al., 2024). In preclinical pharmacology, water-soluble salt forms such as harmine hydrochloride have been used, and medicinal chemistry analogs with higher potency than the parent have been reported, supporting tractability for formulation and structure–activity optimization (Singh et al., 2024).

The mechanistic disease context relevant to dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is dominated by lysosomal and autophagy dysfunction in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), where impaired lysosomal degradation, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and autophagic flux promote lipofuscin accumulation, oxidative stress, complement/inflammasome activation, and RPE death (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Master regulators of lysosomal biogenesis and degradative capacity include TFEB/TFE3, which are controlled by mTORC1, AMPK, Ca2+/calcineurin, and lysosomal signaling nodes; TFEB drives expression of the CLEAR gene network to expand lysosomal/autophagy capacity and has been repeatedly highlighted as a central therapeutic axis for restoring RPE degradative function (Boya et al., 2023). The CLEAR program directly impacts lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP2 and proteases like cathepsins, and TFEB activity is constrained by nutrient-sensing mTORC1 signaling on the lysosomal surface (Boya et al., 2023). Because LAMP2 deficiency impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation and yields AMD-like phenotypes, and cathepsin D (CTSD) is the primary POS protease in RPE, TFEB-mediated enhancement of these systems is mechanistically aligned with dry AMD pathobiology (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Note, however, that the provided evidence base contains no direct data linking harmine to TFEB activation, CLEAR gene induction, or DYRK1A inhibition in RPE or neural cells; those specific connections are absent in the cited retinal/lysosome literature excerpts (Boya et al., 2023).

Therapeutic History  
No registered clinical trials were identified on ClinicalTrials.gov for the search terms “Harmine retinal pigment epithelium” or “Harmine dry age-related macular degeneration,” indicating no publicly registered clinical evaluation of harmine for dry AMD or closely related RPE indications under those exact phrases (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The negative registry findings were reiterated in independent queries and associated summaries, which emphasize that these are specific to the exact search terms and this registry, and do not exclude preclinical studies, trials registered elsewhere, or studies indexed under alternative nomenclature; nonetheless, they demonstrate a lack of registered clinical activity for harmine in dry AMD on this platform (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Outside ophthalmology, harmine has a preclinical pharmacology history in neurodegenerative disease models, including antiparkinsonian activity comparable in some studies to levodopa, anti-cataleptogenic effects in haloperidol models at 2.5–5 mg/kg, and reduction of MPTP-induced oligokinesia, with some analogs achieving desired effects at 2 mg/kg compared with 20 mg/kg for harmine (Singh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, harmine promotes time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species via upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and enhanced PKA phosphorylation, supporting a proteostasis-modulating mechanism in CNS models (Singh et al., 2024). Additional pharmacology reported in the literature includes MAO and AChE inhibition in preclinical models, consistent with multi-target neuromodulatory activity of β-carbolines (Singh et al., 2024). The excerpts provided here do not document any prior use of harmine in ocular disease models or clinical settings for retinal disease, nor do they offer ocular pharmacokinetic/tissue exposure or ocular tolerability data (Singh et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action  
Known pharmacology of harmine in the supplied materials centers on: (1) enhancement of proteasome-dependent clearance of aggregation-prone proteins through upregulation of the PSMD1 subunit and PKA-mediated mechanisms, leading to time- and dose-dependent degradation of α-synuclein species; and (2) inhibition of monoamine oxidase (MAO) and acetylcholinesterase (AChE), along with reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in diverse preclinical systems (Singh et al., 2024). These activities position harmine as a multi-modal agent influencing proteostasis and neurotransmitter pathways in the CNS (Singh et al., 2024).

By contrast, the specific hypothesis under evaluation—that harmine will inhibit DYRK1A in RPE, increase TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, and thereby promote CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis, acidification, and CTSD activity—is not supported by direct evidence in the provided context; the retinal/lysosomal references explicitly discuss TFEB/TFE3 regulation, RPE lysosome biology, and autophagy dysfunction in AMD, but do not report DYRK1A involvement or link harmine to TFEB modulation (Boya et al., 2023). The mechanistic literature excerpts instead highlight established regulatory routes by which TFEB/TFE3 control lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy: mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation prevents TFEB nuclear import, whereas AMPK activation and lysosomal Ca2+/calcineurin signaling can promote TFEB/TFE3 dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation to induce the CLEAR program (Boya et al., 2023). In the RPE, upstream lysosomal amino-acid sensing via V-ATPase–Ragulator–Rag GTPases coordinates mTORC1 activity at the lysosomal membrane, and disruptions in these nodes (e.g., βA3/A1-crystallin deficits) impair TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene expression, contributing to AMD-like phenotypes (Boya et al., 2023; Sinha et al., 2016).

The RPE’s degradative workload is extraordinary—daily heterophagy of shed photoreceptor outer segments and continuous autophagy—so lysosomal membrane proteins and hydrolytic enzyme systems are critical to homeostasis: LAMP2 is a TFEB/CLEAR target whose deficiency delays POS degradation and produces AMD-like retinal changes, and CTSD is the principal lysosomal protease mediating POS/rhodopsin degradation; impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion and elevated lysosomal pH (e.g., due to A2E or lipofuscin) reduce cathepsin activity and drive lipofuscinogenesis and RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Consequences of lysosomal failure include LMP with cytosolic release of cathepsins, DAMP emission, complement activation, and necroptotic cell death; interventions that stabilize lysosomal membranes (e.g., Hsp70 induction) or normalize pH have restored lysosomal function and reduced retinal degeneration in preclinical models, underscoring the therapeutic relevance of lysosome-centric strategies (Boya et al., 2023). Therapeutic interventions that restore lysosomal enzyme function (e.g., cathepsin D gene therapy) and enhance CMA or autophagy have also attenuated retinal degeneration and preserved visual function in vivo, further supporting this axis (Boya et al., 2023).

In summary, while TFEB activation and lysosomal rejuvenation are compelling, disease-relevant mechanisms for dry AMD, the materials provided do not document harmine as a DYRK1A inhibitor in RPE, or as an agent that increases TFEB nuclear translocation, CLEAR gene expression, LAMP1/2 abundance, or CTSD activity in ocular systems; these specific mechanistic links remain unsubstantiated in this evidence set (Boya et al., 2023).

Expected Effect  
If the hypothesized mechanism were correct—that harmine inhibits a TFEB-restraining kinase and thereby drives TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene activation in RPE—the expected cellular outcomes would include increased lysosomal biogenesis, improved lysosomal acidification and ion homeostasis, higher LAMP2/LAMP1 expression, augmented cathepsin content and activity (including CTSD), enhanced autophagic flux, and improved phagosome–lysosome fusion and degradation of POS, together leading to reduced lipofuscin burden, mitigation of LMP, and protection from necroptosis and chronic inflammation (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023). TFEB is the master transcriptional regulator of the CLEAR program, and its dephosphorylation/nuclear localization induces expression of genes that collectively increase lysosomal number and degradative competence; in the RPE, CLEAR-dependent targets include LAMP2, whose deficiency causes delayed POS clearance and AMD-like degeneration (Boya et al., 2023). A direct functional prediction is that promoting TFEB activity would increase lysosome number and cathepsin activity; indeed, pharmacologic Ezrin inhibition—through a distinct regulatory route—has been shown to increase lysosomal number and cathepsin activity in RPE, reduce vision loss, and thus serves as proof-of-concept that boosting lysosomal protease capacity is salutary in retinal disease models (Boya et al., 2023). Because CTSD is the primary POS protease in RPE and is inhibited by elevated lysosomal pH or phototoxic lipofuscin constituents such as A2E, a TFEB-driven program that improves acidification and enzymatic capacity would be predicted to restore POS processing and limit lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Boya et al., 2023).

Autophagy and mitophagy readouts should similarly improve: TFEB/CLEAR activation increases autophagosome formation and lysosomal fusion, restoring autophagic flux diminished with age and in AMD, and reducing SQSTM1/p62 accumulation and associated proteostatic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). Enhanced lysosomal function is expected to reduce DAMP release and intracellular complement activation, attenuate inflammasome/ferroptosis cascades associated with reduced autophagy, and stabilize mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk via AMPK-dependent signaling and TFEB-induced biogenesis (Boya et al., 2023). Because mTORC1 hyperactivation in the RPE causes lysosomal dysfunction and AMD-like degeneration, an agent that indirectly reduces mTORC1 activity or relieves TFEB from mTORC1/AKT constraints could restore lysosomal-autophagic balance and improve RPE survival (Boya et al., 2023).

However, the materials provided include no experimental data demonstrating that harmine produces these outcomes in RPE or retina, nor do they show ocular pharmacokinetics or local tolerability; thus, in the proposed assays, any expected effects of harmine on TFEB/CLEAR, lysosomal acidification, LAMP1/2, CTSD, POS clearance, autophagic flux, or inflammatory readouts should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require direct testing (Singh et al., 2024). In designing such assays, relevant endpoints and models include: TFEB nuclear translocation and CLEAR gene panels; Lysotracker-based pH measurements; LAMP1/LAMP2 abundance; total and active CTSD and cathepsin activity assays; live-cell phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics with POS; A2E/lipofuscin-loaded RPE to model elevated lysosomal pH and LMP susceptibility; LC3-II turnover and SQSTM1/p62 levels to quantify autophagic flux; markers of LMP (cytosolic cathepsin activity) and necroptosis; complement activation and inflammasome markers (e.g., IL-1β) in stressed RPE—each aligned with disease-relevant mechanisms in the cited literature (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Mechanistic alignment with RPE pathobiology: The dry AMD literature strongly implicates lysosomal dysfunction, autophagy decline, impaired phagosome–lysosome fusion, and defective degradative capacity in RPE degeneration; TFEB-directed lysosomal biogenesis and restoration of lysosomal pH/ion homeostasis are repeatedly identified as rational therapeutic axes (Boya et al., 2023). CLEAR-dependent targets such as LAMP2 and cathepsins (including CTSD) are essential for POS processing and retinal homeostasis, and their failure yields AMD-like phenotypes—consistent with the proposed direction of effect (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
- Proof-of-concept for lysosome-centric interventions: Stabilization of lysosomal membranes, normalization of lysosomal pH, enhancement of cathepsin activity, activation of CMA, and direct correction of lysosomal enzyme deficits each attenuate retinal degeneration and preserve function in preclinical models, providing a diverse set of precedents that validate the therapeutic strategy at the pathway level (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Proteostasis-modulating activity of harmine: In CNS models, harmine promotes clearance of misfolded/aggregation-prone proteins via the ubiquitin–proteasome system, upregulating PSMD1 and enhancing PKA-dependent proteasomal activity; this establishes harmine as a proteostasis-active scaffold with in vivo pharmacology, a potentially favorable feature for diseases characterized by toxic protein/lipid waste accumulation (Singh et al., 2024).  
- Formulation and medicinal chemistry tractability: A water-soluble hydrochloride salt has been used in vivo, and analogs with markedly improved potency over harmine have been reported, supporting a path for optimization if ocular exposure or target engagement proves limiting (Singh et al., 2024).

Weaknesses and Critical Gaps  
- No direct evidence for the central hypothesis: The provided evidence base lacks demonstrations that harmine inhibits DYRK1A, increases TFEB dephosphorylation/nuclear localization, induces CLEAR gene expression, or elevates LAMP1/2 and CTSD in RPE or neural cells; consequently, the core premise—DYRK1A→TFEB→CLEAR engagement by harmine in RPE—remains unsubstantiated here (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Absence of ophthalmic data: There are no ocular pharmacokinetics, retina/RPE exposure, or local ocular tolerability data for harmine in the materials provided, which constitute major translational risks for an ocular indication (Singh et al., 2024).  
- No registered clinical activity in dry AMD: Multiple ClinicalTrials.gov queries under relevant phrases returned zero trials, indicating an absence of publicly registered clinical development for harmine in RPE/dry AMD; this constrains assessment of clinical feasibility, ocular target engagement, and dose–response in humans for this indication (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- Potential systemic off-target liabilities: Harmine’s MAO and AChE inhibitory activities in preclinical models indicate multi-target pharmacology that could complicate systemic dosing for ocular indications, although the present excerpts do not provide human tolerability or safety data to quantify this risk; nonetheless, the profile reinforces the need for careful exposure–response characterization and possibly local delivery strategies (Singh et al., 2024).  
- Unclear linkage to mTORC1/AMPK axes in RPE: The TFEB pathway in RPE is tightly regulated by mTORC1, AMPK, lysosomal Ca2+/calcineurin, and V-ATPase–Ragulator signaling; the provided materials do not show harmine’s effects on these nodes in ocular systems, leaving mechanistic plausibility at the level of generic TFEB activation rather than compound-specific evidence (Boya et al., 2023).

Decision Context and Recommended Next Steps  
- Evidence-based conclusion: On the evidence provided here, harmine is not yet a validated candidate for dry AMD, because the central mechanism-of-action claims (DYRK1A inhibition leading to TFEB/CLEAR activation in RPE) are not supported by direct data in these materials, and there is no ocular PK/tolerability or registered clinical experience to de-risk translation (Boya et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
- High-priority experiments to test the hypothesis:  
  • In vitro RPE mechanistic assays: quantify TFEB nuclear translocation, TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation status, and CLEAR gene panels after harmine exposure; measure LAMP1/LAMP2 abundance, cathepsin content and activity (CTSD), lysosomal pH (Lysotracker/LysoSensor), and phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics in POS-fed RPE; evaluate autophagic flux via LC3-II turnover and SQSTM1/p62; determine effects under A2E/lipofuscin load and oxidative stress to model AMD-relevant stressors (Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Boya et al., 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023).  
  • Inflammation/complement readouts: assess DAMP release, complement activation, inflammasome markers (e.g., IL-1β), and ferroptosis regulators, given the link between reduced autophagy and inflammasome–ferroptosis activation in RPE (Boya et al., 2023).  
  • Pathway positioning: determine harmine’s impact on mTORC1 (p-S6K, p-4E-BP1), AMPK activation, and Ca2+/calcineurin signaling, to map its position relative to TFEB regulatory inputs in RPE (Boya et al., 2023).  
  • Ocular pharmacokinetics and tolerability: quantify retina/RPE exposure after systemic and local (intravitreal/subconjunctival) dosing of harmine and harmine·HCl; evaluate local ocular tolerability (inflammation, IOP, ERG, retinal histopathology); these data are entirely missing in the provided materials and are essential for translational assessment (Singh et al., 2024).  
  • Comparative benchmarking: include positive controls known to enhance lysosomal function in RPE (e.g., mTORC1 inhibitors, AMPK activators, Ezrin pathway modulators) to calibrate the magnitude of effect needed for translational relevance (Boya et al., 2023).

- Literature and registry expansion: Because ClinicalTrials.gov queries under narrow terms returned no trials, broaden searches to other registries (WHO ICTRP, EU CTR), synonyms/related classes (β-carbolines, DYRK1A inhibitors) and biomedical literature (PubMed/Embase) for any published RPE/ocular data on harmine or close analogs; this is explicitly recommended in the ClinicalTrials.gov query notes to ensure a comprehensive landscape assessment (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Programmatic Risk–Benefit Assessment  
- Potential upside: If harmine or an optimized analog demonstrates robust TFEB/CLEAR activation and lysosomal rejuvenation in RPE—with measurable restoration of LAMP2 and CTSD activity, improved POS clearance, reduced lipofuscin/LMP, and downstream anti-inflammatory benefits—then it would sit squarely on a well-validated pathophysiological axis in dry AMD, akin to other successful lysosome-targeted interventions in retinal models (Boya et al., 2023).  
- Key derisking milestones: Demonstrating ocular exposure at pharmacologically relevant levels without ocular toxicity, and confirming TFEB/CLEAR pathway engagement with functional rescue of RPE degradative capacity, are gating requirements for progression (Singh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023).  
- Principal uncertainties: The absence of direct evidence tying harmine to TFEB activation in RPE or neural systems in the provided materials, the lack of ocular PK/tolerability data, and the multi-target CNS pharmacology (MAO/AChE inhibition) that may complicate systemic dosing strategies collectively elevate development risk (Boya et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024).

Bottom Line  
Harmine presents as a proteostasis-active, neuropharmacologically tractable scaffold with preclinical in vivo CNS efficacy and formulation/medicinal chemistry precedent, but the specific mechanism-of-action proposed for dry AMD—DYRK1A inhibition leading to TFEB/CLEAR-mediated lysosomal rejuvenation in RPE—lacks direct support in the provided evidence base, and there is no ocular pharmacokinetic or tolerability information to enable translational planning (Singh et al., 2024; Boya et al., 2023). Given the strong independent rationale for TFEB-directed lysosomal restoration in RPE and the centrality of CTSD/LAMP2 to POS processing and retinal integrity, harmine remains an intriguing, but currently unvalidated, hypothesis-driven candidate whose advancement should be contingent on near-term generation of rigorous RPE mechanistic data and ocular PK/tolerability profiles, alongside expanded literature/registry searches for any unpublished or non-ClinicalTrials.gov evidence (Boya et al., 2023; Si et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Proposal for GSK126 (Selleckchem S7061)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
GSK126 is a small‐molecule, synthetic compound originally developed as a selective inhibitor of the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) enzyme. As a S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-competitive inhibitor, GSK126 belongs to the class of epigenetic modulators that work by impairing the catalytic activity of EZH2, a methyltransferase that deposits H3K27me3 repressive marks on chromatin. These compounds were discovered and optimized initially for use in cancer, where aberrant EZH2 activity drives tumor progression through silencing of tumor suppressor genes. The chemical structure of GSK126 and its mode of synthesis have been well characterized in the oncology literature, and the compound has been extensively used in preclinical models and early phase clinical studies to assess its ability to relieve polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-mediated gene silencing (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). As such, GSK126 represents a prototypical member of a therapeutic class that has been used predominantly in oncology, with recent efforts to repurpose its epigenetic modulatory properties to other diseases where aberrant gene repression plays a role.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development of EZH2 inhibitors such as GSK126 has been focused predominantly on oncological applications. Several clinical trials have evaluated EZH2 inhibitors in hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, where deregulated EZH2 activity supports cancer cell proliferation and survival. For example, while related compounds (e.g., GSK2816126) were investigated in dose escalation studies in patients with hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, GSK126 itself has been studied preclinically and in clinical contexts for its anti-proliferative effects in cancer models (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014). In addition, high-content screening initiatives in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells have identified EZH2 inhibitors among a range of epigenetic drug candidates, with studies reporting that GSK126 can upregulate p16 expression in RPE models as part of broader efforts to identify modulators of senescence (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). However, there is no published record to date of GSK126 being deployed specifically for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or for directly targeting lysosomal dysfunction in ocular tissues. Open Targets Platform data reveal a very weak association between EZH2 and AMD, with minimal documented evidence tying EZH2 activity directly to disease pathogenesis in the retina (Buniello et al., 2025). Thus, while extensive preclinical and clinical data substantiate the use of EZH2 inhibitors in cancer, their specific application to dry AMD remains an emerging hypothesis that has not yet been validated either in biochemical in vitro studies or in in vivo ocular models.

Mechanism of Action:  
The primary mechanism of action of GSK126 is based on its inhibition of EZH2 activity. EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) that methylates lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3), a modification generally associated with transcriptional silencing of target genes. By competitively binding to the SAM-binding pocket of EZH2, GSK126 prevents the addition of methyl groups to H3K27, thereby reducing the global levels of H3K27me3 and leading to a derepression of genes normally silenced by this epigenetic mark (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17). In cancer cells, this mechanism leads to reactivation of tumor suppressor genes such as p16, and similar findings have been observed in epigenetic drug screens using RPE cells where treatment with GSK126 resulted in upregulation of p16 expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53).

The repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD suggests that similar chromatin-level mechanisms could be exploited in RPE cells to relieve the suppression of the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network, a collection of genes regulated by the master transcription factor TFEB responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function. Under stress conditions, the epigenetic repression mediated by EZH2 via H3K27me3 may contribute to the diminished expression of lysosomal genes, including those coding for components of the acidification machinery such as vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) subunits and lysosomal proteases like cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7). The rationale is that inhibition of EZH2 with GSK126 will alleviate H3K27me3 deposition at promoters of lysosomal genes, allowing TFEB to more effectively activate the transcription of these CLEAR genes. In cancer models, related observations have been made where EZH2 inhibition leads to increased expression of V-ATPase subunits and CTSD (cathepsin D) as well as enhancement of autophagy (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17, 22–23). Although most of these studies have been conducted in cancer or other non-ocular cell types, the underlying biochemical interactions between EZH2, histone modifications, and gene expression remain consistent and serve as the basis for the proposed mechanism in RPE cells. In summary, by reducing H3K27me3-mediated repression, GSK126 is expected to derepress genes that are essential for maintaining proper lysosomal acidification, proteolysis, and overall cell homeostasis, thereby addressing one potential pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The therapeutic hypothesis posits that in the context of dry AMD, RPE cells suffer from lysosomal dysfunction—manifested by aberrant acidification and insufficient activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin D—that contributes to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and cellular debris. TFEB, a transcription factor known to drive the expression of the CLEAR network, plays a critical role in regulating lysosomal biogenesis and function. Notably, in aging retina and AMD, the activation of TFEB-mediated gene expression is impaired, leading to reduced levels of essential lysosomal enzymes and V-ATPase subunits, as well as the accumulation of lipofuscin-like material (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 9–10). The proposed effect of GSK126 in RPE cells is to inhibit EZH2 and relieve the epigenetic repression imposed by H3K27me3 at lysosomal gene promoters. This derepression should allow TFEB to more robustly activate the transcription of its target genes, thereby enhancing the expression of V-ATPase subunits and cathepsin D. Enhanced V-ATPase expression will improve lysosomal acidification—a key determinant of lysosome function—while increased levels of cathepsin D will bolster the degradative capacity of the lysosome. In other cellular contexts, such as in certain cancer cell lines, EZH2 inhibition has been shown to upregulate autophagy-related genes, including those involved in lysosomal function, which supports the plausibility of this mechanism in RPE cells (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 16–17; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15).

Given that RPE cells are highly metabolically active and rely on efficient lysosomal degradation for the phagocytosis and recycling of photoreceptor outer segments, the expected outcome of GSK126 treatment would be an improvement in lysosomal clearance. This improvement could translate into a reduction of the toxic protein aggregates and lipofuscin accumulation that are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology. In vitro, one would anticipate observing an increase in TFEB nuclear translocation, upregulation of CLEAR network genes, enhanced lysosomal acidification (as measured by V-ATPase activity) and restored cathepsin D levels in treated RPE cells, thereby validating the hypothesized mechanism (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 17–18; Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 3–4). In vivo, similar effects might lead to improved RPE function and a potentially slower progression of dry AMD. However, it is important to note that while there is evidence for the role of EZH2 in regulating p16 and autophagy in various models, direct evidence linking GSK126 treatment to restored lysosomal gene networks in RPE cells remains to be generated.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposal to repurpose GSK126 for dry AMD represents an innovative application of epigenetic therapy beyond its established role in oncology. One of the major strengths of this candidate is the robust preclinical and clinical safety data that have been accumulated in cancer studies. The availability of dosing and pharmacokinetic profiles from oncology clinical trials offers a significant advantage in terms of de-risking the development timeline for repurposing efforts (GlaxoSmithKline, 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Moreover, the mechanistic rationale is scientifically sound: EZH2 is a well-characterized repressor of gene transcription via H3K27me3, and its inhibition could indeed lead to the derepression of genes critical for lysosomal maintenance (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 5–7).

However, there are several weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, despite the compelling mechanistic hypothesis, there is a paucity of direct evidence demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition in RPE cells leads to upregulation of lysosomal genes, specifically those involved in the acidification machinery and cathepsin D expression (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53). Second, comprehensive target-disease association analyses using platforms such as Open Targets reveal a very weak connection between EZH2 and AMD, which raises the possibility that EZH2’s role in the pathogenesis of dry AMD may be limited, or that other compensatory pathways might diminish the impact of EZH2 inhibition in the retinal environment (Buniello et al., 2025). Third, while studies in cancer cell lines have indicated that EZH2 inhibition can upregulate V-ATPase subunits and lysosomal enzyme expression, cancer cells and RPE cells exhibit markedly different epigenetic landscapes and stress responses; therefore, extrapolation from oncology models to the RPE must be approached with caution (Shu et al., 2023, pp. 20–21, 22–23).

Furthermore, targeting epigenetic regulators always carries the risk of off-target effects since these enzymes regulate the expression of a broad spectrum of genes. In the context of the retina—an organ with complex cellular interdependencies—the potential for unintended consequences on RPE differentiation, survival, or interactions with photoreceptors must be thoroughly evaluated prior to clinical translation (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 7–8; Ferret, 2024, pp. 171–173).

Another point of consideration is the durability of the epigenetic modification induced by EZH2 inhibition. While durable enhancement of lysosomal capacity through chromatin-level changes is an attractive prospect, the reversibility and specificity of these modifications in the context of chronic degenerative diseases like dry AMD remain uncertain. It will be crucial to determine whether the epigenetic changes induced by GSK126 are sustained over time in RPE cells and whether they translate to meaningful improvements in visual function or retinal integrity in preclinical models.

From a translational perspective, the repurposing strategy for GSK126 should include comprehensive in vitro studies using RPE cell lines and primary cultures, with endpoints that directly assess lysosomal acidification, cathepsin D activity, and clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. Furthermore, in vivo studies in animal models of dry AMD are needed to evaluate whether EZH2 inhibition can restore lysosomal function and slow disease progression under physiologically relevant conditions (Abokyi & Tse, 2025, pp. 2–3, 9–10). Comparative studies with other epigenetic modulators and TFEB activators could also provide context regarding the relative efficacy of GSK126 in reactivating the CLEAR network.

In conclusion, the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is a promising, yet exploratory, approach that leverages a clear mechanistic hypothesis: by inhibiting EZH2, GSK126 may relieve repressive histone marks at lysosomal gene promoters, thereby promoting TFEB-driven transcription of genes essential for lysosomal acidification and proteolytic activity. This approach could conceivably ameliorate the lysosomal defects observed in RPE cells in dry AMD. The strengths of this candidate lie in its well-defined molecular target, its established clinical safety profile in oncology studies, and the potential for a durable, chromatin-level correction of lysosomal dysfunction. However, significant challenges remain, including the need for direct evidence linking EZH2 inhibition to enhancements in the CLEAR gene network within RPE cells, the potential off-target effects inherent to epigenetic therapies, and the overall weak association between EZH2 and AMD pathogenesis as indicated by current target-disease databases.

Given these considerations, while the mechanistic rationale is robust and the repurposing strategy innovative, the current level of evidence is insufficient for immediate clinical application. It is imperative that future research generate direct preclinical data in ocular models of dry AMD to confirm that GSK126 can, in fact, restore lysosomal function in RPE cells via TFEB activation and increased cathepsin D and V-ATPase expression. Further investigation should also focus on clarifying the broader gene expression changes induced by GSK126 in RPE cells to ensure that the desired effects on lysosomal pathways are achieved without detrimental off-target consequences.

The forthcoming research should aim to delineate the dose-response relationships, optimize delivery to the ocular compartment, and ensure that sustained improvements in lysosomal capacity correlate with clinical endpoints relevant to AMD progression (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 13–15; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72; Ferret, 2024, pp. 103–106).

In summary, while the repurposing of GSK126 for dry AMD is conceptually attractive and supported by a reasonable mechanistic framework, the endeavor is in its nascent stages. The existing literature does not yet provide direct evidence that GSK126 elicits the specific lysosomal benefits hypothesized in RPE cells. As such, this candidate represents a high-risk, high-reward opportunity that merits further in-depth investigation through rigorous preclinical studies, with a view toward eventual clinical translation if the mechanistic hypotheses are confirmed (Coryell, 2019, pp. 48–53; Sharif, 2015, pp. 68–72).

Proposal for SB290157 (Sigma SML0390)

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of SB290157 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD), with a focus on its chemical origin, its therapeutic history, the detailed mechanism of action at the molecular level, the expected pharmacological effects in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, and an overall assessment of strengths and weaknesses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB290157 is a fully synthetic, nonpeptidic small‐molecule agent originally discovered as a selective antagonist of the complement anaphylatoxin C3a receptor (C3aR). Chemically, it is defined as N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine and was identified via high-throughput screening of chemical libraries using membranes from cells stably expressing human C3aR, such as RBL-2H3 cells (Ames et al., 2001). The lead compound was chemically optimized from an initial hit (SKF 63649) to improve affinity and potency, and its synthesis has been well described using peptide–like solid‐phase synthetic strategies (e.g., Fmoc protecting group chemistry on Wang resin) thereby yielding a compound with high purity (≥95%) and reproducible physicochemical properties (Ames et al., 2001). SB290157 belongs to a class of compounds that modulate G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), in this case a complement receptor, and similar nonpeptidic small‐molecule ligands have been employed in preclinical studies to probe inflammatory pathways in various disease states (Iyer et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2001). Its discovery set an important precedent for the therapeutic targeting of complement receptors, especially given the historical absence of potent, selective C3aR antagonists, and it has been widely used as a research tool in animal models and cell-based assays to interrogate the physiological roles of C3a/C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History:  
SB290157 has been extensively employed in preclinical models to examine the role of C3aR in inflammation and immune modulation. In early studies, it was shown to antagonize C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization and receptor internalization in RBL-2H3 cells and human neutrophils, with reported IC50 values in the low-nanomolar range (approximately 27–30 nM), suggesting robust antagonism under defined experimental conditions (Ames et al., 2001). In vivo, SB290157 demonstrated antiinflammatory efficacy by reducing neutrophil recruitment in guinea pig models of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced airway neutrophilia and by decreasing paw edema in rat adjuvant-induced arthritis models through intraperitoneal dosing (Ames et al., 2001). Although valuable as a pharmacological probe, its history is mired by concerns as several subsequent investigations indicated that SB290157 can exhibit partial agonist activity—depending on the assay system and receptor expression context—and even engage an off-target complement receptor, C5aR2, to induce β-arrestin recruitment (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). With more than 70 publications referencing its use, SB290157 remains one of the most commonly used C3aR inhibitors; however, it is essentially confined to the research arena and has never reached clinical development for AMD or other indications (Li et al., 2021).  
There is emerging evidence in ophthalmologic research relevant to dry AMD. For example, an in vitro human fetal RPE cell model has shown that complement fragment C3a can drive the formation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits via dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway; importantly, co-application of SB290157 with recombinant C3a in these cultures prevented the abnormal deposit formation, suggesting that C3aR blockade can modulate key pathological events relevant to AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Despite this promising mechanistic link, SB290157 itself has not been advanced clinically, and its use in retinal models remains primarily exploratory. Moreover, the existence of antagonistic and agonistic properties in various assay systems necessitates careful interpretation of its efficacy when contemplating the translation to human ocular diseases (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB290157 has been characterized as a competitive antagonist that binds to the orthosteric site of the C3a receptor, thereby inhibiting the native ligand, C3a, from eliciting its downstream signaling responses. In classic radioligand binding assays using 125I-labeled C3a, SB290157 displaces the radiolabeled peptide with an IC50 of ~200 nM, indicating it competes effectively with C3a (Ames et al., 2001). Functionally, this displacement correlates with inhibition of C3a-induced intracellular calcium mobilization, a key second messenger response mediated via G-protein coupling to pertussis-toxin–sensitive Gi/o proteins (Ames et al., 2001). Additionally, SB290157 has been shown to block C3a-mediated receptor internalization in immune cells, further supporting its role in antagonizing C3aR activation (Ames et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Beyond the canonical receptor blockade, several studies have pointed out that SB290157’s activity is highly context-dependent. In systems where C3aR is overexpressed—such as recombinant CHO or transfected RBL cells—SB290157 can paradoxically act as an agonist to trigger intracellular signaling cascades like ERK phosphorylation, potentially due to rapid receptor desensitization or kinetic differences in ligand-receptor interaction (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Moreover, its off-target partial agonism at the closely related receptor C5aR2 has been documented, wherein it mediates β-arrestin recruitment at higher concentrations, thereby dampening C5a-induced ERK signaling in primary macrophages (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such dual or biased pharmacological properties underscore that SB290157’s molecular actions cannot be solely categorized as pure antagonism without considering assay conditions and cell contexts (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
In the context of RPE cells, C3a binding to C3aR is hypothesized to disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis, leading to lysosomal alkalinization—a key factor that impairs the maturation and proteolytic activity of lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin D (CTSD). Cathepsin D is critical for proper turnover of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and degradation of proteinaceous aggregates; its dysfunction is implicated in drusen formation, a hallmark of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). By competitively inhibiting C3a binding, SB290157 is expected to mitigate abnormal Ca2+ signaling, maintain lysosomal acidification, and therefore preserve CTSD processing and activity, which in turn would prevent or lessen the accumulation of drusen-like deposits (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). This proposed mechanism is supported by the observation that in hfRPE cultures, SB290157 co-application with C3a prevented both the upregulation of C3aR expression and the subsequent deposition of abnormal ECM structures (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Nonetheless, the precise molecular interactions at the receptor—the positioning of the diphenylethoxy moiety and arginine side chain—is critical for binding affinity and selectivity (Iyer et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2025), and minor alterations in these interactions might contribute to the observed functional variability.

Expected Effect:  
Based on the hypothesis for dry AMD, SB290157 is expected to act on RPE cells by antagonizing the C3aR, thereby preventing the cascade of intracellular events that lead to lysosomal stress. In a typical RPE culture assay where C3a is exogenously added—thereby simulating enhanced complement activity as observed in AMD—SB290157 should block C3a binding, which would normally result in the perturbation of lysosomal pH homeostasis. The blockade of this receptor is envisaged to preserve the normally acidic lysosomal environment required for the optimal maturation and proteolytic function of cathepsin D (CTSD), an enzyme whose dysfunction is implicated in the formation of drusen and the progression of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, by preserving lysosomal function, SB290157 is expected to reduce subsequent activation of the inflammasome—a multi-protein complex that is triggered when lysosomal destabilization occurs—and thus attenuate the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β. This cascade is particularly relevant because chronic inflammation is thought to drive many of the degenerative changes associated with AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vitro, RPE cells pre-treated with SB290157 before C3a challenge would be anticipated to maintain normal lysosomal acidity (measured by appropriate pH-sensitive dyes), exhibit proper CTSD processing (as observed by Western blot analysis for mature cathepsin D forms), and display reduced markers of inflammasome activation such as caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β release. Gene expression studies in these cells might also reveal normalized levels of key ECM components and proteases, ultimately leading to a reduction in sub-RPE deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
It is important to note that C3aR is expressed on RPE cells and its activation has been implicated in additional downstream effects—including modulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway and extracellular matrix turnover—which further contribute to cell dysfunction and deposit formation. Therefore, antagonism of C3aR by SB290157, if effective and selective, could theoretically interrupt this pathogenic cascade and offer a protective effect against drusen-mediated RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Ames et al., 2001).

Overall Evaluation:  
SB290157 offers a compelling mechanistic rationale for repurposing in dry AMD given the central role of complement dysregulation in the pathogenesis of the disease. Among its strengths is a well-documented ability to block C3a-induced signaling events across multiple preclinical models. Early characterizations demonstrated that SB290157 effectively inhibited intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, receptor internalization, and other pro-inflammatory events in both immune cells and engineered cell systems (Ames et al., 2001). Its application in an hfRPE model demonstrated that C3a-induced sub-RPE deposit formation can be reversed upon treatment with SB290157, underscoring its potential utility in preventing one of the critical pathological features of dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Furthermore, the known rodent tolerability and defined in vivo pharmacokinetics observed in other disease models—such as LPS-induced airway inflammation and adjuvant-induced arthritis—support the concept that SB290157 can be delivered systemically with demonstrable pharmacodynamic effects (Ames et al., 2001).  

However, several weaknesses temper enthusiasm for immediate clinical translation. A significant concern is the compound’s context-dependent pharmacology. Multiple studies have reported that SB290157 can function as a partial or even full agonist under certain conditions, particularly in overexpression systems, and paradoxically activate C3aR instead of inhibiting it (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005). Such functional divergence is critical when considering a therapy designed to block a deleterious signal in a delicate tissue such as the retina. Moreover, SB290157 has been shown to exhibit off-target effects, including partial agonism at C5aR2—a related complement receptor—which may confound downstream anti-inflammatory responses and produce unintended biological effects (Li et al., 2021; Mathieu et al., 2005).  
Additionally, while there is evidence of efficacy in non-ocular models and even in an hfRPE culture system, there is a paucity of robust in vivo data specifically demonstrating efficacy in ocular or AMD preclinical models. Modern translational approaches demand rigorous evaluation of pharmacokinetics, tissue penetration, ocular tolerability, and local off-target activity in the complex microenvironment of the eye—data that remain limited for SB290157 in the AMD setting (Iyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021). Furthermore, owing to its reputation as a “controversial” tool compound, some in the field recommend the use of complementary genetic models (e.g., C3aR knockout mice) to validate findings derived from its use (Coulthard, 2015; Li et al., 2021). This underscores the need for next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved selectivity and a more predictable pharmacodynamic profile if the goal is clinical translation for dry AMD.  

In summary, SB290157 has strong theoretical appeal as a means to interrupt a pathological complement cascade that leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired CTSD maturation, and ultimately drusen formation in dry AMD. Its prior use in various inflammatory and in vitro RPE models, along with the biochemistry linking C3aR activation to intracellular Ca2+ dysregulation and lysosomal stress, supports the hypothesis that C3aR blockade may be beneficial in preserving RPE function (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Iyer et al., 2017). Nonetheless, the intrinsic limitations of SB290157—including its potential for agonistic behavior, off-target C5aR2 activity, and inconsistent effects across different cellular contexts—present significant challenges that must be addressed prior to advancing this candidate into clinical trials for AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In conclusion, SB290157 is a well-characterized research tool with documented efficacy in blocking complement-mediated inflammatory responses in several animal models as well as in an hfRPE culture system, making it a promising candidate to test the hypothesis that C3aR blockade can prevent lysosomal alkalinization and CTSD dysfunction in dry AMD. Its strengths include a defined mechanism of competitive antagonism at C3aR, cross-species activity, and experimentally demonstrated protective effects against abnormal sub-RPE deposit formation. However, its context-dependent agonist behavior and off-target activation of C5aR2 raise significant concerns about its selectivity and reliability as a clinical therapeutic. Additionally, the limited data regarding ocular pharmacokinetics and direct efficacy in robust in vivo dry AMD models suggest that further validation is required. Thus, while the underlying rationale for targeting complement-mediated lysosomal dysfunction remains compelling, SB290157 is best viewed as a stepping stone toward the development of next-generation C3aR antagonists with improved pharmacological profiles for potential clinical application in dry AMD (Ames et al., 2001; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Li et al., 2021).

Proposal for GDC-0941 (Pictilisib; Selleckchem S1066)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GDC-0941 (pictilisib) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, ATP-competitive, pan–class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) inhibitor discovered through structure-guided medicinal chemistry at Genentech as an optimization beyond early tool compounds and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor PI-103, with substantially improved selectivity for class I PI3Ks and favorable pharmacokinetics (PK) suitable for systemic dosing in humans (Garces, n.d.; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2024). At the biochemical level, pictilisib exhibits low-nanomolar potency against p110α and p110δ, with activity across class I isoforms (representative IC₅₀s: α ≈ 3 nM, β ≈ 33 nM, δ ≈ 3 nM, γ ≈ 75 nM) and weak activity on mTOR (~0.58 μM), consistent with selective targeting of class I PI3Ks over mTOR kinase (Huang et al., 2023; Garces, n.d.; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Co-crystal structural analysis shows an ATP-mimetic thieno[3,2-d]pyrimidine core in which the morpholine oxygen donates a hinge hydrogen bond (Val882), the indazole engages an affinity pocket (Asp841/Tyr867), and a methanesulfonyl-piperazine tail projects toward solvent; these interactions underpin its potency and selectivity within the class I PI3K ATP site (PDB 3DBS) (Garces, n.d.). Pictilisib belongs to the pan-class I PI3K inhibitor class, a therapeutic category widely advanced in oncology to suppress the PI3K→AKT→mTOR signaling axis that governs cell growth, survival, and metabolism; multiple agents in this class have reached clinical testing or approval, providing a clear translational precedent for pathway engagement and safety management in humans (Schmitz et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Therapeutic History  
The development history of pictilisib is anchored in oncology, where first-in-human Phase I trials established a recommended Phase II dose of 330 mg once daily, dose-proportional PK (Tₘₐₓ ≈ 2 h, t₁/₂ ≈ 13–24 h), and robust pharmacodynamic (PD) target engagement—up to ~90% inhibition of phosphorylated AKT (Ser473) in platelet-rich plasma within 1–3 h of dosing and suppression of p-AKT and p-S6 in tumor biopsies at sufficient exposure (AUC > 20 μM·h) (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Across Phase I combination studies, pictilisib showed a manageable safety profile and some antitumor activity, with common adverse events including nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, hyperglycemia, and cytopenias; dose-limiting toxicity in some settings was grade 3 maculopapular rash (Mishra et al., 2021; Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015). Although pathway suppression was clear, randomized combination trials in breast and lung cancer variably met efficacy endpoints and broader development was limited by tolerability in multi-drug regimens and modest efficacy as monotherapy—experience that nonetheless provides clinically validated PK/PD tools and class-effect safety benchmarks (Mishra et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2017).

No preclinical or clinical use of pictilisib or other class I PI3K inhibitors has been reported for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or RPE-centered retinal disease models in the provided literature, and a recent review emphasizes that no ongoing clinical trials directly target autophagy in AMD, underscoring an evidence gap for PI3K inhibitors in this indication (Blasiak et al., 2025). By contrast, direct downstream pathway modulation in RPE—mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin—has shown that activating the lysosome–TFEB axis reduces POS-derived autofluorescent granules in vitro in a hydrolase-dependent manner, but clinical testing in advanced AMD returned limited efficacy and adverse effects, illustrating both the mechanistic plausibility of modulating this pathway and translational challenges (Falcão et al., 2024). Collectively, the therapeutic history supports that class I PI3K inhibitors achieve systemic PI3K pathway inhibition in humans with tractable but nontrivial toxicities; however, there is no published RPE- or AMD-focused body of work with pictilisib to date in the provided context (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Mechanism of Action  
Class I PI3Ks phosphorylate PIP₂ to PIP₃, recruiting PH-domain effectors including PDK1 and AKT to the plasma membrane, where AKT is activated by phosphorylation at Thr308 (PDK1) and Ser473 (mTORC2) (Huang et al., 2023). Activated AKT phosphorylates multiple substrates that converge on mTORC1 activation (via TSC2/PRAS40), leading to phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E-BP1 to promote protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, thereby integrating growth-factor status with anabolic programs (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), AKT/mTOR signaling is an established regulator of cell proliferation and autophagy; mTORC1 activation inhibits autophagy by blocking ULK1 signaling and autolysosomal biogenesis, whereas rapamycin-mediated mTORC1 inhibition activates autophagy and preserves photoreceptor function in preclinical models (Chang et al., 2015). PI3K inhibition upstream of AKT is thus expected to reduce PIP₃ generation, limit AKT membrane recruitment/activation, and secondarily depress mTORC1 signaling in RPE (Castel et al., 2021; Chang et al., 2015).

PI3K→AKT signaling intersects directly with TFEB/TFE3—the master transcription factors of lysosomal biogenesis and the CLEAR regulon—through both mTORC1-dependent and mTORC1-independent routes (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Nutrient-driven mTORC1 activity at the lysosome phosphorylates TFEB/TFE3 to retain them in the cytosol; conversely, mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and induction of lysosomal/autophagy genes (Falcão et al., 2024). Importantly, AKT2 directly phosphorylates TFEB (at Ser467) and TFE3 (Ser321), promoting 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic sequestration independent of mTORC1, thereby repressing CLEAR gene expression and lysosomal programs in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). In AMD-relevant contexts—human dysmorphic macular RPE, CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE, and Akt2 RPE-specific knock-in mice—AKT2 upregulation increases TFEB/TFE3 phosphorylation, reduces lysosomal hydrolases (cathepsin D/L) and CLEAR target expression, impairs autophagic flux, and shifts autophagy toward secretory pathways characterized by increased FKBP51/SNAP23, autophagosome fusion with the plasma membrane, and extracellular release of IL-1β/HMGB1 (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). TFEB rescue via a phospho-deficient TFEB-S467A mutant or pharmacologic TFEB activation with trehalose restores cathepsin D/L and autophagy genes, normalizes autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and improves RPE structure in AMD-like mouse models, establishing TFEB/TFE3 as actionable nodes downstream of AKT2 in RPE (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).

SIRT5 and mitochondrial metabolism integrate with AKT2–TFEB signaling in RPE. SIRT5 interacts with AKT2 and reduces lysine malonylation on AKT2, modulating AKT2 activity; AKT2, via inhibition of PGC-1α, downregulates SIRT5, creating a bidirectional circuit that affects TFEB-dependent lysosomal function and mitochondrial respiration (Ghosh et al., 2023). AKT2 upregulation impairs mitochondrial respiration (maximal and ATP-linked), which is rescued by SIRT5, linking mitochondrial–lysosomal crosstalk to RPE proteostasis (Ghosh et al., 2023). Functionally, failure of the AKT2/SIRT5/TFEB axis elevates secretory autophagy and likely contributes to drusen pathogenesis by exporting inflammatory cargo (Ghosh et al., 2023).

These mechanistic data converge with mTORC1→TFEB observations in POS-fed RPE models. Synchronous POS phagocytosis transiently activates mTORC1 early, with TFEB protein increasing but remaining phosphorylated during late maturation, indicating a bottleneck at TFEB activation (Falcão et al., 2024). Pharmacologic mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin after AFGs have formed lowers POS-derived autofluorescence by ~30% in hfRPE/ARPE-19, reduces pS6, decreases the pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increases LAMP1, and requires active lysosomal hydrolases: cathepsin D knockout or protease/lipase inhibition abolishes the rapamycin effect (Falcão et al., 2024). Human AMD RPE exhibits hyperphosphorylated TFEB with decreased nuclear localization and lower cathepsin D/L protein levels and activities, consistent with impaired lysosome proteolysis; constitutively active TFEB boosts CLEAR genes, including hydrolases and V-ATPase subunits (e.g., ATP6V0A1), supporting enhanced acidification capacity (Falcão et al., 2025).

Pictilisib’s proximal pharmacology—ATP-competitive inhibition of class I PI3Ks—has been shown to produce substantial pathway suppression in human tissues (reduced pAKT, reduced pS6) and in tumor models; such upstream inhibition is expected to depress both AKT→mTORC1 signaling and AKT2-mediated TFEB phosphorylation, potentially enabling TFEB/TFE3 nuclear translocation and restoration of CLEAR programs in RPE (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Two caveats are central. First, class III PI3K/VPS34 activity is required for autophagosome nucleation; thus class I–selective inhibition (as with pictilisib) is mechanistically appropriate, whereas class III inhibition would be detrimental to autophagy flux (Wang et al., 2023). Second, while AKT inhibitors (e.g., MK-2206) and TFEB activators (trehalose) have directly increased autophagy and TFEB nuclear translocation in RPE, no direct evidence of class I PI3K inhibitors reproducing these effects in RPE has been reported in the provided literature (Karim et al., 2020; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Expected Effect  
In RPE cell assays designed to model dry AMD–relevant lysosomal stress (e.g., POS feeding, A2E/oxidant exposure, or CFH risk-allele iPSC-RPE), pictilisib is expected to reduce PI3K-dependent PIP₃ generation, lowering membrane recruitment and phosphorylation of AKT, thereby secondarily suppressing mTORC1 and directly relieving AKT2-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB/TFE3 (Huang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021; Ghosh et al., 2024). Mechanistically, this should dephosphorylate TFEB/TFE3, promote nuclear translocation, and activate the CLEAR transcriptional program to increase components of lysosomal biogenesis and function (e.g., LAMP1/2, cathepsin D/L, and V-ATPase subunits), thereby enhancing degradative capacity and autophagic flux (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

Operationally testable expected effects include:  
• Signaling: decreased pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 (Ser235/236) within hours of dosing in RPE, mirroring PD seen in tumors and platelet-rich plasma in human trials, establishing target engagement (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021).  
• TFEB/TFE3 activation: reduction in pTFEB/TFEB ratio, increased nuclear TFEB/TFE3, and induction of CLEAR genes; in RPE systems, TFEB activation correlates with increased LAMP1 and rescue of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy mediators (e.g., ATG9B), as seen upon TFEB S467A expression or trehalose treatment (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Lysosomal function: increased abundance and maturation of cathepsin D (pro→intermediate→mature chain) and cathepsin L, and improved degradative flux, consistent with observations that AMD RPE shows diminished cathepsin levels/activities and that hydrolase function is required for rapamycin-mediated clearance of POS-derived AFGs (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), reduced p62/SQSTM1 accumulation, restored autophagosome–lysosome fusion (e.g., GFP-LC3 and LysoTracker/LAMP1 colocalization), and decreased accumulation of double-membrane autophagosomes on EM, reversing the AKT2-driven flux block (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• POS-derived autofluorescence: reduction in POS-dependent autofluorescent granules in preventive and resolving paradigms, analogous to mTORC1 inhibition or TFEB activation effects; efficacy will depend on intact lysosomal hydrolase activity (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Secretory autophagy: decreased FKBP51/SNAP23 elevation, reduced plasma-membrane fusion of autophagosomes, and lower extracellular release of IL-1β and HMGB1 from RPE, mirroring effects seen with SIRT5 co-expression or AKT2 inhibition (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Acidification: although lysosomal pH has not been directly measured after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE, TFEB activation increases expression of V-ATPase subunits, and improved hydrolase activities imply normalization of the acidic lumen; direct pH assays (LysoSensor/LysoTracker) should be incorporated because efficacy of rapamycin/TFEB approaches depends on intact lysosomal acid hydrolases (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024).

These expectations rest on the well-documented presence and dysregulation of the AKT2→TFEB/TFE3→CLEAR axis in RPE and the dependence of POS clearance on mTOR/TFEB-governed lysosomal function (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024). AKT2 is upregulated in macular RPE from AMD donors and in AMD-like mouse models, and RPE-specific Akt2 overexpression is sufficient to induce AMD-like pathology, supporting target relevance in the cell type and disease context of interest (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Because PI3K is upstream of AKT, class I PI3K inhibition should, in principle, reduce AKT2 activity and thereby favor TFEB activation; however, no direct studies in the provided literature demonstrate pictilisib (or any class I PI3K inhibitor) inducing TFEB nuclear translocation or improving cathepsin D maturation/activity in RPE, so these are testable, evidence-generating predictions rather than established facts (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Karim et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with disease biology: Dry AMD features impaired RPE autophagy–lysosome function, diminished cathepsin D/L levels/activities, and TFEB hyperphosphorylation with reduced nuclear TFEB, all of which converge on lysosomal insufficiency and accumulation of lipofuscin-like material and extracellular drusen; upstream PI3K inhibition is a coherent strategy to relieve AKT2- and mTORC1-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and restore CLEAR-driven lysosomal biogenesis and flux (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Drug tractability and translational readiness: Pictilisib achieves robust systemic target engagement in humans (pAKT/pS6 suppression), has well-characterized PK/PD and class-effect safety, and is chemically and biophysically optimized, enabling accelerated preclinical testing and dosage/formulation exploration for ocular delivery or low systemic exposure strategies (Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021; Garces, n.d.).  
• Selectivity profile appropriate for autophagy enhancement: Because autophagosome nucleation requires class III PI3K/VPS34, class I selectivity of pictilisib avoids this liability while suppressing AKT→mTOR signaling and AKT2-dependent TFEB phosphorylation, in contrast to nonselective PI3K inhibition which would be deleterious (Wang et al., 2023; Castel et al., 2021).

Risks and Gaps  
• No direct RPE/AMD data with class I PI3K inhibitors: In contrast to clear benefits from rapamycin and TFEB activation, the literature presented contains no direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition, or pictilisib specifically, improves TFEB activation/nuclear entry, lysosomal biogenesis, cathepsin D maturation/activity, lysosomal acidification, autophagy flux, or POS handling in RPE; thus, the central hypothesis remains unvalidated experimentally in the disease-relevant cell type (Blasiak et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). By comparison, AKT inhibition (MK-2206) and trehalose have been shown to increase autophagy and nuclear TFEB in RPE, and AKT2 inhibitors reduced lipid/apoE in CFH(H/H) RPE, but these are not PI3K inhibitors and may differ in cellular selectivity and compensatory signaling (Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
• Complexity of autophagy modulation and context dependence: Autophagy is a double-edged sword with biphasic responses to stress; overactivation or mistimed activation could exacerbate RPE stress or impair other retinal cell types, and some autophagy inhibitors display retinal toxicity (e.g., chloroquine class), emphasizing the need for precise control and safety profiling (Blasiak et al., 2025; Kaarniranta et al., 2013). Rapamycin has shown only limited clinical efficacy in advanced AMD despite mechanistic benefits in vitro, illustrating translational friction between pathway modulation and clinical outcomes (Falcão et al., 2024).  
• Safety, delivery, and exposure management: Systemic class I PI3K inhibition induces hyperglycemia, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicities; while these were generally manageable, ocular delivery strategies (intravitreal or periocular) and ocular pharmacokinetics for pictilisib are uncharacterized in the provided literature, and tissue-specific PD (e.g., drug levels at the RPE/Bruch’s complex) is likely to determine efficacy and safety (Josephs & Sarker, 2016; Sarker et al., 2015; Mishra et al., 2021). Tissue PD variability seen in tumors versus blood suggests careful intratissue PD assays are necessary (Sarker et al., 2015).  
• Isoform and cell-type specificity: AKT2 is the isoform implicated in RPE TFEB repression and secretory autophagy; upstream PI3K isoform contributions in RPE are not defined here, and pan-class I inhibition could affect neighboring retinal cells, choroidal endothelium, and immune cells, potentially altering retinal immunity and angiogenesis in unintended ways (Ghosh et al., 2024; Castel et al., 2021). Given the evidence favoring AKT2-selective inhibition or direct TFEB activation in RPE models, PI3K-level intervention may be broader than necessary and carry off-target tissue consequences (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020).  
• Acidification endpoint uncertainty: The hypothesis specifically posits enhanced lysosomal acidification, yet none of the provided sources report direct lysosomal pH measurements after class I PI3K inhibition in RPE; while CLEAR induction can increase V-ATPase subunits and rapamycin-mediated clearance requires active hydrolases, direct acidification effects remain to be demonstrated (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2024; Blasiak et al., 2025).

Go/No-Go Evidence Plan  
Given the strong mechanistic rationale but absence of direct RPE data, a staged validation program is warranted:  
– In vitro RPE target engagement and TFEB activation: Demonstrate pictilisib decreases pAKT (Ser473) and pS6 in primary human fetal RPE, ARPE-19, and iPSC-RPE, and increases nuclear TFEB/TFE3 with induction of CLEAR genes (CTSD, CTSL, LAMP2, ATP6V0A1) assessed by Western, RT-qPCR, and ChIP-qPCR (Falcão et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Lysosome function readouts: Quantify cathepsin D maturation and enzymatic activity, LAMP1/2 abundance, and lysosomal pH using ratiometric probes; include hydrolase inhibition controls to assess dependence analogous to the rapamycin data (Falcão et al., 2024).  
– Autophagic flux and modality: Assess LC3-II turnover (± bafilomycin A₁), p62 dynamics, autolysosome number (LC3–LAMP1 colocalization), and EM confirmation; evaluate secretory-autophagy markers (FKBP51, SNAP23) and extracellular cargo (HMGB1, IL-1β) to test reversal of the AKT2-driven phenotype (Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– Functional disease readouts: Test POS-dependent autofluorescence reduction in preventive and resolving paradigms and POS degradation assays; evaluate lipid/apoE accumulation in CFH(H/H) iPSC-RPE and Cryba1 cKO explants to compare with reported trehalose and AKT2 inhibitor effects (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
– In vivo and delivery: Establish ocular PK and tolerability for local delivery (intravitreal/periocular) in rodents, then test efficacy in RPE-driven AMD-like models (Akt2 KI, Cryba1 cKO, NaIO₃) with TFEB activation, lysosomal and functional endpoints (ERG/SD-OCT) (Ghosh et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).  
– Benchmarking: Include rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibition), MK-2206 (AKT inhibition), and trehalose (mTOR-independent TFEB activation) comparators to position PI3K inhibition within the therapeutic landscape (Falcão et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2023).

Conclusion  
Pictilisib offers a mechanistically coherent, drug-like approach to modulate an RPE pathway of clear pathogenic relevance—AKT2/mTOR-mediated repression of TFEB/TFE3 and the CLEAR network—backed by robust human PK/PD experience and a selectivity profile compatible with enhancing autophagy without impeding VPS34-dependent nucleation (Ghosh et al., 2024; Sarker et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2023). However, the absence of direct evidence that class I PI3K inhibition rectifies TFEB activity, lysosomal hydrolase function (notably cathepsin D), lysosomal acidification, autophagic flux, or POS clearance in RPE is a critical gap that precludes immediate advancement; by contrast, downstream interventions (rapamycin, TFEB activation, AKT2 inhibition) already demonstrate these benefits in RPE models (Falcão et al., 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). On balance, pictilisib is plausible and testable but not yet justified for translational progression without focused RPE and ocular studies; an AKT2-selective inhibitor or TFEB-directed strategies may offer a higher probability of effect with narrower network perturbation, and should be run in parallel as mechanistic benchmarks (Ghosh et al., 2024; Karim et al., 2020). If the proposed RPE experiments confirm that pictilisib restores TFEB-driven lysosomal programs, improves cathepsin D maturation/activity, normalizes autophagy flux, and reduces POS-derived autofluorescence with acceptable ocular tolerability, the candidate would merit advancement to in vivo ocular efficacy testing; absent such confirmation, resources should pivot to agents with demonstrated RPE TFEB engagement (Ghosh et al., 2024; Falcão et al., 2024).
